sections.title: Study Notes · Part 1: Individuals
sections.summary: Study notes for every domain of SEE Part 1: Individuals.

blocks.text: This domain covers the groundwork before a return is prepared: confirming taxpayer identity, gathering source documents, determining filing requirements, and applying due diligence. The exam tests whether you know who must file, what information is needed, and how prior-year data and identity protections affect the current return.
Key points

items: Each filer needs a valid TIN: SSN, ITIN (Form W-7), or ATIN; ITINs not used on a return in 3 consecutive years expire.
Filing requirement depends on gross income, filing status, age, and dependency status; 2024 standard deduction sets most thresholds.
2024 standard deduction: $14,600 single/MFS, $29,200 MFJ, $21,900 head of household.
Self-employed taxpayers must file if net self-employment earnings are $400 or more.
Dependents have separate (lower) filing thresholds and may owe the kiddie tax on unearned income.
Source documents include W-2, 1099-NEC, 1099-MISC, 1099-K, 1099-INT/DIV/B, K-1s, 1098, and 1095-A/B/C.
The 1099-K reporting threshold remained transitionally at $5,000 for 2024 (IRS phase-in).
Identity Protection PINs (IP PINs) are six digits and required on the return when issued.
Prior-year AGI or a Self-Select PIN is used to e-file and validate identity.
Preparers should review prior-year returns for carryovers: NOLs, capital losses, charitable carryforwards, and credits.
Form 8867 paid-preparer due diligence applies to EITC, CTC/ACTC/ODC, AOTC, and head-of-household filing status.
Keep records supporting income, deductions, and credits; substantiation rules vary by item.

blocks.text:
Preliminary work is about setting the return up correctly before any numbers are entered. The first task is establishing identity and a valid taxpayer identification number. U.S. citizens and most residents use a Social Security number; nonresidents and others ineligible for an SSN use an ITIN obtained on Form W-7. Adopted children pending an SSN may use an ATIN. Remember that ITINs expire if not used on a filed return for three consecutive years, which can stall processing.

Next you determine whether a return is even required. The thresholds track the standard deduction for the taxpayer's filing status and age, with add-ons for taxpayers who are 65 or older or blind. Special rules override these: anyone with $400 or more of net self-employment income must file to report self-employment tax, and dependents face their own lower thresholds keyed to earned versus unearned income.

Gathering source documents is the practical heart of this domain. Wages appear on Form W-2; nonemployee compensation on 1099-NEC; interest, dividends, and broker proceeds on the 1099-INT, 1099-DIV, and 1099-B; and partnership, S corporation, estate, and trust income on Schedule K-1. Health coverage and marketplace subsidies arrive on Forms 1095-A, B, and C, with the 1095-A being essential to reconcile the premium tax credit.

Reviewing the prior-year return is a high-yield habit. Carryovers such as net operating losses, capital loss carryforwards (limited to $3,000 of net capital loss deductible against ordinary income per year), disallowed passive losses, and charitable carryforwards all flow into the current year and are easy to miss.

Finally, due diligence is tested heavily. Form 8867 must accompany returns claiming the EITC, child tax credit and its variants, the American Opportunity Tax Credit, or head-of-household status. The preparer must ask reasonable questions, document answers, and keep records. Identity protections such as the IP PIN also belong here: when the IRS issues a six-digit IP PIN, it must be entered or the e-filed return will reject.

This domain covers what counts as gross income, how different income streams are taxed, and the basis and reporting rules for assets. Expect questions on wages, interest, dividends, retirement distributions, capital transactions, and the taxability of fringe benefits and other receipts.
Key points

items: Gross income includes all income from whatever source derived unless specifically excluded by law.
Qualified dividends and long-term capital gains use preferential rates of 0%, 15%, or 20%.
Long-term holding period is more than one year; one year or less is short-term (ordinary rates).
Tax-exempt municipal bond interest is excluded from income but reported on the return.
Series EE/I savings bond interest may be excludable when used for qualified higher education.
Basis of purchased property is cost; inherited property gets a stepped-up (date-of-death) FMV basis.
Gifted property keeps the donor's carryover basis (with a special dual-basis rule for losses).
Roth qualified distributions are tax-free; traditional IRA/401(k) distributions are generally ordinary income.
Required minimum distributions begin at age 73 under SECURE 2.0; the missed-RMD penalty is 25% (10% if timely corrected).
Early distributions before 59 1/2 generally face a 10% additional tax unless an exception applies.
Social Security benefits are 0%, 50%, or up to 85% taxable based on provisional income.
Sale of a primary residence can exclude $250,000 of gain ($500,000 MFJ) under Section 121.
Cancellation of debt is generally taxable unless an exclusion (insolvency, bankruptcy, qualified principal residence) applies.
Wash sale rules disallow a loss when substantially identical securities are bought within 30 days.

blocks.text:
Section 61 defines gross income broadly as all income from whatever source derived, so the analytical default is that a receipt is taxable unless a specific exclusion applies. The exam rewards knowing the common exclusions: gifts and inheritances, life insurance proceeds paid by reason of death, qualified municipal bond interest, certain scholarships, and qualifying employer fringe benefits.

Investment income carries its own rate structure. Ordinary dividends and short-term gains are taxed at regular rates, but qualified dividends and long-term capital gains (assets held more than one year) enjoy 0%, 15%, or 20% rates depending on taxable income. The 3.8% net investment income tax can apply on top of these for higher-income taxpayers. The wash sale rule is a frequent trap: a loss is disallowed if substantially identical securities are repurchased within 30 days before or after the sale, and the disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement shares.

Basis drives gain and loss, so master the three acquisition patterns. Purchased property takes a cost basis. Inherited property generally receives a step-up (or step-down) to fair market value at the date of death, which can erase pre-death appreciation. Gifted property uses carryover basis, but a special dual-basis rule applies when the donor's basis exceeds fair market value at the gift date and the donee later sells at a loss.

Retirement income is heavily tested. Distributions from traditional IRAs and pre-tax 401(k)s are ordinary income; qualified Roth distributions are tax-free. Required minimum distributions now begin at age 73, and failing to take one triggers a 25% excise tax that drops to 10% if corrected promptly. Distributions before age 59 1/2 generally add a 10% penalty unless an exception (disability, first home up to $10,000 for IRAs, higher education, substantially equal payments) applies.

Two recurring asset topics round out the domain. Social Security benefits are taxable on a sliding scale of 0%, 50%, or 85% based on provisional income. And the Section 121 exclusion lets taxpayers exclude up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 for joint filers) on the sale of a principal residence owned and used as a main home for at least two of the prior five years.

This domain covers adjustments to income, the standard versus itemized deduction choice, and the major individual credits. The exam tests thresholds, phaseouts, and the critical distinction between deductions (reduce taxable income) and credits (reduce tax dollar-for-dollar).
Key points

items: Above-the-line adjustments reduce AGI: educator expenses ($300 for 2024), HSA, IRA, student loan interest, SE tax (half), SE health insurance.
2024 standard deduction: $14,600 single, $29,200 MFJ, $21,900 HoH; extra amount for 65+/blind.
Itemized deductions include medical (over 7.5% of AGI), SALT (capped at $10,000), home mortgage interest, and charitable gifts.
Charitable cash gifts to public charities are deductible up to 60% of AGI; appreciated property generally 30%.
Child Tax Credit is $2,000 per qualifying child under 17; up to $1,700 refundable (ACTC) for 2024.
CTC phases out at $400,000 MFJ / $200,000 others, reduced $50 per $1,000 over the threshold.
Credit for Other Dependents (ODC) is $500, nonrefundable.
EITC requires earned income, valid SSNs, and is fully refundable; max ~$7,830 with three or more children for 2024.
American Opportunity Tax Credit: up to $2,500 per student, 40% refundable, first four years of college.
Lifetime Learning Credit: 20% of up to $10,000 expenses ($2,000 max), nonrefundable, no year limit.
Child and Dependent Care Credit: up to $3,000 (one) or $6,000 (two+) of expenses, 20-35% rate.
Saver's Credit rewards retirement contributions for lower-income taxpayers at 10/20/50%.
Refundable credits can generate a refund; nonrefundable credits only reduce tax to zero.

blocks.text:
The structural backbone of this domain is the difference between deductions and credits. Deductions reduce the amount of income subject to tax, so their value depends on the marginal bracket. Credits reduce the tax itself dollar-for-dollar, making them far more valuable per dollar. Within credits, the refundable versus nonrefundable distinction is constantly tested: refundable credits (EITC, the additional child tax credit, the refundable portion of the AOTC) can produce a refund even with no tax liability, while nonrefundable credits only zero out tax.

Adjustments to income, often called above-the-line deductions, reduce AGI and are available even to taxpayers who take the standard deduction. Common ones include the educator expense deduction ($300 for 2024), the deductible portion of self-employment tax, self-employed health insurance, HSA contributions, traditional IRA contributions, and up to $2,500 of student loan interest subject to phaseout.

Most taxpayers compare the standard deduction against itemized deductions and take the larger. Itemizing on Schedule A includes medical expenses exceeding 7.5% of AGI, state and local taxes capped at $10,000, qualified home mortgage interest, and charitable contributions. Charitable cash gifts to public charities are generally limited to 60% of AGI, while gifts of appreciated long-term capital gain property are limited to 30% of AGI and deducted at fair market value.

The family credits are exam favorites. The Child Tax Credit is $2,000 per qualifying child under 17, with up to $1,700 refundable as the additional child tax credit for 2024, phasing out above $400,000 (MFJ) or $200,000 (all others). The $500 Credit for Other Dependents covers older children and qualifying relatives. The Earned Income Tax Credit requires earned income and valid Social Security numbers and is fully refundable, peaking near $7,830 for taxpayers with three or more qualifying children in 2024.

Education and care credits complete the picture. The American Opportunity Tax Credit gives up to $2,500 per student for the first four years of postsecondary education and is 40% refundable; the Lifetime Learning Credit gives 20% of up to $10,000 in expenses with no year limit but is nonrefundable. The Child and Dependent Care Credit applies a 20-35% rate to up to $3,000 of expenses for one qualifying person or $6,000 for two or more.

This domain covers how the individual tax liability is computed: applying the rate schedules, the alternative minimum tax, additional taxes like NIIT and the Additional Medicare Tax, and self-employment tax. The exam tests the mechanics of moving from taxable income to total tax owed.
Key points

items: Federal individual rates for 2024 are 10, 12, 22, 24, 32, 35, and 37 percent across seven brackets.
Capital gains and qualified dividends use a separate 0/15/20 percent rate schedule.
Self-employment tax is 15.3% on net SE earnings (12.4% Social Security + 2.9% Medicare).
2024 Social Security wage base for SE and FICA is $168,600; Medicare has no wage cap.
Net SE earnings are net profit times 92.35% before applying the 15.3% rate.
One-half of self-employment tax is deductible above the line.
Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% applies to wages/SE income over $200,000 single / $250,000 MFJ.
Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) is 3.8% on the lesser of NII or MAGI over $200,000/$250,000.
Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) recomputes tax with fewer preferences; 2024 exemption $85,700 single / $133,300 MFJ.
AMT exemption phases out at higher income; rates are 26% and 28%.
Kiddie tax taxes a child's unearned income above a threshold at the parents' rate.
Estimated tax safe harbors: pay 90% of current year or 100% of prior year (110% if prior AGI over $150,000).

blocks.text:
Computing the individual tax begins with the progressive rate schedule. For 2024 the seven brackets run 10, 12, 22, 24, 32, 35, and 37 percent, and the bracket dollar ranges differ by filing status. Crucially, long-term capital gains and qualified dividends are pulled out and taxed on their own 0/15/20 percent schedule stacked on top of ordinary income, so a taxpayer can have ordinary income taxed at one rate while gains are taxed at another.

Self-employment tax is one of the most computational topics on the exam. A self-employed person owes both halves of Social Security and Medicare, totaling 15.3% on net earnings. You first multiply net profit by 92.35% to get net SE earnings, then apply 12.4% for the Social Security portion (only up to the $168,600 wage base for 2024) and 2.9% for Medicare, which has no cap. Half of the resulting tax is deductible as an adjustment to income.

Several surtaxes layer onto high earners. The 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies to wages and self-employment income above $200,000 (single) or $250,000 (joint), and importantly there is no employer match for this piece. The 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax applies to the lesser of net investment income or the amount by which modified AGI exceeds those same thresholds.

The alternative minimum tax is a parallel system that recomputes income by adding back certain preferences and disallowing some deductions, then subtracts a large exemption ($85,700 single, $133,300 joint for 2024) that itself phases out at high income. The remaining base is taxed at 26% up to a breakpoint and 28% above it; the taxpayer pays the higher of regular tax or AMT.

Finally, the exam expects you to handle estimated taxes and the kiddie tax. To avoid an underpayment penalty, taxpayers generally must pay the smaller of 90% of the current year's tax or 100% of the prior year's tax (110% if prior-year AGI exceeded $150,000). The kiddie tax pulls a dependent child's unearned income above an annual threshold up to the parents' marginal rate to discourage shifting investment income to children.

This domain covers proactive guidance: tax planning, recordkeeping, estimated payments, and how life events affect future returns. The exam tests your ability to recommend sound, legal strategies and to recognize the tax consequences of decisions before they are made.
Key points

items: Advise on timing income and deductions to manage marginal brackets across years.
Recommend retirement contributions: 2024 IRA limit $7,000 ($8,000 if 50+); 401(k) $23,000 ($30,500 if 50+).
HSA contribution limits for 2024: $4,150 self-only, $8,300 family, plus $1,000 catch-up at 55+.
Roth conversions accelerate tax now for tax-free growth later; weigh current vs. future brackets.
Estimated tax payments are due quarterly: April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.
Recordkeeping: keep returns and support generally 3 years; 6 years if income understated by 25%+; indefinitely if fraud or no return.
Marriage, divorce, birth, and death change filing status, dependents, and credits.
Capital loss harvesting can offset gains plus $3,000 of ordinary income per year.
Qualified charitable distributions (QCDs) let those 70 1/2+ give up to $105,000 (2024) from IRAs tax-free.
529 plans grow tax-free for qualified education; gift-tax superfunding allows 5 years of exclusions at once.
Advise on withholding adjustments via Form W-4 to avoid surprises.
Penalties for underpayment, late filing (5%/month), and late payment (0.5%/month) should guide planning.

blocks.text:
Advising is forward-looking work, so the emphasis shifts from reporting what happened to shaping what will happen. A core technique is managing the timing of income and deductions. By accelerating deductions into a high-income year or deferring income to a lower-bracket year, a taxpayer can smooth taxable income across the rate schedule. Bunching itemized deductions, such as charitable gifts every other year, can push a taxpayer above the standard deduction in alternating years.

Retirement and health savings vehicles are central planning tools. For 2024 a taxpayer can contribute up to $7,000 to an IRA ($8,000 if age 50 or older) and up to $23,000 to a 401(k) ($30,500 with catch-up). Health Savings Accounts offer a triple tax benefit and allow $4,150 self-only or $8,300 family contributions, plus a $1,000 catch-up at 55. Roth conversions deserve careful counsel: they accelerate tax today in exchange for tax-free growth, which makes sense when current brackets are lower than expected future brackets.

Estimated taxes and withholding management prevent unpleasant April surprises. Estimated payments fall due on April 15, June 15, September 15, and the following January 15, and a well-advised taxpayer either hits a safe harbor or adjusts Form W-4 withholding to cover liability. Underpayment, late-filing (5% per month, up to 25%), and late-payment (0.5% per month) penalties give clients concrete reasons to plan ahead.

Life events reshape the return and should trigger proactive review. Marriage and divorce change filing status and may alter eligibility for credits; the birth or adoption of a child adds dependents and the child tax credit; the death of a spouse opens qualifying surviving spouse status for two years. Each event is a planning opportunity to revisit withholding, beneficiary designations, and estimated payments.

Giving and education strategies close out the advisory toolkit. Qualified charitable distributions let taxpayers 70 1/2 or older direct up to $105,000 (2024) from an IRA to charity tax-free, satisfying RMDs without raising AGI. Capital loss harvesting offsets gains and up to $3,000 of ordinary income annually, with the rest carried forward. And 529 plans let education savings grow tax-free, with a superfunding election that front-loads five years of gift-tax annual exclusions into one contribution.

This domain covers individual situations beyond the standard return: estate and gift tax, international taxpayers, and special reporting like foreign accounts. The exam tests filing requirements, exclusions, and the forms unique to these specialized scenarios.
Key points

items: 2024 estate and gift lifetime exemption is $13.61 million per individual (unified credit).
2024 annual gift tax exclusion is $18,000 per donee; unlimited for spouse (U.S. citizen) and direct tuition/medical payments.
Form 709 reports taxable gifts; Form 706 reports the estate of a decedent.
Portability lets a surviving spouse use the deceased spouse's unused exclusion (DSUE) via a timely 706.
FBAR (FinCEN Form 114) is required when foreign accounts exceed $10,000 aggregate at any time in the year.
Form 8938 (FATCA) reports specified foreign financial assets above higher thresholds with the return.
Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (Form 2555) for 2024 is up to $126,500 for qualifying taxpayers abroad.
Foreign Tax Credit (Form 1116) offsets U.S. tax on foreign-source income to avoid double taxation.
Nonresident aliens file Form 1040-NR and are generally taxed only on U.S.-source income.
The substantial presence test determines U.S. resident status for tax purposes.
Generation-skipping transfer (GST) tax applies to transfers to grandchildren or beyond.
Step-up in basis at death generally applies to inherited property included in the estate.

blocks.text:
Specialized individual returns branch off in three main directions: transfer taxes, international issues, and the reporting that accompanies them. Transfer taxes use a unified system in which the gift and estate taxes share one lifetime exemption, set at $13.61 million per individual for 2024. Because the exemption is so large, most clients never pay transfer tax, but they still may need to file.

Gift tax mechanics are heavily tested. The 2024 annual exclusion lets a donor give $18,000 per recipient with no gift tax filing, and gifts within this limit do not consume the lifetime exemption. Gifts to a U.S.-citizen spouse are unlimited, and amounts paid directly to a school for tuition or to a provider for medical care are excluded entirely. Gifts above the annual exclusion are reported on Form 709 and draw down the lifetime exemption. At death, Form 706 reports the estate, and portability allows a timely filing to transfer a deceased spouse's unused exclusion to the survivor.

The international side starts with residency. The substantial presence test counts days in the U.S. over a three-year weighted formula to decide whether someone is a resident (taxed on worldwide income, Form 1040) or a nonresident alien (taxed mostly on U.S.-source income, Form 1040-NR). Resident citizens abroad have relief tools: the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion on Form 2555 can exclude up to $126,500 of 2024 earnings, and the Foreign Tax Credit on Form 1116 offsets U.S. tax with taxes paid to other countries.

Foreign asset reporting trips up many taxpayers and is a reliable exam topic. The FBAR, FinCEN Form 114, must be filed when the aggregate value of foreign financial accounts exceeds $10,000 at any point during the year; it is filed separately from the tax return. Form 8938 under FATCA reports specified foreign financial assets when higher thresholds are met and is attached to the return; the two regimes overlap but are distinct.

Finally, basis and the generation-skipping transfer tax deserve attention. Inherited property generally receives a stepped-up basis to date-of-death fair market value, a major planning point for appreciated assets. The GST tax is an additional layer imposed on transfers that skip a generation, such as gifts or bequests to grandchildren, designed to prevent families from avoiding a layer of estate tax.

A quick decision framework for choosing the correct filing status, which drives the standard deduction, bracket thresholds, and credit eligibility. Filing-status questions are common and often hinge on the precise definitions of dependents and household maintenance.
Key points

items: Marital status is generally determined as of December 31 of the tax year.
Married Filing Jointly combines both spouses' income and offers the widest brackets.
Married Filing Separately limits many credits and uses the narrowest brackets.
A spouse who dies during the year still allows MFJ for that year.
Qualifying Surviving Spouse status lasts two years after the spouse's death if a dependent child is maintained.
Head of Household requires being unmarried (or considered unmarried) and paying over half the cost of a home for a qualifying person.
A 'considered unmarried' taxpayer can file HoH if living apart from a spouse for the last 6 months and maintaining a child's home.
Qualifying child tests: relationship, age, residency, support, and joint return.
Qualifying relative tests: not a qualifying child, relationship/member of household, gross income under $5,050 (2024), and support.
HoH gives a larger standard deduction and more favorable brackets than single.
Single applies to unmarried taxpayers who do not qualify for HoH or surviving spouse.
Choosing MFS may help when separating liability or when one spouse has large miscellaneous deductions.

blocks.text:
Filing status is the first fork in any individual return because it sets the standard deduction, the bracket breakpoints, and eligibility for numerous credits. The threshold question is marital status, which is generally fixed as of the last day of the tax year: a taxpayer married on December 31 is treated as married for the whole year, and one divorced by then is unmarried for the whole year.

For married couples the choice is between joint and separate filing. Married Filing Jointly combines both incomes, provides the widest brackets and largest standard deduction, and unlocks the most credits, which is why it is usually the better choice. Married Filing Separately narrows the brackets, disallows or reduces credits like the EITC and education credits, and forces both spouses to either itemize or take the standard deduction together; it is chosen mainly to separate liability or in unusual deduction situations.

Two statuses provide relief after a spouse's death. In the year of death the surviving spouse may still file jointly. For the two years after, a Qualifying Surviving Spouse who maintains a household for a dependent child keeps the favorable joint brackets and standard deduction, a meaningful benefit during a hard transition.

Head of Household is the most frequently litigated status on the exam because its requirements are specific. The taxpayer must be unmarried or considered unmarried, must pay more than half the cost of keeping up a home, and must have a qualifying person living there for more than half the year. A married taxpayer can be considered unmarried, and thus eligible for HoH, by living apart from a spouse for the last six months of the year while maintaining a home for a child.

Underlying all of this is the dependency analysis. A qualifying child must meet relationship, age, residency, support, and joint-return tests, while a qualifying relative must not be a qualifying child, must satisfy a relationship or member-of-household test, must have gross income under $5,050 for 2024, and must receive over half of their support from the taxpayer. Because the right status often turns on whether someone is a dependent, master these tests and the filing-status questions resolve themselves.

A focused reference on the capital gains rules: holding periods, rate categories, netting, and special asset types. These mechanics appear throughout Parts 1 and 2 and reward precise knowledge of the cutoffs and rates.
Key points

items: Short-term: held one year or less, taxed at ordinary rates.
Long-term: held more than one year, taxed at 0%, 15%, or 20%.
Holding period starts the day after acquisition and includes the date of sale.
Inherited property is automatically long-term regardless of actual holding period.
Collectibles (art, coins, metals) are taxed at a maximum 28% rate.
Unrecaptured Section 1250 gain on real estate depreciation is taxed up to 25%.
Net capital losses offset gains; up to $3,000 of excess loss offsets ordinary income per year.
Unused capital losses carry forward indefinitely (individuals).
Section 1231 gains can be long-term capital gain; Section 1231 losses are ordinary.
Depreciation recapture under Sections 1245/1250 converts gain to ordinary income.
Wash sale rule disallows losses on repurchase within 30 days before/after the sale.
Qualified dividends are taxed at the same 0/15/20 long-term capital gains rates.
The 3.8% net investment income tax can apply on top of capital gains for high earners.

blocks.text:
Capital gains rules reward exact knowledge of two things: how long the asset was held and what type of asset it is. The holding period dividing line is one year. Property held one year or less produces short-term gain taxed at ordinary rates, while property held more than one year produces long-term gain eligible for the preferential 0%, 15%, or 20% rates. Counting matters: the holding period begins the day after acquisition and runs through the date of sale, so a position acquired on a given date must be held through the same date the following year plus one day to be long-term.

Netting is the next mechanical layer. Short-term gains and losses are combined, long-term gains and losses are combined, and the two categories are then netted against each other. If a net capital loss remains, an individual may deduct up to $3,000 against ordinary income each year ($1,500 if married filing separately) and carry the rest forward indefinitely. Knowing the order of netting and the $3,000 cap answers a surprising number of questions.

Special asset types carry their own ceilings. Collectibles such as art, antiques, coins, and precious metals are taxed at a maximum 28% rate rather than the usual 20%. Real estate that was depreciated triggers unrecaptured Section 1250 gain, taxed at up to 25%. These elevated rates apply only to the relevant slice of gain, not the entire transaction, which is a common point of confusion.

Business property follows the Section 1231 and recapture framework. Section 1231 assets are depreciable property and real estate used in a trade or business; a net Section 1231 gain is generally treated as long-term capital gain, while a net Section 1231 loss is fully ordinary, giving taxpayers the best of both worlds. However, depreciation recapture under Section 1245 (personal property) and Section 1250 (real property) recharacterizes part of the gain as ordinary income to claw back prior depreciation deductions.

Finally, remember the rules that interact with capital gains. The wash sale rule disallows a loss when substantially identical securities are repurchased within 30 days before or after the sale, deferring the loss into the replacement basis. Qualified dividends ride the same 0/15/20 schedule as long-term gains. And for higher-income taxpayers the 3.8% net investment income tax stacks on top, so the effective rate on long-term gains can reach 23.8%.

A step-by-step walkthrough of the section 199A qualified business income deduction, including the taxable-income thresholds, the SSTB limitation, and the wage and property cap. The QBI deduction is one of the most heavily tested individual topics. Master the threshold ranges and the W-2 wage/UBIA limit.
Key points

items: QBI deduction is generally 20% of qualified business income from a pass-through (sole prop, partnership, S corp).
It is a deduction from AGI (below the line) but does not require itemizing.
2024 taxable income thresholds: full deduction below $191,950 single / $383,900 MFJ.
Phase-in (phase-out) range: $191,950-$241,950 single and $383,900-$483,900 MFJ.
Above the upper threshold, a Specified Service Trade or Business (SSTB) gets no QBI deduction.
SSTBs include health, law, accounting, consulting, athletics, financial services, and any trade where the principal asset is the reputation/skill of owners.
Above the threshold, non-SSTBs are limited to the greater of 50% of W-2 wages, or 25% of W-2 wages plus 2.5% of UBIA of qualified property.
Overall, the deduction cannot exceed 20% of (taxable income minus net capital gains).
QBI excludes capital gains, dividends, interest income not allocable to the business, and reasonable compensation/guaranteed payments.
Qualified REIT dividends and qualified PTP income get a separate 20% deduction not subject to the wage/property limit.
Net QBI losses carry forward and reduce QBI in the following year.
The deduction is claimed on Form 8995 (simplified, under threshold) or Form 8995-A (above threshold).

blocks.text:
The section 199A deduction lets owners of pass-through businesses deduct up to 20% of their qualified business income. QBI is the net income from a qualified trade or business; it excludes investment-type income (capital gains, dividends, most interest) and excludes amounts paid to the owner as reasonable compensation (S corp wages) or guaranteed payments (partnerships). The deduction reduces taxable income but is taken whether or not the taxpayer itemizes.

The analysis turns entirely on taxable income relative to the 2024 thresholds. Below $191,950 (single) or $383,900 (MFJ), the calculation is simple: 20% of QBI, subject only to the overall cap of 20% of taxable income less net capital gains. No SSTB or wage limits apply in this lower band.

Within the phase-in range ($191,950-$241,950 single; $383,900-$483,900 MFJ), two limitations phase in proportionally. First, SSTB income begins to be excluded. Second, the W-2 wage and property limitation begins to apply. An SSTB is a service business in fields like health, law, accounting, consulting, athletics, or financial services, or any business whose principal asset is the reputation or skill of its owners.

Above the upper threshold, the rules are fully in effect: SSTBs receive no QBI deduction at all, and non-SSTBs are capped at the greater of 50% of the business's W-2 wages or 25% of W-2 wages plus 2.5% of the unadjusted basis (UBIA) of qualified depreciable property. This wage/property cap is why capital-intensive or wage-paying businesses can still claim the deduction at high incomes while service businesses cannot. Report the deduction on Form 8995 if under the threshold or Form 8995-A if above it.

A focused note on the character of gains and losses from property sales, including the preferential rates for long-term capital gains and the recapture rules for depreciated business property. These topics span individual and business returns. The ordering of the 1231 netting and recapture is a frequent exam trap.
Key points

items: Long-term (held more than one year) capital gains and qualified dividends are taxed at 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on taxable income.
Short-term gains (held one year or less) are taxed at ordinary rates.
Net capital losses for individuals are deductible against ordinary income up to $3,000 per year ($1,500 MFS); excess carries forward indefinitely.
Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) adds 3.8% on investment income above MAGI of $200,000 single / $250,000 MFJ.
Section 1231 property is depreciable property and real property used in a trade or business and held more than one year.
Net 1231 gains are treated as long-term capital gain; net 1231 losses are treated as ordinary loss - the best of both worlds.
Section 1231 lookback: net 1231 gain is recharacterized as ordinary to the extent of nonrecaptured net 1231 losses in the prior 5 years.
Section 1245 (depreciable personal property) recaptures ALL prior depreciation as ordinary income up to the gain.
Section 1250 (real property) recaptures only depreciation taken in excess of straight-line as ordinary income (usually zero under MACRS).
Unrecaptured section 1250 gain is the straight-line depreciation portion, taxed at a maximum 25% rate.
Collectibles long-term gain is taxed at a maximum 28% rate.
Recapture (1245/1250) is computed first; any remaining gain is netted under section 1231.

blocks.text:
The character of a gain - ordinary or capital - controls its tax rate, and depreciation recapture is the mechanism that converts what would be capital gain back into ordinary income to the extent of prior deductions. Start with holding period: assets held more than one year produce long-term capital gain eligible for the preferential 0/15/20% rates, while assets held a year or less produce short-term gain taxed as ordinary income.

Section 1231 governs depreciable and real property used in a business and held over a year. Its hybrid treatment is favorable: net 1231 gains become long-term capital gains, but net 1231 losses are fully deductible as ordinary losses. A lookback rule prevents abuse - net 1231 gain is recharacterized as ordinary income to the extent the taxpayer deducted net 1231 losses in the prior five years.

Before 1231 netting, recapture is applied asset by asset. Section 1245 covers depreciable personal property (machinery, equipment) and recaptures all prior depreciation as ordinary income, up to the amount of the gain. Because depreciation reduced ordinary income, recapture restores it. Section 1250 covers real property but only recaptures depreciation taken in excess of straight-line; since MACRS real property uses straight-line, true 1250 recapture is usually zero.

What remains for real property is unrecaptured section 1250 gain - the portion of the gain attributable to straight-line depreciation - which is taxed at a maximum rate of 25%, higher than the regular long-term rate but lower than ordinary rates. Two other special rates appear: collectibles get a maximum 28% rate, and high-income taxpayers may owe the additional 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax on net gains. Compute recapture first, then net any residual gain under 1231.

A comparison of the major retirement savings vehicles, their 2024 contribution limits, tax treatment, and distribution rules. Retirement topics appear across individual income, deductions, and penalties. Focus on the traditional-versus-Roth distinction and the RMD and early-distribution rules.
Key points

items: 2024 IRA contribution limit: $7,000, plus a $1,000 catch-up for those 50 and older ($8,000 total).
2024 401(k)/403(b) elective deferral limit: $23,000, plus a $7,500 catch-up at 50+ ($30,500 total).
Traditional IRA contributions may be deductible; deductibility phases out if covered by a workplace plan above income limits.
Roth IRA contributions are never deductible; eligibility phases out at higher MAGI ($146,000-$161,000 single; $230,000-$240,000 MFJ for 2024).
Roth qualified distributions (account 5+ years and age 59 1/2, death, disability, or first home) are entirely tax-free.
Traditional IRA/401(k) distributions are taxed as ordinary income; basis (nondeductible contributions) returns tax-free pro rata.
Required Minimum Distributions begin at age 73 (SECURE 2.0); Roth IRAs have no RMD during the owner's lifetime.
Missed-RMD excise tax is 25%, reduced to 10% if corrected within the correction window.
Early distributions before 59 1/2 generally incur a 10% additional tax unless an exception applies.
SEP-IRA: employer contributions up to 25% of compensation, max $69,000 for 2024 (good for self-employed).
SIMPLE IRA: 2024 employee deferral limit $16,000 plus $3,500 catch-up; mandatory employer match or contribution.
Roth 401(k) accounts no longer require lifetime RMDs starting in 2024 under SECURE 2.0.

blocks.text:
Retirement accounts split into two tax models. Traditional accounts (traditional IRA, 401(k), SEP, SIMPLE) generally give an upfront deduction or pretax deferral, grow tax-deferred, and tax distributions as ordinary income. Roth accounts (Roth IRA, Roth 401(k)) take after-tax money in, grow tax-free, and pay out qualified distributions tax-free. Choosing between them is essentially a bet on whether the taxpayer's rate will be higher now or in retirement.

For 2024, the IRA limit is $7,000 with a $1,000 age-50 catch-up, while 401(k)-type plans allow $23,000 of elective deferrals plus a $7,500 catch-up. Traditional IRA deductibility phases out when the taxpayer (or spouse) is an active participant in a workplace plan and income exceeds the applicable range. Roth IRA contributions are themselves phased out at higher MAGI - $146,000 to $161,000 for single filers and $230,000 to $240,000 for joint filers in 2024.

Distributions are where the exam concentrates. Roth qualified distributions are tax-free once the account is at least five years old and the owner is 59 1/2 (or meets death, disability, or first-home exceptions). Traditional distributions are fully ordinary income except for any basis from nondeductible contributions, which returns tax-free on a pro-rata basis. Distributions before age 59 1/2 trigger a 10% additional tax unless an exception applies, such as disability, qualified higher-education expenses, a first-home purchase up to $10,000, or substantial medical expenses.

Required minimum distributions force money out of traditional accounts starting at age 73 under SECURE 2.0. Failing to take an RMD triggers a 25% excise tax on the shortfall, reduced to 10% if corrected promptly. Roth IRAs require no distributions during the owner's lifetime, and starting in 2024 Roth 401(k) accounts also escape lifetime RMDs. Self-employed taxpayers have additional options: a SEP-IRA allows employer contributions up to 25% of compensation (max $69,000 for 2024), and a SIMPLE IRA permits $16,000 of deferrals with a required employer contribution.

A comparison of the education tax credits, deductions, and savings vehicles, with their 2024 limits and coordination rules. Education benefits generate many individual questions because of overlapping rules and phaseouts. The key is matching the right benefit to the facts and avoiding double-dipping.
Key points

items: American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC): up to $2,500 per student (100% of first $2,000 + 25% of next $2,000) for first 4 years of postsecondary education.
AOTC is 40% refundable (up to $1,000); requires at least half-time enrollment in a degree program.
AOTC MAGI phaseout: $80,000-$90,000 single, $160,000-$180,000 MFJ; no credit if MFS.
Lifetime Learning Credit (LLC): up to $2,000 per return (20% of up to $10,000 of expenses), nonrefundable, no enrollment minimum.
LLC same phaseout as AOTC for 2024 ($80,000-$90,000 single, $160,000-$180,000 MFJ).
AOTC and LLC cannot both be claimed for the same student in the same year.
Student loan interest deduction: up to $2,500 above-the-line, phasing out at MAGI $80,000-$95,000 single, $165,000-$195,000 MFJ (2024).
529 plan: contributions grow tax-free; qualified distributions for education (including up to $10,000/year K-12 tuition) are tax-free.
Coverdell ESA: $2,000 annual contribution limit per beneficiary; tax-free for qualified K-12 and higher-education expenses.
Qualified expenses for AOTC include tuition, fees, and required course materials; room and board do NOT qualify for the credits.
Series EE/I savings bond interest may be excluded when redeemed for qualified higher education (income limits apply).
You cannot use the same expenses for more than one benefit (no double benefit).

blocks.text:
Education benefits come in three flavors: credits that reduce tax directly, a deduction for student loan interest, and tax-advantaged savings accounts. The two credits are the headliners. The American Opportunity Tax Credit is the more generous: up to $2,500 per student for each of the first four years of postsecondary education, calculated as 100% of the first $2,000 of qualified expenses plus 25% of the next $2,000. It is partially refundable - up to $1,000 - and requires at least half-time enrollment in a degree program.

The Lifetime Learning Credit is broader but smaller. It provides up to $2,000 per return (not per student), equal to 20% of up to $10,000 of qualified expenses, and has no enrollment-level or year-limit requirement, making it useful for graduate students, part-timers, and job-skills courses. It is nonrefundable. Both credits share the same 2024 MAGI phaseout ranges and cannot both be claimed for the same student in the same year, so practitioners pick whichever yields more.

The student loan interest deduction is an above-the-line deduction of up to $2,500 of interest paid, available even to non-itemizers, with its own MAGI phaseout. It is taken by the person legally obligated on the loan. This deduction can be claimed alongside the credits as long as the same dollars are not counted twice.

Savings vehicles defer or eliminate tax on earnings. A 529 plan grows tax-free and pays out tax-free for qualified education, including up to $10,000 per year of K-12 tuition and, more recently, certain student loan repayments. A Coverdell ESA allows $2,000 per beneficiary per year with similar tax-free treatment. The overarching rule across all benefits is no double-dipping: the same expense cannot support more than one benefit, and amounts paid by tax-free 529 or scholarship funds reduce the expenses available for the credits. Note that room and board never qualify for the credits, though they can qualify for 529 distributions.

sections.title: Study Notes · Part 2: Businesses
sections.summary: Study notes for every domain of SEE Part 2: Businesses.

blocks.text: This domain covers the choice and characteristics of business entities: sole proprietorships, partnerships, C corporations, S corporations, and LLCs. The exam tests formation, liability, taxation differences, and the default and elective classification rules.
Key points

items: Sole proprietorships report on Schedule C; income flows to the owner and is subject to SE tax.
Partnerships file Form 1065 (informational) and pass income to partners on Schedule K-1.
C corporations file Form 1120 and pay a flat 21% corporate tax; dividends create double taxation.
S corporations file Form 1120-S, pass through income, and avoid double taxation.
S corp eligibility: domestic, 100 or fewer shareholders, one class of stock, eligible shareholders only.
S corp election is made on Form 2553; generally due by the 15th day of the 3rd month of the tax year.
LLCs default to disregarded (single-member) or partnership (multi-member) but can elect corporate status via Form 8832.
General partners and sole proprietors have unlimited personal liability; corporations and LLCs offer limited liability.
Partnership and S corp income retains its character (capital gain, ordinary, etc.) when passed through.
Reasonable compensation must be paid to S corp shareholder-employees before distributions.
Self-employment tax applies to general partners' distributive share but not to S corp distributions.
Guaranteed payments to partners are deductible by the partnership and ordinary income to the partner.

blocks.text:
Entity choice drives both liability and taxation, and the exam expects you to compare the structures fluently. A sole proprietorship is the simplest: there is no separate entity, income lands on Schedule C of the owner's 1040, and the owner bears unlimited personal liability and self-employment tax. At the other extreme, a C corporation is a fully separate taxpayer that files Form 1120, pays a flat 21% rate, and shields owners from liability, but its earnings are taxed again as dividends, producing the classic double taxation.

Pass-through entities sit in between and avoid entity-level tax. A partnership files Form 1065 as an information return and allocates income, deductions, and credits to partners on Schedule K-1; the character of each item is preserved, so a long-term capital gain at the partnership level stays long-term for the partner. General partners pay self-employment tax on their distributive share, and guaranteed payments for services or capital are deductible by the partnership and ordinary income to the recipient partner.

The S corporation is a pass-through with strict eligibility rules that are frequently tested. It must be a domestic corporation with no more than 100 shareholders, only one class of stock, and only eligible shareholders, which generally means individuals, certain trusts, and estates, but not partnerships, corporations, or nonresident aliens. The election is made on Form 2553, generally by the 15th day of the third month of the tax year for which it is to take effect.

The LLC is a state-law entity with flexible federal tax treatment. By default a single-member LLC is disregarded and reported like a sole proprietorship, while a multi-member LLC is taxed as a partnership. Either can elect to be taxed as a corporation, and then as an S corporation, by filing Form 8832 and/or Form 2553. This flexibility makes the LLC a popular vehicle that you must analyze by its tax election, not its legal label.

Two cross-cutting issues recur. First, reasonable compensation: an S corporation must pay its shareholder-employees a reasonable salary subject to payroll taxes before making distributions, because distributions escape self-employment and FICA tax and the IRS polices attempts to disguise wages as distributions. Second, liability: general partners and sole proprietors are personally exposed, while corporate shareholders, LLC members, and limited partners enjoy limited liability, which often weighs as heavily as the tax analysis in choosing a structure.

This domain covers preparing business returns: computing business income, deductions, depreciation, and cost recovery, plus accounting methods and inventory. The exam tests Section 179, bonus depreciation, the QBI deduction, and the ordinary-and-necessary expense standard.
Key points

items: Deductible business expenses must be ordinary and necessary under Section 162.
Section 179 expensing limit for 2024 is $1,220,000 with a phaseout beginning at $3,050,000 of purchases.
Bonus depreciation is 60% for property placed in service in 2024 (phasing down 20% per year).
MACRS is the standard depreciation system; common recovery periods are 5, 7, 27.5, and 39 years.
The Section 199A QBI deduction is up to 20% of qualified business income for pass-throughs.
QBI is limited above $191,950 single / $383,900 MFJ (2024) by wages, UBIA, and SSTB rules.
Cash method recognizes income when received and expenses when paid; accrual when earned/incurred.
Businesses with average gross receipts under $30 million (2024) may use the cash method.
Business meals are generally 50% deductible; most entertainment is nondeductible.
Startup costs: up to $5,000 deductible in year one, the rest amortized over 15 years.
Net operating losses can offset up to 80% of taxable income and carry forward indefinitely.
Self-employed taxpayers may deduct a home office using actual or simplified ($5/sq ft, max 300) methods.
Vehicle expenses use either the standard mileage rate (67 cents/mile for 2024) or actual costs.

blocks.text:
Preparing a business return starts with measuring income and then subtracting the costs of earning it. The governing standard for deductions is Section 162: an expense must be both ordinary (common in the trade) and necessary (helpful and appropriate). Capital expenditures are not deducted immediately; instead they are recovered over time through depreciation, amortization, or depletion.

Cost recovery is the most computational part of the domain. Most tangible business property is depreciated under MACRS, with familiar recovery periods of five years for vehicles and computers, seven years for office furniture, 27.5 years for residential rental, and 39 years for nonresidential real property. Two accelerated tools layer on top: Section 179 lets a business immediately expense up to $1,220,000 of qualifying property in 2024 (phasing out dollar-for-dollar once purchases exceed $3,050,000), and bonus depreciation allows an additional 60% write-off in 2024 as the bonus percentage steps down 20 points each year.

The qualified business income deduction under Section 199A is a signature Part 2 topic. It allows owners of pass-through businesses to deduct up to 20% of qualified business income. Below the income thresholds of $191,950 single or $383,900 joint for 2024 the deduction is straightforward, but above them it is limited by W-2 wages paid and the unadjusted basis of qualified property, and specified service businesses such as law, accounting, and consulting phase out entirely.

Accounting methods and inventory affect timing. The cash method recognizes income when actually or constructively received and expenses when paid, while the accrual method recognizes income when earned and expenses when incurred. Many small businesses qualify for the cash method because their average annual gross receipts fall under the $30 million (2024) threshold, which also relieves them of certain inventory and uniform capitalization requirements.

Finally, several recurring deductions show up on the exam. Business meals are generally 50% deductible while entertainment is not. Startup costs allow an immediate $5,000 deduction with the remainder amortized over 15 years. A home office can be claimed using actual expenses or the simplified $5 per square foot method capped at 300 square feet. Vehicle costs use either the 67-cents-per-mile standard rate for 2024 or actual expenses. And net operating losses can now offset only 80% of taxable income but carry forward indefinitely.

This domain covers returns and taxpayers beyond ordinary businesses: trusts and estates, tax-exempt organizations, retirement plans, and employment tax reporting. The exam tests the distinct forms, filing thresholds, and compliance rules for each.
Key points

items: Estates and trusts file Form 1041; they are separate taxable entities with compressed tax brackets.
Trust/estate income distributed to beneficiaries is reported on Schedule K-1 and deducted via DNI.
The 2024 top trust tax bracket (37%) is reached at only $15,200 of taxable income.
Tax-exempt organizations apply on Form 1023 (501(c)(3)) or 1024 and file annual Form 990 series.
Small exempt orgs file Form 990-N (e-Postcard) if gross receipts are normally $50,000 or less.
Unrelated business income tax (UBIT) applies to exempt orgs on income from unrelated trade or business (Form 990-T).
Employers file Form 941 quarterly for payroll taxes; Form 940 annually for FUTA.
FUTA tax is 6.0% on the first $7,000 of wages, usually reduced to 0.6% with state credit.
Forms W-2 and W-3 are due to the SSA by January 31; 1099-NEC also due January 31.
Qualified retirement plans must meet nondiscrimination, vesting, and coverage rules; report on Form 5500.
Excise taxes on prohibited transactions and excess contributions are reported on Form 5330.
Gift and estate returns (Forms 709/706) overlap here for high-net-worth and fiduciary clients.

blocks.text:
This domain gathers the entities and returns that fall outside the mainstream business filings. Fiduciary returns come first. Estates and trusts are separate taxable entities that file Form 1041, but they use highly compressed brackets that reach the top 37% rate at only $15,200 of taxable income in 2024. To avoid that harsh rate, fiduciaries distribute income to beneficiaries, who then report it on Schedule K-1; the entity deducts these distributions up to its distributable net income (DNI), which also limits how much income the beneficiaries must report.

Tax-exempt organizations form the second cluster. A charity seeking 501(c)(3) status applies on Form 1023 (or the streamlined 1023-EZ), while other exempt types use Form 1024. Once recognized, the organization files an annual return in the Form 990 series, with the smallest organizations (gross receipts normally $50,000 or less) filing the simple 990-N e-Postcard. Even exempt organizations owe tax on income from a regularly carried-on trade or business unrelated to their exempt purpose; this unrelated business income tax is reported on Form 990-T.

Employment tax reporting is a practical, high-frequency topic. Employers report income tax withholding and the employer and employee shares of Social Security and Medicare on Form 941 each quarter, and they report federal unemployment tax on Form 940 annually. FUTA is nominally 6.0% on the first $7,000 of each employee's wages but is usually reduced to an effective 0.6% by the credit for state unemployment taxes paid. Wage statements on Forms W-2 and W-3, along with 1099-NEC forms, are due by January 31.

Retirement plan administration adds compliance layers. Qualified plans must satisfy nondiscrimination, minimum coverage, and vesting standards to preserve their tax-favored status, and most file an annual Form 5500 information return. When prohibited transactions or excess contributions occur, the resulting excise taxes are reported on Form 5330.

The boundary between this domain and individual specialized returns is porous. High-net-worth planning and fiduciary work bring in the gift tax return (Form 709) and the estate tax return (Form 706), and an enrolled agent serving business and wealthy clients should recognize when a death, a trust funding, or a large gift pulls these forms into play.

A practical guide to recovering the cost of business property through MACRS, bonus depreciation, and the section 179 election. These rules drive many Part 2 questions about timing and amount of deductions. Know the 2024 limits and the ordering of the three methods.
Key points

items: MACRS is the default cost-recovery system; common recovery periods: 5-year (autos, computers), 7-year (office furniture), 27.5-year (residential rental), 39-year (nonresidential real property).
Most personal property uses the 200% declining balance method switching to straight-line; real property uses straight-line.
Half-year convention applies to most personal property; mid-quarter convention if over 40% of property is placed in service in Q4.
Real property uses the mid-month convention.
Section 179 expensing limit for 2024 is $1,220,000, phasing out dollar-for-dollar once purchases exceed $3,050,000.
Section 179 cannot create or increase a loss - it is limited to business taxable income (carryover allowed).
Bonus depreciation under section 168(k) is 60% for property placed in service in 2024 (phasing down from 100%).
Ordering: take section 179 first, then bonus depreciation on the remaining basis, then regular MACRS.
Section 179 applies to tangible personal property and qualified improvement property; it does not apply to land or most buildings.
Listed property (passenger autos) has annual depreciation caps; luxury auto first-year cap is around $20,400 with bonus for 2024.
Bonus depreciation applies automatically unless the taxpayer elects out by class; section 179 must be affirmatively elected.
Section 179 recapture occurs if business use drops to 50% or less before the end of the recovery period.

blocks.text:
Depreciation spreads the cost of long-lived business assets over their useful lives. MACRS, the Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System, is the default. The key inputs are the asset's recovery period, the applicable convention, and the depreciation method. Personal property such as machinery, computers, and furniture typically uses 200% declining balance over 5 or 7 years; real property uses straight-line over 27.5 years (residential rental) or 39 years (commercial).

Conventions determine how much depreciation is allowed in the first and last years. The half-year convention treats all personal property as placed in service at the midpoint of the year. However, if more than 40% of the year's personal property is placed in service in the fourth quarter, the mid-quarter convention applies instead, which usually reduces the first-year deduction. Real property always uses the mid-month convention.

Two accelerators can front-load deductions. The section 179 election lets a business immediately expense up to $1,220,000 of qualifying property in 2024, with a dollar-for-dollar phaseout beginning at $3,050,000 of purchases. Critically, section 179 cannot create a taxable loss; any amount disallowed by the income limit carries forward. Bonus depreciation under section 168(k) is 60% for 2024 and, unlike section 179, can create a loss and applies automatically unless the taxpayer elects out.

The deductions are taken in a specific order: first section 179, then bonus depreciation on the remaining basis, then regular MACRS on whatever is left. Watch for recapture: if business use of section 179 property falls to 50% or less before the recovery period ends, the excess of the section 179 deduction over what straight-line MACRS would have allowed is recaptured as ordinary income. Passenger autos are listed property subject to annual dollar caps that override the general rules.

topics.title: Partnership vs S-Corp vs C-Corp Comparison

blocks.text: A side-by-side comparison of the three main business entity types tested on Part 2, covering taxation, owner compensation, basis, and distributions. Choosing and understanding entity type underlies many business questions. The pass-through versus double-taxation distinction is central.
Key points

items: C-corp: separate taxpayer, flat 21% corporate rate; earnings taxed again as dividends to shareholders (double taxation).
S-corp and partnership: pass-through entities; income flows to owners and is taxed once at the owner level.
Partnership owners pay self-employment tax on their distributive share of trade-or-business income (general partners).
S-corp shareholders are NOT subject to SE tax on pass-through profits but must take reasonable W-2 wages for services.
S-corp eligibility: 100 shareholder limit, one class of stock, only eligible (generally individual, certain trust/estate) U.S. shareholders.
Partnership basis includes the partner's share of partnership liabilities; S-corp stock basis does NOT include entity-level debt (only direct shareholder loans).
Loss deductions are limited to basis; partners can also count debt basis, S-corp shareholders need separate debt basis from direct loans.
C-corp distributions are dividends to the extent of earnings and profits (E&P); partnership/S-corp distributions are generally tax-free return of basis first.
Guaranteed payments to partners are deductible by the partnership and ordinary income to the partner.
C-corps can have unlimited shareholders, multiple stock classes, and corporate or foreign owners.
Pass-through income may qualify for the 20% QBI deduction; C-corp income does not.
Filing: partnership Form 1065 + K-1; S-corp Form 1120-S + K-1; C-corp Form 1120 (no K-1).

blocks.text:
The defining difference among entities is how many times income is taxed. A C corporation is a separate taxpayer that pays a flat 21% tax on its income; when it distributes earnings as dividends, shareholders pay tax again, producing the classic double taxation. Partnerships and S corporations are pass-through entities: income is reported by the entity for information purposes but taxed only once, at the owner level, on Schedule K-1.

Self-employment tax treatment is a major planning point. A general partner pays self-employment tax on the full distributive share of trade-or-business income, including guaranteed payments. By contrast, an S corporation shareholder pays no self-employment tax on pass-through profits but must receive reasonable compensation as W-2 wages for services rendered - and the IRS scrutinizes unreasonably low wages designed to dodge payroll taxes.

Basis rules differ in a way the exam loves to test. A partner's basis includes a share of the partnership's liabilities, so partnership debt can support loss deductions and tax-free distributions. An S corporation shareholder's stock basis does not include entity-level debt; only loans the shareholder makes directly to the corporation create debt basis. Losses pass through only to the extent of basis (and then must clear at-risk and passive limits).

Eligibility and flexibility favor C corporations for raising capital: they allow unlimited shareholders, multiple classes of stock, and corporate or foreign owners. S corporations are restricted to 100 eligible shareholders, generally individuals and certain trusts/estates, and a single class of stock. Distributions also differ: C-corp distributions are dividends to the extent of earnings and profits, while partnership and S-corp distributions are first a tax-free return of basis. Finally, pass-through income may qualify for the 20% QBI deduction, an advantage C corporations do not share.

The qualified business income deduction lets eligible noncorporate taxpayers deduct up to 20 percent of qualified business income from pass-through entities and sole proprietorships. Mastering the taxable-income thresholds, the SSTB rules, and the wage/UBIA limits is essential for Part 2.
Key points

items: QBI deduction is generally 20 percent of qualified business income from a qualified trade or business.
2024 taxable income thresholds: $191,950 single / $383,900 MFJ where limitations begin to phase in.
Below the threshold: simple 20 percent of QBI, no wage or SSTB limits apply.
Above the upper threshold (phase-in is $50,000 single / $100,000 MFJ): full limitations apply.
Specified service trades or businesses (SSTBs) lose the deduction entirely above the upper threshold.
SSTBs include health, law, accounting, consulting, athletics, financial services, and businesses relying on owner reputation/skill.
Above-threshold non-SSTB limit: greater of 50% of W-2 wages, OR 25% of W-2 wages plus 2.5% of UBIA of qualified property.
Deduction is also capped at 20 percent of (taxable income minus net capital gain).
QBI excludes capital gains, dividends, interest income not allocable to the business, and reasonable compensation/guaranteed payments.
S corporation shareholder wages and partnership guaranteed payments are not QBI.
The deduction is taken below the line but does not require itemizing; it reduces taxable income, not AGI.
REIT dividends and qualified PTP income get a separate 20 percent component.
Losses create negative QBI that carries forward to offset future QBI.
Form 8995 (simplified) or Form 8995-A (complex, above threshold) computes the deduction.

blocks.text:
Start every QBI question by locating taxable income relative to the 2024 thresholds ($191,950 single, $383,900 MFJ). If the taxpayer is below the threshold, the answer is almost always the simple 20 percent of QBI, even for an SSTB, with no wage or property testing. This single check resolves many exam questions instantly.

Above the threshold, two things change. First, the deduction for any business is limited to the greater of 50 percent of W-2 wages paid, or 25 percent of wages plus 2.5 percent of the unadjusted basis immediately after acquisition (UBIA) of qualified property. Second, SSTBs phase out and are fully disallowed above the upper end of the range. The phase-in range is $50,000 wide for single filers and $100,000 for joint filers, and within it both the SSTB disallowance and the wage limit apply proportionally.

Remember what is not QBI: investment income, reasonable S corporation wages, and guaranteed payments to partners are excluded. The overall deduction is then capped at 20 percent of taxable income minus net capital gain. Tie these pieces together on Form 8995 (below threshold) or 8995-A (above threshold), and watch for QBI loss carryforwards that reduce a later year's deduction.

Basis determines gain, loss, depreciation, and the limit on deductible losses. The exam tests three flavors heavily: property basis, partnership outside basis, and S corporation stock and debt basis. Knowing the ordering rules for adjustments is the key to consistent answers.
Key points

items: Property basis starts at cost: purchase price plus acquisition costs, sales tax, freight, and installation.
Gifted property: donee takes donor's basis for gain; uses lower of donor basis or FMV for loss (dual basis rule).
Inherited property: basis is generally FMV at date of death (stepped-up basis), holding period automatically long-term.
Partnership outside basis increases by contributions, share of income, and share of partnership liabilities.
Partnership basis decreases by distributions, share of losses, and decreases in liabilities; never below zero.
A partner's share of partnership debt counts in outside basis (a key difference from S corp basis).
S corp stock basis increases by income/gains and additional contributions; decreases by distributions then losses.
S corp shareholders do NOT get basis from corporate-level debt; only direct shareholder loans add debt basis.
Losses are deductible only to the extent of basis (stock then debt for S corps); excess suspends and carries forward.
Distributions reduce basis before losses are applied in the ordering rules.
Nontaxable stock dividends spread original basis across all shares (per-share basis decreases).
Like-kind (1031) exchanges of real property carry over basis adjusted for boot and recognized gain.
Basis adjustments follow a strict order each year; apply increases before decreases, distributions before losses.

blocks.text:
Property basis questions usually reduce to one of three acquisition methods. Purchased property starts at cost including the expenditures needed to put the asset in service. Gifted property triggers the dual-basis rule: the donee uses the donor's carryover basis to figure gain but the lower of that basis or fair market value to figure a loss, which can produce a 'no gain, no loss' zone. Inherited property steps up (or down) to date-of-death fair market value and is automatically long-term.

Partnership outside basis is dynamic. It rises with cash and property contributions and the partner's distributive share of income, and it includes the partner's share of partnership liabilities, which is a frequent exam distinction. It falls with distributions, the share of losses, and reductions in liabilities, but never below zero. A distribution exceeding basis produces capital gain.

S corporation basis looks similar but with a crucial difference: shareholders get basis only from their own capital and direct loans to the corporation, never from third-party corporate debt. Each year, adjust stock basis up for income, down for distributions, and then down for losses, applying debt basis for losses only after stock basis is exhausted. Losses that exceed total basis are suspended and carry forward until basis is restored.

Depreciation is one of the densest and most tested Part 2 topics. You must distinguish MACRS recovery periods and conventions, the Section 179 election and its limits, bonus depreciation phase-down, and when ADS straight-line is required.
Key points

items: MACRS is the default depreciation system for most tangible property placed in service after 1986.
Common recovery periods: 5-year (autos, computers), 7-year (office furniture, equipment), 27.5-year (residential rental), 39-year (nonresidential real).
Personal property uses 200% or 150% declining balance; real property uses straight-line.
Half-year convention applies to most personal property; mid-quarter applies if >40% placed in service in Q4.
Real property uses the mid-month convention.
Section 179 2024 expensing limit: $1,220,000, with phase-out beginning at $3,050,000 of property placed in service.
Section 179 cannot create or increase a business loss (limited to business taxable income; excess carries forward).
Bonus depreciation for 2024 is 60% (phasing down: 80% in 2023, 60% in 2024, 40% in 2025).
Bonus applies to new and used qualifying property with a recovery period of 20 years or less.
Ordering: take Section 179 first, then bonus depreciation, then regular MACRS on the remaining basis.
ADS (Alternative Depreciation System) uses straight-line over longer lives; required for listed property used 50% or less for business and for certain tax-exempt/foreign use.
Listed property (passenger autos) is subject to annual luxury-auto depreciation caps.
Section 179 can be applied to qualified improvement property and certain roofs/HVAC/security on nonresidential real property.
Land is never depreciable.

blocks.text:
Begin a depreciation question by classifying the asset and its recovery period. Autos and computers are 5-year property; furniture and most equipment are 7-year; residential rental real estate is 27.5-year straight-line; nonresidential real property is 39-year straight-line. The convention follows: half-year for most personal property, mid-quarter if more than 40 percent of personal property went into service in the last quarter, and mid-month for real property.

Next, layer the elective accelerations in the correct order. Section 179 lets a business expense up to $1,220,000 in 2024, phased out dollar-for-dollar once total qualifying purchases exceed $3,050,000, and it cannot push the business into a loss (any excess carries forward). After Section 179, apply bonus depreciation, which is 60 percent in 2024 as the provision phases down, on the remaining basis of qualifying property with a recovery period of 20 years or less. Finally, depreciate whatever basis is left under regular MACRS.

Watch for the special cases the exam loves. Passenger automobiles face annual luxury-auto caps regardless of cost. Listed property used 50 percent or less for business must use ADS straight-line and loses both Section 179 and bonus. ADS is also required for certain tax-exempt use property and electing real property trades or businesses. And land never depreciates, so always strip land value out of a building's basis before computing depreciation.

Character of gain or loss drives the tax rate and is a heavily tested concept. You must separate capital assets from Section 1231 business assets, apply the netting process, and convert otherwise favorable gain back to ordinary income through depreciation recapture.
Key points

items: Capital assets are everything except inventory, receivables, depreciable business property, and real property used in business.
Holding period: more than one year is long-term; one year or less is short-term.
2024 long-term capital gains rates: 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on taxable income brackets.
Section 1231 property is depreciable property and real property used in a trade or business held more than one year.
Net Section 1231 gain is treated as long-term capital gain; net Section 1231 loss is treated as ordinary loss (best of both).
Section 1245 recapture: gain up to prior depreciation on personal property is recaptured as ordinary income.
Section 1250 recapture: applies to excess (accelerated over straight-line) depreciation on real property, now largely historical.
Unrecaptured Section 1250 gain (straight-line depreciation on real property) is taxed at a maximum 25% rate.
Section 1231 five-year lookback: prior unrecaptured 1231 losses recharacterize current 1231 gains as ordinary.
Capital losses offset capital gains; net capital loss deducts up to $3,000 against ordinary income ($1,500 MFS).
Excess capital losses carry forward indefinitely for individuals (retain character).
Wash sale rule disallows a loss when substantially identical securities are bought within 30 days before or after.
Collectibles and certain small business stock gain can be taxed at a maximum 28% rate.

blocks.text:
The exam wants you to determine character before computing tax. First decide whether an asset is a capital asset, a Section 1231 business asset, or ordinary (inventory, receivables). Capital assets net short-term against short-term and long-term against long-term, with a net long-term gain qualifying for the preferential 0/15/20 percent rates in 2024.

Section 1231 gives business taxpayers the best of both worlds: net 1231 gains become long-term capital gains, while net 1231 losses become fully deductible ordinary losses. But two recapture mechanisms claw back the favorable treatment. Section 1245 recaptures depreciation taken on personal property (machinery, equipment) as ordinary income up to the amount of depreciation claimed. For real property, modern straight-line depreciation creates 'unrecaptured Section 1250 gain' taxed at a maximum 25 percent rather than 20 percent.

Do not forget the five-year lookback rule: if you deducted net Section 1231 losses as ordinary in the prior five years, current-year net 1231 gains are recharacterized as ordinary income to the extent of those unrecaptured losses. Finally, manage capital losses correctly. They offset capital gains first, then up to $3,000 of ordinary income per year for individuals, with the remainder carrying forward indefinitely and retaining its short- or long-term character. The wash sale rule disallows losses on substantially identical securities repurchased within the 30-day window before or after the sale.

Fiduciary income tax on Form 1041 applies to estates and trusts. The exam tests the concept of distributable net income, the distinction between simple and complex trusts, and how the income distribution deduction shifts tax to beneficiaries.
Key points

items: Form 1041 is the income tax return for estates and trusts; it is separate from the estate tax return (Form 706).
A trust or estate is a separate taxpaying entity but generally acts as a conduit, taxing income to beneficiaries.
Distributable net income (DNI) limits and characterizes the deduction for distributions and the income beneficiaries report.
Simple trusts must distribute all income annually, make no charitable contributions, and distribute no corpus.
Complex trusts may accumulate income, distribute principal, and make charitable gifts.
The income distribution deduction lets the entity deduct amounts distributed (up to DNI), avoiding double tax.
Beneficiaries report distributed income on Schedule K-1, retaining its character (interest, dividends, capital gain).
Trusts and estates reach the top 37% bracket at a very low threshold (about $15,200 of taxable income in 2024).
Estates get a $600 exemption; simple trusts get $300; complex trusts get $100.
Capital gains are usually taxed to the trust (allocated to corpus) unless required or actually distributed.
Estates may elect a fiscal year; trusts (except certain 645-election cases) must use a calendar year.
The 3.8% net investment income tax applies to undistributed NII above the top bracket threshold.
Grantor trusts are disregarded; income is taxed directly to the grantor, not on a separate 1041.

blocks.text:
Form 1041 treats an estate or non-grantor trust as a separate taxpayer, but its design is a conduit: income that flows out to beneficiaries is taxed to them, while income retained is taxed to the entity. The mechanism is the income distribution deduction, which equals the lesser of the amount distributed or distributable net income (DNI). DNI both caps the deduction and tells beneficiaries how much income, and of what character, to report on their Schedule K-1.

Know the simple-versus-complex distinction cold. A simple trust must distribute all of its income currently, cannot make charitable contributions, and cannot distribute corpus; it gets a $300 exemption. A complex trust may accumulate income, distribute principal, and give to charity; it gets a $100 exemption. Estates get a $600 exemption and, unlike most trusts, may choose a fiscal year.

The compressed rate schedule is a favorite exam point. Trusts and estates hit the top 37 percent ordinary rate at only about $15,200 of taxable income in 2024, and the 3.8 percent net investment income tax kicks in at the same low threshold. This compression is why fiduciaries often distribute income to beneficiaries in lower brackets. Capital gains generally stay with the trust as part of corpus and are taxed at the entity level unless the governing instrument or fiduciary allocates them to income and they are distributed.

Tax-exempt organizations are tested for their qualification requirements, annual filing obligations, and the unrelated business income tax. Knowing the differences among 501(c)(3) categories and the public charity versus private foundation distinction is high-yield.
Key points

items: Section 501(c)(3) covers religious, charitable, scientific, literary, and educational organizations.
501(c)(3) status requires an organizational test and an operational test; no private inurement allowed.
501(c)(3)s are restricted from political campaign activity and limited in lobbying (substantial-part or 501(h) election).
Most organizations apply for recognition using Form 1023 (or streamlined 1023-EZ); 501(c)(4) and others use Form 1024.
Annual return is Form 990, 990-EZ, or 990-N (e-Postcard) depending on gross receipts and assets.
990-N e-Postcard is for organizations with gross receipts normally $50,000 or less.
