Failure to file a 990-series return for three consecutive years results in automatic revocation of exemption.
Public charities have broad public support; private foundations are typically funded by a few sources.
Private foundations face excise taxes (e.g., on net investment income, self-dealing, failure to distribute).
Unrelated business income tax (UBIT) applies to income from a regularly carried-on trade or business unrelated to the exempt purpose.
UBIT is reported on Form 990-T; a $1,000 specific deduction is allowed.
Exceptions to UBI include volunteer-run activities, items sold for the convenience of members, and donated-merchandise sales.
Churches are exempt without applying and generally need not file Form 990.

blocks.text:
A 501(c)(3) organization must satisfy both an organizational test (its governing documents limit it to exempt purposes and dedicate assets to charity on dissolution) and an operational test (it actually operates primarily for those purposes). No part of net earnings may inure to a private individual, the organization may not engage in political campaign activity, and lobbying must be insubstantial unless it makes the 501(h) expenditure election. Recognition is usually obtained by filing Form 1023, with smaller organizations eligible for the streamlined 1023-EZ.

Filing obligations scale with size. The smallest organizations file the Form 990-N e-Postcard (gross receipts normally $50,000 or less), mid-size organizations file Form 990-EZ, and larger ones file the full Form 990. The exam frequently tests the automatic revocation rule: failing to file any 990-series return for three consecutive years revokes exemption by operation of law, and reinstatement requires a new application.

Unrelated business income tax is the other heavily tested area. Even a tax-exempt organization owes tax (on Form 990-T, after a $1,000 specific deduction) on net income from a trade or business that is regularly carried on and not substantially related to its exempt purpose. Statutory exceptions soften this: activities conducted substantially by volunteers, the sale of donated merchandise, and activities for the convenience of members are not unrelated business income. Distinguishing public charities (broad public support) from private foundations (narrow funding, subject to special excise taxes on self-dealing and minimum distributions) rounds out the topic.

sections.title: Study Notes · Part 3: Representation
sections.summary: Study notes for every domain of SEE Part 3: Representation.

blocks.text: This domain covers the rules governing tax practitioners: Circular 230, preparer responsibilities, due diligence, and the sanctions for misconduct. The exam tests who may practice, the standards they must meet, and the penalties for violations.
Key points

items: Circular 230 (31 CFR Part 10) governs practice before the IRS by attorneys, CPAs, EAs, and others.
Enrolled agents, attorneys, and CPAs have unlimited practice rights before the IRS.
EAs must complete 72 hours of continuing education per three-year cycle, with 16 hours minimum per year (2 ethics).
A valid PTIN is required for anyone who prepares returns for compensation.
Practitioners must exercise due diligence in preparing returns and advising clients.
Tax return positions generally need substantial authority or at least a reasonable basis with disclosure.
Section 6694 penalizes preparers for understatements: greater of $1,000 or 50% of fee (unreasonable position).
Section 6695 imposes penalties for failure to sign, furnish a copy, keep records, or due diligence ($635 per 8867 failure in 2024).
Conflicts of interest require informed written consent retained for 36 months.
Practitioners may not charge unconscionable fees and generally may not use contingent fees except in limited situations.
The Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) enforces Circular 230; sanctions include censure, suspension, and disbarment.
Best practices include clear communication, fact verification, and advising clients of potential penalties.

blocks.text:
Practices and procedures is the ethics and professional-conduct heart of Part 3, anchored by Circular 230, the Treasury regulation that governs who may practice before the IRS and how. Attorneys, CPAs, and enrolled agents enjoy unlimited practice rights, meaning they can represent any taxpayer on any matter before any IRS office. Other categories, such as annual filing season program participants, have limited rights tied to returns they prepared.

Enrolled agents have specific maintenance obligations that the exam expects you to know. An EA must complete 72 hours of continuing education over each three-year enrollment cycle, averaging 24 hours per year with a floor of 16 hours in any single year, including two hours of ethics annually. Anyone preparing returns for compensation must also hold a current preparer tax identification number (PTIN) and renew it each year.

The standards for taking positions on a return are tested with precision. To avoid preparer penalties, an undisclosed position generally needs substantial authority, while a disclosed position needs only a reasonable basis; for tax shelters and reportable transactions the bar rises to more-likely-than-not. The Section 6694 preparer penalty for an unreasonable position is the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived, and it climbs for willful or reckless conduct.

Section 6695 collects a set of procedural penalties every practitioner must respect: failing to sign the return, failing to furnish a copy to the taxpayer, failing to retain records, and failing to meet due diligence each carry penalties, with the due diligence failure on Form 8867 set at $635 per failure for 2024. Because a single return claiming the EITC, CTC, AOTC, and head-of-household status involves four due diligence items, the penalties can stack quickly.

Conduct rules round out the domain. A practitioner facing a conflict of interest may proceed only with informed written consent from each affected client, retained for at least 36 months. Unconscionable fees are prohibited, and contingent fees are barred except in narrow circumstances such as IRS examinations of original returns. The Office of Professional Responsibility enforces these rules and can censure, suspend, or disbar practitioners, making compliance a career-protecting necessity rather than a formality.

This domain covers how a practitioner represents a taxpayer in dealings with the IRS: powers of attorney, the examination and appeals process, and the taxpayer's rights. The exam tests forms, procedures, and the practitioner's authority and obligations.
Key points

items: Form 2848 (Power of Attorney) authorizes representation and the right to receive confidential information.
Form 8821 (Tax Information Authorization) allows information access but not representation.
Examinations come in three types: correspondence, office, and field audits.
Taxpayers may appeal exam results to the IRS Independent Office of Appeals.
The 30-day letter proposes changes and offers Appeals; the 90-day letter is the statutory notice of deficiency.
A statutory notice of deficiency (90-day letter) gives the right to petition the U.S. Tax Court without paying first.
The Tax Court hears deficiency cases pre-payment; refund suits go to district court or the Court of Federal Claims after payment.
The general assessment statute of limitations is 3 years; 6 years for a 25%+ omission; unlimited for fraud or no return.
The collection statute of limitations is generally 10 years from assessment.
The Taxpayer Bill of Rights guarantees ten fundamental rights, including representation and appeal.
Practitioners must be authorized; unenrolled preparers have limited representation rights.
The Taxpayer Advocate Service helps with unresolved hardships and systemic problems.

blocks.text:
Representation begins with authority. To act for a taxpayer before the IRS, a practitioner files Form 2848, the power of attorney, which both authorizes representation and permits receipt of confidential return information for specified tax matters and periods. When a client only needs someone to access information, not to advocate, Form 8821, the tax information authorization, is the lighter-weight tool because it grants information access without representation rights.

Most representation work flows from examinations. Audits arrive in three forms of escalating intensity: correspondence audits handled by mail for narrow issues, office audits conducted at an IRS office, and field audits where an agent visits the taxpayer's home or business for complex matters. Throughout, the practitioner manages the flow of documents and arguments, and the Taxpayer Bill of Rights guarantees the client the right to representation, to be informed, and to challenge the IRS position.

The dispute path is defined by two key letters. After an exam, a 30-day letter proposes adjustments and offers the right to take the case to the IRS Independent Office of Appeals, an internal forum designed to resolve disputes without litigation. If no agreement is reached, the IRS issues a statutory notice of deficiency, the 90-day letter, which is the taxpayer's ticket to petition the United States Tax Court without first paying the disputed tax.

Choosing a court matters. The Tax Court is unique in allowing a taxpayer to litigate before paying, making it the common forum for deficiency disputes. Alternatively, a taxpayer can pay the tax, file a claim for refund, and if denied sue in a U.S. district court or the Court of Federal Claims. The pre-payment versus pay-first distinction is a reliable exam point.

Statutes of limitations frame the entire process and must be memorized. The IRS generally has three years from filing to assess additional tax, extended to six years when more than 25% of gross income is omitted, and with no limit at all in cases of fraud or an unfiled return. Once tax is assessed, the IRS generally has ten years to collect. When normal channels fail and a taxpayer faces hardship or a systemic problem, the Taxpayer Advocate Service provides an independent avenue for relief.

This domain covers particular representation matters: collection alternatives, penalty relief, innocent spouse relief, and resolving liabilities. The exam tests installment agreements, offers in compromise, penalty abatement, and the specialized forms each requires.
Key points

items: Installment agreements (Form 9465) let taxpayers pay over time; streamlined options exist for balances up to $50,000.
An Offer in Compromise (Form 656) settles a liability for less than owed based on collection potential.
OIC grounds: doubt as to collectibility, doubt as to liability, or effective tax administration.
Currently Not Collectible (CNC) status pauses collection when a taxpayer cannot pay basic living expenses.
Innocent spouse relief (Form 8857) can relieve a spouse from joint liability for the other's errors.
Three relief types: innocent spouse (6015(b)), separation of liability (6015(c)), and equitable relief (6015(f)).
First-Time Abatement (FTA) waives certain penalties for taxpayers with a clean 3-year compliance history.
Reasonable cause can abate penalties when failure was due to circumstances beyond the taxpayer's control.
A federal tax lien attaches to property; a levy actually seizes property or funds.
Collection Due Process (Form 12153) gives a hearing right after a lien or levy notice.
Trust fund recovery penalty (TFRP) holds responsible persons personally liable for unpaid payroll taxes.
Penalty abatement requests can be made by phone, letter, or Form 843.

blocks.text:
This domain narrows representation to the specific remedies practitioners pursue when a client owes money or disputes a penalty. The most common collection alternative is the installment agreement, requested on Form 9465, which spreads payment over time. Streamlined agreements are available for balances up to $50,000 with minimal financial disclosure, while larger or more complex cases require detailed financial statements and direct negotiation.

When full payment is genuinely impossible, the offer in compromise lets the IRS accept less than the full liability. The most common basis is doubt as to collectibility, where the offer reflects the taxpayer's reasonable collection potential, but offers can also rest on doubt as to liability or on effective tax administration where paying in full would be inequitable. The offer is submitted on Form 656. For taxpayers who cannot pay anything without sacrificing basic living expenses, Currently Not Collectible status temporarily halts collection, though interest continues to accrue.

Innocent spouse relief is a frequently tested protection for taxpayers harmed by a joint return. Filed on Form 8857, it comes in three flavors under Section 6015: traditional innocent spouse relief for understatements the requesting spouse did not know about, separation of liability that splits the deficiency between former spouses, and equitable relief as a catch-all when the other two do not apply but holding the spouse liable would be unfair.

Penalty relief is its own toolkit. First-Time Abatement administratively waives failure-to-file, failure-to-pay, and failure-to-deposit penalties for taxpayers with a clean three-year compliance record. Where FTA does not apply, reasonable cause relief can abate penalties when the failure resulted from circumstances beyond the taxpayer's control, such as serious illness, natural disaster, or reliance on incorrect professional advice. Requests can be made by phone, by written explanation, or on Form 843.

Collection enforcement and its safeguards close the domain. A federal tax lien is a claim against the taxpayer's property that protects the government's interest, while a levy actually seizes assets like bank accounts or wages. After receiving a lien filing or final levy notice, a taxpayer has Collection Due Process rights, requested on Form 12153, to a hearing before Appeals. Practitioners representing businesses must also watch the trust fund recovery penalty, which makes responsible individuals personally liable for the withheld payroll taxes a business failed to remit.

topics.title: Completion of the Filing Process
topics.reference: Domain 3D: Completion of the Filing Process

blocks.text: This domain covers finishing and filing the return correctly: signatures, e-filing rules, recordkeeping, amended returns, and electronic filing mandates. The exam tests preparer signing duties, e-file requirements, and post-filing corrections.
Key points

items: Paid preparers must sign returns and include their PTIN.
The e-file mandate generally requires preparers filing 11 or more covered returns to e-file.
Form 8879 is the e-file signature authorization the taxpayer signs to permit electronic filing.
Taxpayers e-sign using a Self-Select PIN or Practitioner PIN method.
Amended individual returns use Form 1040-X; can now be e-filed for recent years.
Refund claims via 1040-X must generally be filed within 3 years of filing or 2 years of payment.
Form 4868 grants an automatic 6-month extension to file (not to pay) for individuals.
Form 7004 provides an automatic extension for many business returns.
Preparers must give the taxpayer a complete copy of the return.
Records supporting the return should generally be retained at least 3 years.
Direct deposit speeds refunds; preparers cannot deposit a client's refund into their own account.
EFINs (Electronic Filing Identification Numbers) authorize firms to e-file; PTINs identify the individual preparer.

blocks.text:
The filing process is where preparation becomes a legally filed return, and the domain emphasizes doing the final steps correctly. A paid preparer must sign the return and include a valid PTIN; an unsigned return or a missing PTIN exposes the preparer to Section 6695 penalties. The taxpayer must also sign, and for electronic returns this happens through an e-file signature authorization on Form 8879, which the taxpayer signs to let the practitioner transmit the return.

Electronic filing is now the norm and carries its own mandate. A preparer who reasonably expects to file 11 or more covered returns in a year must e-file them unless an exception or taxpayer opt-out applies. Two identifiers govern e-filing: the firm uses an Electronic Filing Identification Number (EFIN) to transmit, while each individual preparer is tracked by a PTIN. Taxpayers authenticate electronically using either the Self-Select PIN method, which relies on prior-year AGI, or the Practitioner PIN method documented on Form 8879.

Extensions and timing are routinely tested. Individuals get an automatic six-month extension to file by submitting Form 4868, and many businesses use Form 7004. The critical caveat is that an extension to file is not an extension to pay; tax owed is still due by the original deadline, and interest and the failure-to-pay penalty run from that date regardless of the extension.

Correcting a filed return is the amended return process. Individuals file Form 1040-X, which can now be e-filed for recent tax years. The refund statute of limitations governs how long a taxpayer has to claim money back: generally the later of three years from when the original return was filed or two years from when the tax was paid. Missing this window forfeits the refund permanently, so calendaring it is essential.

Good housekeeping completes the process. The preparer must furnish the taxpayer a complete copy of the return, and both should retain records supporting income, deductions, and credits for at least three years, longer when the six-year omission rule or fraud could apply. Direct deposit accelerates refunds, but a strict ethical line forbids a preparer from directing any portion of a client's refund into the preparer's own account, a rule designed to prevent fee-skimming and fraud.

A condensed reference to Circular 230, the rulebook for practice before the IRS. Part 3 of the exam tests these duties, restrictions, and sanctions heavily, and many questions can be answered directly from this framework.
Key points

items: Circular 230 is found at 31 CFR Part 10 and governs practice before the IRS.
Practitioners with unlimited rights: attorneys, CPAs, and enrolled agents.
Subpart A defines who may practice; Subpart B sets duties and restrictions; Subpart C covers sanctions.
Must promptly submit records/information lawfully requested by the IRS unless privileged.
Must exercise due diligence as to accuracy of returns and representations.
May rely on client information in good faith but cannot ignore obvious errors or inconsistencies.
Must advise clients of noncompliance, errors, or omissions and their consequences.
Contingent fees are generally prohibited except for examinations, refund claims, and judicial proceedings.
Conflicts of interest require informed written consent retained 36 months.
Cannot endorse or negotiate a client's refund check.
Best practices: clear engagement, fact-based advice, and acting fairly and with integrity.
Sanctions by OPR: censure (public reprimand), suspension, disbarment, and monetary penalties.
Due diligence and competence are affirmative, ongoing obligations, not one-time checks.

blocks.text:
Circular 230 is the single most important authority for Part 3, and structuring it in your mind by subpart makes the questions far easier. Subpart A answers who may practice: attorneys, CPAs, and enrolled agents have unlimited rights to represent any taxpayer on any matter, while other preparers have limited rights tied to the returns they prepared. Subpart B lists the duties and restrictions practitioners owe, and Subpart C sets out the sanctions for violating them.

The duties in Subpart B are the substance of most exam questions. A practitioner must promptly submit records and information lawfully requested by the IRS unless a good-faith belief that they are privileged applies. They must exercise due diligence in preparing returns and in any oral or written representations to the IRS, and while they may rely in good faith on information furnished by a client, they cannot ignore implications that the information is incorrect, inconsistent, or incomplete.

A distinct and tested duty is the obligation to advise. When a practitioner learns that a client has not complied with the law, or has made an error or omission on a return, they must promptly tell the client about the noncompliance and the consequences of failing to fix it. The practitioner is not required to correct the error themselves or to report the client, but silence is not an option.

Fee and conduct restrictions form a cluster worth memorizing. Contingent fees are generally prohibited, with narrow exceptions for IRS examinations, claims for refund, and judicial proceedings. Unconscionable fees are barred outright. A practitioner facing a conflict of interest may continue only with each affected client's informed written consent, retained for 36 months. And a practitioner may never endorse or otherwise negotiate a client's refund check, a bright-line rule designed to prevent fraud.

Subpart C supplies the teeth. The Office of Professional Responsibility investigates violations and can impose censure, which is a public reprimand, suspension for a defined period, or disbarment that ends practice rights, and monetary penalties up to the gross income derived from the offending conduct can also apply. Because these sanctions threaten a practitioner's livelihood, the exam frames Circular 230 not as abstract ethics but as the operating license every enrolled agent must protect.

A comparison of the main IRS collection alternatives a representative can pursue for a taxpayer who cannot pay in full: installment agreements, offers in compromise, and currently-not-collectible status. Part 3 tests when each is appropriate and the forms and consequences involved. Each has distinct eligibility and effects on the statute of limitations.
Key points

items: Installment Agreement (IA): taxpayer pays the full liability over time; request on Form 9465 or online.
Guaranteed IA available for individuals owing $10,000 or less who meet compliance conditions.
Streamlined IA available for balances up to $50,000 payable within 72 months without detailed financial disclosure.
Offer in Compromise (OIC): settles the debt for less than the full amount; filed on Form 656 with Form 433-A(OIC) and an application fee plus initial payment.
OIC grounds: doubt as to collectibility, doubt as to liability, or effective tax administration.
OIC reasonable collection potential (RCP) = net realizable equity in assets + future income; the offer must generally meet or exceed RCP.
Filing an OIC suspends the 10-year collection statute while it is pending plus 30 days.
Currently Not Collectible (CNC): IRS halts active collection because payment would cause hardship; the debt is not forgiven.
Penalties and interest continue to accrue during CNC status, and the IRS may file a federal tax lien.
The collection statute expiration date (CSED) is generally 10 years from assessment.
A federal tax lien may still attach under an IA or CNC; a levy is generally released once an IA is in effect.
All options require the taxpayer to be in filing compliance (all required returns filed).

blocks.text:
When a taxpayer owes more than they can pay, a representative chooses among three core paths based on the taxpayer's ability to pay and asset picture. An installment agreement is the simplest: the taxpayer commits to pay the full liability over time. Guaranteed agreements (under $10,000) and streamlined agreements (under $50,000 over 72 months) require little or no financial disclosure, while larger balances require a Form 433 financial statement and may demand asset liquidation first.

An offer in compromise settles the debt for less than the full amount. The most common ground is doubt as to collectibility, where the IRS accepts that it cannot collect the full liability before the statute expires. The offer must generally equal or exceed the reasonable collection potential, computed as the net realizable equity in the taxpayer's assets plus a multiple of future monthly disposable income. Filing an offer suspends the collection statute while it is pending plus an additional 30 days, and the taxpayer must stay compliant for the next five years or the compromise defaults.

Currently not collectible status is appropriate when collection would create economic hardship. The IRS stops active collection - no levies - but this is a pause, not forgiveness. Penalties and interest keep accruing, the IRS will likely file a federal tax lien to protect its interest, and the account is periodically reviewed; if the taxpayer's finances improve, collection resumes.

Two themes cut across all three. First, the collection statute expiration date generally gives the IRS ten years from assessment to collect, and any option that suspends that clock (like a pending OIC) extends the government's window. Second, every option requires filing compliance: the taxpayer must have filed all required returns before the IRS will consider any collection alternative. Matching the right option to the taxpayer's facts - full pay over time, settle for less, or pause - is the core skill Part 3 tests.

A concise summary of the assessment, collection, and refund limitation periods that govern IRS and taxpayer actions. These dates appear throughout Part 3 and in procedural questions on Parts 1 and 2. Knowing the triggers and exceptions prevents missed deadlines and wrong answers.
Key points

items: Assessment statute (ASED): generally 3 years from the later of the due date or the date the return was filed.
6-year assessment period if the taxpayer omits more than 25% of gross income.
No assessment limit for a false or fraudulent return, a willful attempt to evade, or a return never filed.
Omission of foreign financial asset income over $5,000 also extends assessment to 6 years.
Collection statute (CSED): generally 10 years from the date of assessment.
Refund claim: the later of 3 years from filing the return or 2 years from paying the tax.
Refund amount is limited by the lookback rule (the 'look-back' to taxes paid within the applicable 3- or 2-year window).
Filing an OIC, bankruptcy, a CDP hearing request, or being outside the U.S. can suspend/extend the CSED.
A taxpayer can consent to extend the assessment period by signing Form 872 (or 872-A, open-ended).
A claim filed within the period but no return ever filed limits refund to amounts paid in the prior 2 years.
The mailbox rule (timely mailed = timely filed) applies to returns and claims using proper postmark or designated private delivery service.
An amended return filed near the deadline does not by itself extend the assessment statute on the original return.

blocks.text:
Limitation periods set the outer boundaries on when the IRS can assess and collect tax and when a taxpayer can claim a refund. The assessment statute, the ASED, is generally three years from the later of the return's due date or its actual filing date. This means filing early does not start the clock early - a return filed in February for a April-due year still runs the three years from the April due date.

Several exceptions lengthen the assessment window. A substantial omission of income - more than 25% of gross income - extends the period to six years, as does omitting more than $5,000 of income from specified foreign financial assets. Most importantly, there is no statute of limitations at all on a fraudulent return, a willful attempt to evade tax, or a return that was never filed; the IRS can assess those at any time.

The collection statute, the CSED, gives the IRS ten years from the date of assessment to collect an assessed liability. Various events suspend this clock, including a pending offer in compromise, bankruptcy proceedings, a collection due process hearing request, and periods when the taxpayer is outside the United States. Taxpayers may also voluntarily extend the assessment period by signing a consent on Form 872.

The refund statute protects taxpayers. A claim for refund must be filed by the later of three years from the date the return was filed or two years from the date the tax was paid. Even a timely claim is subject to a lookback limit: the refund cannot exceed the tax paid within the applicable three-year (or two-year) window preceding the claim. The mailbox rule treats a return or claim as filed on the postmark date if properly mailed or sent by a designated private delivery service. Mastering these triggers - what starts each clock and what stops it - is essential for procedural questions.

A focused cheat sheet on Treasury Circular 230, which governs who may practice before the IRS and the duties practitioners owe. This is the core of Part 3 ethics questions. Know the practice rights, the diligence and competence duties, and the sanction process.
Key points

items: Circular 230 governs practice before the IRS by attorneys, CPAs, enrolled agents, enrolled actuaries, and enrolled retirement plan agents.
Enrolled agents have unlimited practice rights - any taxpayer, any tax matter, any IRS office.
Unenrolled preparers have only limited representation rights (returns they prepared and signed, with an AFSP record of completion).
Practitioners must exercise due diligence in preparing returns and in representations to the IRS and clients.
A practitioner must promptly notify a client of any error or omission in a return or document and the consequences.
Practitioners must return client records on request, even if a fee dispute exists (state law may allow withholding the practitioner's own work product).
Contingent fees are generally prohibited except in limited situations (e.g., IRS examination of an original return, certain refund claims).
Practitioners may not charge an unconscionable fee or unreasonably delay any matter before the IRS.
Conflicts of interest are permitted only with informed, written consent retained for 36 months.
Sanctions for violations: censure (public reprimand), suspension, disbarment, and monetary penalties.
The Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) handles practitioner discipline; the Return Preparer Office handles PTINs and enrollment.
Best-practice standards encourage clear client communication, advising on penalties, and acting fairly with integrity.

blocks.text:
Circular 230 is the rulebook for practicing before the IRS, and Part 3 leans heavily on it. The first concept is who may practice and how broadly. Enrolled agents, like attorneys and CPAs, have unlimited practice rights: they can represent any taxpayer on any matter before any IRS office. Unenrolled return preparers have only limited rights, generally restricted to representing taxpayers for returns they personally prepared and signed, and only if they hold an Annual Filing Season Program record of completion.

The diligence and competence duties form the ethical core. A practitioner must exercise due diligence in preparing and filing returns and in any oral or written representations to the IRS or to clients. When a practitioner learns of an error or omission on a client's return, Circular 230 requires prompt notice to the client of the error and its potential consequences - though it does not require the practitioner to fix it without the client's consent or to report the client to the IRS.

Several practice-management rules are frequently tested. Practitioners must promptly return a client's records upon request even amid a fee dispute, though they may generally retain their own work product subject to state law. Contingent fees are largely prohibited, with narrow exceptions such as representing a client in an IRS examination of an original return or in connection with certain refund claims. Conflicts of interest can be waived only with each affected client's informed, written consent, which must be retained for at least 36 months.

Discipline runs through the Office of Professional Responsibility. The available sanctions, in increasing severity, are censure (a public reprimand), suspension, and disbarment from practice, and the IRS may also impose monetary penalties. Knowing the ladder and the conduct that triggers each level - along with the affirmative duties of diligence, candor, and prompt client communication - covers the heart of the ethics material on the exam.

After an assessment, the IRS pursues collection through a defined sequence of notices, liens, and levies. Enrolled agents must know the taxpayer's rights, the collection alternatives, and the deadlines that govern appeals and the collection statute.
Key points

items: Collection begins after assessment and the first balance-due notice (CP14).
The Collection Statute Expiration Date (CSED) is generally 10 years from the date of assessment.
A federal tax lien arises automatically; the IRS files a Notice of Federal Tax Lien to establish priority against other creditors.
A levy actually seizes property; it requires a Final Notice of Intent to Levy and notice of CDP rights.
Collection Due Process (CDP) hearing must be requested within 30 days of the Final Notice to preserve Tax Court review.
A late CDP request (within one year) gets an equivalent hearing but no Tax Court appeal.
Installment agreements let taxpayers pay over time; streamlined agreements apply under set balance thresholds.
An Offer in Compromise (Form 656) can settle for less based on doubt as to collectibility, liability, or effective tax administration.
Currently Not Collectible (CNC) status pauses active collection when the taxpayer cannot pay.
Certain levies are exempt by statute (e.g., some wages, unemployment, certain pensions, tools of trade up to limits).
The IRS must release a levy if it creates economic hardship.
Seriously delinquent tax debt can lead to passport certification/denial by the State Department.
Trust fund recovery penalty can hold responsible persons personally liable for unpaid payroll taxes.

blocks.text:
Collection follows assessment. Once tax is assessed and the first notice (CP14) goes unpaid, the IRS escalates through a series of letters. A federal tax lien attaches automatically to the taxpayer's property; filing the Notice of Federal Tax Lien is what gives the government priority over later creditors. A levy goes further and actually seizes assets, but it cannot proceed until the IRS issues a Final Notice of Intent to Levy that also informs the taxpayer of Collection Due Process rights.

The 30-day CDP deadline is the single most important date to memorize. Requesting a CDP hearing within 30 days of the Final Notice of Intent to Levy (or the lien filing notice) preserves the right to petition Tax Court if the taxpayer disagrees with the appeals determination. Miss the 30 days but file within a year and the taxpayer gets only an 'equivalent hearing' with no judicial review. At the hearing, the taxpayer can raise collection alternatives but generally cannot contest the underlying liability if they already had a chance to do so.

Collection alternatives are the practical core of representation work. Installment agreements (including streamlined options under balance thresholds) spread payments over time. An Offer in Compromise on Form 656 can settle the debt for less, most commonly on doubt as to collectibility. Currently Not Collectible status pauses active collection for taxpayers facing hardship. Throughout, the 10-year Collection Statute Expiration Date runs in the background, and certain events (offers, CDP hearings, bankruptcy) suspend and extend it.

The exam tests common civil penalties, how they are calculated, and the reasonable cause and first-time abatement relief options. Distinguishing the failure-to-file penalty from the failure-to-pay penalty is essential.
Key points

items: Failure-to-file penalty: 5% of unpaid tax per month (or part), up to 25% maximum.
Failure-to-pay penalty: 0.5% of unpaid tax per month, up to 25% maximum.
When both apply in the same month, the failure-to-file penalty is reduced by the failure-to-pay penalty (net 4.5%).
Minimum failure-to-file penalty for returns over 60 days late: the lesser of a set dollar amount or 100% of the tax due.
Estimated tax penalty (Form 2210) applies when withholding plus estimates fall short of safe-harbor amounts.
Safe harbor: pay 90% of current-year tax or 100% of prior-year tax (110% if prior-year AGI over $150,000).
Accuracy-related penalty: 20% for negligence or substantial understatement of income tax.
Substantial understatement means understating tax by more than 10% (or $5,000 for individuals), whichever is greater.
Civil fraud penalty is 75% of the underpayment attributable to fraud.
Interest accrues on unpaid tax (and on penalties) from the original due date until paid; it compounds daily.
Reasonable cause can abate penalties but generally not interest tied to the underlying tax.
First-Time Abatement (FTA) can remove failure-to-file/pay penalties with a clean three-year compliance history.
Trust fund recovery and information-return penalties have their own separate regimes.

blocks.text:
The two penalties candidates confuse most are failure-to-file and failure-to-pay. Failure to file is the harsher of the two at 5 percent of unpaid tax per month, capped at 25 percent. Failure to pay is only 0.5 percent per month, also capped at 25 percent. When both apply in the same month, the failure-to-file penalty is reduced by the failure-to-pay amount so the combined rate is 5 percent (4.5 percent file plus 0.5 percent pay). This is why filing on time even when you cannot pay is always advisable.

The estimated tax penalty operates differently; it is essentially interest for underpaying throughout the year. Taxpayers avoid it by meeting a safe harbor: paying at least 90 percent of the current year's tax or 100 percent of the prior year's tax, with the prior-year figure rising to 110 percent if prior-year AGI exceeded $150,000. The accuracy-related penalty of 20 percent applies to negligence or a substantial understatement, defined for individuals as understating tax by more than 10 percent or $5,000, whichever is larger. Fraud raises the stakes to a 75 percent civil penalty.

Relief comes in two main forms. Reasonable cause abates penalties when the taxpayer exercised ordinary business care but still could not comply (illness, disaster, reliance on a professional in limited circumstances), though it rarely touches interest on the tax itself. First-Time Abatement is an administrative waiver available to taxpayers with a clean three-year compliance record and removes the failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties without needing to prove reasonable cause. Interest, by contrast, accrues from the original due date, compounds daily, and generally cannot be abated unless it resulted from an IRS error or delay.

Knowing when a return can be amended and how long the IRS has to assess or a taxpayer has to claim a refund is core representation knowledge. The assessment and refund statutes have several important exceptions the exam likes to test.
Key points

items: Individuals amend with Form 1040-X; it can now be e-filed for many recent tax years.
Refund claim statute: the later of 3 years from filing or 2 years from when the tax was paid.
A return filed early is treated as filed on the original due date for starting the statute clock.
General assessment statute (ASED): 3 years from the later of the due date or the date filed.
6-year assessment statute applies if gross income is understated by more than 25%.
No statute of limitations on assessment for a false/fraudulent return or for failure to file.
The collection statute (CSED) is generally 10 years from the date of assessment.
Filing Form 1040-X does not extend the assessment statute on its own.
An amended return showing more tax due should be filed and paid to limit penalties and interest.
Carryback claims (e.g., certain NOLs) have their own timing rules tied to the loss year.
Form 843 is used to claim refunds/abatements of certain taxes, interest, penalties, and fees (not income tax shown on a return).
The IRS generally has 45 days to pay a timely-filed original return refund before owing interest to the taxpayer.
A protective claim preserves a refund right when the amount depends on a contingent future event.

blocks.text:
The refund statute and the assessment statute run on different clocks, and the exam tests both. To claim a refund, a taxpayer must file within the later of three years from the date the return was filed or two years from the date the tax was paid. A return filed before the due date is treated as filed on the due date, so the three-year window typically runs from April 15. Miss this window and the refund is lost even if the overpayment is genuine.

The assessment statute (ASED) gives the IRS three years from the later of the due date or the actual filing date to assess additional tax. Two big exceptions extend or eliminate it: a more-than-25-percent omission of gross income stretches the period to six years, and a false or fraudulent return or a failure to file leaves the statute open indefinitely. The separate collection statute (CSED) then gives the IRS ten years from assessment to collect.

For amendments, individuals use Form 1040-X, which is now electronically filable for many recent years. Filing a 1040-X does not by itself extend the assessment statute, so an amended return claiming a refund must still fall within the refund window. When an amendment increases tax, filing and paying promptly minimizes the failure-to-pay penalty and interest that accrue from the original due date. Form 843 covers refund and abatement claims for certain penalties, interest, and excise items that are not income tax reported on a return, and a protective claim can hold a refund right open when the outcome depends on a pending event such as litigation.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.summary: 232 step-by-step calculations across all three parts.

topics.title: Social Security Provisional Income / Taxable Portion

blocks.text: A married-filing-jointly couple receives $30,000 in Social Security benefits. Their other income is $40,000 (pension and interest), including $2,000 of tax-exempt municipal bond interest. How much of their Social Security is taxable?
Steps

items: Step 1: Compute provisional income = other income $40,000 (which already includes the $2,000 tax-exempt interest) + 1/2 of SS benefits ($30,000 / 2 = $15,000) = $55,000.
Step 2: MFJ thresholds: base $32,000 and upper $44,000. Provisional $55,000 exceeds both.
Step 3: Tier 1 amount: 50% x (lesser of [provisional - $32,000] or [$44,000 - $32,000]) = 50% x $12,000 = $6,000.
Step 6: Cap at 85% of benefits: 85% x $30,000 = $25,500. The $15,350 is the lesser, so taxable SS = $15,350.

blocks.text: Answer: $15,350 of the $30,000 Social Security benefit is taxable. Takeaway: tax-exempt interest still counts in provisional income and can increase taxable Social Security.

topics.title: Net Investment Income Tax (3.8%) on High Earners

blocks.text: A single taxpayer has wages of $230,000 and net investment income (interest, dividends, capital gains) of $50,000, for MAGI of $280,000. What is the Net Investment Income Tax for 2024?
Steps

items: Step 1: The NIIT threshold for single filers is $200,000.
Step 2: Excess MAGI over threshold = $280,000 - $200,000 = $80,000.
Step 3: NIIT base = lesser of net investment income ($50,000) and excess MAGI ($80,000) = $50,000.
Step 5: Wages are not investment income, but they raise MAGI above the threshold, exposing the investment income to the tax.

blocks.text: Answer: The NIIT is $1,900. Takeaway: NIIT applies 3.8% to the lesser of net investment income or MAGI over the filing-status threshold.

A single taxpayer is an active participant in a workplace 401(k). For 2024 his MAGI is $80,000. The 2024 phaseout range for a single active participant is $77,000 to $87,000. He contributes the $7,000 maximum to a traditional IRA. How much is deductible?
Steps

items: Step 1: Phaseout range width = $87,000 - $77,000 = $10,000.
Step 2: Amount into the phaseout = MAGI $80,000 - $77,000 = $3,000.
Step 3: Fraction phased out = $3,000 / $10,000 = 30%; deductible fraction = 70%.
Step 4: Tentative deductible = 70% x $7,000 = $4,900.
Step 5: Round up to the nearest $10 (special rule, but not below $200 if any deduction remains): deductible = $4,900.
Step 6: The nondeductible portion of $2,100 may still be contributed as basis (Form 8606).

blocks.text: Answer: $4,900 of the $7,000 IRA contribution is deductible; $2,100 is nondeductible basis. Takeaway: active-participant status phases out the IRA deduction proportionally within the MAGI band.

topics.title: Self-Employment Tax and the 1/2 SE Tax Deduction

blocks.text: A sole proprietor has $100,000 of net profit from Schedule C in 2024 (no wages from any job). Compute the self-employment tax and the above-the-line deduction for half of it.
Steps

items: Step 1: Net earnings from self-employment = $100,000 x 92.35% = $92,350.
Step 2: This $92,350 is below the $168,600 Social Security wage base, so all of it is subject to the 12.4% Social Security portion.
Step 3: Social Security tax = 12.4% x $92,350 = $11,451.40.
Step 6: Deduction for 1/2 of SE tax (above the line) = $14,130 / 2 = $7,065.

blocks.text: Answer: SE tax is about $14,130; the deduction for half is about $7,065. Takeaway: SE tax is computed on 92.35% of net profit, and half of it is an above-the-line deduction.
A married-filing-jointly couple has AGI of $42,000 in 2024 and together contributed $3,000 to IRAs. For 2024 MFJ, AGI up to $46,000 qualifies for the 50% credit rate. Compute the Saver's Credit.
Steps

items: Step 1: The Saver's Credit applies to up to $2,000 of contributions per person ($4,000 combined for MFJ).
Step 2: Their $3,000 of combined contributions is under the $4,000 ceiling, so all $3,000 counts.
Step 3: At AGI of $42,000 (under $46,000 for MFJ), the credit rate is 50%.
Step 4: Saver's Credit = 50% x $3,000 = $1,500.
Step 5: This is a nonrefundable credit limited to tax liability; it stacks on top of any IRA deduction.

blocks.text: Answer: The Saver's Credit is $1,500. Takeaway: lower-income savers get a 10%-50% nonrefundable credit on up to $2,000 of retirement contributions per person.

topics.title: Kiddie Tax on a Child's Unearned Income

blocks.text: A 15-year-old dependent has $5,000 of unearned income (interest and dividends) and no earned income in 2024. The 2024 standard deduction floor for the kiddie tax is $1,300, and the next $1,300 is taxed at the child's rate. Compute the income taxed at the parents' rate.
Steps

items: Step 1: First $1,300 of unearned income is offset by the child's standard deduction (tax-free).
Step 2: Next $1,300 is taxed at the child's own (typically 10%) rate.
Step 3: Unearned income above $2,600 ($1,300 + $1,300) is taxed at the parents' marginal rate (kiddie tax).
Step 4: Amount subject to kiddie tax = $5,000 - $2,600 = $2,400.
Step 5: That $2,400 is taxed at the parents' rate; the prior $1,300 is taxed at the child's 10% = $130.

blocks.text: Answer: $2,400 of the child's unearned income is taxed at the parents' rate. Takeaway: for 2024, the first $1,300 is tax-free, the next $1,300 is at the child's rate, and unearned income over $2,600 hits the kiddie tax.

topics.title: Filing Status: Qualifying Surviving Spouse Eligibility and Tax

blocks.text: Maria's husband died in March 2022. She has not remarried and maintains a home for her dependent son. In 2024 she has taxable income of $90,000. She wants to know her correct filing status and the standard deduction-based comparison for 2024.
Steps

items: Step 1: Determine eligibility. Qualifying Surviving Spouse (QSS) is available for the two tax years AFTER the year of death if the taxpayer has a dependent child and has not remarried. Spouse died 2022, so 2023 and 2024 qualify.
Step 2: Confirm 2024 is the second qualifying year and she maintains a home for her dependent son: she qualifies for QSS in 2024.
Step 3: QSS uses the same tax brackets and standard deduction as Married Filing Jointly. The 2024 MFJ/QSS standard deduction is $29,200.
Step 4: Compare to Head of Household, which she would otherwise use: HoH standard deduction is $21,900. QSS gives $29,200 - $21,900 = $7,300 more deduction.
Step 5: QSS brackets are also wider (MFJ schedule), reducing the marginal rate on her $90,000 taxable income versus HoH.
Step 6: Conclusion: File as Qualifying Surviving Spouse for 2024; in 2025 she must switch to Head of Household (assuming the dependent child remains).

blocks.text: Answer: Maria files as Qualifying Surviving Spouse for 2024, using MFJ brackets and the $29,200 standard deduction ($7,300 more than HoH). Takeaway: QSS lasts only the two years after the year of death and requires a dependent child plus an unmarried taxpayer.

topics.title: Dependency: Qualifying Relative Gross Income and Support Tests

blocks.text: Tom supports his 67-year-old mother, who lives in her own apartment. In 2024 his mother received $4,500 of taxable interest/dividends and $11,000 of nontaxable Social Security benefits. Tom paid $9,000 of her $14,000 total support; she paid the remaining $5,000 from her Social Security. Can Tom claim her as a dependent?
Steps

items: Step 1: Apply the gross income test. A qualifying relative's gross income must be less than the 2024 limit of $5,050. Tax-exempt Social Security is excluded from gross income.
Step 2: Mother's gross income for the test = $4,500 (taxable interest/dividends only). $4,500 < $5,050, so the gross income test is MET.
Step 3: Apply the support test. Tom must provide more than half of total support. Total support = $14,000.
Step 4: Tom's share = $9,000 / $14,000 = 64.3%, which is more than half. Support test is MET.
Step 5: A parent does not need to live with the taxpayer to be a qualifying relative, and the relationship test is satisfied.
Step 6: All tests met (gross income, support, relationship, not a qualifying child of another). Tom may claim his mother as a qualifying relative.

blocks.text: Answer: Tom can claim his mother as a qualifying relative; she may also qualify him for the $500 Credit for Other Dependents. Takeaway: nontaxable Social Security is ignored for the $5,050 gross income test, and parents need not live with the taxpayer.

Mark and Lisa file jointly for 2024. Mark's W-2 wages are $82,000 and Lisa's are $46,000. They have $1,200 of taxable interest and $800 of qualified dividends. Mark contributed $4,000 to a traditional IRA (fully deductible) and paid $3,000 of student loan interest (limited to $2,500). They use the standard deduction of $29,200. Compute their taxable income.
Steps

items: Step 2: Add other income: $128,000 + $1,200 interest + $800 dividends = $130,000 total income.
Step 3: Apply above-the-line adjustments: IRA deduction $4,000 + student loan interest (capped at $2,500) = $6,500.
Step 5: Subtract the standard deduction: $123,500 - $29,200 = $94,300.
Step 6: There are no QBI or other below-the-line items, so taxable income = $94,300.

blocks.text: Answer: Taxable income is $94,300. Above-the-line adjustments reduce AGI before the standard deduction is applied.

topics.title: Taxable Portion of Social Security Benefits

blocks.text: A married couple filing jointly receives $24,000 in Social Security benefits and has $40,000 of other income (no tax-exempt interest). Determine provisional income and the maximum taxable portion of benefits using the 85% test thresholds ($32,000 and $44,000 for MFJ).
Steps

items: Step 1: Provisional income = other income + half of benefits = $40,000 + ($24,000 / 2) = $52,000.
Step 2: Provisional income $52,000 exceeds the upper MFJ threshold of $44,000, so the 85% tier applies.
Step 3: 85% of benefits = 0.85 x $24,000 = $20,400 (the absolute cap on taxable benefits).
Step 4: Lower-tier amount: 50% of (lesser of provisional over $32,000, or $12,000 band) plus 85% of excess over $44,000.
Step 6: Taxable benefits = lesser of $12,800 or the $20,400 cap = $12,800.

blocks.text: Answer: $12,800 of the Social Security benefits is taxable. The 85% cap limits taxability even when provisional income is high.

A single taxpayer has MAGI of $260,000 in 2024, including $30,000 of net investment income (interest, dividends, and capital gains). The NIIT threshold for single filers is $200,000. Compute the Net Investment Income Tax.
Steps

items: Step 1: Excess MAGI over the threshold = $260,000 - $200,000 = $60,000.
Step 2: Net investment income = $30,000.
Step 3: The NIIT base is the lesser of net investment income or excess MAGI: lesser of $30,000 and $60,000 = $30,000.
Step 5: The tax applies because both MAGI exceeds the threshold and there is net investment income.

blocks.text: Answer: Net Investment Income Tax is $1,140. The 3.8% tax applies to the lesser of net investment income or MAGI over the threshold.

A single taxpayer is an active participant in an employer plan in 2024 and has MAGI of $82,000. The IRA deduction phaseout range for a single active participant is $77,000 to $87,000, a $10,000 range. The contribution limit is $7,000. Compute the deductible IRA amount.
Steps

items: Step 1: MAGI within the phaseout range: $82,000 is between $77,000 and $87,000.
Step 2: Amount into the range = $82,000 - $77,000 = $5,000.
Step 3: Fraction phased out = $5,000 / $10,000 range = 50%.
Step 4: Reduction = 50% x $7,000 contribution limit = $3,500.
Step 5: Deductible amount = $7,000 - $3,500 = $3,500 (rounded to the nearest $10).

blocks.text: Answer: The deductible IRA amount is $3,500. The deduction phases out proportionally across the $10,000 income range.

A single taxpayer in 2024 has potential itemized deductions of $4,000 state income tax, $6,000 mortgage interest, $2,500 charitable gifts, and $1,000 of medical expenses (but AGI is $80,000, so only medical over 7.5% of AGI counts). The standard deduction is $14,600. Should they itemize?
Steps

items: Step 1: Medical deductible portion = $1,000 - (7.5% x $80,000 = $6,000) = negative, so $0 medical is deductible.
Step 2: SALT is fully under the $10,000 cap: state income tax $4,000 is allowed.
Step 3: Total itemized = $4,000 SALT + $6,000 mortgage interest + $2,500 charity + $0 medical = $12,500.
Step 4: Compare to the $14,600 standard deduction: $12,500 < $14,600.
Step 5: Take the standard deduction because it is larger.

blocks.text: Answer: Take the $14,600 standard deduction; itemized total is only $12,500. Medical expenses are deductible only above 7.5% of AGI.

Walter and Iris file jointly for 2024. They receive $36,000 in Social Security benefits. Their other income is a $40,000 pension, $5,000 of taxable interest, and $3,000 of tax-exempt municipal bond interest. Determine how much of their Social Security benefits is taxable.
Steps

items: Step 1: Compute provisional (combined) income = other income + tax-exempt interest + one-half of benefits. One-half of benefits = $36,000 / 2 = $18,000.
Step 2: Provisional income = $40,000 pension + $5,000 interest + $3,000 tax-exempt + $18,000 = $66,000.
Step 3: MFJ thresholds are $32,000 (first) and $44,000 (second). Provisional income $66,000 exceeds both, so use the 85% computation.
Step 4: Amount over second threshold = $66,000 - $44,000 = $22,000; 85% of that = $18,700.
Step 5: Lesser of (a) $18,700 + smaller of [$6,000 fixed MFJ add-on or 50% of benefits] and (b) 85% of benefits. Smaller of $6,000 and $18,000 = $6,000, so (a) = $18,700 + $6,000 = $24,700.
Step 6: 85% of benefits = 0.85 x $36,000 = $30,600. Taxable amount = lesser of $24,700 and $30,600 = $24,700.
Step 7: Taxable Social Security = $24,700 of the $36,000 received.

blocks.text: Answer: $24,700 of the $36,000 benefits is taxable. Tax-exempt interest still counts in provisional income and can push benefits into the 85% tier.

A married couple has one child in their second year of college with $4,500 of qualified tuition. Their modified AGI is $168,000. Compute their American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC) after the phaseout.
Steps

items: Step 1: Tentative AOTC = 100% of first $2,000 + 25% of next $2,000 = $2,000 + $500 = $2,500 (qualified expenses of $4,500 exceed $4,000).
Step 2: MFJ phaseout range is MAGI $160,000 to $180,000 (width $20,000).
Step 4: Reduction ratio = $8,000 / $20,000 = 0.40, so 40% is phased out and 60% remains.
Step 6: Final AOTC = $1,500 (40% of which, $600, is refundable as up to 40% of the credit).

blocks.text: Answer: AOTC is $1,500 after the 40% phaseout. The credit is reduced ratably across the $20,000 MFJ MAGI band.

topics.title: EITC Disqualified by Investment Income Limit (2024)

blocks.text: Nina is single with two qualifying children and $19,000 of earned income from wages. She also has $12,000 of taxable interest and dividends (investment income). For 2024 the investment-income limit for EITC is $11,600. Determine her EITC eligibility.
Steps

items: Step 1: Identify her investment income: $12,000 of interest and dividends.
Step 2: The 2024 EITC investment-income ceiling is $11,600.
Step 3: Compare: $12,000 > $11,600, so she exceeds the limit.
Step 4: Exceeding the investment-income limit by even $1 disqualifies the taxpayer entirely; there is no phase-down.
Step 5: Although her $19,000 earned income with two children would otherwise generate a sizable EITC, the credit is $0.
Step 6: Result: EITC = $0 for 2024 solely due to the investment-income test.

blocks.text: Answer: EITC is $0 because investment income of $12,000 exceeds the $11,600 limit. The investment-income test is a hard cliff, not a phaseout.

topics.title: Annualized Income Installment Method for Estimated Tax

blocks.text: Priya, single, has uneven income. Her annual projected tax is $24,000. By the end of the first quarter (3 months, through March 31), her annualized taxable income computation yields an annualized tax of $18,000. Required annual payment is 90% of $24,000. Determine the minimum first-quarter estimated payment under the annualized method (annualization factor 4 for the 3-month period; applicable percentage 22.5% for Q1).
Steps

items: Step 1: Annualized tax for the period = $18,000 (already annualized using factor of 4).
Step 2: The cumulative required installment through Q1 uses the 22.5% applicable percentage.
Step 3: Cumulative amount due through Q1 = 22.5% x $18,000 = $4,050.
Step 4: Compare to the regular (even) method: 22.5% x (90% x $24,000) = 22.5% x $21,600 = $4,860.
Step 5: The annualized method allows the smaller $4,050 because early income was lower.
Step 6: Minimum Q1 payment to avoid penalty under the annualized method = $4,050.

blocks.text: Answer: Minimum first-quarter payment is $4,050. The annualized method lets taxpayers with back-loaded income pay less early in the year.

Grace, single, has wages of $190,000, net investment income of $60,000 (dividends, interest, and net capital gain), and no other income. The NIIT threshold for single filers is $200,000. Compute her 3.8% NIIT.
Steps

items: Step 1: Modified AGI = $190,000 wages + $60,000 investment income = $250,000.
Step 3: NIIT applies to the lesser of net investment income ($60,000) or MAGI excess ($50,000).
Step 4: Lesser amount = $50,000.

blocks.text: Answer: NIIT is $1,900 (3.8% on the lesser of $60,000 NII or $50,000 MAGI excess). The threshold is not indexed for inflation.

topics.title: Individual AMT Computation with Exemption Phaseout (Single, 2024)

blocks.text: Logan is single. His alternative minimum taxable income (AMTI) for 2024 is $620,000. The 2024 single AMT exemption is $85,700, phasing out at 25 cents per dollar of AMTI over $609,350. The 26% rate applies up to $232,600 of the AMT base and 28% above. His regular tax is $150,000. Compute the AMT, if any.
Steps

items: Step 2: Allowed exemption = $85,700 - $2,663 = $83,037.
Step 5: Compare TMT $145,698 to regular tax $150,000.
Step 6: AMT = TMT - regular tax = $145,698 - $150,000 = negative, so AMT = $0.

blocks.text: Answer: No AMT is owed because tentative minimum tax ($145,698) is below regular tax ($150,000). AMT only applies when TMT exceeds regular tax.

Tanya is single with two qualifying children. Her 2024 earned income (and AGI) is $40,000. The 2024 maximum EITC for two children is $6,960, with a 21.06% phaseout that begins at $22,720 for non-joint filers. Estimate her EITC.
Steps

items: Step 1: Her income $40,000 is above the phaseout start of $22,720, so she is in the phaseout band.
Step 2: Income over the phaseout threshold = $40,000 - $22,720 = $17,280.
Step 3: Phaseout reduction = 21.06% x $17,280 = $3,639.17, round to $3,639.
Step 5: Confirm she is below the completed-phaseout income (about $55,768 for two children, non-joint), so a partial credit remains.

blocks.text: Answer: Estimated EITC is about $3,321. In the phaseout band the credit drops 21.06 cents per dollar of income for two-child filers.

Devon, single, paid $9,000 of qualified graduate tuition in 2024. His modified AGI is $85,000. The 2024 LLC phaseout range for single filers is MAGI $80,000 to $90,000. Compute his Lifetime Learning Credit.
Steps

items: Step 1: Tentative LLC = 20% of up to $10,000 of expenses = 20% x $9,000 = $1,800.
Step 2: Phaseout range width = $90,000 - $80,000 = $10,000.
Step 4: Reduction fraction = $5,000 / $10,000 = 0.50 (50% phased out).

blocks.text: Answer: Lifetime Learning Credit is $900 after a 50% phaseout. The LLC is nonrefundable and capped at 20% of the first $10,000 of expenses per return.

topics.title: Required Minimum Distribution Shortfall: Excise Tax (2024)

blocks.text: Ruth, age 75, had a traditional IRA balance of $500,000 on December 31, 2023. Her RMD life-expectancy factor for 2024 is 24.6. She withdrew only $8,000 during 2024. Compute her 2024 RMD, the shortfall, and the SECURE 2.0 excise tax (25%, reduced to 10% if timely corrected).
Steps

items: Step 1: 2024 RMD = prior year-end balance / factor = $500,000 / 24.6 = $20,325.20, round to $20,325.
Step 2: Amount actually taken = $8,000.
Step 4: Standard excise tax = 25% x $12,325 = $3,081.25, round to $3,081.
Step 5: If corrected within the SECURE 2.0 correction window, the rate drops to 10% = $1,232.50, round to $1,233.

blocks.text: Answer: RMD is $20,325; shortfall $12,325. Excise tax is $3,081 (25%) or $1,233 if timely corrected (10%).

topics.title: Qualified Charitable Distribution Reducing Taxable RMD

blocks.text: Frank, age 73, must take a $26,000 RMD from his traditional IRA in 2024. He directs $18,000 of it straight to a qualified charity as a QCD and takes the remaining $8,000 as cash. The 2024 QCD limit is $105,000. How much of the distribution is taxable, and how does this interact with the standard deduction?
Steps

items: Step 1: A QCD counts toward the RMD but is excluded from gross income.
Step 2: QCD portion = $18,000, fully excluded from income.
Step 3: Cash portion taken personally = $8,000, fully taxable as ordinary income.
Step 4: Taxable IRA income = $26,000 RMD - $18,000 QCD = $8,000.
Step 5: The $18,000 is NOT a Schedule A charitable deduction (already excluded), so Frank can still claim the standard deduction.
Step 6: QCD is under the $105,000 cap, so the full exclusion stands.

blocks.text: Answer: Only $8,000 is taxable; the $18,000 QCD is excluded yet satisfies part of the RMD. QCDs benefit standard-deduction filers because income is reduced directly.

topics.title: Charitable Contribution AGI Limits: Cash vs. Appreciated Stock

blocks.text: Theo has AGI of $200,000 in 2024. He donates $130,000 cash to a public charity and long-term appreciated stock worth $50,000 (basis $10,000) to the same public charity. Cash is limited to 60% of AGI; appreciated capital-gain property to 30% of AGI. Compute the deductible amount this year and any carryover.
Steps

items: Step 1: 60% cash limit = 60% x $200,000 = $120,000; cash given $130,000 exceeds this, so cash deduction = $120,000.
Step 2: 30% appreciated-property limit = 30% x $200,000 = $60,000; stock FMV $50,000 is within this limit.

Step 3: But total cannot exceed the overall 50%/60% ceiling; cash already uses $120,000, leaving $80,000 of the $120,000 (60%) overall room... the 30% category is separately capped, and combined deductions cannot exceed 50% of AGI for the non-cash category stacking. Apply ordering: cash first up to 60% = $120,000.

Step 4: Remaining AGI ceiling for the stock = lesser of its 30% limit ($60,000) and overall 50% limit reduced by cash. Since cash already exceeds 50% of AGI ($100,000), no additional room remains this year for the 30% property.
Step 5: Deductible this year = $120,000 cash only; the $50,000 stock is fully carried over.
Step 6: Carryovers (5 years): cash carryover $10,000 and stock carryover $50,000.

blocks.text: Answer: Deduct $120,000 cash this year; carry forward $10,000 cash and $50,000 stock for up to 5 years. Cash donations that hit the 60% ceiling crowd out the 30% appreciated-property category.

topics.title: Qualified Business Income (QBI) Deduction Below the Threshold

blocks.text: A single taxpayer has $90,000 of qualified business income from a sole proprietorship and taxable income (before the QBI deduction) of $130,000, which includes $5,000 of net capital gain. Taxable income is below the 2024 single threshold of $191,950, so no wage/SSTB limits apply. Compute the QBI deduction.
Steps

items: Step 1: Below the threshold, the QBI deduction is 20% of QBI, subject to an overall income cap.
Step 2: Tentative QBI deduction = 20% x $90,000 = $18,000.
Step 3: Overall cap = 20% x (taxable income - net capital gain) = 20% x ($130,000 - $5,000) = 20% x $125,000 = $25,000.
Step 4: QBI deduction = lesser of $18,000 and $25,000 = $18,000.
Step 5: The deduction is taken below the line but does not reduce AGI or self-employment tax.

blocks.text: Answer: QBI deduction is $18,000 (20% of QBI, under the income cap). Below the threshold, no W-2 wage or property limit applies.

A single taxpayer has a net long-term capital loss of $9,000 and a net short-term capital gain of $1,000 for 2024, with no other capital transactions. Compute the deductible capital loss, the amount applied against ordinary income, and the carryover.
Steps

items: Step 1: Net capital result = short-term gain $1,000 - long-term loss $9,000 = net loss of $8,000.
Step 2: Individuals may deduct net capital losses against ordinary income up to $3,000 per year.
Step 3: Deducted against ordinary income in 2024 = $3,000.
Step 4: Remaining loss carried forward = $8,000 - $3,000 = $5,000.
Step 5: The $5,000 carryover retains its long-term character into 2025.

blocks.text: Answer: Deduct $3,000 against ordinary income; carry forward $5,000 (long-term). The annual ordinary-income offset for net capital losses is capped at $3,000 ($1,500 if MFS).

topics.title: Additional Medicare Tax (0.9%) on High Wages (MFJ)

blocks.text: A married couple filing jointly has combined Medicare wages of $300,000 (one spouse $200,000, the other $100,000). The Additional Medicare Tax is 0.9% on wages above the MFJ threshold of $250,000. Compute the Additional Medicare Tax owed on the return.
Steps

items: Step 1: Combined Medicare wages = $200,000 + $100,000 = $300,000.
Step 2: MFJ threshold = $250,000.
Step 3: Wages over threshold = $300,000 - $250,000 = $50,000.
Step 4: Additional Medicare Tax = 0.9% x $50,000 = $450.
Step 5: Employers withhold the 0.9% only on individual wages over $200,000, so reconciliation on Form 8959 may show under- or over-withholding.

blocks.text: Answer: Additional Medicare Tax is $450 (0.9% on $50,000 over the $250,000 MFJ threshold). The threshold is per return, but employer withholding is per individual at $200,000.

A married-filing-jointly couple in 2024 paid $9,200 state income tax, $7,500 real estate property tax, and $1,100 personal property (vehicle) tax. They also paid $14,000 of qualified home mortgage interest and gave $3,000 cash to charity. What is their total itemized deduction?
Steps

items: Step 1: Add all state and local taxes (SALT): $9,200 + $7,500 + $1,100 = $17,800.
Step 2: Apply the SALT cap. For 2024, total SALT is limited to $10,000 (MFJ). The $17,800 is reduced to $10,000.
Step 3: Add the non-SALT itemized items: mortgage interest $14,000 + charity $3,000 = $17,000.
Step 4: Total itemized deductions = $10,000 (capped SALT) + $17,000 = $27,000.
Step 5: Compare to 2024 MFJ standard deduction of $29,200. Itemizing ($27,000) is LESS than the standard deduction.
Step 6: They should claim the standard deduction of $29,200 instead.

blocks.text: Answer: Itemized total is $27,000 after the $10,000 SALT cap, but the $29,200 standard deduction is larger, so they take the standard deduction. Takeaway: the SALT cap can push taxpayers back to the standard deduction.
In 2024 a single taxpayer bought a home with a $900,000 acquisition mortgage. Interest paid for the year totaled $40,500 at an average 4.5% rate. How much mortgage interest is deductible?
Steps

items: Step 1: The 2024 acquisition-debt limit is $750,000 of principal for loans taken after Dec 15, 2017.
Step 2: Find the deductible fraction: $750,000 / $900,000 = 0.8333.
Step 3: Apply the fraction to interest paid: $40,500 x 0.8333 = $33,750.
Step 4: The remaining $40,500 - $33,750 = $6,750 of interest on the excess $150,000 of debt is nondeductible personal interest.
Step 5: Verify: $750,000 x 4.5% = $33,750, matching the deductible amount.

blocks.text: Answer: Deductible mortgage interest is $33,750; $6,750 is nondeductible. Takeaway: interest on acquisition debt above $750,000 is disallowed proportionally.

A taxpayer with 2024 AGI of $100,000 donated $70,000 cash to a public charity (60% AGI limit). In 2025 her AGI is $80,000 and she makes no new gifts. How much can she deduct each year and what carries over?
Steps

items: Step 2: 2024 deduction = $60,000 (the lesser of the $70,000 gift and the $60,000 limit).
Step 4: 2025 cash limit = 60% x $80,000 = $48,000. The $10,000 carryover is well under this.
Step 5: 2025 deduction = $10,000 (full carryover used). Carryovers last up to 5 years.
Step 6: Total deducted over both years = $60,000 + $10,000 = $70,000, the full gift.

blocks.text: Answer: Deduct $60,000 in 2024 and $10,000 in 2025 (carryover). Takeaway: excess charitable gifts carry forward up to 5 years, subject to the AGI limit each year.

topics.title: Medical Expense Deduction Over 7.5% AGI Floor

blocks.text: A taxpayer with AGI of $90,000 had $12,000 of unreimbursed qualified medical expenses in 2024. How much is deductible as an itemized deduction?
Steps

items: Step 1: Compute the AGI floor: 7.5% x $90,000 = $6,750.
Step 2: Deductible medical = qualified expenses minus floor = $12,000 - $6,750 = $5,250.
Step 3: Only expenses above the floor count; the first $6,750 is nondeductible.
Step 4: This $5,250 is added to other itemized deductions on Schedule A.
Step 5: Compare total itemized to the standard deduction before deciding to itemize.

blocks.text: Answer: Deductible medical expenses are $5,250. Takeaway: only the portion of medical costs exceeding 7.5% of AGI is deductible.

A degree candidate received a $30,000 scholarship in 2024. She paid $18,000 for tuition and required fees and $4,000 for required books. The remaining scholarship was used for room and board ($8,000). How much of the scholarship is taxable?
Steps

items: Step 1: Identify qualified education expenses that make scholarship amounts tax-free: tuition, required fees, and required course materials (books/supplies).
Step 2: Add qualified expenses: tuition/fees $18,000 + required books $4,000 = $22,000.
Step 3: The portion of the scholarship up to qualified expenses is tax-free: $22,000 is excluded.
Step 4: The remainder used for room and board is taxable: $30,000 - $22,000 = $8,000.
Step 5: Room and board are NOT qualified education expenses, so the $8,000 must be reported as taxable income (on the wages line, noted 'SCH').
Step 6: Confirm: tax-free $22,000 + taxable $8,000 = $30,000 total scholarship.

blocks.text: Answer: $8,000 of the scholarship is taxable (the room-and-board portion); $22,000 is tax-free. Takeaway: scholarships are tax-free only to the extent used for tuition, required fees, and required course materials.

topics.title: Cancellation of Debt Income With Insolvency Exclusion

blocks.text: A taxpayer had a $40,000 credit card balance settled for $15,000 in 2024, generating a Form 1099-C for the forgiven amount. Immediately before the cancellation, the taxpayer's total liabilities were $120,000 and the fair market value of total assets was $95,000. How much cancellation of debt (COD) income is taxable?
Steps

items: Step 1: Compute the forgiven (cancelled) debt: $40,000 owed - $15,000 paid = $25,000 of COD income reported on the 1099-C.
Step 2: Measure insolvency immediately before cancellation: liabilities $120,000 - asset FMV $95,000 = $25,000 insolvent.
Step 3: The insolvency exclusion lets the taxpayer exclude COD income up to the amount of insolvency.
Step 4: Excludable amount = lesser of COD ($25,000) or insolvency ($25,000) = $25,000.
Step 5: Taxable COD income = $25,000 COD - $25,000 excluded = $0.
Step 6: Note: the taxpayer must reduce tax attributes (e.g., NOLs, basis) by the excluded amount on Form 982.

blocks.text: Answer: $0 of the $25,000 COD is taxable because the taxpayer was insolvent by $25,000. Takeaway: the insolvency exclusion (Form 982) shelters COD income only up to the extent of insolvency, with required attribute reduction.

topics.title: Gambling Winnings and Loss Deduction Limit

blocks.text: A casual (non-professional) gambler won $12,000 at the casino in 2024 and has documented losses of $15,000 for the year. The taxpayer itemizes deductions. How are these reported and what is the net tax effect?
Steps

items: Step 1: Report all gambling winnings as 'other income': $12,000 is included in gross income (cannot be netted against losses on the income side).
Step 2: Gambling losses are deductible only as an itemized deduction (not subject to the 2% floor) and only up to the amount of winnings.
Step 3: Deductible loss = lesser of actual losses ($15,000) or winnings ($12,000) = $12,000.
Step 4: The excess $15,000 - $12,000 = $3,000 of losses is disallowed and does NOT carry over.
Step 5: Net income effect: $12,000 winnings included, $12,000 loss deducted (only if itemizing) = $0 net taxable gambling income for an itemizer.
Step 6: If the taxpayer took the standard deduction instead, the full $12,000 of winnings would be taxed with no offset for losses.

blocks.text: Answer: The taxpayer reports $12,000 of winnings and may deduct $12,000 of losses (capped at winnings) only if itemizing; $3,000 of losses is lost. Takeaway: gambling losses are capped at winnings, never create a net loss, and require itemizing.
Hal, single, received $24,000 of Social Security benefits. His other income is $30,000 of taxable pension and interest, plus $2,000 of tax-exempt interest. How much of his benefits is taxable?
Steps

items: Step 1: Provisional income = $30,000 + $2,000 + one-half of benefits ($12,000) = $44,000.
Step 2: Base amounts for single filers are $25,000 and $34,000, so provisional income exceeds both.
Step 3: Amount between the two bases: 50% × ($34,000 − $25,000) = $4,500 (lesser of that or 50% of benefits).

blocks.text: Answer: $13,000 of Hal's benefits is taxable. Tax-exempt interest increases provisional income but is not itself taxed.

topics.title: Home Sale Exclusion with Selling Costs

blocks.text: Ben, single, sells his main home of six years for $520,000. Selling costs are $30,000 and his adjusted basis is $200,000. He has not used the exclusion in the past two years. What gain is taxable?
Steps

Step 5: The $40,000 is long-term capital gain reported on Form 8949 and Schedule D.

blocks.text: Answer: $40,000 of long-term capital gain is taxable. A married couple filing jointly with the same facts would exclude up to $500,000 and owe nothing.

An investor exchanges rental land (adjusted basis $300,000, FMV $500,000) for other investment land worth $450,000 plus $50,000 cash. Find realized gain, recognized gain, and the basis of the new land.
Steps

items: Step 3: Recognized gain is limited to boot received = $50,000.
Step 4: New basis = old basis $300,000 + gain recognized $50,000 − boot received $50,000 = $300,000.
Step 5: Deferred gain = $200,000 − $50,000 = $150,000, which is preserved in the lower basis.

blocks.text: Answer: Recognized gain is $50,000 and the new land's basis is $300,000. Report on Form 8824.
A taxpayer sells land for $300,000. Her adjusted basis is $180,000. She receives $60,000 in the year of sale and the rest in later years. What gain is reported in the year of sale?
Steps

items: Step 2: Gross profit percentage = $120,000 ÷ $300,000 = 40%.
Step 3: Gain in the year of sale = 40% × $60,000 payment = $24,000.
Step 4: Each later payment is multiplied by 40% to find the gain recognized.
Step 5: Interest on the note is reported separately as ordinary income; use Form 6252.

blocks.text: Answer: $24,000 of gain is reported in the year of sale. If depreciation recapture existed it would be recognized in the year of sale regardless.
An investor buys 100 shares at $50 ($5,000) and sells them at $40 ($4,000). Twelve days later she buys 100 shares of the same stock for $42 each ($4,200). What happens to the $1,000 loss?
Steps

items: Step 1: The repurchase occurred within 30 days after the sale, so the wash sale rule applies.
Step 2: The $1,000 loss is disallowed in the current year.
Step 3: The disallowed loss is added to the basis of the new shares: $4,200 + $1,000 = $5,200.
Step 4: The holding period of the old shares tacks onto the new shares.
Step 5: When the new shares are sold, the larger basis reduces gain or increases loss.

blocks.text: Answer: No loss is deductible now. The new shares have a basis of $5,200, preserving the $1,000 loss for later.

In 2024 Dana has the following sales: a long-term gain of $9,000, a long-term loss of $3,000, a short-term gain of $2,000, and a short-term loss of $7,000. Determine the net capital gain or loss and its character.
Steps

items: Step 1: Net long-term: $9,000 gain - $3,000 loss = $6,000 net long-term gain.
Step 2: Net short-term: $2,000 gain - $7,000 loss = $5,000 net short-term loss.
Step 3: Combine the two net figures: $6,000 LT gain - $5,000 ST loss = $1,000 net gain.
Step 4: Because the surviving net amount came from the long-term column, the $1,000 is a net long-term capital gain.
Step 5: The $1,000 net long-term gain is taxed at preferential capital gains rates.

blocks.text: Answer: Net long-term capital gain of $1,000. Net short-term losses offset long-term gains, and the surviving character is long-term.
Single taxpayer Raj has a net capital loss of $9,500 for 2024 and no capital gains. How much can he deduct against ordinary income this year, and what carries forward?
Steps

items: Step 1: The annual capital loss deduction limit against ordinary income is $3,000 (single or MFJ).
Step 2: Deduct $3,000 of the $9,500 loss on the 2024 return.
Step 4: The $6,500 retains its long-term or short-term character and carries to 2025.
Step 5: In 2025 he again deducts up to $3,000 (or offsets future gains) until the carryover is used up.

blocks.text: Answer: Deduct $3,000 in 2024 and carry $6,500 forward. The $3,000 ordinary-income limit forces multi-year use of large net losses.

A married couple filing jointly sells their main home for $850,000. Their adjusted basis is $400,000, and selling expenses are $50,000. They owned and used the home as their principal residence for the last 5 years. How much gain is taxable?
Steps
