items: Step 1: Amount realized = $850,000 - $50,000 selling expenses = $800,000.
Step 2: Realized gain = $800,000 - $400,000 basis = $400,000.
Step 3: They meet the 2-of-5-year ownership and use tests, so the MFJ exclusion is $500,000.
Step 4: Excludable gain = lesser of $400,000 gain or $500,000 cap = $400,000.

blocks.text: Answer: Taxable gain is $0. The full $400,000 gain fits under the $500,000 MFJ Section 121 exclusion.

topics.title: Wash Sale Disallowed Loss and Replacement Basis

blocks.text: Owen sells 100 shares of XYZ for $4,000 (basis $7,000), realizing a $3,000 loss. Eleven days later he buys 100 replacement XYZ shares for $4,500. Determine the deductible loss and the basis of the new shares.
Steps

items: Step 1: Loss realized = $4,000 proceeds - $7,000 basis = -$3,000.
Step 2: Replacement purchase within 30 days (11 days) triggers the wash-sale rule.
Step 3: The $3,000 loss is fully disallowed for current deduction.
Step 4: Disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement shares: $4,500 + $3,000 = $7,500.
Step 5: The holding period of the old shares tacks onto the new shares.
Step 6: Net effect: no current deduction, but the loss is preserved in the higher $7,500 basis.

blocks.text: Answer: Deductible loss is $0; replacement shares' basis is $7,500. Wash-sale losses are deferred into the new shares' basis, not lost permanently.

topics.title: Qualified Dividends and Capital Gains Stacking

blocks.text: A single taxpayer has $50,000 of ordinary taxable income and $20,000 of qualified dividends, for $70,000 total taxable income (2024). The 0% LTCG bracket for singles ends at $47,025 and the 15% bracket applies above that. Compute the tax on the qualified dividends.
Steps

items: Step 1: Qualified dividends stack on top of ordinary income for rate purposes.
Step 2: Ordinary income of $50,000 already fills the 0% LTCG bracket (which ends at $47,025).
Step 3: Because ordinary income exceeds $47,025, none of the dividends fall in the 0% band.
Step 4: The full $20,000 of qualified dividends falls in the 15% LTCG bracket (under the $518,900 top for 2024).
Step 5: Tax on dividends = 15% x $20,000 = $3,000.
Step 6: The ordinary income is taxed separately at ordinary rates.

blocks.text: Answer: Tax on the qualified dividends is $3,000 (all at 15%). Ordinary income is stacked first, so it can fully consume the 0% capital-gains bracket.

Single taxpayer Owen bought his home in March 2024 and sold it in September 2024 after only 18 months... actually he owned and lived in it 15 months before a qualifying job relocation 400 miles away forced the sale. His gain is $190,000. He had no prior exclusion. Compute his maximum excludable gain.
Steps

items: Step 1: Full single exclusion is $250,000, but it requires 2 of the last 5 years of ownership and use; Owen has only 15 months.
Step 2: A change-of-employment relocation (>50 miles farther) qualifies for a reduced exclusion based on time.
Step 3: Reduced-exclusion fraction = months used / 24 = 15 / 24 = 0.625.
Step 4: Maximum reduced exclusion = $250,000 x 0.625 = $156,250.
Step 5: Gain of $190,000 exceeds the $156,250 limit.
Step 6: Taxable gain = $190,000 - $156,250 = $33,750 (long-term capital gain).

blocks.text: Answer: Owen excludes $156,250 and reports $33,750 of taxable gain. The reduced exclusion prorates the cap by months over 24, not the actual gain.

A sole proprietor places $50,000 of 5-year MACRS property in service in 2024 with no Section 179 or bonus depreciation elected. The half-year convention applies. The 5-year MACRS percentages are 20.00%, 32.00%, 19.20%, 11.52%, 11.52%, 5.76%. Build the depreciation for years 1 through 3 and state total depreciation taken by end of year 3.
Steps

items: Step 1: Year 1 depreciation = 20.00% x $50,000 = $10,000.
Step 2: Year 2 depreciation = 32.00% x $50,000 = $16,000.
Step 3: Year 3 depreciation = 19.20% x $50,000 = $9,600.
Step 4: Cumulative through year 3 = $10,000 + $16,000 + $9,600 = $35,600.
Step 5: Remaining basis after year 3 = $50,000 - $35,600 = $14,400 (to be recovered in years 4-6).

blocks.text: Answer: Year 1 $10,000, year 2 $16,000, year 3 $9,600; cumulative $35,600 with $14,400 of basis remaining. 5-year MACRS uses 200% declining balance with a half-year convention.

topics.title: Section 179 Expensing Limited by Business Taxable Income

blocks.text: A sole proprietor buys $90,000 of qualifying equipment in 2024 (well under the $1,220,000 limit and $3,050,000 phaseout). Before any Section 179 deduction, the business has taxable income of $52,000. The owner elects to expense the full $90,000 under Section 179. How much is deductible in 2024?
Steps

items: Step 1: Section 179 cannot exceed the aggregate taxable income from the active conduct of the business.
Step 2: Business taxable income limit = $52,000.
Step 3: Elected Section 179 = $90,000, but it is capped at $52,000 for 2024.
Step 4: Allowed 2024 Section 179 deduction = $52,000.
Step 5: Disallowed amount carried forward = $90,000 - $52,000 = $38,000, available in future years subject to the income limit.

blocks.text: Answer: Only $52,000 is deductible in 2024; $38,000 carries forward. Section 179 cannot create or increase a business loss.

topics.title: Like-Kind Exchange with Boot: Recognized Gain and New Basis

blocks.text: An investor exchanges real property (used in business) with an adjusted basis of $80,000 and FMV of $130,000 for like-kind real property worth $110,000 plus $20,000 cash boot. Compute the realized gain, recognized gain, and basis of the replacement property under Section 1031.
Steps

items: Step 1: Realized gain = FMV received ($110,000 property + $20,000 cash) - adjusted basis $80,000 = $130,000 - $80,000 = $50,000.
Step 2: Recognized gain = lesser of realized gain ($50,000) and boot received ($20,000) = $20,000.
Step 4: Basis of replacement property = adjusted basis of old property + gain recognized - boot received = $80,000 + $20,000 - $20,000 = $80,000.
Step 5: Check: replacement FMV $110,000 - deferred gain $30,000 = $80,000, matching the computed basis.

blocks.text: Answer: Recognized gain is $20,000 (the boot) and replacement-property basis is $80,000. Boot triggers gain recognition up to the lesser of boot or realized gain; the rest is deferred.

topics.title: Section 1245 Depreciation Recapture on Equipment Sale

blocks.text: A business sells machinery for $45,000. Its original cost was $60,000 and accumulated depreciation taken was $40,000 (adjusted basis $20,000). Compute the total gain, the ordinary-income recapture under Section 1245, and any Section 1231 gain.
Steps

items: Step 1: Adjusted basis = cost $60,000 - depreciation $40,000 = $20,000.
Step 2: Total gain = sale price $45,000 - adjusted basis $20,000 = $25,000.
Step 3: Section 1245 recapture = lesser of total gain ($25,000) or depreciation taken ($40,000) = $25,000.
Step 4: Because the entire gain is within depreciation taken, all $25,000 is ordinary income.
Step 5: Section 1231 gain = total gain - recapture = $25,000 - $25,000 = $0 (sale price did not exceed original cost).

blocks.text: Answer: All $25,000 of gain is ordinary income (Section 1245 recapture); no Section 1231 gain. Recapture is the lesser of gain or prior depreciation.

topics.title: EITC With Two Qualifying Children in the Phaseout Range

blocks.text: A single parent with two qualifying children has 2024 earned income and AGI both equal to $40,000. The 2-child EITC parameters for 2024 are: maximum credit $6,960, phaseout begins at $22,720 (single), and phaseout rate 21.06%. Estimate the EITC.
Steps

items: Step 1: Income $40,000 exceeds the phaseout start of $22,720, so the credit is reduced from the maximum.
Step 2: Excess over threshold = $40,000 - $22,720 = $17,280.
Step 3: Phaseout reduction = $17,280 x 21.06% = $3,639.17, round to $3,639.
Step 5: Confirm income is below the complete-phaseout point ($55,768 for 2-child single), so a partial credit remains.

blocks.text: Answer: Estimated EITC is about $3,321. Takeaway: in the phaseout range, the credit drops by 21.06 cents per extra dollar of the greater of earned income or AGI.

topics.title: Child and Dependent Care Credit With Two Earners

blocks.text: A married couple paid $9,000 for daycare for their two children under 13 in 2024. Spouse A earned $60,000; Spouse B earned $5,500. Their AGI is $65,500, giving a 20% credit rate. What is the credit?
Steps

items: Step 1: Expense cap for two or more qualifying persons is $6,000. The $9,000 paid exceeds this, so start with $6,000.
Step 2: Apply the earned-income limit: eligible expenses cannot exceed the LOWER earner's earned income. Spouse B earned $5,500.
Step 3: Limited expenses = lesser of $6,000 (cap) and $5,500 (lower earner) = $5,500.
Step 4: Apply the AGI-based credit rate. At AGI over $43,000 the rate floors at 20%.

blocks.text: Answer: The child and dependent care credit is $1,100. Takeaway: eligible expenses are capped at the lower-earning spouse's earned income, not just the $6,000 dollar limit.

A married couple has three qualifying children under 17 and 2024 earned income of $30,000. Their tax liability is $0, so none of the $6,000 Child Tax Credit ($2,000 x 3) can offset tax. How much refundable Additional Child Tax Credit can they receive?
Steps

items: Step 1: The refundable ACTC is the lesser of (a) the unused CTC, or (b) 15% of earned income over $2,500, capped at $1,700 per child for 2024.
Step 4: Per-child cap = $1,700 x 3 children = $5,100.
Step 5: Refundable ACTC = lesser of $4,125 and $5,100 = $4,125 (the unused CTC of $6,000 is larger still).

blocks.text: Answer: They receive $4,125 as a refundable ACTC. Takeaway: with no tax liability, the refundable portion is limited to 15% of earned income above $2,500, up to $1,700 per child.

A single taxpayer paid $2,800 of qualified student loan interest in 2024. Her MAGI (before this deduction) is $82,500. The 2024 single phaseout range is $80,000 to $95,000. What is her deductible student loan interest?
Steps

items: Step 1: Cap the interest at the statutory maximum of $2,500. Although she paid $2,800, only $2,500 is potentially deductible.
Step 2: Determine the phaseout. For single filers in 2024, the deduction phases out ratably over MAGI from $80,000 to $95,000 (a $15,000 range).
Step 3: Compute excess MAGI over the floor: $82,500 - $80,000 = $2,500.
Step 5: Reduction = $2,500 x 0.16667 = $417 (rounded).
Step 6: Deductible interest = $2,500 - $417 = $2,083.

blocks.text: Answer: She may deduct $2,083 of student loan interest as an above-the-line adjustment. Takeaway: the $2,500 cap applies first, then a ratable phaseout over the $80,000-$95,000 single MAGI range for 2024.

topics.title: Educator Expense and HSA Above-the-Line Adjustments (2024)

blocks.text: A married couple files jointly for 2024. Both spouses are eligible K-12 educators who each spent $400 on classroom supplies. One spouse also made a $4,000 contribution to a self-only HSA (the 2024 self-only HSA limit is $4,150; she is under 55). What are their total above-the-line adjustments from these items?
Steps

items: Step 1: Apply the educator expense deduction. The 2024 limit is $300 per eligible educator. Each spouse spent $400 but is capped at $300.
Step 2: Two eligible educators: $300 + $300 = $600 educator expense deduction.
Step 3: Apply the HSA deduction. The 2024 self-only limit is $4,150; she contributed $4,000, which is below the limit, so the full $4,000 is deductible.
Step 4: Confirm the HSA contribution does not exceed the limit: $4,000 < $4,150, fully allowed.
Step 5: Total above-the-line adjustments = educator $600 + HSA $4,000 = $4,600.
Step 6: These reduce AGI directly and are available whether or not the couple itemizes.

blocks.text: Answer: Total above-the-line adjustments are $4,600 ($600 educator + $4,000 HSA). Takeaway: the educator deduction is capped at $300 per educator (so $600 for two), and HSA contributions are deductible up to the annual limit regardless of itemizing.
Lena, single, bought a new U.S.-assembled car in 2025 with a loan secured by the car and paid $4,500 of interest. Her MAGI is $110,000. What is her deduction?
Steps

items: Step 1: The annual cap is $10,000, which the $4,500 does not exceed.
Step 2: The phase-out begins above $100,000 of MAGI for single filers.
Step 3: Excess MAGI = $110,000 − $100,000 = $10,000, or 10 increments of $1,000.
Step 4: Reduction = 10 × $200 = $2,000.

blocks.text: Answer: Lena deducts $2,500. The loan must have been originated after 2024, the vehicle must be new, and she must report the VIN.
A married couple filing jointly has MAGI of $540,000 for 2025 and paid $45,000 of state income and property taxes. They itemize. What is the maximum state and local tax deduction?
Steps

items: Step 1: The 2025 SALT cap is $40,000 for a joint return.
Step 2: The cap phases down for MAGI above $500,000, by 30% of the excess.
Step 5: Reduced cap = $40,000 − $12,000 = $28,000, which is above the $10,000 floor.

blocks.text: Answer: The couple can deduct $28,000 of the $45,000 paid. The cap cannot fall below $10,000.

topics.title: QBI Deduction Below the Income Threshold

blocks.text: A single sole proprietor has qualified business income of $60,000 and taxable income before the QBI deduction of $100,000, of which $0 is net capital gain. What is her QBI deduction?
Steps

items: Step 1: Taxable income is below the threshold where wage and property limits and the SSTB rules apply, so only the general limit is needed.
Step 3: Taxable income limit = 20% × ($100,000 − $0 net capital gain) = $20,000.
Step 4: The deduction is the lesser of $12,000 and $20,000.
Step 5: Report on Form 8995.

blocks.text: Answer: Her QBI deduction is $12,000. It reduces taxable income but not AGI or self-employment tax.
A married couple, both working, has AGI of $60,000 and pays $7,000 for care of their two children under 13. Both spouses earned more than $6,000. What is the credit for 2025?
Steps

items: Step 1: The expense limit for two or more qualifying persons is $6,000, so $7,000 is capped at $6,000.
Step 2: The credit percentage is 35% at AGI of $15,000 or less and falls by one point for each $2,000 of AGI over $15,000, to a floor of 20% for AGI above $43,000.
Step 3: At AGI of $60,000 the percentage is 20%.
Step 5: Report on Form 2441; employer-provided dependent care benefits would reduce the limit.

blocks.text: Answer: The credit is $1,200. The credit is nonrefundable.
A first-year student's qualified tuition and required fees are $3,500. The parents' MAGI is below the phase-out. Compute the credit and the refundable portion.
Steps

items: Step 1: AOTC = 100% of the first $2,000 of expenses = $2,000.
Step 2: Plus 25% of the next $2,000: expenses remaining are $1,500, so 25% × $1,500 = $375.
Step 3: Total credit = $2,000 + $375 = $2,375.
Step 4: 40% of the credit is refundable = 0.40 × $2,375 = $950.
Step 5: The remaining $1,425 is nonrefundable and limited by tax liability.

blocks.text: Answer: The credit is $2,375, of which $950 is refundable. Form 8863 and the student's Form 1098-T are required.

topics.title: Adjusted Basis of a Personal Residence

blocks.text: Tom bought a home for $260,000. He added a $30,000 finished basement and a $12,000 new roof, and received a $5,000 insurance reimbursement for storm damage he did not repair structurally. He also deducted $0 depreciation (personal use). Compute his adjusted basis.
Steps

items: Step 1: Start with original cost basis = $260,000.
Step 2: Add capital improvements: $30,000 basement + $12,000 roof = $42,000.
Step 3: Basis after improvements = $260,000 + $42,000 = $302,000.
Step 4: Subtract the $5,000 insurance reimbursement (a return of basis for the casualty): $302,000 - $5,000 = $297,000.
Step 5: No depreciation applies to a personal residence, so adjusted basis = $297,000.

blocks.text: Answer: Adjusted basis is $297,000. Capital improvements increase basis; reimbursements for unrepaired casualty losses decrease it.

A taxpayer inherits stock from a parent who died in 2024. The parent's original cost was $20,000, and the fair market value on the date of death was $75,000. The heir sells the stock 8 months later for $80,000. Compute the heir's basis, gain, and holding period character.
Steps

items: Step 1: Inherited property generally takes a basis equal to FMV at date of death: $75,000.
Step 2: The decedent's original $20,000 cost is irrelevant for the heir's basis.
Step 3: Gain on sale = $80,000 sale price - $75,000 stepped-up basis = $5,000.
Step 4: Inherited property is automatically treated as long-term regardless of how long the heir holds it.
Step 5: The $5,000 gain is therefore a long-term capital gain.

blocks.text: Answer: Basis is $75,000 (stepped up), and the $5,000 gain is long-term. Inherited property gets a date-of-death FMV basis and automatic long-term treatment.

topics.title: Section 1031 Like-Kind Exchange With Boot Received

blocks.text: Diego exchanges rental land with an adjusted basis of $120,000 and FMV of $200,000 for replacement land worth $170,000 plus $30,000 cash (boot). Compute realized gain, recognized gain, and the basis of the new land.
Steps

items: Step 1: Amount realized = $170,000 (new land) + $30,000 (cash) = $200,000.
Step 2: Realized gain = $200,000 - $120,000 basis = $80,000.
Step 3: Recognized gain = lesser of realized gain ($80,000) or boot received ($30,000) = $30,000.
Step 5: Basis of new land = old basis + gain recognized - boot received = $120,000 + $30,000 - $30,000 = $120,000.
Step 6: Check: FMV of new land $170,000 - deferred gain $50,000 = $120,000, confirming the substituted basis.

blocks.text: Answer: Realized gain $80,000; recognized gain $30,000 (limited to boot); new-land basis $120,000. Boot received triggers gain only up to the cash, and the rest defers into a carryover basis.

topics.title: Installment Sale Gross Profit Percentage and Annual Gain

blocks.text: Maya sells investment land for $250,000. Her adjusted basis is $150,000 and selling expenses are $10,000. The buyer pays $50,000 down in the year of sale and the balance over later years. Compute the gross profit percentage and the gain reported in the year of sale.
Steps

items: Step 1: Contract price = $250,000 (no mortgage assumed).
Step 2: Gross profit = selling price - (basis + selling expenses) = $250,000 - ($150,000 + $10,000) = $90,000.
Step 3: Gross profit percentage = $90,000 / $250,000 = 36%.
Step 4: Payments received in year of sale = $50,000 down payment.
Step 5: Gain recognized year of sale = 36% x $50,000 = $18,000.
Step 6: The remaining deferred gross profit = $90,000 - $18,000 = $72,000, recognized at 36% as later principal payments are collected.

blocks.text: Answer: Gross profit percentage is 36% and year-of-sale gain is $18,000. Each principal dollar collected carries 36 cents of taxable gain.

topics.title: Section 1245 Depreciation Recapture on Equipment Sale

blocks.text: A business sells a machine for $42,000. It was bought for $50,000 and $35,000 of MACRS depreciation has been taken, leaving an adjusted basis of $15,000. Determine the total gain and how much is ordinary income under Section 1245 versus Section 1231 gain.
Steps

items: Step 1: Adjusted basis = $50,000 cost - $35,000 depreciation = $15,000.
Step 2: Total gain = $42,000 sale price - $15,000 basis = $27,000.
Step 3: Section 1245 recapture = lesser of total gain ($27,000) or depreciation taken ($35,000) = $27,000.
Step 4: Because the gain does not exceed depreciation taken, the entire $27,000 is ordinary income.
Step 5: Section 1231 gain = total gain - ordinary recapture = $27,000 - $27,000 = $0.
Step 6: Result: all $27,000 of gain is taxed as ordinary income; none is favorable Section 1231 gain.

blocks.text: Answer: All $27,000 of gain is ordinary under Section 1245. When the sale price stays below original cost, gain is recaptured as ordinary up to the depreciation taken.

topics.title: Unrecaptured Section 1250 Gain on Rental Building

blocks.text: An investor sells a rental building for a $90,000 gain. Straight-line depreciation of $60,000 was claimed (no excess accelerated depreciation). Determine the unrecaptured Section 1250 gain (25% rate) versus the long-term capital gain taxed at regular LTCG rates.
Steps

items: Step 1: Real property depreciated straight-line has no Section 1250 ordinary recapture (excess over straight-line = $0).
Step 2: However, gain attributable to straight-line depreciation is 'unrecaptured Section 1250 gain,' taxed at a maximum 25%.
Step 3: Unrecaptured 1250 gain = lesser of depreciation taken ($60,000) or total gain ($90,000) = $60,000.
Step 4: Remaining gain = $90,000 - $60,000 = $30,000, taxed at regular long-term capital gains rates (0/15/20%).
Step 5: So $60,000 is taxed up to 25% and $30,000 at the normal LTCG rate.
Step 6: No portion is ordinary income because all depreciation was straight-line.

blocks.text: Answer: $60,000 is unrecaptured Section 1250 gain (max 25%) and $30,000 is regular LTCG. Straight-line real-estate depreciation creates a 25%-rate layer, not ordinary recapture.

topics.title: MACRS Plus Section 179 and Bonus Depreciation (2024)

blocks.text: A calendar-year business places $80,000 of 5-year MACRS equipment in service in 2024 (mid-year, not last quarter). It elects $30,000 of Section 179, then 60% bonus depreciation (2024 rate) on the remainder, then regular MACRS on what is left (Year-1 5-year rate 20%). Compute total first-year depreciation.
Steps

items: Step 1: Apply Section 179 first: $30,000. Remaining basis = $80,000 - $30,000 = $50,000.
Step 2: Apply 2024 bonus depreciation of 60% to the $50,000: 60% x $50,000 = $30,000. Remaining basis = $50,000 - $30,000 = $20,000.
Step 3: Apply regular MACRS Year-1 (half-year, 5-year property, 20%): 20% x $20,000 = $4,000.
Step 4: Total first-year deduction = $30,000 + $30,000 + $4,000 = $64,000.
Step 5: Remaining depreciable basis carried to later years = $20,000 - $4,000 = $16,000.
Step 6: Order matters: Section 179, then bonus, then MACRS on the residual.

blocks.text: Answer: First-year depreciation is $64,000. The stacking order is Section 179, then 60% bonus (2024), then MACRS on the residual basis.

topics.title: Section 121 Home-Sale Exclusion With Nonqualified Use

blocks.text: A single taxpayer sells a home for a $400,000 gain. They owned it 10 years but rented it out (nonqualified use) for 2 of those years before living in it for the remaining 8 years. The Section 121 exclusion is $250,000 (single). Compute the taxable gain after allocating for nonqualified use (ignore depreciation recapture).
Steps

items: Step 1: Nonqualified-use fraction = years of nonqualified use / total years owned = 2 / 10 = 20%.
Step 2: Gain allocated to nonqualified use (not excludable) = 20% x $400,000 = $80,000.
Step 3: Gain eligible for exclusion = $400,000 - $80,000 = $320,000.
Step 4: Apply the $250,000 single exclusion to the eligible gain: $320,000 - $250,000 = $70,000 still taxable.
Step 5: Total taxable gain = nonqualified-use gain $80,000 + remaining $70,000 = $150,000.
Step 6: Result: $250,000 excluded, $150,000 taxable as capital gain.

blocks.text: Answer: Taxable gain is $150,000. Gain allocable to nonqualified (rental) periods cannot be excluded under Section 121, even within the ownership window.

A business has a net Section 1231 gain of $40,000 this year. In the prior five years it deducted nonrecaptured net Section 1231 losses of $15,000 (all from two years ago, not yet recaptured). Determine how much of the current gain is ordinary versus long-term capital gain.
Steps

items: Step 1: Net Section 1231 gain this year = $40,000, which would normally be long-term capital gain.
Step 2: The 5-year lookback requires recapturing prior unrecaptured net 1231 losses as ordinary income.
Step 3: Nonrecaptured net 1231 losses available = $15,000.
Step 4: Ordinary income (recaptured) = lesser of current gain ($40,000) or prior losses ($15,000) = $15,000.
Step 5: Remaining gain = $40,000 - $15,000 = $25,000, treated as long-term capital gain.
Step 6: Result: $15,000 ordinary income and $25,000 long-term capital gain.

blocks.text: Answer: $15,000 is ordinary income and $25,000 is long-term capital gain. The 5-year lookback recharacterizes current 1231 gain as ordinary up to recent unrecaptured 1231 losses.

topics.title: Rental Loss Limited by the $25,000 Active Participation Allowance

blocks.text: Dana actively participates in a residential rental she owns 100%. In 2024 the rental produces a $32,000 tax loss. Dana's modified AGI before the rental loss is $128,000, all from wages. She has no other passive activities. How much rental loss can she deduct in 2024?
Steps

items: Step 1: Rental real estate is passive, but active participants may deduct up to $25,000 of loss against nonpassive income (special allowance).
Step 2: The $25,000 allowance phases out at 50 cents per dollar of MAGI over $100,000, fully gone at $150,000.
Step 4: Phaseout reduction = 50% x $28,000 = $14,000.
Step 5: Allowance remaining = $25,000 - $14,000 = $11,000.
Step 6: Deductible loss = lesser of actual loss ($32,000) and allowance ($11,000) = $11,000.
Step 7: Suspended (carryover) passive loss = $32,000 - $11,000 = $21,000, carried to 2025.

blocks.text: Answer: Dana deducts $11,000 in 2024 and carries $21,000 forward. The $25,000 allowance shrinks $0.50 per dollar of MAGI above $100,000.

Priya is self-employed and uses a 240-square-foot room exclusively as her principal place of business; her home is 1,600 square feet. For 2024 she paid $14,000 mortgage interest, $3,000 real estate tax, $2,400 utilities, $1,200 homeowner's insurance, and $800 repairs to the office only. Her Schedule C net income before the home-office deduction is $9,500. Compute the home office deduction.
Steps

items: Step 1: Business-use percentage = 240 / 1,600 = 15%.
Step 2: Indirect expenses (whole home) = $14,000 + $3,000 + $2,400 + $1,200 = $20,600; allocated portion = 15% x $20,600 = $3,090.
Step 3: Direct expense (office only repairs) = $800 (100% deductible).
Step 4: Tentative home-office deduction = $3,090 + $800 = $3,890.
Step 5: The deduction cannot exceed gross income from the business use ($9,500 here), so the full $3,890 is allowed.
Step 6: Net Schedule C profit after home office = $9,500 - $3,890 = $5,610.

blocks.text: Answer: Home office deduction is $3,890. Indirect costs are allocated by the 15% business-use percentage; direct office repairs are fully deductible.

topics.title: Vehicle Deduction: Actual Cost vs. Standard Mileage (2024)

blocks.text: Marco drove his car 18,000 total miles in 2024, of which 12,600 were for his sole proprietorship (70% business use). Actual costs for the year were $9,200 (gas, repairs, insurance, plus $4,000 depreciation). The 2024 standard mileage rate is 67 cents per mile. Which method gives the larger deduction?
Steps

items: Step 1: Standard mileage method = 12,600 business miles x $0.67 = $8,442.
Step 2: Actual cost method = total actual costs x business-use % = $9,200 x 70% = $6,440.
Step 3: Compare: standard mileage $8,442 vs. actual $6,440.
Step 4: Standard mileage yields the larger deduction by $8,442 - $6,440 = $2,002.
Step 5: Note: to use standard mileage Marco must have chosen it in the car's first business year; switching from actual (with accelerated depreciation) back to standard is restricted.

blocks.text: Answer: Standard mileage gives $8,442 vs. $6,440 actual, a $2,002 advantage. Always compute both when eligible.

Bianca has $120,000 of net Schedule C profit in 2024 and no wages from any employer. The 2024 Social Security wage base is $168,600; the SE tax rates are 12.4% (OASDI) and 2.9% (Medicare). Compute her self-employment tax and the deductible half.
Steps

items: Step 1: Net earnings from SE = 92.35% x $120,000 = $110,820.
Step 2: OASDI portion = 12.4% x $110,820 (below the $168,600 base) = $13,741.68.
Step 3: Medicare portion = 2.9% x $110,820 = $3,213.78.
Step 5: Deductible half (above-the-line) = $16,955 / 2 = $8,478 (rounded).

blocks.text: Answer: SE tax is about $16,955, with roughly $8,478 deductible as an adjustment to income. Net earnings are first reduced to 92.35% of profit.

topics.title: Net Operating Loss 80% Limitation With Carryforward

blocks.text: An individual has a $120,000 NOL carryforward from 2023 (post-2017 NOL). In 2024 taxable income before the NOL deduction is $100,000. How much NOL can be used in 2024 and what carries forward?
Steps

items: Step 1: Post-2017 NOLs are limited to 80% of taxable income computed before the NOL deduction.
Step 3: NOL deduction allowed in 2024 = lesser of available $120,000 and the $80,000 limit = $80,000.
Step 4: 2024 taxable income after NOL = $100,000 - $80,000 = $20,000.
Step 5: Remaining NOL carryforward = $120,000 - $80,000 = $40,000, carried forward indefinitely.

blocks.text: Answer: Use $80,000 of the NOL in 2024 (leaving $20,000 taxable); $40,000 carries forward. Takeaway: post-2017 NOLs cannot offset more than 80% of taxable income.

A married couple finalized a domestic adoption in 2024 and paid $20,000 of qualified adoption expenses. The 2024 maximum adoption credit is $16,810, and the phaseout range begins at MAGI of $252,150 and ends at $292,150. Their MAGI is $262,150. What adoption credit may they claim?
Steps

items: Step 1: Limit qualified expenses to the 2024 maximum credit: expenses are $20,000 but the credit cap is $16,810.
Step 2: Tentative credit before phaseout = $16,810.
Step 3: Compute excess MAGI over the phaseout floor: $262,150 - $252,150 = $10,000.
Step 4: Phaseout fraction = $10,000 / $40,000 range = 0.25 (25% phased out).
Step 5: Reduction = $16,810 x 0.25 = $4,202.50, rounded to $4,203.
Step 6: Allowed credit = $16,810 - $4,203 = $12,607 (nonrefundable; unused amount carries forward up to 5 years).

blocks.text: Answer: They may claim a $12,607 adoption credit. Takeaway: cap expenses at $16,810, then phase out ratably over the $40,000 MAGI range; the credit is nonrefundable but carries forward 5 years.

A homeowner installed qualifying rooftop solar panels in 2024 at a total cost of $28,000, plus $9,000 for a qualifying battery storage system. Their tax liability before the credit is $7,500. What is the Residential Clean Energy Credit and how much can be used this year?
Steps

items: Step 1: Identify the credit rate. The Residential Clean Energy Credit is 30% of qualified property costs for 2022-2032, with no annual dollar cap for solar and battery storage.
Step 2: Total qualified costs = solar $28,000 + battery storage $9,000 = $37,000.
Step 4: The credit is nonrefundable. Current-year liability is $7,500, so only $7,500 can offset tax this year.
Step 5: Unused credit = $11,100 - $7,500 = $3,600 carries forward to future years.
Step 6: Result: $7,500 reduces 2024 tax to $0, with $3,600 carried forward.

blocks.text: Answer: The credit is $11,100; $7,500 offsets 2024 tax and $3,600 carries forward. Takeaway: the Residential Clean Energy Credit is 30% with no cap for solar/battery and carries forward when nonrefundable limits apply.

topics.title: Self-Employment Tax on $80,000 of Net Profit (2025)

blocks.text: Dana is a sole proprietor with $80,000 of Schedule C net profit for 2025 and no wages. Compute her self-employment tax and the deduction for half of it.
Steps

items: Step 1: Net earnings from self-employment = $80,000 × 92.35% = $73,880.
Step 2: Social Security portion = $73,880 × 12.4% = $9,161.12 (below the 2025 wage base of $176,100).
Step 3: Medicare portion = $73,880 × 2.9% = $2,142.52.
Step 5: Deduction for one-half of SE tax = $11,303.64 ÷ 2 = $5,651.82, taken on Schedule 1 as an adjustment to income.

blocks.text: Answer: SE tax is $11,303.64, and Dana deducts $5,651.82 above the line. The deduction reduces income tax but not SE tax.
Marco, a single bartender, received $20,000 of qualified tips in 2025. His MAGI (before this deduction) is $162,000. How much can he deduct under the qualified tips deduction?
Steps

items: Step 1: The deduction cap is $25,000, so the $20,000 of tips is initially fully eligible.
Step 2: The phase-out begins when MAGI exceeds $150,000 for single filers.
Step 3: Excess MAGI = $162,000 − $150,000 = $12,000, which is 12 increments of $1,000.
Step 4: Reduction = 12 × $100 = $1,200.

blocks.text: Answer: Marco may deduct $18,800. The deduction is claimed on Schedule 1-A and is available even if he takes the standard deduction.
Priya and Sam file jointly for 2025. Qualified overtime premium pay (the 'half' of time-and-a-half) is $20,000 total, and MAGI is $310,000 before the deduction. What is their overtime deduction?
Steps

items: Step 1: The joint cap is $25,000, so $20,000 is within the cap.
Step 2: The joint phase-out begins at $300,000 of MAGI.
Step 3: Excess MAGI = $310,000 − $300,000 = $10,000, or 10 increments of $1,000.
Step 4: Reduction = 10 × $100 = $1,000.

blocks.text: Answer: The couple deducts $19,000. Only the premium portion of overtime pay qualifies, not the full overtime wages.
Walter, 68, is single with MAGI of $85,000 for 2025. What additional senior deduction can he claim?
Steps

items: Step 1: The base senior deduction is $6,000 for a taxpayer age 65 or older by year end.
Step 2: The phase-out threshold for single filers is $75,000.
Step 4: Reduction = 6% × $10,000 = $600.

blocks.text: Answer: Walter's senior deduction is $5,400, in addition to the extra standard deduction for age 65 or older.
A married couple filing jointly has MAGI of $320,000, including $90,000 of net investment income. Compute the NIIT.
Steps

items: Step 1: The MFJ threshold is $250,000 and is not indexed for inflation.
Step 2: Excess of MAGI over threshold = $320,000 − $250,000 = $70,000.
Step 3: NIIT base = lesser of net investment income ($90,000) or the excess ($70,000) = $70,000.
Step 5: Report on Form 8960; it is added to the tax on Schedule 2.

blocks.text: Answer: The NIIT is $2,660.
Ava, age 12, has $5,000 of interest and dividend income in 2025 and no earned income. Her parents are in the 24% bracket. Explain how her income is taxed.
Steps

items: Step 1: The dependent standard deduction for 2025 is the greater of $1,350 or earned income plus $450, so $1,350 here.
Step 2: The first $1,350 of unearned income is offset by the standard deduction and is untaxed.
Step 3: The next $1,350 is taxed at the child's rate (10%).
Step 4: Unearned income above $2,700 is net unearned income: $5,000 − $2,700 = $2,300.
Step 5: The $2,300 is taxed at the parents' marginal rate (24%) using Form 8615, or the parents may elect Form 8814.

blocks.text: Answer: $1,350 is untaxed, $1,350 is taxed at Ava's rate (10% = $135), and $2,300 is taxed at 24% ($552). Total tax is $687 before any other items.

topics.title: Tax on Capital Gains and Ordinary Income (Single, 2025)

blocks.text: Sam, single, has 2025 taxable income of $70,000, which includes $10,000 of long-term capital gain and $60,000 of ordinary income. Estimate his tax using the 2025 brackets and the 0%/15% capital gain thresholds (0% up to $48,350 of taxable income).
Steps

items: Step 1: Ordinary income of $60,000 is taxed first using the 2025 single brackets: 10% to $11,925, 12% to $48,475, 22% above.
Step 3: The capital gain stack begins at $60,000, which is above the 0% limit of $48,350, so all $10,000 is taxed at 15%.

blocks.text: Answer: Sam's regular tax is $9,614. Had the ordinary income been low enough to leave part of the gain below $48,350, that part would be taxed at 0%.

A married couple has three qualifying children under 17 and a modified AGI of $445,000 in 2024. The Child Tax Credit is $2,000 per child and phases out at $50 per $1,000 (or fraction) of MAGI over the $400,000 MFJ threshold. Compute their allowable CTC.
Steps

items: Step 1: Tentative CTC = 3 children x $2,000 = $6,000.
Step 3: Round up to the next $1,000: 45 increments.
Step 4: Phaseout reduction = 45 x $50 = $2,250.
Step 5: Allowable CTC = $6,000 - $2,250 = $3,750.

blocks.text: Answer: Allowable Child Tax Credit is $3,750. The credit drops $50 for each $1,000 of MAGI above the $400,000 MFJ threshold.

topics.title: Earned Income Tax Credit on the Phaseout Range

blocks.text: Maria is single with one qualifying child in 2024. Her earned income and AGI are both $30,000. For one child, the maximum EITC is $4,213, the phaseout begins at $22,720, and the phaseout rate is 15.98%. Estimate her EITC.
Steps

items: Step 1: Her income exceeds the phaseout start, so begin from the maximum credit of $4,213.
Step 2: Income over the phaseout threshold = $30,000 - $22,720 = $7,280.
Step 3: Phaseout reduction = $7,280 x 15.98% = $1,163.34, rounded to $1,163.
Step 5: Because AGI equals earned income here, the credit is computed on the same figure.

blocks.text: Answer: Estimated EITC is approximately $3,050. On the phaseout range the credit equals the maximum minus 15.98% of income over the threshold.

A single taxpayer has $250,000 of Medicare wages in 2024. The employer withheld additional Medicare tax on wages over $200,000. The taxpayer's filing-status threshold is $200,000. Compute the total Additional Medicare Tax owed and reconcile with employer withholding.
Steps

items: Step 1: Wages over the $200,000 threshold = $250,000 - $200,000 = $50,000.
Step 2: Additional Medicare Tax = 0.9% x $50,000 = $450.
Step 3: Employer must withhold 0.9% on wages over $200,000 = 0.9% x $50,000 = $450.
Step 4: Because withholding ($450) equals the liability ($450), no additional amount is due on Form 8959.
Step 5: Result reconciles to $0 balance for the Additional Medicare Tax.

blocks.text: Answer: Additional Medicare Tax is $450, fully covered by employer withholding. The 0.9% applies only to wages above the filing-status threshold.

A single parent with AGI of $50,000 paid $6,000 of qualifying care expenses for two children under 13 while working. The expense limit is $6,000 for two or more qualifying persons, and at this income the applicable credit rate is 20%. Compute the credit.
Steps

items: Step 1: Qualifying expenses paid = $6,000, which equals the $6,000 cap for two or more children.
Step 2: Eligible expense base = lesser of actual $6,000 or the $6,000 limit = $6,000.
Step 3: At AGI of $50,000 the applicable percentage has dropped to the 20% floor.
Step 5: The credit is nonrefundable and limited to expenses that allow the parent to work.

blocks.text: Answer: The Child and Dependent Care Credit is $1,200. At higher AGI the rate floors at 20% of up to $6,000 of expenses for two or more children.

topics.title: Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) for a Single Filer (2024)

blocks.text: Cole is single with wages of $190,000, net investment income (interest, dividends, capital gains) of $40,000, and no other income. MAGI equals AGI of $230,000. Compute his 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax.
Steps

items: Step 1: NIIT applies to the lesser of (a) net investment income or (b) MAGI over the threshold. Single threshold is $200,000.
Step 2: Net investment income = $40,000.
Step 3: MAGI over threshold = $230,000 - $200,000 = $30,000.
Step 6: Wages are not investment income, but they raise MAGI and thus the excess-over-threshold base.

blocks.text: Answer: NIIT is $1,140. It applies to the smaller of net investment income or the MAGI excess over the $200,000 single threshold.

Helena (single) has alternative minimum taxable income (AMTI) of $650,000 for 2024. The 2024 AMT exemption for single filers is $85,700, phasing out at 25 cents per dollar of AMTI above $609,350. Compute her tentative minimum tax using the 26%/28% rates (28% applies above $232,600).
Steps

items: Step 1: Determine exemption phaseout. AMTI over $609,350 = $650,000 - $609,350 = $40,650.
Step 2: Phaseout = 25% x $40,650 = $10,162.50, rounded to $10,162.
Step 3: Allowed exemption = $85,700 - $10,162 = $75,538.
Step 6: Tentative minimum tax = $60,476 + $95,721 = $156,197 (rounded).
Step 7: The TMT is compared to regular tax; AMT equals the excess of TMT over regular tax.

blocks.text: Answer: Tentative minimum tax is about $156,197. High AMTI both shrinks the exemption (25% phaseout) and pushes income into the 28% AMT bracket.

Reyes has $300,000 of total taxable income, including $60,000 of foreign-source income. His total U.S. tax before credits is $66,000. He paid $18,000 of foreign income tax. Compute the foreign tax credit limitation and the allowed credit.
Steps

items: Step 1: FTC limitation = U.S. tax x (foreign-source taxable income / total taxable income).
Step 4: Foreign tax actually paid = $18,000.
Step 5: Allowed credit = lesser of paid ($18,000) or limitation ($13,200) = $13,200.
Step 6: Excess of $18,000 - $13,200 = $4,800 carries back 1 year then forward 10 years.

blocks.text: Answer: Allowed FTC is $13,200 with $4,800 carried over. The credit cannot exceed the U.S. tax on the foreign-source portion of income.

topics.title: Gift Tax: Annual Exclusion and Taxable Gift (2024)

blocks.text: In 2024 Helen, a widow, gives her son $40,000 in cash and her daughter $12,000 in cash. The 2024 gift tax annual exclusion is $18,000 per donee. She makes no gift-splitting election. Compute her total taxable gifts for the year.
Steps

items: Step 1: Son's gift $40,000 less annual exclusion $18,000 = $22,000 taxable.
Step 2: Daughter's gift $12,000 is below the $18,000 exclusion, so $0 taxable (excess exclusion is not transferable).
Step 3: Total taxable gifts = $22,000 + $0 = $22,000.
Step 4: The $22,000 reduces Helen's lifetime exclusion (2024 basic exclusion $13.61 million) but produces no out-of-pocket gift tax.
Step 5: A Form 709 is required because a gift to one donee exceeded $18,000.

blocks.text: Answer: Taxable gifts total $22,000; Form 709 is required. The annual exclusion is per donee and unused exclusion does not carry between donees.

topics.title: Basis of Gifted Property: Dual-Basis Rule for a Loss

blocks.text: Mother gifts stock to her son. Her adjusted basis was $30,000; fair market value on the date of gift was $20,000. No gift tax was paid. The son later sells the stock. Determine his recognized gain or loss if he sells at (a) $35,000, (b) $15,000, and (c) $25,000.
Steps

items: Step 1: Because FMV ($20,000) is below the donor's basis ($30,000), the dual-basis rule applies.
Step 2: For gain, use the donor's carryover basis of $30,000; for loss, use FMV at gift of $20,000.
Step 5: Sale at $25,000: between $20,000 and $30,000, so neither gain nor loss is recognized = $0.

blocks.text: Answer: (a) $5,000 gain, (b) $5,000 loss, (c) $0. Selling within the FMV-to-donor-basis range produces no recognized gain or loss.

A single taxpayer below the threshold has $80,000 of qualified business income from a sole proprietorship and $10,000 of qualified REIT dividends in 2024. Taxable income before the QBI deduction is $120,000 (net capital gain is $0). What is the QBI deduction?
Steps

items: Step 1: Component 1 (QBI): 20% x $80,000 = $16,000.
Step 2: Component 2 (REIT/PTP): 20% x $10,000 qualified REIT dividends = $2,000.
Step 3: Combined QBI amount = $16,000 + $2,000 = $18,000.
Step 4: Overall limit = 20% x (taxable income - net capital gain) = 20% x ($120,000 - $0) = $24,000.
Step 5: QBI deduction = lesser of $18,000 and $24,000 = $18,000.

blocks.text: Answer: The Section 199A deduction is $18,000. Takeaway: qualified REIT dividends get a separate 20% component not subject to wage/UBIA limits, then the total is capped at 20% of taxable income minus net capital gain.

topics.title: QBI Deduction in the Phase-In Range for a Specified Service Trade

blocks.text: A single taxpayer owns a consulting firm (a specified service trade or business, SSTB) with $150,000 of QBI. Taxable income before QBI is $210,000. The 2024 single threshold is $191,950 and the phase-out range is $50,000 (fully phased out at $241,950). Compute the QBI deduction.
Steps

items: Step 1: For an SSTB above the threshold, the allowed QBI is reduced as income rises through the phase-out range.
Step 2: Excess over threshold = $210,000 - $191,950 = $18,050.
Step 3: Applicable percentage = 1 - (excess / phase-out range) = 1 - ($18,050 / $50,000) = 1 - 0.361 = 0.639 (63.9%).
Step 4: Allowed QBI for the SSTB = $150,000 x 63.9% = $95,850.
Step 5: Tentative deduction = 20% x $95,850 = $19,170 (wage/UBIA limit would also apply at the same applicable percentage, ignored here for simplicity).
Step 6: Compare to 20% of taxable income; assume not limiting, so QBI deduction = $19,170.

blocks.text: Answer: The QBI deduction is about $19,170. Takeaway: SSTB income phases out over a $50,000 (single) range above the threshold and is fully disallowed at the top.

topics.title: Excess Social Security Tax Withholding Credit (Two Employers, 2024)

blocks.text: In 2024 a single taxpayer worked for two employers. Employer A paid $120,000 in wages and withheld $7,440 of Social Security tax; Employer B paid $80,000 and withheld $4,960. The 2024 Social Security wage base is $168,600 (max employee SS tax = $10,453.20). How much excess Social Security tax can the taxpayer claim as a credit?
Steps

items: Step 1: Total Social Security tax withheld = $7,440 (Employer A) + $4,960 (Employer B) = $12,400.
Step 2: Determine the 2024 maximum employee Social Security tax: wage base $168,600 x 6.2% = $10,453.20.
Step 3: Excess withheld = total withheld $12,400 - maximum $10,453.20 = $1,946.80.
Step 4: The excess arises because two employers each withheld without knowledge of the other; this is allowed only when there are multiple employers.
Step 5: Round to $1,947. This excess is claimed as a refundable credit (additional payment) on Schedule 3.
Step 6: Note: a single employer over-withholding must instead refund the employee directly; the credit method applies only to multiple-employer situations.

blocks.text: Answer: The taxpayer claims $1,947 of excess Social Security tax as a credit against tax. Takeaway: with two or more employers, Social Security tax withheld above the annual maximum ($10,453.20 for 2024) is a refundable credit on Schedule 3.

A single taxpayer received $6,000 in advance premium tax credit (APTC) for 2024 marketplace coverage. After year-end, the computed allowed premium tax credit based on actual income is only $4,200. The taxpayer's household income is 350% of the federal poverty line (no repayment limitation applies at this income level). What is the reconciliation result?
Steps

items: Step 1: Compare advance payments to the allowed credit. APTC received = $6,000; allowed PTC = $4,200.
Step 2: Because APTC ($6,000) exceeds the allowed credit ($4,200), the taxpayer has excess advance payments to repay.

Step 4: Check the repayment limitation. At 350% of FPL the income is at/above 400%? No - it is 350%, but the limitation caps apply below 400% FPL. At 300%-400% the single-filer cap for 2024 is $1,575.
Step 5: Apply the cap: required repayment = lesser of excess ($1,800) or limitation ($1,575) = $1,575.
Step 6: The taxpayer repays $1,575 as additional tax; $225 of the excess is forgiven by the limitation.

blocks.text: Answer: The taxpayer must repay $1,575 of excess advance premium tax credit (capped from $1,800). Takeaway: excess APTC is reconciled on Form 8962, and repayment is limited by income-based caps for households under 400% of the federal poverty line.

A self-employed client's 2024 total tax was $18,000 and her 2024 AGI was $120,000. She expects 2025 tax of $22,000. What is the smallest amount she can pay through withholding and estimates to avoid the underpayment penalty?
Steps

items: Step 1: Prior-year safe harbor: 100% of 2024 tax = $18,000 (AGI under $150,000, so 110% does not apply).
Step 2: Current-year safe harbor: 90% of expected 2025 tax = 0.90 × $22,000 = $19,800.
Step 3: The required annual payment is the smaller of the two: $18,000.
Step 4: Quarterly installments = $18,000 ÷ 4 = $4,500 due April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.
Step 5: Any remaining balance due on filing is not penalized if the safe harbor is met.

blocks.text: Answer: She must pay at least $18,000 for 2025, or $4,500 per installment. The remaining $4,000 of expected tax can be paid with the return.
Maria turns 75 in 2025. Her traditional IRA balance on December 31, 2024 was $600,000. Using the Uniform Lifetime Table factor of 24.6 for age 75, compute her RMD.
Steps

items: Step 1: Use the prior December 31 account balance: $600,000.
Step 2: Find the factor from the Uniform Lifetime Table for her age at year end: 24.6.
Step 4: If she takes less, the excise tax is 25% of the shortfall (10% if corrected within the correction window).
Step 5: She may satisfy the RMD with a qualified charitable distribution to a charity.

blocks.text: Answer: Her 2025 RMD is about $24,390. Withdrawals from multiple IRAs can be aggregated, but 401(k) RMDs must come from each plan separately.

topics.title: Roth Conversion with After-Tax Basis (Pro-Rata Rule)

blocks.text: A taxpayer has one traditional IRA worth $100,000, of which $20,000 is after-tax basis (from nondeductible contributions). She converts $30,000 to a Roth IRA. How much is taxable?
Steps

items: Step 1: Basis ratio = $20,000 ÷ $100,000 = 20%, so 80% of the IRA is pre-tax.
Step 2: Taxable portion of the conversion = 80% × $30,000 = $24,000.
Step 3: Nontaxable portion = $30,000 − $24,000 = $6,000.
Step 4: Basis remaining in the traditional IRA = $20,000 − $6,000 = $14,000.
Step 5: Form 8606 tracks the computation.

blocks.text: Answer: $24,000 of the conversion is taxable. The pro-rata rule prevents converting only the after-tax dollars.

Priya's 2023 AGI was $180,000 and her 2023 total tax was $40,000. She expects 2024 tax of $55,000. Because her prior-year AGI exceeds $150,000, her safe harbor is 110% of prior-year tax. What minimum total must she pay through withholding and estimates to avoid an underpayment penalty?
Steps

items: Step 1: Option A (current year): 90% x $55,000 = $49,500.
Step 2: Option B (prior year): because AGI > $150,000, use 110% x $40,000 = $44,000.
Step 3: The required annual payment is the smaller of the two: min($49,500, $44,000) = $44,000.
Step 4: She must pay at least $44,000 across withholding and four equal estimates of $11,000.
Step 5: Paying $44,000 avoids the penalty even though actual tax is $55,000.

blocks.text: Answer: She must pay at least $44,000 to be safe. High earners (prior AGI over $150,000) use the 110% prior-year safe harbor.

A single taxpayer has $90,000 of qualified business income from a sole proprietorship and taxable income before the QBI deduction of $120,000, which includes $4,000 of net capital gain. Their income is below the 2024 single threshold of $191,950, so no wage/UBIA limit applies. Compute the QBI deduction.
Steps

items: Step 1: Tentative QBI deduction = 20% x $90,000 QBI = $18,000.
Step 2: Compute the taxable-income limit base: taxable income before QBI minus net capital gain = $120,000 - $4,000 = $116,000.
Step 3: Overall limit = 20% x $116,000 = $23,200.
Step 4: QBI deduction = lesser of $18,000 or $23,200 = $18,000.
Step 5: Subtract from taxable income: $120,000 - $18,000 = $102,000 taxable income.

blocks.text: Answer: QBI deduction is $18,000. Below the threshold it is simply 20% of QBI, capped by 20% of taxable income less net capital gain.

A married couple has alternative minimum taxable income (AMTI) of $1,300,000 in 2024. The MFJ AMT exemption is $133,300 and phases out at 25 cents per dollar of AMTI over $1,218,700. Compute the allowable exemption and tentative minimum tax base.
Steps

items: Step 1: AMTI over the phaseout start = $1,300,000 - $1,218,700 = $81,300.
Step 2: Exemption reduction = 25% x $81,300 = $20,325.
Step 3: Allowable exemption = $133,300 - $20,325 = $112,975.
Step 4: AMT base = AMTI - exemption = $1,300,000 - $112,975 = $1,187,025.
Step 5: This base is then taxed at 26%/28% to find tentative minimum tax.

blocks.text: Answer: The allowable AMT exemption is $112,975, leaving an AMT base of $1,187,025. The exemption shrinks 25 cents per dollar above the phaseout threshold.

topics.title: Kiddie Tax on a Child's Unearned Income (2024)

blocks.text: A 15-year-old dependent has $6,000 of unearned income (interest and dividends) and no earned income for 2024. The first $1,300 is tax-free (standard deduction for unearned income), the next $1,300 is taxed at the child's rate, and the remainder is taxed at the parents' marginal rate (24%). Assume the child's own rate is 10%. Compute the child's tax.
Steps

items: Step 1: Total unearned income = $6,000.
Step 2: First $1,300 is offset by the standard deduction = $0 tax.
Step 3: Next $1,300 is taxed at the child's 10% rate = $130.
Step 4: Remaining unearned income = $6,000 - $1,300 - $1,300 = $3,400.
Step 5: The $3,400 is taxed at the parents' 24% rate = $816.
Step 6: Total kiddie tax = $130 + $816 = $946.

blocks.text: Answer: The child's tax is $946. Unearned income above $2,600 is taxed at the parents' marginal rate under the kiddie tax.

topics.title: Additional Medicare Tax for a Single Filer (2024)

blocks.text: A single taxpayer has Medicare wages of $260,000 and no self-employment income. The Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% applies to wages above the $200,000 single threshold. Compute the Additional Medicare Tax.
Steps

items: Step 1: Single threshold for the Additional Medicare Tax is $200,000.
Step 2: Wages over the threshold = $260,000 - $200,000 = $60,000.
Step 3: Additional Medicare Tax = 0.9% x $60,000 = $540.
Step 4: The employer withholds 0.9% on wages over $200,000 regardless of filing status.
Step 5: Any over- or under-withholding is reconciled on Form 8959 with the return.
Step 6: Total Additional Medicare Tax owed = $540.

blocks.text: Answer: The Additional Medicare Tax is $540 (0.9% of the $60,000 over the $200,000 threshold). It applies only to earnings above the filing-status threshold.

topics.title: Capital Loss Limitation and Carryover for an Individual

blocks.text: A single taxpayer has a net capital loss of $11,000 for 2024 (after netting all gains and losses). How much is deductible this year and what carries forward?
Steps

items: Step 1: Individuals may deduct net capital losses against ordinary income up to $3,000 per year ($1,500 if MFS).
Step 2: Current deduction = $3,000.
Step 4: The carryover keeps its character (here long-term or short-term as originally classified) and carries forward indefinitely.
Step 5: Next year the $8,000 first offsets capital gains, then up to $3,000 of ordinary income again.

blocks.text: Answer: Deduct $3,000 in 2024; carry $8,000 forward. Takeaway: individuals' net capital losses offset ordinary income only up to $3,000/year, with indefinite carryforward.

topics.title: Section 121 Home Sale Exclusion With Partial Use Period

blocks.text: A single taxpayer sells her main home for a $400,000 gain. She owned and used it as her main home for only 18 of the last 60 months because of a job relocation (a qualifying reduced-exclusion reason). What gain can she exclude?
Steps

items: Step 1: The full Section 121 exclusion is $250,000 (single) but requires 2 of 5 years of ownership and use; she falls short.
Step 2: She qualifies for a reduced (prorated) exclusion due to a qualifying job-related move.
Step 3: Proration fraction = months of use / 24 months = 18 / 24 = 0.75.
Step 4: Reduced maximum exclusion = $250,000 x 0.75 = $187,500.
Step 5: Taxable gain = $400,000 - $187,500 = $212,500, taxed as long-term capital gain.

blocks.text: Answer: She can exclude $187,500; $212,500 is taxable LTCG. Takeaway: a qualifying early sale (job, health, unforeseen circumstances) gives a prorated exclusion based on months of use over 24.

topics.title: Wash Sale Loss Disallowance and Basis Adjustment

blocks.text: An investor sells 100 shares of XYZ for $4,000 (basis $6,000), realizing a $2,000 loss. Within 30 days she buys 100 replacement shares of XYZ for $4,200. What loss is allowed and what is the basis of the new shares?
Steps

items: Step 1: The wash sale rule disallows a loss when substantially identical stock is bought within 30 days before or after the sale.
Step 2: Realized loss = $4,000 - $6,000 = -$2,000. Because replacement shares were purchased in the window, the loss is disallowed.
Step 3: Allowed loss this year = $0.
Step 4: The disallowed $2,000 loss is added to the basis of the new shares.
Step 5: New shares' basis = purchase price $4,200 + disallowed loss $2,000 = $6,200.
Step 6: The holding period of the old shares tacks onto the new shares.

blocks.text: Answer: The $2,000 loss is disallowed; the replacement shares' basis is $6,200. Takeaway: a wash sale defers the loss into the basis of the replacement shares rather than eliminating it.

A business pays a contractor $20,000 during 2024 but the contractor failed to provide a valid TIN (Form W-9). Backup withholding applies. The current backup withholding rate is 24%. How much must the payer withhold and remit, and what does the contractor receive?
Steps

items: Step 1: Identify when backup withholding applies: a missing or incorrect TIN (or IRS notification) triggers it on reportable payments such as nonemployee compensation.
Step 2: Apply the backup withholding rate of 24% to the reportable payment of $20,000.
Step 3: Backup withholding = 24% x $20,000 = $4,800.
Step 4: The payer remits the $4,800 to the IRS (via Form 945) and pays the contractor the net: $20,000 - $4,800 = $15,200.
Step 5: The full $20,000 is reported on Form 1099-NEC, with the $4,800 shown as federal income tax withheld.
Step 6: The contractor reports $20,000 of income and claims the $4,800 as withholding credit on their return.

blocks.text: Answer: The payer withholds and remits $4,800 (24% of $20,000), paying the contractor $15,200 net. Takeaway: a missing/invalid TIN triggers 24% backup withholding, remitted on Form 945 and creditable to the payee.

topics.title: Simple Trust Taxable Income and Distribution

blocks.text: A simple trust has $20,000 of DNI and distributes $18,000 to its beneficiary during the year. Compute the trust's taxable income and the beneficiary's income from the trust.
Steps

items: Step 1: A simple trust must distribute all income currently, and the distribution deduction is the lesser of distributions or DNI: $18,000.
Step 2: Trust income before deduction = $20,000.
Step 3: Trust taxable income = $20,000 − $18,000 − $300 exemption = $1,700.
Step 4: The beneficiary reports $18,000 (limited to DNI) on Schedule K-1 with the same character as the income.
Step 5: If the trust is required to distribute all income, $20,000 would be treated as distributed and taxed to the beneficiary.

blocks.text: Answer: The trust has taxable income of $1,700 and the beneficiary is taxed on $18,000.

A business places $50,000 of computer equipment (5-year MACRS property) in service in March 2024. No Section 179 or bonus depreciation is elected. Using the half-year convention table rates (Year 1: 20.00%, Year 2: 32.00%), compute depreciation for years 1 and 2 and the remaining basis.
Steps

items: Step 1: Year 1 depreciation = $50,000 x 20.00% = $10,000.
Step 2: Year 2 depreciation = $50,000 x 32.00% = $16,000.
Step 3: Total depreciation taken through Year 2 = $10,000 + $16,000 = $26,000.
Step 4: Adjusted basis after Year 2 = $50,000 - $26,000 = $24,000.
Step 5: The half-year convention treats the asset as in service mid-year regardless of the March date.

blocks.text: Answer: Year 1 = $10,000 and Year 2 = $16,000, leaving $24,000 of basis. MACRS percentages are applied to the original cost, not the declining balance.

topics.title: Section 179 Expensing with the Investment Limit

blocks.text: In 2024 a business buys $3,200,000 of qualifying equipment. The Section 179 maximum deduction is $1,220,000 and the phaseout (investment) threshold begins at $3,050,000, reducing the limit dollar-for-dollar. Compute the maximum Section 179 deduction available.
Steps

items: Step 1: Total qualifying purchases = $3,200,000.
Step 3: Reduce the $1,220,000 cap dollar-for-dollar by $150,000.
Step 4: Maximum Section 179 deduction = $1,220,000 - $150,000 = $1,070,000.
Step 5: The remaining cost above $1,070,000 may be recovered via bonus depreciation or regular MACRS.

blocks.text: Answer: Maximum Section 179 deduction is $1,070,000. Purchases above the $3,050,000 threshold reduce the deduction dollar-for-dollar.

A sole proprietor has $100,000 of net profit on Schedule C in 2024 and no wages. The SE tax rate is 15.3% on net earnings, applied to 92.35% of net profit, and the deductible portion is half the SE tax. Compute SE tax and the above-the-line deduction.
Steps

items: Step 1: Net earnings from self-employment = $100,000 x 92.35% = $92,350.
Step 2: All $92,350 is below the 2024 Social Security wage base of $168,600, so the full 15.3% applies.
Step 4: Deductible (employer-equivalent) portion = 50% x $14,130 = $7,065.
Step 5: The $7,065 is an above-the-line deduction that reduces AGI.

blocks.text: Answer: SE tax is about $14,130 with a $7,065 above-the-line deduction. SE tax is figured on 92.35% of net profit at 15.3%.

An S corporation has one shareholder-employee who provides all services. The company nets $200,000 before any owner pay and distributes the entire amount as a $200,000 distribution with $0 wages. A reasonable salary for the role is $90,000. Show the FICA exposure and the correct recharacterization.
Steps

items: Step 1: Paying $0 wages avoids all payroll tax on $200,000, which the IRS challenges as unreasonable.
Step 2: Reasonable compensation for the services is $90,000, which must be run through payroll.
Step 3: Recharacterize: $90,000 becomes W-2 wages, $110,000 remains a distribution.
Step 4: Combined FICA on the wages = 15.3% x $90,000 = $13,770 (employer + employee share).
Step 5: The $110,000 distribution is not subject to FICA, so only the wage portion is taxed for payroll.

blocks.text: Answer: $90,000 must be wages (about $13,770 of FICA) and $110,000 a distribution. S corp owner-employees must take reasonable compensation before distributions.

topics.title: Business Use of Vehicle: Standard Mileage

blocks.text: A self-employed consultant drives 18,000 total miles in 2024, of which 12,000 are documented business miles. The 2024 standard mileage rate is 67 cents per mile. She also paid $400 in business-related parking and tolls. Compute her deductible vehicle expense.
Steps

items: Step 1: Determine business-use percentage: 12,000 / 18,000 = 66.67% (used only for actual-cost method, noted for context).
Step 2: Standard mileage deduction = 12,000 business miles x $0.67 = $8,040.
Step 3: Parking and tolls are deductible in addition to the mileage rate: $400.
Step 4: Total deductible vehicle expense = $8,040 + $400 = $8,440.
Step 5: Under the standard mileage method, depreciation and gas are already built into the rate.

blocks.text: Answer: Deductible vehicle expense is $8,440. Parking and tolls are added on top of the standard mileage allowance.

A business places $100,000 of new 7-year MACRS equipment in service in 2024. The 2024 bonus depreciation rate is 60%. After bonus, the remaining basis is depreciated under MACRS (Year 1 rate 14.29% for 7-year property). Compute first-year depreciation.
Steps

items: Step 1: Bonus depreciation = 60% x $100,000 = $60,000.
Step 2: Remaining basis after bonus = $100,000 - $60,000 = $40,000.
Step 3: Regular MACRS Year 1 on the remaining basis = 14.29% x $40,000 = $5,716.
Step 4: Total first-year depreciation = $60,000 + $5,716 = $65,716.
Step 5: Bonus depreciation phases down to 60% in 2024 (from 80% in 2023).

blocks.text: Answer: First-year depreciation is $65,716. In 2024 bonus depreciation is 60%, with the remaining basis recovered through MACRS.

Sophia (single) owns a consulting firm (an SSTB) generating $180,000 of qualified business income. Her taxable income before the QBI deduction is $216,100. For 2024 the single QBI phase-out range is $191,950 to $241,950 (width $50,000). Compute her allowed QBI deduction.
Steps

items: Step 1: Because it is an SSTB and taxable income is within the phase-out range, the QBI is partially allowed.
Step 2: Excess over threshold = $216,100 - $191,950 = $24,150.
Step 3: Phase-in percentage = $24,150 / $50,000 = 48.3%; applicable (includible) percentage = 1 - 0.483 = 51.7%.
Step 4: Includible QBI = 51.7% x $180,000 = $93,060.
Step 5: Tentative deduction = 20% x $93,060 = $18,612.
Step 6: Compare to 20% of taxable income limit = 20% x $216,100 = $43,220; the smaller $18,612 controls.
Step 7: Allowed QBI deduction = $18,612.

blocks.text: Answer: QBI deduction is $18,612. For an in-range SSTB, only the applicable percentage (51.7% here) of QBI counts before the 20% computation.

topics.title: Section 199A Wage/UBIA Limit Above the Threshold

blocks.text: Marcus (single) owns a non-SSTB manufacturing business with $400,000 of QBI. His taxable income of $300,000 is fully above the 2024 phase-out (over $241,950), so the wage/UBIA limit fully applies. The business paid $90,000 of W-2 wages and holds $200,000 of qualified property (UBIA). Compute the QBI deduction.
Steps

items: Step 1: Tentative QBI deduction = 20% x $400,000 = $80,000.
Step 2: Wage/UBIA limit = greater of (a) 50% of W-2 wages or (b) 25% of wages + 2.5% of UBIA.
Step 5: Greater of (a) and (b) = $45,000.
Step 6: Allowed QBI = lesser of tentative ($80,000) or wage/UBIA limit ($45,000) = $45,000.
Step 7: Final deduction (also under 20% of taxable income $60,000) = $45,000.

blocks.text: Answer: QBI deduction is $45,000, capped by the 50%-of-wages limit. Above the threshold, the W-2 wage/UBIA test can sharply reduce the 20% deduction.

topics.title: Self-Employment Tax and the One-Half SE Deduction

blocks.text: A sole proprietor has $110,000 of net profit from Schedule C and no wages. For 2024 the Social Security wage base is $168,600. Compute the self-employment tax and the deductible one-half adjustment.
Steps

items: Step 1: Net earnings subject to SE tax = 92.35% x $110,000 = $101,585.
Step 2: This is below the $168,600 Social Security wage base, so the full 15.3% rate applies.
Step 4: (Components: 12.4% Social Security = $12,596.54 + 2.9% Medicare = $2,945.97.)
Step 5: One-half SE tax deduction (above the line) = $15,543 / 2 = $7,771 (using $7,771.50, rounded).
Step 6: The deduction reduces AGI but not the SE tax itself.

blocks.text: Answer: SE tax is about $15,543 and the above-the-line deduction is about $7,771. The 92.35% factor and one-half deduction are the core SE-tax mechanics.

topics.title: Home Office Deduction Using the Regular Method

blocks.text: A self-employed designer uses a 300-square-foot office in her 2,000-square-foot home exclusively for business. Annual home expenses: $18,000 mortgage interest and property tax, $4,000 utilities and insurance, and $6,000 depreciation on the home. Net Schedule C income before the home-office deduction is $50,000. Compute the home-office deduction.
Steps

items: Step 1: Business-use percentage = 300 / 2,000 = 15%.
Step 3: Income limitation: deduction cannot exceed net business income of $50,000.
Step 4: $4,200 is well below the $50,000 limit, so the full amount is deductible.
Step 5: Home-office deduction = $4,200.
Step 6: (The depreciation portion, 15% x $6,000 = $900, reduces the home's basis for later sale.)

blocks.text: Answer: Home-office deduction is $4,200 under the regular method. The 15% business-use share applies to all qualifying home expenses, subject to an income limit.

A single taxpayer has a $700,000 business loss from a sole proprietorship and $200,000 of wages and other non-business income. For 2024 the excess-business-loss threshold for single filers is $305,000. Determine the currently deductible business loss and the disallowed amount.
Steps

items: Step 1: Aggregate business loss = $700,000.
Step 2: The 2024 single threshold caps the business loss usable against non-business income at $305,000.
Step 3: Excess business loss disallowed = $700,000 - $305,000 = $395,000.
Step 4: Currently allowed business loss = $305,000.
Step 5: The disallowed $395,000 becomes a net operating loss carryforward to next year.
Step 6: The $305,000 loss offsets the $200,000 of other income; remaining $105,000 of loss may create a current-year NOL as well.

blocks.text: Answer: Allowed business loss is $305,000; $395,000 is disallowed and carried forward as an NOL. The excess-business-loss rule caps how much business loss can offset non-business income.

topics.title: S-Corporation Loss Limited by Stock Basis, Then Carryover

blocks.text: Carmen owns 100% of an S corporation. Her stock basis at the start of 2024 is $30,000 and she has made no loans to the corporation. The S corporation passes through a $46,000 ordinary loss for 2024. How much loss can she deduct, and what happens to the rest?
Steps

items: Step 1: A shareholder may deduct pass-through losses only up to stock basis plus debt basis.
Step 2: Stock basis = $30,000; debt basis = $0; total basis limit = $30,000.
Step 3: Allowed loss in 2024 = lesser of loss ($46,000) and basis ($30,000) = $30,000.
Step 4: Stock basis after loss = $30,000 - $30,000 = $0.
Step 5: Suspended loss carried forward = $46,000 - $30,000 = $16,000.
Step 6: The $16,000 is deductible in a future year when Carmen restores basis (additional capital or income).

blocks.text: Answer: Carmen deducts $30,000 in 2024 and carries $16,000 forward. S-corp losses stop at stock plus debt basis; unlike partnerships, shareholder guarantees of corporate debt do not create basis.

topics.title: Partnership Section 704(c) Allocation of Built-In Gain

blocks.text: Aaron contributes land to a new 50/50 partnership. The land has a fair market value of $100,000 and an adjusted basis to Aaron of $60,000 (a $40,000 built-in gain). Two years later the partnership sells the land for $110,000. How is the $50,000 total gain allocated under Section 704(c)?
Steps

items: Step 1: Section 704(c) requires the pre-contribution built-in gain to be allocated to the contributing partner.
Step 2: Built-in gain at contribution = FMV $100,000 - basis $60,000 = $40,000 (all to Aaron).
Step 3: Total gain on sale = sale price $110,000 - partnership basis $60,000 = $50,000.
Step 4: Post-contribution appreciation = $110,000 - $100,000 = $10,000, shared 50/50 = $5,000 each.
Step 5: Aaron's total gain = $40,000 (704(c) built-in) + $5,000 (his half of post-contribution) = $45,000.
Step 6: Other partner's gain = $5,000.

blocks.text: Answer: Aaron recognizes $45,000 and the other partner $5,000. Section 704(c) prevents shifting a contributor's built-in gain to other partners.

topics.title: Partner's Outside Basis After Distributions and Loss

blocks.text: Nadia's beginning partnership outside basis is $50,000. During 2024 her share of partnership ordinary income is $12,000, her share of tax-exempt income is $2,000, the partnership distributes $20,000 cash to her, and her share of nondeductible expenses is $1,000. Compute her year-end outside basis.
Steps

items: Step 1: Start with beginning basis = $50,000.
Step 2: Increase for income items: + $12,000 ordinary income + $2,000 tax-exempt income = +$14,000.
Step 3: Subtotal before distributions = $50,000 + $14,000 = $64,000.
Step 4: Decrease for cash distribution = - $20,000.
Step 5: Decrease for nondeductible, noncapital expense = - $1,000.

blocks.text: Answer: Year-end outside basis is $43,000. Tax-exempt income increases basis and nondeductible expenses decrease it, preserving the single-tax character of a partnership.

topics.title: Reasonable Compensation: S-Corp Payroll Tax Exposure

blocks.text: Owen is the sole shareholder-employee of an S corporation that nets $200,000 before any owner compensation. He pays himself only $30,000 in W-2 wages and takes the rest as a distribution. The IRS asserts reasonable compensation should be $110,000. Estimate the additional employment tax exposure on the recharacterized wages (use combined 15.3% on the wage shortfall, ignoring the wage base for simplicity here since amounts are below $168,600).
Steps

items: Step 1: Reasonable wages asserted = $110,000; wages actually paid = $30,000.
Step 2: Wage shortfall subject to recharacterization = $110,000 - $30,000 = $80,000.
Step 3: Combined Social Security + Medicare rate (employer + employee) = 15.3%.
Step 4: Additional FICA exposure = 15.3% x $80,000 = $12,240.
Step 5: Penalties and interest may be added; the distribution does not avoid payroll tax to the extent it substitutes for reasonable compensation.

blocks.text: Answer: About $12,240 of additional employment tax on the $80,000 wage shortfall. S-corp owners must pay reasonable wages before taking distributions free of FICA.

An estate has distributable net income (DNI) of $40,000 for 2024, all from taxable interest. It distributes $50,000 of cash to its sole beneficiary during the year. How much can the estate deduct as an income distribution deduction, and how much is taxable to the beneficiary?
Steps

items: Step 1: The income distribution deduction is limited to the lesser of distributions or DNI.
Step 2: Distributions = $50,000; DNI = $40,000.
Step 3: Income distribution deduction = lesser of the two = $40,000.
Step 4: Beneficiary's taxable income from the estate = $40,000 (carries the interest character).
Step 5: The extra $10,000 distributed beyond DNI is a tax-free distribution of corpus (principal), neither deducted nor taxed.

blocks.text: Answer: The estate deducts $40,000 and the beneficiary reports $40,000 of interest; the $10,000 excess is a nontaxable distribution of principal. DNI caps the deduction and the beneficiary's income.

topics.title: Guaranteed Payments and Partner's Distributive Share

blocks.text: A two-partner LLC pays Partner A a $40,000 guaranteed payment for services. After deducting that payment, the partnership has ordinary business income of $60,000, allocated 50/50. Compute Partner A's total income from the partnership and the partnership's reported ordinary income.
Steps

items: Step 1: A guaranteed payment is deductible by the partnership and is ordinary income (and SE income) to the recipient regardless of partnership profit.
Step 2: Partnership ordinary income after the guaranteed payment = $60,000.
Step 3: Partner A's distributive share = 50% x $60,000 = $30,000.
Step 4: Partner A's total income from partnership = guaranteed payment $40,000 + distributive share $30,000 = $70,000.
Step 5: Partner B's income = 50% x $60,000 = $30,000.

blocks.text: Answer: Partner A reports $70,000 ($40,000 guaranteed payment + $30,000 share); the partnership's ordinary income (after the deductible payment) is $60,000. Guaranteed payments are deducted before computing distributive shares.

topics.title: Partner Basis Ordering With Distribution and Loss

blocks.text: A partner's outside basis at the start of 2024 is $20,000. During the year the partnership reports a $5,000 cash distribution to her and allocates her a $30,000 ordinary loss. In what order are these applied and what is deductible?
Steps

items: Step 1: Order of basis adjustments: (1) add current-year income items, (2) subtract distributions, (3) subtract losses.
Step 2: No income items here, so start at $20,000.
Step 3: Subtract the cash distribution first: $20,000 - $5,000 = $15,000 basis. (Distribution is within basis, no gain.)
Step 4: Apply the loss against remaining basis: loss allowed is limited to $15,000 basis.
Step 5: Deductible loss in 2024 = $15,000; ending basis = $0.
Step 6: Suspended loss carried forward = $30,000 - $15,000 = $15,000 (deductible when basis is restored).

blocks.text: Answer: She deducts $15,000 of loss; $15,000 is suspended; basis is $0. Takeaway: distributions reduce basis BEFORE losses, so they shrink the loss a partner can currently deduct.

topics.title: S Corporation Distribution: AAA vs Dividend From E&P

blocks.text: An S corporation (formerly a C corporation) has accumulated adjustments account (AAA) of $40,000 and accumulated E&P of $25,000 from its C years. The sole shareholder has stock basis of $50,000 and receives a $75,000 distribution in 2024. Characterize the distribution.
Steps

items: Step 1: First tier - tax-free to the extent of AAA: $40,000 reduces AAA to $0 and reduces stock basis to $50,000 - $40,000 = $10,000.
Step 2: Second tier - distributions next come from accumulated C-corp E&P and are a taxable dividend: $25,000 is an ordinary dividend (does NOT reduce stock basis).
Step 3: Remaining distribution after AAA and E&P = $75,000 - $40,000 - $25,000 = $10,000.
Step 4: Third tier - this $10,000 is tax-free return of capital to the extent of remaining basis ($10,000), reducing basis to $0.
Step 5: No distribution remains, so no capital gain results.

blocks.text: Answer: Of the $75,000: $40,000 tax-free (AAA), $25,000 taxable dividend (E&P), $10,000 tax-free return of capital; basis ends at $0. Takeaway: an S corp with C-corp E&P layers distributions AAA first, then taxable E&P dividend, then return of capital.

A C corporation receives three dividends in 2024: $100,000 from a company it owns 10% of, $100,000 from one it owns 30% of, and $100,000 from a company it owns 85% of (same affiliated group). Compute the dividends-received deduction (assume no taxable-income limit applies).
Steps

items: Step 1: Ownership under 20% gets a 50% DRD: 50% x $100,000 = $50,000.
Step 2: Ownership of 20% to less than 80% gets a 65% DRD: 65% x $100,000 = $65,000.
Step 3: Ownership of 80% or more (affiliated) gets a 100% DRD: 100% x $100,000 = $100,000.
Step 5: The $300,000 of dividend income is reported but offset by the $215,000 deduction, leaving $85,000 net.

blocks.text: Answer: The total DRD is $215,000. Takeaway: the DRD percentage rises with ownership - 50% under 20%, 65% for 20-80%, and 100% at 80%+.

topics.title: Partnership Guaranteed Payment vs Distributive Share

blocks.text: A partner is entitled to a $50,000 guaranteed payment for services regardless of income. The partnership has $120,000 of ordinary income BEFORE the guaranteed payment, and the partner has a 25% interest. Compute the partner's total income from the partnership.
Steps

items: Step 1: The guaranteed payment is deductible by the partnership in computing partnership ordinary income.
Step 2: Partnership ordinary income after guaranteed payment = $120,000 - $50,000 = $70,000.
Step 3: Partner's distributive share = 25% x $70,000 = $17,500.
Step 4: Partner's total income = guaranteed payment $50,000 + distributive share $17,500 = $67,500.
Step 5: Both amounts are self-employment income to the partner; the guaranteed payment is ordinary income reported on Schedule K-1.

blocks.text: Answer: The partner reports $67,500 ($50,000 guaranteed payment + $17,500 distributive share). Takeaway: guaranteed payments reduce partnership income before the remaining profit is allocated to partners.

topics.title: S Corporation Reasonable Compensation and Payroll Tax

blocks.text: A sole shareholder-employee of an S corporation takes only a $20,000 salary while the corporation has $130,000 of net profit, distributing $110,000 to him. The IRS determines reasonable compensation should have been $80,000. What is the additional FICA exposure on reclassification (2024, employer + employee, ignoring the wage base for this size)?
Steps

items: Step 1: The IRS recharacterizes $80,000 - $20,000 = $60,000 of distributions as wages.
Step 2: Social Security tax: 12.4% combined (6.2% employer + 6.2% employee) on the $60,000 (still under the $168,600 wage base) = $7,440.
Step 3: Medicare tax: 2.9% combined (1.45% + 1.45%) on $60,000 = $1,740.
Step 4: Total additional FICA = $7,440 + $1,740 = $9,180.
Step 5: Distributions are NOT subject to FICA, which is why the original underpayment of salary triggers the adjustment.
