blocks.text: Answer: Reclassifying $60,000 of distributions to wages creates about $9,180 of additional FICA. Takeaway: S-corp owners must pay reasonable W-2 wages; understating salary to dodge payroll tax invites reclassification.

topics.title: Corporate Charitable Contribution 10% Taxable Income Limit

blocks.text: A C corporation has taxable income of $500,000 before any charitable deduction (and before the DRD). It donated $70,000 cash to qualified charities in 2024. How much is deductible and what carries over?
Steps

items: Step 1: The corporate charitable deduction is limited to 10% of taxable income computed before the charitable deduction, DRD, and certain other items.
Step 3: Current deduction = lesser of contribution $70,000 and limit $50,000 = $50,000.
Step 4: Carryover = $70,000 - $50,000 = $20,000, carried forward up to 5 years.
Step 5: The carryover is usable in a future year only after that year's own contributions, within that year's 10% limit.

blocks.text: Answer: Deduct $50,000 now; carry $20,000 forward up to 5 years. Takeaway: corporate charity is capped at 10% of taxable income, with a 5-year carryforward.

A C corporation (not a personal service or holding company) has accumulated taxable income of $400,000 it cannot justify retaining for business needs. It has never accumulated earnings before. What is the accumulated earnings tax, and how does the credit apply?
Steps

items: Step 1: The accumulated earnings credit allows a minimum accumulation of $250,000 (standard, non-service corporation) without penalty.
Step 2: Accumulated taxable income subject to tax = $400,000 - $250,000 credit = $150,000 (assuming no greater reasonable business need is shown).
Step 3: The accumulated earnings tax rate is 20% (matching the qualified dividend rate).
Step 4: Accumulated earnings tax = 20% x $150,000 = $30,000.
Step 5: This is a penalty tax in addition to regular corporate income tax, intended to discourage hoarding earnings to avoid shareholder dividend tax.

blocks.text: Answer: The accumulated earnings tax is $30,000. Takeaway: corporations get a $250,000 accumulation credit ($150,000 for service firms); excess unjustified accumulations are taxed at 20%.

topics.title: Built-In Gains Tax on a Converted S Corporation

blocks.text: A C corporation elects S status. At conversion it holds an asset with a built-in gain of $100,000. Within the 5-year recognition period it sells the asset, recognizing the full $100,000 gain. The corporate tax rate is 21%. Compute the built-in gains tax.
Steps

items: Step 1: The built-in gains (BIG) tax applies when an S corporation sells appreciated assets that had net unrealized built-in gain at conversion, within the 5-year recognition period.
Step 2: Recognized built-in gain = $100,000.
Step 3: BIG tax rate = the highest corporate rate, 21%.
Step 4: Built-in gains tax = 21% x $100,000 = $21,000 (paid at the corporate level).
Step 5: The gain net of the BIG tax ($100,000 - $21,000 = $79,000) then passes through to shareholders, reduced by the BIG tax already paid.

blocks.text: Answer: The built-in gains tax is $21,000. Takeaway: selling appreciated assets within 5 years of converting C to S triggers a 21% corporate-level BIG tax.

A new partner buys a 1/3 interest for $90,000. At that time her share of the partnership's inside basis in assets is $60,000, and the partnership has a valid Section 754 election in place. Compute her Section 743(b) basis adjustment.
Steps

items: Step 1: A Section 754 election allows the partnership to adjust the inside basis of its assets when an interest is transferred.
Step 2: The buyer's outside basis = purchase price = $90,000.
Step 3: Her proportionate share of the partnership's inside basis in assets = $60,000.
Step 4: Section 743(b) adjustment = outside basis - share of inside basis = $90,000 - $60,000 = $30,000 (a positive step-up).
Step 5: This $30,000 adjustment is personal to the buyer and increases her share of depreciation and reduces gain on later asset sales.

blocks.text: Answer: The Section 743(b) step-up is $30,000, special to the new partner. Takeaway: a 754 election lets a purchasing partner adjust inside basis to match the price paid, eliminating the inside/outside basis disparity.

topics.title: C Corporation Income Tax (Flat 21%) With NOL Limit

blocks.text: A C corporation has 2024 taxable income of $500,000 before any NOL deduction and has a $300,000 post-2017 NOL carryforward. Compute the corporate tax after applying the NOL.
Steps

items: Step 1: Post-2017 NOLs offset at most 80% of taxable income.
Step 3: NOL used = lesser of $300,000 available and $400,000 limit = $300,000 (full NOL fits).
Step 4: Taxable income after NOL = $500,000 - $300,000 = $200,000.
Step 5: Corporate tax = 21% x $200,000 = $42,000.
Step 6: NOL carryforward remaining = $0.

blocks.text: Answer: Corporate tax is $42,000 after using the full $300,000 NOL. Takeaway: C corporations pay a flat 21%, and post-2017 NOLs are capped at 80% of taxable income (here the full NOL was within the cap).

topics.title: Hobby vs. Business: Tax Treatment of Hobby Income

blocks.text: An individual earns $9,000 from an activity the IRS classifies as a hobby (not engaged in for profit) in 2024 and incurs $6,500 of related expenses. The taxpayer wonders how income and expenses are reported under current law.
Steps

items: Step 1: Determine income inclusion. All hobby income is taxable and reported as other income: $9,000 is included in gross income.
Step 2: Determine expense treatment. For 2018-2025, miscellaneous itemized deductions subject to the 2% floor are suspended; hobby expenses fall in this category.
Step 3: Therefore the $6,500 of hobby expenses is NOT deductible at all under current law.
Step 4: Taxable amount from the hobby = $9,000 income with $0 deductible expenses = $9,000 fully taxed.
Step 5: Contrast with a genuine trade or business (Schedule C), where the $6,500 would be deductible against the $9,000, leaving $2,500 net profit subject to income and SE tax.
Step 6: Conclusion: hobby classification is unfavorable - full income, no expense offset.

blocks.text: Answer: All $9,000 of hobby income is taxable and none of the $6,500 expenses is deductible (2018-2025 suspension). Takeaway: hobby losses cannot offset income; only a for-profit business on Schedule C can deduct expenses.

topics.title: Net Operating Loss Carryforward for an Individual (Post-2017 Rules)

blocks.text: A sole proprietor has a 2024 net operating loss of $90,000 carried to 2025. In 2025 the taxpayer has taxable income of $100,000 before applying the NOL (and before the NOL deduction, with no other special items). How much of the NOL can be used in 2025 and what carries forward?
Steps

items: Step 1: Apply the post-2017 rule: NOLs arising after 2017 may not be carried back (generally) and carry forward indefinitely.
Step 2: The NOL deduction is limited to 80% of taxable income computed without the NOL deduction.
Step 4: NOL available is $90,000, but the deduction is capped at the $80,000 limit.
Step 5: 2025 NOL deduction = $80,000; taxable income after NOL = $100,000 - $80,000 = $20,000.
Step 6: Remaining NOL carryforward = $90,000 - $80,000 = $10,000 carried to 2026 (indefinitely).

blocks.text: Answer: The taxpayer deducts $80,000 of the NOL in 2025 (80% limit), leaving $20,000 of taxable income and a $10,000 NOL carryforward. Takeaway: post-2017 NOLs carry forward indefinitely but are limited to 80% of taxable income each year.

topics.title: Passive Activity Loss Release on Full Disposition

blocks.text: An investor owns a passive rental partnership interest with $40,000 of suspended passive losses carried over from prior years. In 2024 the activity itself generates a $5,000 passive loss, and the investor sells the entire interest in a fully taxable sale to an unrelated party, recognizing a $12,000 gain. What is the net effect on the investor's 2024 income from this activity?
Steps

items: Step 1: On a fully taxable disposition of an entire passive interest, all suspended passive losses are released and become fully deductible.
Step 2: Total suspended/current passive losses = $40,000 prior suspended + $5,000 current-year loss = $45,000.
Step 3: The gain on sale is $12,000 (this gain is itself passive income for netting purposes).
Step 4: Net the released losses against the gain and other income: $12,000 gain - $45,000 losses = $33,000 net loss.
Step 5: Because of the full disposition, the entire $33,000 net loss is deductible against any income (no longer limited to passive income).
Step 6: Net 2024 effect: a $33,000 ordinary/non-passive-limited loss available against other income.

blocks.text: Answer: A fully taxable disposition frees all $45,000 of losses; netted against the $12,000 gain, the investor deducts a $33,000 loss against any income. Takeaway: complete disposition of a passive activity to an unrelated party releases all suspended passive losses.

topics.title: Sole Proprietor Self-Employed Health Insurance Deduction Limit

blocks.text: A self-employed consultant reports $25,000 of net profit on Schedule C for 2024 and pays $18,000 in health insurance premiums for herself. Her deductible one-half of SE tax is $1,766. She has no other earned income and was not eligible for any employer-subsidized health plan. What is her self-employed health insurance deduction?
Steps

items: Step 1: The self-employed health insurance deduction is limited to net SE earnings from the business after subtracting the deductible half of SE tax.
Step 2: Earned income limit = Schedule C net profit $25,000 - one-half SE tax $1,766 = $23,234.
Step 3: Premiums paid = $18,000; compare to the earned income limit of $23,234.
Step 4: Since $18,000 < $23,234, the premiums are not limited by earnings.
Step 5: Deductible amount = $18,000 (the full premiums).
Step 6: This is an above-the-line deduction (Schedule 1), reducing AGI but not Schedule C profit or SE tax.

blocks.text: Answer: She may deduct the full $18,000 of premiums above the line because it is below her $23,234 earnings limit. Takeaway: the self-employed health insurance deduction cannot exceed net SE earnings (net profit minus the deductible half of SE tax).

Jordan contributes $30,000 cash and equipment with an adjusted basis of $20,000 (FMV $35,000) to a partnership. The partnership also assumes a $10,000 share of liabilities that Jordan bears. In the first year Jordan's share of ordinary income is $15,000, and the partnership distributes $25,000 cash to Jordan. Find Jordan's ending outside basis.
Steps

items: Step 1: Initial basis = cash $30,000 + adjusted basis of equipment $20,000 = $50,000 (carryover basis under section 722).
Step 2: Add Jordan's share of partnership liabilities (section 752): $50,000 + $10,000 = $60,000.
Step 3: Add share of income: $60,000 + $15,000 = $75,000.
Step 4: Subtract the cash distribution: $75,000 − $25,000 = $50,000.
Step 5: The distribution ($25,000) is less than basis ($75,000), so no gain is recognized.

blocks.text: Answer: Ending outside basis is $50,000. The $15,000 built-in gain on the equipment ($35,000 − $20,000) is allocated to Jordan under section 704(c).

Nia starts the year with stock basis of $10,000 and no loan basis. The S corporation allocates her $15,000 of ordinary income, $1,000 of tax-exempt interest, $2,000 of nondeductible expenses, and a $7,000 separately stated capital loss. It also distributes $20,000 to her. What is her ending stock basis and which loss is allowed?
Steps

items: Step 1: Increase basis for income items first: $10,000 + $15,000 + $1,000 = $26,000.
Step 2: Reduce basis for distributions next: $26,000 − $20,000 = $6,000.
Step 3: Reduce basis for nondeductible expenses: $6,000 − $2,000 = $4,000.
Step 4: Reduce basis for losses last, but not below zero: the $7,000 loss is limited to $4,000.
Step 5: The disallowed $3,000 carries forward and can be used when basis increases.

blocks.text: Answer: Ending basis is $0; Nia deducts $4,000 of the loss and carries forward $3,000. The ordering is income, distributions, nondeductible expenses, then losses.
A C corporation owns 25% of another domestic corporation and receives $100,000 of dividends. Its taxable income before the DRD is $400,000. Compute the DRD.
Steps

items: Step 1: Ownership of 20% or more but less than 80% gives a 65% deduction.
Step 3: The deduction is limited to 65% of taxable income before the DRD: 65% × $400,000 = $260,000, which is not binding.
Step 5: Taxable income = $400,000 − $65,000 = $335,000, before other deductions.

blocks.text: Answer: The DRD is $65,000. If the corporation owned less than 20%, the deduction would be 50%.

Alex starts the year with a $40,000 outside basis in a partnership. During the year his share of partnership income is $25,000, his share of tax-exempt income is $2,000, he receives a $15,000 cash distribution, and his share of nondeductible expenses is $1,000. Compute his year-end basis.
Steps

items: Step 1: Beginning basis = $40,000.
Step 2: Add ordinary income share: $40,000 + $25,000 = $65,000.
Step 3: Add tax-exempt income (it still increases basis): $65,000 + $2,000 = $67,000.
Step 4: Subtract the cash distribution: $67,000 - $15,000 = $52,000.
Step 5: Subtract nondeductible expenses: $52,000 - $1,000 = $51,000.
Step 6: Year-end outside basis = $51,000.

blocks.text: Answer: Ending outside basis is $51,000. Income (including tax-exempt) raises basis; distributions and nondeductible items lower it.

Beth owns 100% of an S corporation. Her beginning stock basis is $30,000. The S corp passes through $18,000 of ordinary income, $4,000 of separately stated charitable contributions, and a $20,000 cash distribution. Compute her ending stock basis and the taxability of the distribution.
Steps

items: Step 1: Beginning stock basis = $30,000.
Step 2: Increase for ordinary income: $30,000 + $18,000 = $48,000.
Step 3: Apply the distribution before deductions: $48,000 - $20,000 = $28,000 (distribution is within basis, so tax-free).
Step 4: Decrease for the charitable contribution pass-through: $28,000 - $4,000 = $24,000.
Step 5: Ending stock basis = $24,000, and the $20,000 distribution is nontaxable return of basis.

blocks.text: Answer: Ending stock basis is $24,000 and the $20,000 distribution is tax-free. Distributions reduce basis before loss and deduction items.

A C corporation generates a $200,000 NOL in 2024 and carries it forward to 2025, when it has taxable income of $150,000 before the NOL. Post-2017 NOLs may offset only 80% of taxable income. Compute the NOL used, taxable income, and carryover.
Steps

items: Step 1: 80% limitation on 2025 income = 80% x $150,000 = $120,000.
Step 2: NOL available = $200,000; usable amount = lesser of $200,000 or $120,000 = $120,000.
Step 3: 2025 taxable income after NOL = $150,000 - $120,000 = $30,000.
Step 4: Remaining NOL carryover = $200,000 - $120,000 = $80,000.
Step 5: The $80,000 carries forward indefinitely, again subject to the 80% cap.

blocks.text: Answer: Use $120,000 of NOL, leaving $30,000 taxable income and an $80,000 carryover. Post-2017 NOLs are capped at 80% of taxable income.

topics.title: Partnership Guaranteed Payment and Distributive Share

blocks.text: A two-person partnership earns $160,000 before any guaranteed payments. Partner A receives a $40,000 guaranteed payment for services; the remaining profit is split 50/50. Compute each partner's total income from the partnership.
Steps

items: Step 1: Deduct the guaranteed payment from partnership income: $160,000 - $40,000 = $120,000 remaining profit.
Step 2: Split remaining profit 50/50: each partner's distributive share = $120,000 / 2 = $60,000.
Step 3: Partner A total = $40,000 guaranteed payment + $60,000 distributive share = $100,000.
Step 4: Partner B total = $0 guaranteed payment + $60,000 distributive share = $60,000.
Step 5: Check: $100,000 + $60,000 = $160,000, matching total partnership income.

blocks.text: Answer: Partner A reports $100,000 and Partner B reports $60,000. Guaranteed payments are deducted before splitting the remaining profit.

topics.title: C Corporation Tax with Dividends-Received Deduction

blocks.text: A C corporation has $500,000 of operating income and receives $40,000 in dividends from a domestic corporation in which it owns 25% (qualifying for the 65% dividends-received deduction). The flat corporate rate is 21%. Compute taxable income and the corporate tax.
Steps

items: Step 1: Gross income = $500,000 operating income + $40,000 dividends = $540,000.
Step 2: Dividends-received deduction at 65% ownership tier = 65% x $40,000 = $26,000.
Step 4: Corporate tax = 21% x $514,000 = $107,940.
Step 5: The DRD reduces double taxation on inter-corporate dividends.

blocks.text: Answer: Taxable income is $514,000 and the tax is $107,940. A 20-to-80% owner gets a 65% dividends-received deduction.

An S corporation begins the year with an AAA balance of $50,000. It has $80,000 of ordinary income, $10,000 of tax-exempt income, $5,000 of nondeductible expenses, and makes a $40,000 distribution. Compute the year-end AAA (note tax-exempt income does not increase AAA).
Steps

items: Step 1: Beginning AAA = $50,000.
Step 2: Increase for ordinary income: $50,000 + $80,000 = $130,000.
Step 3: Tax-exempt income does NOT affect AAA, so make no adjustment for the $10,000.
Step 4: Decrease for nondeductible expenses: $130,000 - $5,000 = $125,000.
Step 5: Decrease for the distribution: $125,000 - $40,000 = $85,000.
Step 6: Year-end AAA = $85,000.

blocks.text: Answer: Ending AAA is $85,000. Unlike stock basis, AAA is not increased by tax-exempt income.

topics.title: Partner Outside Basis Including Share of Liabilities

blocks.text: Tara contributes $40,000 cash for a 25% interest in a partnership. The partnership has $120,000 of recourse liabilities allocated by interest, and during the year her distributive share of income is $15,000 and she takes a $10,000 cash distribution. Compute her year-end outside basis.
Steps

items: Step 1: Initial basis = cash contributed $40,000.
Step 2: Add her share of partnership liabilities (treated as a deemed cash contribution): 25% x $120,000 = $30,000.
Step 3: Basis after liabilities = $40,000 + $30,000 = $70,000.
Step 4: Add distributive share of income: $70,000 + $15,000 = $85,000.
Step 5: Subtract cash distribution: $85,000 - $10,000 = $75,000.
Step 6: Year-end outside basis = $75,000 (no liability changes assumed during the year).

blocks.text: Answer: Outside basis is $75,000. A partner's share of partnership liabilities increases outside basis as if cash were contributed.

topics.title: Section 704(c) Built-In Gain Allocation on Contributed Property

blocks.text: Lena contributes land with a basis of $30,000 and FMV of $50,000 to an equal two-person partnership. The partnership later sells the land for $56,000. Under Section 704(c), allocate the gain between Lena and the other partner.
Steps

items: Step 1: Built-in gain at contribution = FMV $50,000 - basis $30,000 = $20,000; this is precontribution gain belonging to Lena.
Step 2: Total gain on sale = $56,000 sale price - $30,000 inside basis = $26,000.
Step 3: Post-contribution appreciation = $56,000 - $50,000 = $6,000 (gain after contribution).
Step 4: Section 704(c) allocates the $20,000 built-in gain entirely to Lena.
Step 5: The remaining $6,000 post-contribution gain is shared 50/50: $3,000 each.
Step 6: Lena's total gain = $20,000 + $3,000 = $23,000; other partner = $3,000.

blocks.text: Answer: Lena is allocated $23,000 and the other partner $3,000. Section 704(c) assigns the precontribution built-in gain to the contributing partner.

topics.title: S Corporation Stock Basis, Debt Basis, and Loss Limitation

blocks.text: An S corporation shareholder begins the year with $20,000 stock basis and a $15,000 direct loan to the corporation (debt basis). The K-1 passes through a $45,000 ordinary loss. Determine the deductible loss and the suspended loss.
Steps

items: Step 1: Loss first reduces stock basis: $20,000 absorbed, leaving stock basis $0.
Step 3: Loss then reduces debt basis: $15,000 absorbed, leaving debt basis $0.
Step 4: Remaining loss = $25,000 - $15,000 = $10,000, which exceeds available basis.
Step 5: Deductible loss this year = $20,000 + $15,000 = $35,000.
Step 6: Suspended loss carried forward = $10,000, deductible when basis is restored.
Step 7: Future income first restores debt basis, then stock basis.

blocks.text: Answer: Deductible loss is $35,000; $10,000 is suspended. S-corp losses are limited to combined stock and debt basis, with the excess carried forward.

topics.title: Guaranteed Payment vs Distributive Share for a Partner

blocks.text: A partnership agreement gives partner Ben a $60,000 guaranteed payment for services plus a 20% share of remaining profits. Before deducting the guaranteed payment, partnership ordinary income is $200,000. Compute Ben's total self-employment income from the partnership.
Steps

items: Step 1: Deduct the guaranteed payment from partnership income: $200,000 - $60,000 = $140,000 remaining profit.
Step 2: Ben's distributive share = 20% x $140,000 = $28,000.
Step 3: Ben's guaranteed payment is ordinary income to him: $60,000.
Step 4: Both items are self-employment income for a general partner.
Step 6: The guaranteed payment is deductible by the partnership and reduces the residual profit shared by all partners.

blocks.text: Answer: Ben reports $88,000 of self-employment income. Guaranteed payments are deducted before computing distributive shares and are themselves taxable to the recipient.

topics.title: Partnership Cash Distribution Exceeding Outside Basis

blocks.text: A partner with an outside basis of $18,000 receives a current cash distribution of $25,000. No property other than cash is distributed. Determine the tax consequences.
Steps

items: Step 1: A cash distribution first reduces outside basis, tax-free, to the extent of basis.
Step 2: Basis absorbs $18,000 of the $25,000 distribution, reducing basis to $0.
Step 3: Excess cash over basis = $25,000 - $18,000 = $7,000.
Step 4: Cash distributions exceeding outside basis are taxable as capital gain.
Step 5: The partner recognizes $7,000 of capital gain.
Step 6: Ending outside basis = $0.

blocks.text: Answer: The partner recognizes $7,000 of capital gain and basis drops to $0. Cash distributions above outside basis trigger gain; distributions within basis are tax-free.

A C corporation receives $100,000 in dividends from a domestic corporation in which it owns 30% (a 20%-or-more but under-80% interest). The corporation's taxable income before the DRD is $90,000. The DRD percentage for 20%-to-80% ownership is 65%. Compute the dividends-received deduction.
Steps

items: Step 1: Tentative DRD = 65% x $100,000 dividends = $65,000.
Step 2: Apply the taxable-income limitation: DRD generally cannot exceed 65% of taxable income for this tier.
Step 3: Taxable-income limit = 65% x $90,000 = $58,500.
Step 4: The limitation does not apply if taking the full DRD creates or increases a net operating loss. Test: taxable income $90,000 - full DRD $65,000 = $25,000 (positive, no NOL).
Step 5: Because no NOL is created, the limitation applies: DRD = lesser of $65,000 and $58,500 = $58,500.

blocks.text: Answer: DRD is $58,500 (limited to 65% of taxable income). The income limit is waived only when the full DRD would create or enlarge an NOL.

topics.title: C-Corporation Net Operating Loss: 80% Taxable-Income Limit

blocks.text: A C corporation generated a $200,000 NOL in 2022 (a post-2017 NOL with no carryback and an 80% usage limit). In 2024 it has taxable income of $150,000 before any NOL deduction. How much NOL can it use in 2024 and what carries forward?
Steps

items: Step 1: Post-2017 NOLs may offset only 80% of taxable income in the carryforward year.
Step 3: Available NOL = $200,000, which exceeds the $120,000 limit.
Step 4: NOL deduction in 2024 = $120,000.
Step 5: 2024 taxable income after NOL = $150,000 - $120,000 = $30,000.
Step 6: Remaining NOL carryforward = $200,000 - $120,000 = $80,000 (carries forward indefinitely).

blocks.text: Answer: Use $120,000 of NOL in 2024, leaving $80,000 to carry forward indefinitely. Post-2017 NOLs cannot reduce taxable income below 20% of pre-NOL income.

topics.title: Accumulated Earnings & Profits and Dividend vs. Return of Capital

blocks.text: A C corporation distributes $80,000 cash to its sole shareholder in 2024. The corporation has accumulated E&P of $30,000 and current-year E&P of $20,000. The shareholder's stock basis is $15,000. Characterize the $80,000 distribution.
Steps

items: Step 1: Distributions are dividends to the extent of current plus accumulated E&P.
Step 2: Total E&P available = $20,000 current + $30,000 accumulated = $50,000.
Step 3: Dividend income (ordinary, possibly qualified) = $50,000.
Step 4: Remaining distribution = $80,000 - $50,000 = $30,000, treated as a return of capital up to stock basis.
Step 5: Return of capital reduces basis: $15,000 of the $30,000 reduces basis to $0 (tax-free).
Step 6: Excess over basis = $30,000 - $15,000 = $15,000, taxed as capital gain.

blocks.text: Answer: $50,000 is a dividend, $15,000 a tax-free return of capital, and $15,000 a capital gain. The ordering is E&P first, then basis, then gain.

A C corporation has taxable income of $400,000 before any charitable deduction and before the dividends-received deduction. It made cash charitable contributions of $50,000. Corporate charitable deductions are limited to 10% of taxable income (computed without the contribution and certain other deductions). Compute the deductible amount and the carryover.
Steps

items: Step 2: Contributions made = $50,000, which exceeds the $40,000 limit.
Step 3: Deductible this year = $40,000.
Step 4: Excess carryover = $50,000 - $40,000 = $10,000.
Step 5: The $10,000 carries forward up to 5 years, subject to the 10% limit in those years.

blocks.text: Answer: Deduct $40,000 now; carry $10,000 forward up to 5 years. Corporations are capped at 10% of taxable income (with specified modifications).

An individual sells a commercial building for $600,000. Original cost was $500,000 and straight-line depreciation taken was $150,000, giving an adjusted basis of $350,000. How is the gain characterized and taxed (assume held long-term, in the 24% bracket)?
Steps

items: Step 1: Total gain = amount realized $600,000 - adjusted basis $350,000 = $250,000.
Step 2: Section 1250 recapture of excess depreciation is $0 because only straight-line was used.
Step 3: Unrecaptured Section 1250 gain = the lesser of total gain or straight-line depreciation = min($250,000, $150,000) = $150,000, taxed at a maximum 25% rate.
Step 4: Remaining Section 1231 gain = $250,000 - $150,000 = $100,000, taxed at the long-term capital gain rate (e.g., 15%).

blocks.text: Answer: Gain is $150,000 unrecaptured 1250 (max 25%) and $100,000 LTCG (15%), totaling about $52,500 of tax. Takeaway: straight-line depreciation on real property is recaptured as unrecaptured 1250 gain at up to 25%, not as ordinary income.

topics.title: Installment Sale With Section 1245 Recapture in Year of Sale

blocks.text: A business sells equipment for $100,000 on an installment note ($20,000 down in 2024; rest later). Adjusted basis is $30,000 (original cost $80,000, depreciation $50,000). How much gain is reported in 2024?
Steps

items: Step 2: Section 1245 depreciation recapture = lesser of depreciation taken ($50,000) or gain ($70,000) = $50,000. ALL recapture is reported in the year of sale, regardless of installments.
Step 3: Gain eligible for installment reporting = total gain $70,000 - recapture $50,000 = $20,000 (Section 1231/capital).
Step 4: Recompute gross profit ratio on the installment portion: $20,000 / $100,000 contract price = 20%.
Step 5: Installment gain on the $20,000 down payment = 20% x $20,000 = $4,000.
Step 6: 2024 reported gain = $50,000 recapture (ordinary) + $4,000 installment = $54,000.

blocks.text: Answer: Report $54,000 of gain in 2024 ($50,000 ordinary recapture + $4,000 installment gain). Takeaway: Section 1245 recapture is fully taxed in the year of sale even when the rest of the gain is spread over installments.

topics.title: Like-Kind Exchange With Boot and Mortgage Relief

blocks.text: A taxpayer exchanges real estate (adjusted basis $200,000, subject to a $60,000 mortgage assumed by the other party) for replacement real estate worth $250,000 plus $10,000 cash received. The relinquished property's FMV is $320,000. Compute realized gain, recognized gain, and new basis.
Steps

items: Step 1: Total consideration received = replacement property $250,000 + cash boot $10,000 + debt relief $60,000 = $320,000.
Step 2: Realized gain = $320,000 - adjusted basis $200,000 = $120,000.
Step 3: Total boot = cash $10,000 + net debt relief $60,000 = $70,000.
Step 4: Recognized gain = lesser of realized gain ($120,000) or boot ($70,000) = $70,000.
Step 5: New basis = old basis $200,000 + recognized gain $70,000 - boot received ($10,000 cash + $60,000 debt relief = $70,000) = $200,000.
Step 6: Check: deferred gain = $120,000 - $70,000 = $50,000, equal to FMV of new property $250,000 - new basis $200,000.

blocks.text: Answer: Realized gain $120,000; recognized gain $70,000; basis in new property $200,000 (deferring $50,000). Takeaway: both cash and mortgage relief count as boot, triggering gain up to the realized amount.

topics.title: Section 1231 Netting of Gains and Losses

blocks.text: A business has the following 2024 results: a $40,000 Section 1231 gain on land sold, a $15,000 Section 1231 loss on equipment, and a $5,000 casualty loss on business property. There are no nonrecaptured 1231 losses from prior years. How is the net result taxed?
Steps

items: Step 1: Casualty/theft losses on business property are netted first separately. Here only a $5,000 loss, no offsetting casualty gain, so it goes directly as an ordinary loss (not into the 1231 hotchpot).
Step 2: Net the remaining Section 1231 items: $40,000 gain - $15,000 loss = $25,000 net 1231 gain.
Step 3: A net Section 1231 GAIN is treated as long-term capital gain (favorable).
Step 4: Check the 5-year lookback: no nonrecaptured 1231 losses, so none of the gain is recharacterized as ordinary.
Step 5: Result: $25,000 long-term capital gain plus a separate $5,000 ordinary casualty loss.

blocks.text: Answer: Net $25,000 Section 1231 gain is taxed as LTCG; the $5,000 casualty loss is ordinary. Takeaway: a net 1231 gain converts to capital gain, but the 5-year lookback can recharacterize it as ordinary if prior 1231 losses exist.

topics.title: Home Office Deduction (Regular Method) With Income Limit

blocks.text: A self-employed consultant uses 300 sq ft of a 1,500 sq ft home (20%) exclusively for business. Annual costs: mortgage interest $12,000, utilities $4,000, insurance $1,500, depreciation on the office portion $2,000. Net business income before the home office deduction is $1,800. Compute the deduction and any carryover.
Steps

items: Step 1: Business-use percentage = 300 / 1,500 = 20%.
Step 2: Indirect expenses x 20%: mortgage interest $12,000 x 20% = $2,400; utilities $4,000 x 20% = $800; insurance $1,500 x 20% = $300; depreciation = $2,000 (already office portion).
Step 3: The deduction cannot exceed net business income of $1,800 (gross income limit).
Step 4: Allocate to the $1,800 limit in order: first the $2,400 of allocable mortgage interest alone exceeds $1,800, so only $1,800 is deductible this year.

Step 5: Disallowed home office expenses carry forward to next year: utilities, insurance, and depreciation ($800 + $300 + $2,000 = $3,100) plus the excess mortgage interest, subject to next year's limit. (Note: mortgage interest portion may instead be deducted on Schedule A.)

blocks.text: Answer: Current home office deduction is limited to $1,800; the excess carries forward. Takeaway: the regular-method home office deduction cannot create or increase a business loss; disallowed amounts carry over.

topics.title: MACRS Half-Year Convention First-Year Depreciation (5-Year Property)

blocks.text: A business places $50,000 of 5-year MACRS property in service in 2024 and elects out of bonus depreciation and Section 179. Using the 200% declining-balance method with the half-year convention (Year 1 rate 20%), compute first- and second-year depreciation.
Steps

items: Step 1: 5-year property uses the 200% DB method; the half-year convention treats it as placed in service mid-year.
Step 2: Year 1 MACRS rate (5-year, half-year) = 20.00%.
Step 3: Year 1 depreciation = $50,000 x 20.00% = $10,000.
Step 4: Year 2 MACRS rate = 32.00%.
Step 5: Year 2 depreciation = $50,000 x 32.00% = $16,000.
Step 6: Accumulated depreciation after 2 years = $10,000 + $16,000 = $26,000.

blocks.text: Answer: Year 1 depreciation is $10,000 and Year 2 is $16,000. Takeaway: 5-year MACRS uses fixed table percentages (20%, 32%, ...) reflecting 200% DB and the half-year convention.

topics.title: Section 179 Expensing With Taxable Income Limit

blocks.text: A business buys $200,000 of qualifying equipment in 2024 (well below the phase-out threshold). Its taxable income from the business before any Section 179 deduction is $120,000. The 2024 Section 179 limit is $1,220,000. How much can be expensed and what carries over?
Steps

items: Step 1: The dollar limit ($1,220,000) and phase-out are not binding here; $200,000 is below them.
Step 2: Section 179 cannot exceed the aggregate taxable income from the active conduct of trades or businesses.
Step 3: Taxable income limit = $120,000.
Step 4: Section 179 deduction this year = lesser of $200,000 (cost) and $120,000 (income limit) = $120,000.
Step 5: Disallowed amount = $200,000 - $120,000 = $80,000, carried forward to future years (subject to future income limits).
Step 6: The remaining $80,000 basis could alternatively be recovered via bonus or regular MACRS depreciation.

blocks.text: Answer: Expense $120,000 now; carry $80,000 of Section 179 forward. Takeaway: Section 179 cannot create a loss - it is limited to business taxable income, with carryover of the excess.

topics.title: Partnership Ordinary Income and Separately Stated Items

blocks.text: A two-person equal partnership reports for 2024: gross receipts $400,000; cost of goods sold $180,000; salaries to non-partner employees $90,000; rent $24,000; a $10,000 long-term capital gain; $3,000 of charitable contributions; and a $5,000 Section 179 expense. What is the partnership's ordinary business income, and what is each partner's share of ordinary income?
Steps

items: Step 1: Identify separately stated items that are NOT in ordinary income: long-term capital gain $10,000, charitable contributions $3,000, and Section 179 expense $5,000.
Step 2: Compute ordinary business income (page 1, Form 1065) using only ordinary items: gross profit = $400,000 - $180,000 = $220,000.
Step 3: Subtract ordinary deductions: $220,000 - salaries $90,000 - rent $24,000 = $106,000 ordinary business income.
Step 4: Do NOT subtract the separately stated items at the entity ordinary-income line (they pass through separately).
Step 5: Each equal partner's share of ordinary income = $106,000 / 2 = $53,000.
Step 6: Each partner also separately receives $5,000 LTCG, $1,500 charitable contribution, and $2,500 Section 179, reported on their own returns.

blocks.text: Answer: Partnership ordinary business income is $106,000; each partner reports $53,000 of ordinary income plus separately stated items. Takeaway: capital gains, charitable contributions, and Section 179 are separately stated and excluded from partnership ordinary income.

topics.title: Partnership Formation: Contribution of Property With a Liability

blocks.text: Anna contributes land with a $30,000 adjusted basis and $100,000 fair market value to a partnership for a 25% interest. The land is subject to a $40,000 mortgage the partnership assumes. What is Anna's recognized gain (if any) and her outside basis after formation?
Steps

items: Step 1: Under Section 721, no gain is generally recognized on a contribution of property to a partnership in exchange for an interest.
Step 2: However, relief of liabilities is treated as a deemed cash distribution. Anna is relieved of $40,000 of debt but reassumes her 25% share: 25% x $40,000 = $10,000.
Step 3: Net debt relief (deemed distribution) = $40,000 - $10,000 = $30,000.
Step 4: Compute Anna's tentative outside basis: contributed basis $30,000 + her share of partnership liabilities $10,000 = $40,000, then reduce by the $40,000 debt relief = $0.
Step 5: Gain is recognized only if the deemed distribution exceeds basis. Compare $30,000 net debt relief to her pre-relief basis of $30,000 (contributed basis) - they are equal, so no gain.
Step 6: Anna's outside basis after formation = $0 (basis cannot go below zero); no gain is recognized.

blocks.text: Answer: Anna recognizes no gain, and her outside basis after formation is $0. Takeaway: liability relief is a deemed distribution; gain results only when net relief exceeds the contributing partner's basis.

topics.title: S Corporation Pass-Through With Health Insurance for a 2% Shareholder

blocks.text: An S corporation pays $14,000 of health insurance premiums for its sole shareholder-employee, who owns 100% (a more-than-2% shareholder) and receives a $60,000 W-2 wage before adding the premiums. The corporation's ordinary business income after deducting wages and premiums is $80,000. How are the premiums treated for the shareholder?
Steps

items: Step 1: For a more-than-2% S corporation shareholder, health insurance premiums paid by the corporation are added to the shareholder's W-2 wages (Box 1).
Step 2: Adjusted W-2 wages = $60,000 base + $14,000 premiums = $74,000 reported in Box 1.
Step 3: The $14,000 is NOT subject to Social Security/Medicare (FICA) tax, so Boxes 3 and 5 remain $60,000.
Step 4: The corporation deducts the $14,000 as compensation (already reflected in the $80,000 ordinary income computation).
Step 5: The shareholder then claims a $14,000 self-employed health insurance deduction above the line on the individual return (limited to W-2 Medicare wages from the S corp).
Step 6: Net result: the premiums are income-tax neutral to the shareholder (included in wages, then deducted) but avoid FICA.

blocks.text: Answer: The $14,000 premium is added to Box 1 wages ($74,000) but excluded from FICA wages; the shareholder deducts $14,000 above the line. Takeaway: 2%+ S shareholder health premiums are W-2 wages for income tax (not FICA) and are deductible above the line.

topics.title: C Corporation Capital Loss Limitation and Carryover

blocks.text: A C corporation has $50,000 of ordinary business income in 2024, a $12,000 long-term capital gain, and a $30,000 short-term capital loss. How much capital loss can the corporation deduct in 2024, and what is the carryover treatment?
Steps

items: Step 1: Net the corporation's capital transactions: $12,000 LTCG - $30,000 STCL = $18,000 net capital loss.
Step 2: Apply the corporate rule: a C corporation may deduct capital losses ONLY against capital gains (no $3,000 ordinary offset like individuals get).
Step 3: Capital losses deductible in 2024 = limited to the $12,000 of capital gains; the $12,000 gain is fully offset, leaving $0 net capital income.
Step 4: The corporation's taxable income is just the ordinary income of $50,000 (no capital loss benefit against ordinary income).
Step 5: The $18,000 net capital loss is carried back 3 years and forward 5 years (corporate rule) to offset capital gains in those years.
Step 6: Carried-over corporate capital losses are always treated as short-term losses in the carryover years.

blocks.text: Answer: The corporation deducts $12,000 of capital loss (only against gains), taxes $50,000 ordinary income, and carries an $18,000 capital loss (back 3/forward 5 years, as short-term). Takeaway: C corporations may use capital losses only against capital gains, never against ordinary income.

topics.title: Corporate Estimated Tax Required Annual Payment

blocks.text: A C corporation expects 2024 tax of $200,000. Its prior-year (2023) tax was $150,000, and it is not a 'large corporation' for the prior-year safe harbor. To avoid an underpayment penalty, what is the smallest total required annual estimated payment, and what is each of the four equal installments?
Steps

items: Step 1: Identify the two safe harbors for a non-large C corporation: (a) 100% of current-year tax, or (b) 100% of prior-year tax.
Step 2: Current-year option = 100% x $200,000 = $200,000.
Step 3: Prior-year option = 100% x $150,000 = $150,000 (allowed only if the prior year was a full 12 months and showed a tax liability).
Step 4: The corporation chooses the smaller required amount: $150,000 (prior-year safe harbor).
Step 5: Required annual payment = $150,000; corporate estimates are due in four equal installments.
Step 6: Each installment = $150,000 / 4 = $37,500, due the 15th of the 4th, 6th, 9th, and 12th months of the tax year.

blocks.text: Answer: The smallest required annual payment is $150,000, paid in four $37,500 installments. Takeaway: non-large C corporations can use the lower of 100% of current-year or 100% of prior-year tax for estimated payment safe harbors.
A business sells machinery for $120,000. It cost $100,000 and $70,000 of depreciation was claimed. How is the gain characterized?
Steps

items: Step 3: Section 1245 recapture = lesser of gain ($90,000) or depreciation ($70,000) = $70,000 ordinary income.
Step 4: Remaining gain = $90,000 − $70,000 = $20,000, which is section 1231 gain.
Step 5: Report on Form 4797; net section 1231 gain flows to Schedule D if there are no lookback losses.

blocks.text: Answer: $70,000 is ordinary income and $20,000 is section 1231 gain (long-term capital gain if the net is a gain). If the machinery sold for $85,000, the entire $55,000 gain would be ordinary.

topics.title: MACRS Five-Year Property: Regular vs. Bonus Depreciation (2025)

blocks.text: A business buys $50,000 of five-year property in 2025 in January (after January 19) and places it in service immediately. It uses the half-year convention. Compare year one depreciation using regular MACRS with using 100% bonus depreciation.
Steps

items: Step 1: MACRS five-year table (half-year) percentages: year 1 20.00%, year 2 32.00%, year 3 19.20%, year 4 11.52%, year 5 11.52%, year 6 5.76%.
Step 2: Regular MACRS year 1 = $50,000 × 20% = $10,000.
Step 3: Regular MACRS year 2 = $50,000 × 32% = $16,000.
Step 4: With 100% bonus depreciation (property acquired after January 19, 2025), year 1 deduction = $50,000.
Step 5: If the taxpayer instead elects section 179, the deduction is limited by taxable income from the business.

blocks.text: Answer: Year-one depreciation is $10,000 under regular MACRS and $50,000 under bonus depreciation. Bonus depreciation can be elected out by class of property.
An employee earns $250,000 in wages in 2025 (single filer). What is the Additional Medicare Tax, and who withholds it?
Steps

items: Step 1: The Additional Medicare Tax rate is 0.9% and applies to wages above $200,000 for withholding purposes.
Step 2: Wages above the threshold = $250,000 − $200,000 = $50,000.
Step 3: Additional Medicare Tax = 0.9% × $50,000 = $450.
Step 4: The employer withholds this tax once wages exceed $200,000, regardless of the employee's filing status.
Step 5: The employer pays no matching amount, since this tax is imposed on the employee only.

blocks.text: Answer: The additional tax is $450, withheld by the employer on pay above $200,000 and reconciled on Form 8959. The regular 1.45% Medicare tax still applies to all wages.

topics.title: Employer Payroll Tax on One Employee

blocks.text: An employer pays an employee $60,000 in 2025. The employer pays state unemployment tax on time. Compute the employer's FICA and FUTA for the employee.
Steps

items: Step 1: Employer Social Security = 6.2% × $60,000 = $3,720.
Step 2: Employer Medicare = 1.45% × $60,000 = $870.
Step 3: Employer FICA = $3,720 + $870 = $4,590.
Step 4: FUTA is 6.0% on the first $7,000 less a 5.4% credit, so the net rate is 0.6%: 0.6% × $7,000 = $42.
Step 5: The employee also pays $4,590 of FICA through withholding.

blocks.text: Answer: Employer cost is $4,590 of FICA plus $42 of FUTA, or $4,632 on top of the $60,000 wages.
A company places $4,300,000 of qualifying property in service in 2025. The §179 limit is $2,500,000 and the phase-out begins at $4,000,000. What is the maximum §179 deduction?
Steps

items: Step 1: Amount over the phase-out threshold = $4,300,000 − $4,000,000 = $300,000.
Step 2: The limit is reduced dollar for dollar: $2,500,000 − $300,000 = $2,200,000.
Step 3: The deduction is also limited to taxable income from the active conduct of the business.
Step 4: Property not expensed under §179 can still receive bonus depreciation (100% for property acquired after January 19, 2025).
Step 5: Report on Form 4562.

blocks.text: Answer: The maximum §179 deduction is $2,200,000 before the taxable income limit.

topics.title: Business Mileage and Home Office Simplified Method (2025)

blocks.text: A sole proprietor drives 12,000 business miles in 2025 and uses 250 square feet of her home regularly and exclusively as an office. Compute the vehicle and home office deductions using the simplest methods.
Steps

items: Step 1: 2025 standard mileage rate for business use is 70 cents per mile.
Step 2: Vehicle deduction = 12,000 × $0.70 = $8,400, plus parking and tolls separately.
Step 3: Simplified home office method = $5 per square foot up to 300 square feet.
Step 4: Home office deduction = 250 × $5 = $1,250.
Step 5: Both deductions reduce Schedule C net profit and therefore self-employment tax.

blocks.text: Answer: Vehicle $8,400 plus home office $1,250 equals $9,650 of deductions, before parking and tolls.

topics.title: Change from Cash to Accrual: Section 481(a) Adjustment

blocks.text: A small business changes from cash to accrual and has $60,000 of accounts receivable at the start of the year of change and no payables. Find the §481(a) adjustment and how it is reported.
Steps

items: Step 1: Switching to accrual brings in income previously not recognized: the receivables are $60,000.
Step 2: The adjustment is positive $60,000 because it increases income.
Step 3: A positive §481(a) adjustment is generally spread over four years, including the year of change.
Step 4: Annual inclusion = $60,000 ÷ 4 = $15,000.
Step 5: File Form 3115 to request the change.

blocks.text: Answer: The adjustment is $60,000, included at $15,000 per year for four years. A negative adjustment would be taken entirely in the year of change.

A taxpayer sells business land for $300,000. Adjusted basis is $180,000 and selling expenses are $20,000. The buyer pays $60,000 down in 2024 and the rest over later years. Compute the gross profit percentage and the gain recognized in 2024.
Steps

items: Step 1: Contract price = $300,000 (no mortgage assumed).
Step 2: Gross profit = $300,000 - $180,000 basis - $20,000 selling expenses = $100,000.
Step 3: Gross profit percentage = $100,000 / $300,000 = 33.33%.
Step 4: Payments received in 2024 = $60,000 down payment.
Step 5: Gain recognized in 2024 = $60,000 x 33.33% = $20,000.
Step 6: The remaining gain is recognized as future principal payments are received.

blocks.text: Answer: Gross profit percentage is 33.33% and 2024 gain is $20,000. Each principal payment is taxed at the gross profit percentage.

A business sells equipment for $35,000. Original cost was $50,000 and accumulated depreciation is $30,000, giving an adjusted basis of $20,000. Determine the total gain and how much is ordinary (Section 1245 recapture) versus Section 1231 gain.
Steps

items: Step 1: Adjusted basis = $50,000 cost - $30,000 depreciation = $20,000.
Step 2: Total gain = $35,000 sale price - $20,000 adjusted basis = $15,000.
Step 3: Section 1245 recapture = lesser of total gain ($15,000) or accumulated depreciation ($30,000) = $15,000.
Step 4: All $15,000 is ordinary income recapture; none exceeds prior depreciation.
Step 5: Section 1231 gain = $15,000 - $15,000 = $0 because the sale price did not exceed original cost.

blocks.text: Answer: Total gain is $15,000, all ordinary Section 1245 recapture. Recapture is the lesser of the gain or the depreciation taken.

A taxpayer exchanges business real estate (adjusted basis $100,000, FMV $150,000) for like-kind real estate worth $130,000 plus $20,000 cash boot. Compute the realized gain, recognized gain, and the basis of the new property.
Steps

items: Step 1: Realized gain = total received ($130,000 property + $20,000 cash) - basis $100,000 = $50,000.
Step 2: Recognized gain = lesser of realized gain ($50,000) or boot received ($20,000) = $20,000.
Step 4: Basis of new property = old basis $100,000 + recognized gain $20,000 - boot received $20,000 = $100,000.
Step 5: The $30,000 deferred gain is preserved in the carryover basis of the new property.

blocks.text: Answer: Recognized gain is $20,000 and new-property basis is $100,000. In a 1031 exchange, gain is recognized only up to boot received.

A C corporation converts to an S corporation. At conversion it held an asset with FMV $200,000 and basis $80,000 (net unrealized built-in gain). Within the recognition period the S corp sells the asset for $210,000. The corporate tax rate is 21%. The S corporation's taxable income limitation is $130,000. Compute the BIG tax.
Steps

items: Step 1: Recognized built-in gain = lesser of (a) actual gain or (b) gain that existed at conversion.
Step 2: Built-in gain at conversion = $200,000 - $80,000 = $120,000.
Step 3: Actual gain on sale = $210,000 - $80,000 = $130,000 (the extra $10,000 arose after conversion).
Step 4: Recognized built-in gain = lesser of $120,000 and $130,000 = $120,000.
Step 5: Apply the taxable income limitation: lesser of $120,000 or $130,000 = $120,000.
Step 7: Post-conversion $10,000 appreciation is not subject to BIG tax.

blocks.text: Answer: BIG tax is $25,200. Only the appreciation that existed at conversion (capped by taxable income) is taxed at 21% at the corporate level.

topics.title: Corporate NOL With 80% of Taxable Income Limitation

blocks.text: A C corporation has a post-2017 NOL carryforward of $500,000. In the current year it has taxable income of $400,000 before the NOL deduction. Compute the allowed NOL deduction and the remaining carryforward.
Steps

items: Step 1: Post-2017 NOLs are limited to 80% of taxable income computed before the NOL deduction.
Step 3: Available NOL = $500,000, which exceeds the limit.
Step 4: Allowed NOL deduction this year = $320,000.
Step 5: Taxable income after NOL = $400,000 - $320,000 = $80,000.
Step 6: Remaining NOL carryforward = $500,000 - $320,000 = $180,000, carried forward indefinitely.

blocks.text: Answer: NOL deduction is $320,000, leaving $180,000 to carry forward. Post-2017 NOLs cannot offset more than 80% of taxable income.

A C corporation receives a $100,000 dividend from a domestic corporation in which it owns 30%. The receiving corporation's taxable income before the DRD (and before the dividend would create/increase an NOL) is $120,000. Compute the dividends-received deduction.
Steps

items: Step 1: Ownership of 30% (at least 20% but under 80%) yields a 65% DRD percentage.
Step 2: Tentative DRD = 65% x $100,000 = $65,000.
Step 3: Taxable-income limitation = 65% x taxable income before DRD = 65% x $120,000 = $78,000.
Step 4: Compare tentative DRD ($65,000) to the limitation ($78,000); the smaller is $65,000.
Step 5: Because the full DRD does not create an NOL, the limitation does not reduce it further.
Step 6: Allowed DRD = $65,000.

blocks.text: Answer: DRD is $65,000 (65% tier for 20-80% ownership). The taxable-income limitation here does not bind because $78,000 exceeds the tentative DRD.

topics.title: Accumulated Earnings and Profits and Dividend Characterization

blocks.text: A C corporation has accumulated E&P of $40,000 and current-year E&P of $10,000. It distributes $80,000 cash to its sole shareholder, whose stock basis is $25,000. Characterize the $80,000 distribution.
Steps

items: Step 1: Total E&P available = current $10,000 + accumulated $40,000 = $50,000.
Step 2: Distribution is a taxable dividend to the extent of E&P: $50,000 is a dividend.
Step 3: Remaining distribution = $80,000 - $50,000 = $30,000, treated next as a return of capital.
Step 4: Return of capital reduces stock basis: $25,000 of the $30,000 reduces basis to $0.
Step 5: Excess over basis = $30,000 - $25,000 = $5,000 is capital gain.
Step 6: Summary: $50,000 dividend, $25,000 tax-free return of capital, $5,000 capital gain.

blocks.text: Answer: Of $80,000: $50,000 is a dividend, $25,000 is tax-free return of capital, and $5,000 is capital gain. Distributions are dividends only up to E&P, then reduce basis, then create gain.

For one quarter an employer pays $80,000 in total taxable wages (all under the Social Security wage base). Compute the total Social Security and Medicare tax (both employer and employee shares) reported on Form 941, plus federal income tax withheld of $9,000. Social Security is 6.2% each side; Medicare is 1.45% each side.
Steps

items: Step 1: Social Security tax = 12.4% (6.2% employee + 6.2% employer) x $80,000 = $9,920.
Step 4: Add federal income tax withheld = $9,000.
Step 5: Total Form 941 tax liability for the quarter = $12,240 + $9,000 = $21,240.

blocks.text: Answer: Total Form 941 liability is $21,240 ($12,240 FICA + $9,000 income tax withheld). The employer matches the employee's Social Security and Medicare shares.

topics.title: Estimated Tax Safe Harbor for a High-Income Taxpayer

blocks.text: A taxpayer had 2023 AGI of $200,000 and a 2023 total tax of $45,000. For 2024 the projected tax is $60,000. What minimum total estimated payments (plus withholding) avoid the underpayment penalty?
Steps

items: Step 1: General safe harbor: pay the lesser of 90% of current-year tax or 100% of prior-year tax.
Step 2: Because 2023 AGI exceeded $150,000, the prior-year safe harbor rises to 110% of prior-year tax.
Step 5: Required annual payment = lesser of $54,000 and $49,500 = $49,500.

blocks.text: Answer: Paying at least $49,500 through withholding and estimates avoids the penalty. Takeaway: when prior-year AGI exceeds $150,000, the prior-year safe harbor is 110%, not 100%.

An employer paid $200,000 of taxable wages in a quarter (all below the Social Security wage base). It withheld $24,000 of federal income tax. Compute the total Form 941 tax liability for the quarter (employer + employee FICA + withheld income tax).
Steps

items: Step 1: Social Security tax = 12.4% of $200,000 (6.2% employer + 6.2% employee) = $24,800.
Step 4: Add withheld federal income tax of $24,000.
Step 5: Total Form 941 liability = $30,600 + $24,000 = $54,600.

blocks.text: Answer: The quarterly Form 941 liability is $54,600. Takeaway: Form 941 reports withheld income tax plus both halves of Social Security and Medicare tax.

topics.title: Trust Tax: Compressed Brackets and the NIIT Threshold (2024)

blocks.text: A complex trust retains all its income in 2024: $16,000 of taxable interest and $4,000 of qualified dividends, with no distributions and $500 of deductible trustee fees. The 2024 trust NIIT threshold is $15,200. Estimate the trust's taxable income and identify the NIIT base.
Steps

items: Step 1: Compute total income: interest $16,000 + qualified dividends $4,000 = $20,000.
Step 2: Subtract deductible trustee fees: $20,000 - $500 = $19,500 before the exemption.
Step 3: Subtract the trust personal exemption. A complex trust gets a $100 exemption: $19,500 - $100 = $19,400 taxable income.
Step 4: Note the compressed brackets - trusts reach the top 37% rate at only $15,200 of taxable income in 2024, so most of this income is taxed at high rates.
Step 5: Identify the NIIT base: undistributed net investment income = $19,500 (all interest and dividends, net of fees), or AGI over the $15,200 threshold, whichever is less.
Step 6: NIIT applies to the lesser amount: AGI over threshold = $19,500 - $15,200 = $4,300, which is less than the $19,500 of net investment income, so the 3.8% NIIT base is $4,300.

blocks.text: Answer: Trust taxable income is about $19,400, and the 3.8% NIIT applies to $4,300 (AGI over the $15,200 threshold). Takeaway: trusts face compressed brackets (top rate at $15,200 in 2024) and a very low NIIT threshold, making distributions to beneficiaries often tax-efficient.

topics.title: Estate Tax: Taxable Estate and Portability (2024)

blocks.text: A decedent dies in 2024 with a gross estate of $9,000,000. Allowable deductions are $1,200,000 (debts, expenses, and a charitable bequest). The decedent made no prior taxable gifts. The 2024 basic exclusion amount is $13,610,000. Is any federal estate tax due, and what unused exclusion may be ported to the surviving spouse?
Steps

items: Step 1: Compute the taxable estate: gross estate $9,000,000 - deductions $1,200,000 = $7,800,000.
Step 2: Add adjusted taxable gifts (prior taxable gifts): $0, so the tax base remains $7,800,000.
Step 3: Compare the taxable estate to the 2024 exclusion of $13,610,000. The estate ($7,800,000) is below the exclusion.
Step 4: Because the taxable estate is fully covered by the exclusion, federal estate tax due = $0.
Step 5: Compute the Deceased Spousal Unused Exclusion (DSUE): $13,610,000 - $7,800,000 used = $5,810,000 of unused exclusion.
Step 6: By timely filing Form 706 and electing portability, the surviving spouse can add $5,810,000 to their own exclusion.

blocks.text: Answer: No estate tax is due, and $5,810,000 of unused exclusion (DSUE) can be ported to the surviving spouse. Takeaway: even with no tax due, filing Form 706 to elect portability preserves the deceased spouse's unused exclusion.

topics.title: Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax on a Direct Skip (2024)

blocks.text: A grandparent makes a 2024 direct gift of $13,000,000 to a grandchild (a 'skip person'). The grandparent has $5,000,000 of GST exemption remaining (the rest was used previously) and elects to apply all of it to this transfer. The GST tax rate is the flat 40%. What is the GST tax on this direct skip?
Steps

items: Step 1: Identify the transfer subject to GST tax: a direct skip of $13,000,000 to a grandchild.
Step 2: Apply available GST exemption: $5,000,000 of the transfer is sheltered.
Step 3: Taxable amount subject to GST = $13,000,000 - $5,000,000 = $8,000,000.
Step 4: Compute the inclusion ratio concept: the portion not covered by exemption ($8,000,000) is taxed at the flat 40% GST rate.
Step 6: Note: this GST tax is in addition to any gift tax owed on the same transfer; the direct skip is also a taxable gift.

blocks.text: Answer: The GST tax on the direct skip is $3,200,000 (40% of the $8,000,000 not covered by GST exemption). Takeaway: transfers to skip persons beyond the GST exemption are taxed at a flat 40%, separate from and in addition to gift tax.

topics.title: PTIN and Continuing Education for Enrolled Agents

blocks.text: An enrolled agent is in a 3-year enrollment cycle that requires 72 hours of continuing education, with a minimum of 16 hours per year (including 2 hours of ethics each year). In years 1 and 2 the EA completed 20 hours each (with ethics). How many hours, including ethics, are still required in year 3 to meet both rules?
Steps

items: Step 1: Total cycle requirement = 72 hours over 3 years.
Step 2: Hours completed in years 1 and 2 = 20 + 20 = 40 hours.
Step 3: Remaining hours needed for the 72-hour total = 72 - 40 = 32 hours in year 3.
Step 4: Check the annual minimum: year 3 must have at least 16 hours; 32 exceeds 16, so that rule is met.
Step 5: Year 3 must also include at least 2 hours of ethics, which fits within the 32 hours.

blocks.text: Answer: The EA needs 32 more hours in year 3, including 2 ethics hours. The cycle requires 72 total hours with a 16-hour annual floor and 2 ethics hours per year.

topics.title: Enrolled Agent Continuing Education Requirement (Three-Year Cycle)

blocks.text: An enrolled agent must satisfy continuing education (CE) over a three-year enrollment cycle. In year one she completed 14 hours (including 2 ethics), year two 18 hours (including 2 ethics), and so far in year three 20 hours (including 2 ethics). Does she meet the requirements, and what minimums apply?
Steps

items: Step 1: State the cycle requirement: 72 total CE hours over the three-year cycle.
Step 2: State the annual minimum: at least 16 hours each year, including at least 2 hours of ethics each year.
Step 3: Check annual minimums. Year one had only 14 hours - this fails the 16-hour minimum, even though ethics (2 hours) was met.
Step 4: Years two (18) and three (20) each meet the 16-hour minimum with 2 ethics hours.
Step 5: Check the cycle total: 14 + 18 + 20 = 52 hours, which is below the 72-hour cycle requirement.
Step 6: Conclusion: she fails both the year-one annual minimum (16 hours) and the 72-hour cycle total; she needs more hours.

blocks.text: Answer: She does NOT meet the requirements: year one fell short of 16 hours, and the cycle total (52) is below 72. Takeaway: EAs need 72 hours per 3-year cycle, with at least 16 hours and 2 ethics hours every year.
A taxpayer owes $10,000 of tax with no extension, files her return three months after the due date, and pays the tax when she files. Compute the penalties (ignoring interest and the minimum penalty).
Steps

items: Step 1: Failure-to-file penalty = 5% per month, but reduced by the 0.5% failure-to-pay penalty for the same months, so 4.5% per month.
Step 3: Failure-to-pay penalty = 0.5% per month × 3 months × $10,000 = $150.
Step 4: Total penalties = $1,350 + $150 = $1,500, or 5% per month × 3 months.
Step 5: Interest accrues separately from the original due date.

blocks.text: Answer: Total penalties are $1,500. A first-time abatement request could remove both penalties if the taxpayer qualifies.
A return shows tax of $78,000. The IRS determines correct tax is $90,000. There was no disclosure and no substantial authority. Is there a substantial understatement, and what is the penalty?
Steps

items: Step 1: Understatement = $90,000 − $78,000 = $12,000.
Step 2: Threshold = the greater of 10% of the correct tax ($9,000) or $5,000 = $9,000.
Step 3: The understatement of $12,000 exceeds $9,000, so it is substantial.
Step 5: The taxpayer can avoid the penalty by showing reasonable cause and good faith or substantial authority.

blocks.text: Answer: Yes, the penalty is $2,400, plus interest on the underpayment.

The IRS assessed tax on March 1, 2019. The taxpayer submitted an offer in compromise on March 1, 2021, which was rejected on September 1, 2021, and the taxpayer filed no appeal. Estimate the new collection statute date.
Steps

items: Step 1: The ten-year collection period starts on assessment: March 1, 2019 to March 1, 2029.
Step 2: The CSED is suspended while an offer is pending, plus 30 days after rejection.
Step 3: Pending period: March 1, 2021 to September 1, 2021 is 184 days.
Step 4: Add 30 days after rejection: 184 + 30 = 214 days.
Step 5: New CSED = March 1, 2029 plus 214 days, which is about October 1, 2029.

blocks.text: Answer: The CSED moves to roughly October 1, 2029. Other suspension events, such as CDP hearings or bankruptcy, add additional time.

A taxpayer's correct tax is $50,000 but the return reported only $35,000. The understatement is substantial if it exceeds the greater of 10% of correct tax or $5,000. The accuracy-related penalty is 20% of the underpayment. Compute the penalty.
Steps

items: Step 1: Understatement = $50,000 correct - $35,000 reported = $15,000.
Step 2: Substantial-understatement threshold = greater of 10% x $50,000 ($5,000) or $5,000 = $5,000.
Step 3: Because $15,000 exceeds $5,000, the understatement is substantial.
Step 4: Accuracy-related penalty = 20% x $15,000 underpayment = $3,000.
Step 5: The penalty applies unless the taxpayer shows reasonable cause and good faith.

blocks.text: Answer: The accuracy-related penalty is $3,000. A 20% penalty applies once the understatement exceeds the greater of 10% of tax or $5,000.

A tax preparer takes an unreasonable position resulting in a $12,000 understatement of a client's tax. The Section 6694(a) penalty for an unreasonable position is the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income the preparer derived. The preparer charged a $1,500 fee for the return. Compute the penalty.
Steps

items: Step 1: Fixed-dollar component = $1,000.
Step 2: Income-based component = 50% x $1,500 fee = $750.
Step 3: The penalty is the greater of the two: greater of $1,000 and $750 = $1,000.
Step 4: If the conduct were willful or reckless (6694(b)), the penalty would rise to the greater of $5,000 or 75% of income.
Step 5: Under 6694(a) here, the penalty is $1,000.

blocks.text: Answer: The Section 6694(a) penalty is $1,000. It is the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the preparer's income from the return.

topics.title: Statute of Limitations: Substantial Omission of Income

blocks.text: A taxpayer filed a 2021 return on April 15, 2022, reporting $200,000 of gross income but omitting $60,000 of additional gross income. The normal assessment period is 3 years; a 6-year period applies if more than 25% of gross income is omitted. Determine the applicable statute and the assessment deadline.
Steps

items: Step 1: Reported gross income = $200,000; omitted = $60,000.
Step 2: 25% of reported gross income = 25% x $200,000 = $50,000.
Step 3: Omission of $60,000 exceeds $50,000, so more than 25% of gross income was omitted.
Step 4: The extended 6-year statute of limitations applies (instead of 3 years).
Step 5: Period runs from the later of the due date or filing date: April 15, 2022.
Step 6: Assessment deadline = April 15, 2028 (6 years).

blocks.text: Answer: The 6-year statute applies, expiring April 15, 2028. Omitting more than 25% of gross income extends the assessment period from 3 to 6 years.

topics.title: Estimated Tax: Annualized Income Installment Method

blocks.text: A taxpayer earns income unevenly. Through the first installment period (3 months, ending March 31), annualized taxable income produces an annualized tax of $24,000. The required annual payment (safe harbor) is $20,000. Under the annualized method, the first installment must cover 22.5% of the annualized tax. Compute the required first installment.
Steps

items: Step 1: The annualized method bases each installment on income earned to date, helpful when income is seasonal.
Step 2: Annualized tax through the first period = $24,000.
Step 3: First-period required cumulative percentage = 22.5%.
Step 4: Required first installment under annualized method = 22.5% x $24,000 = $5,400.
Step 5: Compare to the regular-method quarter (25% of $20,000 safe harbor = $5,000); the annualized method here requires $5,400 because early income was higher.
Step 6: Paying at least $5,400 by April 15 avoids an underpayment penalty for the first period under this method.

blocks.text: Answer: Required first installment is $5,400 (22.5% of annualized tax). The annualized method matches payments to when income is actually earned.

A taxpayer owes $10,000 in tax, files the return 4 months late, and pays nothing until filing. Failure-to-file (FTF) is 5% per month, reduced by any failure-to-pay (FTP) in the same month; FTP is 0.5% per month. Compute the combined penalties for the 4 months (each partial month counts as a full month).
Steps

items: Step 1: FTP = 0.5% per month x 4 months = 2.0% x $10,000 = $200.
Step 2: FTF base = 5% per month, but reduced by the 0.5% FTP in each overlapping month, so net FTF = 4.5% per month.
Step 3: Net FTF for 4 months = 4.5% x 4 = 18.0% x $10,000 = $1,800.
Step 4: FTF combined cap = 25% maximum; 18.0% is under the cap, so no capping needed.
Step 5: Total combined penalties = $1,800 FTF + $200 FTP = $2,000 (plus interest, computed separately).

blocks.text: Answer: Combined penalties are $2,000 ($1,800 FTF + $200 FTP). When both apply in a month, the 5% FTF is reduced by the 0.5% FTP, netting 4.5% per month.

A taxpayer underpaid $8,000 of tax. The applicable IRS underpayment interest rate is 8% per year, and the balance remained unpaid for 180 days. Estimate the interest using simple proration (the exam often tests the rate-times-time concept). Use a 365-day year.
Steps

items: Step 1: Annual interest = rate x balance = 8% x $8,000 = $640 per full year.
Step 2: Fraction of the year unpaid = 180 / 365 = 0.49315.
Step 3: Interest = $640 x 0.49315 = $315.62, round to $316.
Step 4: Note: the IRS actually compounds daily, which would make the figure slightly higher than the simple estimate.
Step 5: Interest accrues on tax and on certain penalties from the original due date until paid and is not abatable for reasonable cause.

blocks.text: Answer: Approximately $316 of interest (simple proration; daily compounding makes the true amount marginally higher). Interest runs from the original due date regardless of extensions.

An individual's correct tax is $50,000 but the return reported only $38,000, an understatement of $12,000. The substantial-understatement threshold is the greater of 10% of correct tax or $5,000. The accuracy-related penalty is 20% of the underpayment attributable to the understatement. Determine whether the penalty applies and compute it.
Steps

items: Step 1: Threshold = greater of 10% x $50,000 = $5,000, or $5,000 fixed; threshold = $5,000.
Step 2: Understatement = $50,000 - $38,000 = $12,000.
Step 3: Because $12,000 exceeds the $5,000 threshold, the understatement is substantial.
Step 4: Penalty = 20% x understated underpayment $12,000 = $2,400.
Step 5: Penalty may be avoided with substantial authority or adequate disclosure with a reasonable basis; otherwise $2,400 applies.

blocks.text: Answer: The penalty applies: $2,400 (20% of the $12,000 understatement). A substantial understatement is the greater of 10% of correct tax or $5,000 for individuals.

topics.title: First-Time Penalty Abatement Effect on Total Balance

blocks.text: A taxpayer qualifies for first-time abatement (FTA). The assessed amounts are: tax $6,000, failure-to-file penalty $900, failure-to-pay penalty $120, and interest $250. FTA waives eligible failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties but not the underlying tax or interest. Compute the balance after FTA (ignore any interest recomputation on abated penalties for simplicity).
Steps

items: Step 1: FTA can waive failure-to-file ($900) and failure-to-pay ($120) penalties for a taxpayer with a clean compliance history.
Step 2: Total penalties abated = $900 + $120 = $1,020.
Step 3: Remaining items not abated = tax $6,000 + interest $250 = $6,250.
Step 5: Balance after FTA = $7,270 - $1,020 = $6,250.
Step 6: Interest tied to the abated penalties would also be reduced in practice, lowering the balance slightly further.

blocks.text: Answer: After FTA the balance is $6,250 ($1,020 of penalties removed). FTA waives FTF and FTP penalties but never the tax itself; interest on the tax remains.

topics.title: Estimated Tax Safe Harbor for a Higher-Income Individual

blocks.text: An individual's 2023 AGI was $200,000 (over $150,000) and the 2023 total tax was $44,000. The 2024 projected tax is $60,000. Higher-income taxpayers must pay the lesser of 90% of current-year tax or 110% of prior-year tax to avoid penalty. Compute the required annual estimated payment.
Steps

items: Step 1: Prior-year safe harbor (AGI over $150,000) = 110% x prior-year tax = 110% x $44,000 = $48,400.
Step 2: Current-year safe harbor = 90% x $60,000 = $54,000.
Step 3: Required annual payment = lesser of the two = $48,400.
Step 4: Quarterly installment = $48,400 / 4 = $12,100.
Step 5: Paying at least $48,400 total (via withholding plus estimates) avoids the underpayment penalty.

blocks.text: Answer: Required annual payment is $48,400 (110% of prior-year tax, the lesser figure). Taxpayers with prior-year AGI over $150,000 use 110% rather than 100%.

topics.title: Statute of Limitations With Substantial Omission of Income

blocks.text: A taxpayer filed a 2021 return on April 15, 2022, reporting $200,000 of gross income but omitting $60,000 of income. By what date can the IRS generally assess additional tax, and which limitations period applies?
Steps

items: Step 1: The normal assessment statute of limitations is 3 years from the filing date.
Step 2: Test the substantial-omission rule: a 6-year statute applies if the taxpayer omits more than 25% of gross income stated on the return.
Step 3: 25% of reported gross income = 25% x $200,000 = $50,000.
Step 4: The omitted $60,000 exceeds $50,000, so the omission is substantial and the 6-year statute applies.
Step 5: Six years from April 15, 2022 = April 15, 2028.

blocks.text: Answer: The 6-year statute applies; the IRS may assess through April 15, 2028. Takeaway: omitting more than 25% of gross income extends the assessment period from 3 to 6 years.

topics.title: Preparer Penalty for Failure to Furnish a Copy and Sign (Section 6695)

blocks.text: A paid preparer completed 40 returns in 2024 but failed to provide a copy of the return to each client and failed to sign 25 of those returns. The 2024 Section 6695 penalties are $60 per failure for failing to furnish a copy and $60 per failure for failing to sign. What is the preparer's total penalty exposure (assume no annual cap is reached)?
Steps

items: Step 1: Identify the failure-to-furnish-a-copy penalty: $60 per return for which a copy was not provided.
Step 2: Failed to furnish a copy on all 40 returns: 40 x $60 = $2,400.
Step 3: Identify the failure-to-sign penalty: $60 per return the preparer failed to sign.
Step 4: Failed to sign 25 returns: 25 x $60 = $1,500.
Step 5: Total Section 6695 penalty exposure = $2,400 + $1,500 = $3,900.
Step 6: Note: each Section 6695 violation has its own annual maximum (e.g., around $30,000 for 2024 per type), so these amounts are within the caps.

blocks.text: Answer: Total preparer penalty exposure is $3,900 ($2,400 for unfurnished copies + $1,500 for unsigned returns). Takeaway: Section 6695 imposes separate $60-per-return penalties for failing to furnish copies and failing to sign, each with its own annual cap.

topics.title: Earned Income Credit Due Diligence Penalty (Section 6695(g))

blocks.text: A preparer filed 30 returns in 2024 claiming the EITC, Child Tax Credit, American Opportunity Credit, and/or Head of Household status without meeting due diligence requirements. On 10 of these returns, the preparer failed due diligence on two separate credits each. The 2024 Section 6695(g) penalty is $635 per failure. What is the total due diligence penalty?
Steps

items: Step 1: Identify the due diligence rule: Section 6695(g) imposes a penalty per failure to comply for EITC, CTC/ACTC, AOTC, and HoH determinations.
Step 2: The penalty applies per credit/status per return, not per return. On each of the 10 returns there were 2 separate failures.
Step 3: Total number of failures = 10 returns x 2 failures each = 20 failures.
Step 4: Apply the 2024 penalty rate: $635 per failure.
Step 5: Total penalty = 20 x $635 = $12,700.
Step 6: Note there is no annual cap on the 6695(g) due diligence penalty, unlike most other 6695 penalties.

blocks.text: Answer: The total due diligence penalty is $12,700 (20 failures x $635). Takeaway: the $635 (2024) due diligence penalty applies separately to each credit/status on each return, with no annual cap.

A taxpayer filed a 2021 return on April 15, 2022, reporting gross income of $200,000 but omitting $60,000 of income. Determine whether the normal 3-year or extended 6-year assessment period applies and the last date the IRS can assess.
Steps

items: Step 1: Compute the omission percentage: $60,000 omitted / $200,000 reported = 30%.
Step 2: The 6-year statute applies when more than 25% of gross income is omitted; 30% exceeds 25%.
Step 3: Therefore the extended 6-year period applies instead of the normal 3 years.
Step 4: Start the clock at the later of the filing date or due date: April 15, 2022.
Step 5: Last assessment date = April 15, 2022 + 6 years = April 15, 2028.

blocks.text: Answer: The 6-year statute applies, allowing assessment through April 15, 2028. Omitting more than 25% of gross income extends the assessment period to six years.

topics.title: Refund Claim Timing Under the Statute

blocks.text: A taxpayer filed a 2021 return on April 15, 2022, and now wants to file an amended return to claim a refund of overpaid tax. The refund statute allows a claim within 3 years from filing or 2 years from payment, whichever is later. The tax was all paid through withholding by April 15, 2022. What is the deadline to claim the refund?
Steps

items: Step 1: Identify the two measuring periods: 3 years from filing or 2 years from the date tax was paid.
Step 2: 3 years from the April 15, 2022 filing = April 15, 2025.
Step 3: 2 years from payment (withholding deemed paid April 15, 2022) = April 15, 2024.
Step 4: Use the later of the two dates: April 15, 2025 is later than April 15, 2024.
Step 5: The refund claim deadline is therefore April 15, 2025.

blocks.text: Answer: The refund claim is due by April 15, 2025. The refund period is the later of 3 years from filing or 2 years from payment.

topics.title: Offer in Compromise: Reasonable Collection Potential (Lump Sum)

blocks.text: A taxpayer owes $90,000. Their net realizable equity in assets is $25,000. Their monthly income exceeds allowable living expenses by $800. For a lump-sum cash offer (paid in 5 or fewer installments), future income is multiplied by 12. Compute the minimum acceptable offer (RCP).
Steps

items: Step 1: Net realizable equity in assets = $25,000.
Step 2: Monthly disposable income = $800.
Step 3: For a lump-sum offer, multiply monthly disposable income by 12: $800 x 12 = $9,600.
Step 4: Reasonable Collection Potential (RCP) = equity + future income = $25,000 + $9,600 = $34,600.
Step 5: RCP $34,600 is less than the $90,000 liability, so doubt as to collectibility exists.
Step 6: Minimum acceptable offer generally equals the RCP = $34,600.

blocks.text: Answer: Minimum lump-sum offer is $34,600 (RCP). RCP equals asset equity plus 12 months of future disposable income for a lump-sum OIC.

topics.title: Offer in Compromise: RCP for a Periodic Payment Offer

blocks.text: The same taxpayer (net asset equity $25,000, monthly disposable income $800) instead proposes a periodic payment offer (paid over 6 to 24 months). For periodic offers, future income is multiplied by 24. Compute the minimum acceptable offer.
Steps

items: Step 1: Net realizable equity in assets = $25,000.
Step 2: Monthly disposable income = $800.
Step 3: For a periodic payment offer, multiply monthly disposable income by 24: $800 x 24 = $19,200.
Step 5: Compared to the lump-sum RCP of $34,600, the periodic offer requires a higher amount.
Step 6: Minimum acceptable periodic offer = $44,200.

blocks.text: Answer: Minimum periodic-payment offer is $44,200. Periodic offers use a 24-month future-income multiplier, raising the required RCP versus the 12-month lump-sum figure.

A corporation failed to remit payroll taxes. The unpaid trust fund portion (employee income tax withheld plus the employee share of FICA) is $48,000, while the employer's matching FICA share is $12,000. A responsible person willfully failed to pay. Compute the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty assessable against the responsible person.
Steps

items: Step 1: The TFRP applies only to the trust fund portion of payroll taxes (amounts withheld from employees).
Step 2: Trust fund amount = withheld income tax + employee share of FICA = $48,000.
Step 3: The employer matching FICA share ($12,000) is NOT a trust fund tax and is excluded.
