Step 4: TFRP = 100% of the trust fund taxes = 100% x $48,000 = $48,000.
Step 5: This penalty can be assessed personally against any willful responsible person.
Step 6: Result: TFRP = $48,000.

blocks.text: Answer: The Trust Fund Recovery Penalty is $48,000. It equals 100% of the employee-withheld (trust fund) taxes only, not the employer's matching share.

topics.title: Statute of Limitations: Substantial Omission of Gross Income

blocks.text: A taxpayer reported gross income of $100,000 on a timely 2021 return filed April 15, 2022, but omitted $30,000 of additional gross income. The normal assessment period is 3 years; it extends to 6 years if more than 25% of gross income is omitted. Determine the applicable assessment deadline.
Steps

items: Step 1: Reported gross income = $100,000; 25% threshold = 25% x $100,000 = $25,000.
Step 2: Omitted income $30,000 exceeds the $25,000 threshold, so the 6-year statute applies.
Step 3: The period begins on the later of the due date or filing date = April 15, 2022.
Step 4: 6-year deadline = April 15, 2022 + 6 years = April 15, 2028.
Step 5: Had the omission been under 25%, the normal 3-year deadline (April 15, 2025) would apply.

blocks.text: Answer: The assessment deadline is April 15, 2028 (6-year statute). Omitting more than 25% of reported gross income doubles the normal 3-year period.

topics.title: Innocent Spouse Relief: Allocation of Understatement (Separation of Liability)

blocks.text: A now-divorced couple filed a joint 2022 return. The IRS later assessed a $20,000 understatement: $16,000 attributable to the ex-husband's unreported self-employment income and $4,000 attributable to the ex-wife's unreported interest. The ex-wife requests separation of liability relief. How is the deficiency allocated to her?
Steps

items: Step 1: Confirm eligibility: separation of liability relief (Section 6015(c)) is available to taxpayers who are divorced, legally separated, or living apart for 12 months - she is divorced.
Step 2: Under separation of liability, the deficiency is allocated as if the spouses had filed separate returns.
Step 3: Allocate the understatement by source: ex-husband's items $16,000; ex-wife's items $4,000; total $20,000.
Step 4: The ex-wife is responsible only for the portion attributable to her items: $4,000.
Step 5: She is relieved of the $16,000 attributable to her ex-husband (absent fraud or actual knowledge of his items).
Step 6: Her remaining liability after relief = $4,000; the IRS pursues the ex-husband for the $16,000.

blocks.text: Answer: Under separation of liability, the ex-wife owes only $4,000 (her own items) and is relieved of the $16,000 from her ex-husband. Takeaway: Section 6015(c) splits a joint deficiency by the source of each spouse's erroneous items for divorced/separated taxpayers.

A taxpayer owes $10,000 in tax and files the return and pays 3 months late. Failure-to-file is 5% per month and failure-to-pay is 0.5% per month, but in any month both apply the FTF penalty is reduced by the FTP penalty for that month. Compute the combined penalty for the 3 months.
Steps

items: Step 1: Gross failure-to-file = 5% per month x 3 months = 15% x $10,000 = $1,500.
Step 2: Failure-to-pay = 0.5% per month x 3 months = 1.5% x $10,000 = $150.
Step 3: For each overlapping month, reduce FTF by the FTP: net FTF rate = 5% - 0.5% = 4.5% per month.
Step 4: Net failure-to-file = 4.5% x 3 months x $10,000 = $1,350.
Step 5: Total penalty = $1,350 FTF + $150 FTP = $1,500.

blocks.text: Answer: Combined penalty is $1,500. The failure-to-file penalty is reduced by the failure-to-pay penalty for any overlapping month.

topics.title: Offer in Compromise Reasonable Collection Potential

blocks.text: A taxpayer owes $90,000. Quick-sale equity in assets is $20,000. Monthly income is $5,000 and allowable monthly living expenses are $4,200. The taxpayer proposes a lump-sum offer, so future income is valued over 12 months. Compute the reasonable collection potential (RCP).
Steps

items: Step 1: Net monthly disposable income = $5,000 income - $4,200 allowable expenses = $800.
Step 2: For a lump-sum cash offer, multiply disposable income by 12: $800 x 12 = $9,600 future income value.
Step 3: Add quick-sale equity in assets: $20,000.
Step 4: RCP = $20,000 asset equity + $9,600 future income = $29,600.
Step 5: The IRS will generally not accept less than RCP, so an offer near $29,600 is the floor.

blocks.text: Answer: Reasonable collection potential is $29,600. RCP equals net asset equity plus the present value of future disposable income.

A taxpayer pays $8,000 of tax 4 months late. The failure-to-pay penalty is 0.5% per month, and interest accrues at an annual rate of 8% (simple, for estimation). Compute the penalty and approximate interest for the 4-month period.
Steps

items: Step 1: Failure-to-pay penalty = 0.5% per month x 4 months = 2% x $8,000 = $160.
Step 2: Convert the 8% annual interest rate to the period: 8% x (4/12) = 2.667%.
Step 3: Interest estimate = 2.667% x $8,000 = $213.33, rounded to $213.
Step 4: Total additions = $160 penalty + $213 interest = $373.
Step 5: The amount due including additions = $8,000 + $373 = $8,373.

blocks.text: Answer: Penalty is $160 and estimated interest is about $213, totaling roughly $373. Penalty and interest accrue separately on unpaid tax.

A taxpayer files a return 3 months late and pays the $10,000 balance due at the same time. The failure-to-file penalty is 5% per month and failure-to-pay is 0.5% per month, but failure-to-file is reduced by the failure-to-pay penalty for overlapping months. Compute the total penalties for the 3 months.
Steps

items: Step 1: Failure-to-pay penalty = 0.5% per month x 3 months x $10,000 = 1.5% x $10,000 = $150.
Step 2: Gross failure-to-file penalty = 5% per month x 3 months = 15% x $10,000 = $1,500.
Step 3: For overlapping months, the 5% FTF is reduced by the 0.5% FTP, leaving a net 4.5% per month for FTF.
Step 4: Net failure-to-file = 4.5% x 3 months x $10,000 = 13.5% x $10,000 = $1,350.
Step 5: Total combined penalty = $1,350 (FTF) + $150 (FTP) = $1,500.
Step 6: The combined monthly rate during overlap is effectively 5% (4.5% + 0.5%).

blocks.text: Answer: Total penalty is $1,500 ($1,350 FTF + $150 FTP). The failure-to-file penalty is reduced by the failure-to-pay penalty in overlapping months.

A taxpayer owes $20,000 of tax that remains unpaid for exactly one year. The IRS underpayment interest rate is 8% per year, compounded daily but approximated here as quarterly compounding at 2% per quarter. Compute the approximate interest owed for the year.
Steps

items: Step 1: Quarterly rate = 8% / 4 = 2% per quarter.
Step 2: Q1 interest = 2% x $20,000 = $400; balance = $20,400.
Step 3: Q2 interest = 2% x $20,400 = $408; balance = $20,808.
Step 5: Q4 interest = 2% x $21,224.16 = $424.48; ending balance = $21,648.64.
Step 6: Total interest for the year = $21,648.64 - $20,000 = $1,648.64.
Step 7: Note compounding makes this slightly more than simple 8% interest of $1,600.

blocks.text: Answer: Approximate interest is $1,648.64. IRS interest compounds, so the effective cost exceeds the stated 8% simple rate of $1,600.

An individual's correct tax is $50,000; the return reported $36,000. The understatement is $14,000. The substantial-understatement threshold is the greater of 10% of correct tax or $5,000. Determine whether the penalty applies and compute it.
Steps

items: Step 1: Understatement = correct tax - reported tax = $50,000 - $36,000 = $14,000.
Step 2: Threshold = greater of 10% x $50,000 = $5,000, or $5,000 fixed = $5,000.
Step 3: Understatement $14,000 exceeds the $5,000 threshold, so it is a substantial understatement.
Step 4: The accuracy-related penalty rate is 20% of the underpayment attributable to the understatement.
Step 6: The penalty may be avoided with substantial authority or adequate disclosure plus reasonable basis.

blocks.text: Answer: The accuracy-related penalty is $2,800 (20% of the $14,000 understatement). It applies because the understatement exceeds the greater of 10% of tax or $5,000.

topics.title: Failure-to-File Penalty Minimum for a Very Late Return

blocks.text: A taxpayer files a return more than 60 days late with a small balance due of $300. The failure-to-file penalty is 5% per month (max 25%), but with a minimum penalty rule for returns over 60 days late. For 2024 the minimum is the lesser of $510 or 100% of the tax due. Compute the penalty.
Steps

items: Step 1: Standard FTF maximum = 25% x $300 = $75.
Step 2: Return is more than 60 days late, so the minimum-penalty rule applies.
Step 3: Minimum penalty = lesser of $510 (2024 amount) or 100% of unpaid tax ($300).
Step 4: Lesser of $510 and $300 = $300.
Step 5: Compare the minimum penalty ($300) to the standard penalty ($75); the larger applies.
Step 6: Failure-to-file penalty = $300.

blocks.text: Answer: The penalty is $300. For returns over 60 days late, the minimum penalty (lesser of $510 or 100% of tax) can exceed the ordinary percentage penalty.

topics.title: Estimated Tax Safe Harbor for a High-Income Taxpayer

blocks.text: A taxpayer's prior-year AGI was $200,000 and prior-year tax was $48,000. Current-year tax is projected at $70,000. Because prior-year AGI exceeded $150,000, the safe harbor requires 110% of prior-year tax. Compute the minimum annual estimated payments needed to avoid an underpayment penalty.
Steps

items: Step 1: Safe harbor option A = 90% of current-year tax = 90% x $70,000 = $63,000.
Step 2: Safe harbor option B = 110% of prior-year tax (AGI over $150,000) = 110% x $48,000 = $52,800.
Step 3: The taxpayer may pay the smaller of the two safe harbors: lesser of $63,000 and $52,800 = $52,800.
Step 4: Required annual estimated payments (plus withholding) = $52,800.
Step 5: Per-quarter minimum = $52,800 / 4 = $13,200.
Step 6: Paying $52,800 avoids the penalty even though actual tax is $70,000.

blocks.text: Answer: Minimum required is $52,800 (110% of prior-year tax). High-income taxpayers use 110%, not 100%, of the prior year for the safe harbor.

topics.title: Offer in Compromise: Future Income (Reasonable Collection Potential)

blocks.text: A taxpayer applies for a lump-sum cash offer in compromise. Net realizable equity in assets is $9,000. Monthly remaining income (income minus allowable expenses) is $500. For a lump-sum offer, future income is calculated as 12 months of remaining monthly income. Compute the minimum acceptable offer (reasonable collection potential).
Steps

items: Step 1: Reasonable collection potential (RCP) = net realizable equity in assets + future income component.
Step 2: Net realizable equity = $9,000.
Step 3: Future income for a lump-sum offer = 12 x monthly remaining income = 12 x $500 = $6,000.
Step 5: The minimum offer the IRS will generally accept equals the RCP, so the offer should be at least $15,000 (assuming it is less than the total liability).

blocks.text: Answer: Minimum acceptable lump-sum offer is $15,000 (RCP). Lump-sum offers multiply remaining monthly income by 12; periodic-payment offers use 24 months.

topics.title: Tax Preparer Penalty for Unreasonable Position (Section 6694)

blocks.text: A paid preparer takes an undisclosed position lacking substantial authority that understates a client's liability by $20,000. The Section 6694(a) penalty is the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived by the preparer for that return. The preparer charged $1,500 for the return. Compute the penalty.
Steps

items: Step 1: Section 6694(a) penalty = greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived from preparing the return.
Step 2: 50% of preparer fee = 50% x $1,500 = $750.
Step 3: Compare $1,000 and $750; the greater is $1,000.
Step 4: Section 6694(a) penalty = $1,000.
Step 5: If the conduct were willful or reckless under 6694(b), the penalty would rise to the greater of $5,000 or 75% of the fee = $5,000.

blocks.text: Answer: The 6694(a) penalty is $1,000 (greater of $1,000 or 50% of the $1,500 fee). Willful or reckless conduct under 6694(b) would instead be the greater of $5,000 or 75% of the fee.
A taxpayer underpaid tax by $25,000 due to negligence on a return. The correct tax was $90,000 but only $65,000 was reported and paid. Compute the accuracy-related penalty under Section 6662.
Steps

items: Step 1: The underpayment attributable to negligence = correct tax $90,000 - reported tax $65,000 = $25,000.
Step 2: The accuracy-related penalty rate is 20% of the underpayment.
Step 4: Note the penalty doubles to 40% for gross valuation misstatements or undisclosed foreign asset transactions (not applicable here).
Step 5: The penalty can be avoided with reasonable cause and good faith, or with adequate disclosure plus a reasonable basis.

blocks.text: Answer: The accuracy-related penalty is $5,000 (20% of $25,000). Takeaway: Section 6662 imposes a 20% penalty on underpayments from negligence or substantial understatement.

topics.title: Combined Failure-to-File and Failure-to-Pay Over 5 Months

blocks.text: A taxpayer owes $10,000 and files the return 5 months late, paying nothing until then. Compute the combined failure-to-file (5%/month) and failure-to-pay (0.5%/month) penalties for the 5 months.
Steps

items: Step 1: Failure-to-file penalty is 5% per month, but reduced by any failure-to-pay penalty running in the same month, so the combined cap per month is 5%.
Step 2: For each of the 5 months: failure-to-file = 5% - 0.5% = 4.5%; failure-to-pay = 0.5%; combined = 5%.
Step 3: Failure-to-file total = 4.5% x 5 months = 22.5% (does not exceed its 25% max).
Step 4: Failure-to-pay total = 0.5% x 5 months = 2.5%.
Step 5: Failure-to-file penalty = 22.5% x $10,000 = $2,250; failure-to-pay penalty = 2.5% x $10,000 = $250.
Step 6: Combined penalties = $2,250 + $250 = $2,500.

blocks.text: Answer: Combined penalties are $2,500 ($2,250 file + $250 pay). Takeaway: when both penalties run, the FTF rate is reduced by the FTP rate to a combined 5% per month, up to the 47.5% overall maximum.

A taxpayer owes $8,000 of tax that remains unpaid for 180 days. The IRS underpayment interest rate is 8% per year (compounded daily, approximated here as simple for the period). Estimate the interest owed.
Steps

items: Step 1: Interest accrues from the original due date until payment at the federal short-term rate plus 3% (here 8% annually).
Step 2: Convert the period: 180 days / 365 days = 0.4932 of a year.
Step 3: Interest = principal x rate x time = $8,000 x 8% x 0.4932 = $8,000 x 0.039452 = $315.62.
Step 4: Daily compounding would make it slightly higher, roughly $318, but $316 is a reasonable estimate.
Step 5: Interest applies to tax AND to penalties; it cannot be abated for reasonable cause (unlike many penalties).

blocks.text: Answer: Underpayment interest is about $316 for 180 days. Takeaway: IRS interest accrues daily on unpaid tax and penalties and generally cannot be waived for reasonable cause.

topics.title: Offer in Compromise - Lump-Sum Reasonable Collection Potential

blocks.text: A taxpayer owes $80,000. Net realizable equity in assets is $15,000. Monthly disposable income (income minus allowable expenses) is $500. He proposes a lump-sum offer (payable in 5 or fewer installments). Compute the minimum acceptable offer (RCP).
Steps

items: Step 1: Reasonable Collection Potential = net realizable equity in assets + future remaining income.
Step 2: For a lump-sum cash offer, future income is multiplied by 12 months.
Step 3: Future income component = $500 x 12 = $6,000.
Step 4: RCP = asset equity $15,000 + $6,000 = $21,000.
Step 5: Because RCP ($21,000) is less than the $80,000 liability, the offer can be accepted at the $21,000 RCP based on doubt as to collectibility.

blocks.text: Answer: The minimum lump-sum OIC is $21,000 (RCP). Takeaway: lump-sum OICs value future income at 12 months; periodic-payment OICs use 24 months.

A taxpayer owes $90,000 with net asset equity of $8,000 and monthly disposable income of $400. She proposes a periodic-payment offer in compromise (paid over 6-24 months). Compute the minimum offer using the 24-month multiplier.
Steps

items: Step 1: For a periodic-payment OIC, future income is multiplied by 24 months.
Step 2: Future income component = $400 x 24 = $9,600.
Step 3: RCP = asset equity $8,000 + future income $9,600 = $17,600.
Step 4: Compare to the liability of $90,000; the RCP of $17,600 is far less, so the offer reflects doubt as to collectibility.
Step 5: During a periodic-payment offer the taxpayer must keep making proposed monthly payments while the IRS evaluates it.

blocks.text: Answer: The minimum periodic-payment OIC is $17,600. Takeaway: periodic offers use a 24-month income multiplier versus 12 months for lump-sum offers, raising the minimum offer.

An employer failed to remit withheld payroll taxes. The unpaid trust fund portion consists of $30,000 in withheld federal income tax and $12,000 in the employees' share of FICA. A responsible person willfully failed to pay. Compute the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty.
Steps

items: Step 1: The TFRP (Section 6672) equals 100% of the unpaid trust fund taxes - the amounts withheld from employees that were held in trust for the government.
Step 2: Trust fund taxes = withheld income tax $30,000 + employee FICA share $12,000 = $42,000.
Step 3: The employer's matching FICA share is NOT part of the trust fund and is excluded from the TFRP.
Step 5: This penalty is assessed personally against responsible persons who willfully failed to remit; it can be collected from their personal assets.

blocks.text: Answer: The Trust Fund Recovery Penalty is $42,000. Takeaway: the TFRP is 100% of withheld income tax plus the employee FICA share, assessed personally against responsible, willful individuals.

topics.title: Installment Agreement User Fee and Monthly Payment Calculation

blocks.text: A taxpayer owes $18,000 and enters a long-term (over 120 days) direct-debit installment agreement applied for online. The penalties and interest accrue at a combined effective rate of about 0.5% per month on the balance. The taxpayer wants to pay it off in 24 equal principal payments (ignoring compounding for estimation). Roughly what is the monthly principal payment, and what is a key advantage of the direct-debit method?
Steps

items: Step 1: Compute the base monthly principal payment to retire $18,000 over 24 months: $18,000 / 24 = $750 per month in principal.
Step 2: Estimate first-month interest/penalty add-on at 0.5%: 0.5% x $18,000 = $90 (declining as the balance falls).
Step 3: Approximate first-month total payment if covering principal plus accrual = $750 + $90 = $840.
Step 4: Identify the user fee. A direct-debit installment agreement applied for online has a lower setup fee (around $31) than a non-direct-debit online agreement (around $130).
Step 5: Note the direct-debit advantage: lower setup fee and reduced risk of default since payments are automatic; low-income taxpayers may have the fee waived or reimbursed.
Step 6: Conclusion: roughly $750/month in principal (about $840 including early-month accrual), with a low ~$31 setup fee for direct debit.

blocks.text: Answer: The taxpayer pays about $750/month in principal (~$840 with early accrual) over 24 months, with a low ~$31 direct-debit online setup fee. Takeaway: direct-debit installment agreements carry the lowest user fees and reduce default risk through automatic payments.

topics.title: Collection Statute Expiration Date (CSED) With a Tolling Event

blocks.text: The IRS assessed a tax on April 15, 2018. The IRS generally has 10 years to collect. The taxpayer filed an Offer in Compromise that was pending for 8 months (which tolls the collection period for that time plus 30 days). When does the collection statute expiration date (CSED) fall?
Steps

items: Step 1: State the base rule: the collection period is 10 years from the date of assessment (Section 6502).
Step 2: Base CSED = assessment date April 15, 2018 + 10 years = April 15, 2028.
Step 3: Identify the tolling event: a pending Offer in Compromise suspends the collection period while pending, plus 30 days afterward.
Step 4: Compute the tolling period: 8 months pending + 30 days ≈ 8 months + 1 month = approximately 9 months.
Step 5: Extend the CSED by the tolling period: April 15, 2028 + 9 months ≈ January 15, 2029.
Step 6: Conclusion: the CSED is pushed from April 15, 2028 to roughly January 15, 2029 due to the OIC tolling.

blocks.text: Answer: The CSED moves from April 15, 2028 to approximately January 15, 2029 because the pending OIC (8 months + 30 days) tolled collection. Takeaway: the 10-year collection statute is suspended by events like a pending OIC, extending the CSED by the tolling period plus required add-ons.
A preparer charges $400 for a return containing an undisclosed position without substantial authority, and the position leads to an understatement. What is the minimum §6694(a) penalty?
Steps

items: Step 1: Section 6694(a) imposes the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived from the return.
Step 3: The greater of $1,000 and $200 is $1,000.
Step 4: Reasonable cause and good faith is a defense, and disclosure on Form 8275 may avoid the penalty.
Step 5: If the conduct were willful or reckless, §6694(b) would apply (the greater of $5,000 or 75% of income).

blocks.text: Answer: The penalty is $1,000, since the dollar floor exceeds 50% of the fee.

sections.title: Glossary
sections.summary: 836 tax terms, grouped by SEE part.

rows: 529 Plan
A state-sponsored education savings plan whose earnings are tax-free when used for qualified education expenses. It can also pay up to $10,000 of K-12 tuition (more beginning in 2026).
60-Day Rollover

The window during which a retirement plan or IRA distribution paid to the taxpayer can be redeposited into another qualified account without tax. Missing the deadline generally makes the distribution taxable and possibly subject to penalty.
65-Day Rule
An election allowing a trustee or executor to treat distributions made in the first 65 days of the following year as made on the last day of the prior year.
ABLE Account
A tax-advantaged savings account for people whose disability began before a set age (26, rising to 46 in 2026) to pay qualified disability expenses.
Above-the-Line Deduction

An adjustment to income subtracted in arriving at AGI, available whether or not the taxpayer itemizes. Examples include educator expenses, HSA contributions, and the deductible part of self-employment tax.
Accountable Plan

An employer reimbursement arrangement that meets IRS rules requiring a business connection, adequate substantiation, and return of excess amounts. Reimbursements under it are excluded from the employee's taxable wages.
Accrued Market Discount Election
An election to include market discount in income annually as it accrues rather than recognizing it all at disposition. It changes the timing but not the ordinary character of the income.
Active Participation
A lower standard than material participation, applied to the $25,000 rental loss allowance. It requires involvement in management decisions such as approving tenants and setting rents.
Active Participation (Rental Real Estate)

A less demanding standard than material participation, met when an owner makes management decisions such as approving tenants and setting rental terms. It is required to claim the special $25,000 rental loss allowance.
Additional Medicare Tax
A 0.9% tax on wages and self-employment income above threshold amounts based on filing status. Employers withhold it on wages over $200,000 regardless of filing status.
Additional Medicare Tax Withholding Threshold

The wage level above which employers must begin withholding the extra 0.9% Medicare tax, currently $200,000, regardless of filing status. Any over- or under-withholding is reconciled on the individual return.
Adjusted Basis

Original basis increased by capital improvements and certain costs, and decreased by items such as depreciation, casualty losses, and return-of-capital distributions. Adjusted basis is subtracted from the amount realized to compute gain or loss.
Adjusted Gross Income (AGI)

A taxpayer's total (gross) income reduced by specific above-the-line adjustments such as IRA contributions, student loan interest, and one-half of self-employment tax. AGI is a key figure because many deductions, credits, and phaseouts are calculated using it.
Adoption Credit

A nonrefundable credit for qualified expenses paid to adopt an eligible child, with a separate exclusion available for employer-provided adoption assistance. The credit phases out at higher income levels and unused amounts can carry forward five years.
Advance Premium Tax Credit
The portion of the premium tax credit paid directly to a health insurer during the year to lower monthly Marketplace premiums. It is reconciled on Form 8962 against the taxpayer's final income.
Aggregation of Trades or Businesses (Section 199A)

An election allowing related qualifying businesses to be combined when applying the wage and property limits of the qualified business income deduction. Aggregation can increase the allowable deduction across commonly controlled businesses.
Alternative Depreciation System

A depreciation method using longer recovery periods and the straight-line method, required for certain property and elective for others. It is mandated for some foreign-use, tax-exempt, and listed property situations.
Alternative Minimum Tax

A parallel tax system that recalculates income with fewer preferences to ensure taxpayers with substantial deductions pay a minimum amount. The taxpayer pays the higher of the regular tax or the tentative minimum tax.
Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT)

A parallel tax system that limits certain deductions and preferences to ensure higher-income taxpayers pay a minimum amount of tax. It is computed on Form 6251 and the taxpayer pays the greater of the regular tax or the tentative minimum tax.
Alternative Minimum Tax Credit

A credit for alternative minimum tax paid in prior years due to timing items such as the spread on incentive stock options. It can be used in later years when regular tax exceeds tentative minimum tax.
Alternative Tax Net Operating Loss Deduction (ATNOLD)

A separately computed net operating loss deduction used in the alternative minimum tax calculation, reflecting AMT adjustments and preferences. It is generally limited to 90% of alternative minimum taxable income.
Amended Return (Form 1040-X)
A return filed to correct a previously filed individual income tax return. It must generally be filed within three years of the original filing or two years of payment to claim a refund.
American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC)

A partially refundable education credit of up to $2,500 per eligible student for the first four years of postsecondary education. It requires at least half-time enrollment in a degree program and phases out at higher incomes.
Amortizable Bond Premium
The excess of a taxable bond's purchase price over its face value, which a holder may elect to amortize as an offset to interest income. The election reduces the bond's basis over its remaining life.
Amount Realized

The total of money plus the fair market value of property and services received on a sale or disposition, reduced by selling expenses. It is compared to adjusted basis to determine realized gain or loss.
AMT Exemption Phaseout
The gradual reduction of the alternative minimum tax exemption as alternative minimum taxable income rises above set thresholds. The phaseout can push effective AMT rates above the stated brackets.
Annual Gift Exclusion
The amount a donor may give to each recipient each year without using lifetime exemption or filing a gift tax return ($19,000 for 2025).
Annualized Income Installment Method

A method of computing estimated tax payments that bases each installment on income actually earned through that point in the year. It helps taxpayers with uneven income avoid penalties for periods when income was lower.
Assignment of Income Doctrine

A principle that income is taxed to the person who earns it or owns the income-producing property, not to whoever ultimately receives it. It prevents taxpayers from shifting tax by directing their income to others.
At-Risk Amount

The amount a taxpayer could actually lose in an activity, generally cash and the adjusted basis of contributed property plus certain borrowed amounts for which the taxpayer is personally liable. Losses are deductible only up to this amount under the at-risk rules.
At-Risk Rules

Limitations that restrict deductible losses from an activity to the amount the taxpayer has economically at risk. Amounts at risk include cash, the adjusted basis of contributed property, and certain borrowed funds for which the taxpayer is personally liable.
Augusta Rule
Informal name for the rule that income from renting a home for fewer than 15 days in a year is excluded and the related expenses are not deductible (section 280A(g)).
Backdoor Roth

A strategy of making a nondeductible traditional IRA contribution and converting it to a Roth IRA, used by taxpayers whose income exceeds the Roth contribution limit. The pro-rata rule can create tax on the conversion.
Backdoor Roth IRA

A strategy where a taxpayer above the Roth income limits makes a nondeductible traditional IRA contribution and then converts it to a Roth IRA. The pro-rata rule can cause part of the conversion to be taxable if other pretax IRA funds exist.
Backup Withholding

Withholding required on certain payments when a payee fails to furnish a correct taxpayer identification number or is subject to IRS notification. The payer withholds a flat percentage and remits it to the IRS.
Backup Withholding Rate

The flat rate of federal income tax a payer must withhold from certain payments when a payee fails to furnish a correct taxpayer identification number or is otherwise subject to backup withholding. The withheld amount is credited against the payee's tax liability.
Basis
A taxpayer's investment in property for tax purposes, generally the cost paid to acquire it. Basis is used to determine gain or loss on disposition and to compute depreciation.
Bona Fide Residence Test

One of two qualifying tests for the foreign earned income exclusion, met when a taxpayer is a genuine resident of a foreign country for an uninterrupted period that includes a full tax year. It depends on intent and ties to the foreign country rather than counting days.
Cafeteria Plan (Section 125)

An employer benefit plan that lets employees choose between taxable cash and certain qualified pretax benefits, such as health coverage or flexible spending accounts. Amounts directed to qualified benefits are excluded from taxable wages.
Cancellation of Debt Income

Income recognized when a debt is forgiven, generally reported on Form 1099-C. Exclusions include bankruptcy, insolvency (to the extent of insolvency), and qualified farm or real property business debt.
Cancellation of Debt Insolvency Exclusion

A provision allowing a taxpayer to exclude canceled debt income to the extent they were insolvent immediately before the discharge. Insolvency is measured by the excess of liabilities over the fair market value of assets.
Capital Asset

Generally any property held by a taxpayer except inventory, depreciable business property, accounts receivable, and certain other excluded items. Sales of capital assets produce capital gains or losses.
Capital Loss
A loss from the sale of a capital asset, deductible against capital gains and up to $3,000 of ordinary income per year. Excess losses are carried forward to future years.
Car Loan Interest Deduction
A deduction of up to $10,000 per year (2025–2028) for interest on a loan for a new, personal-use, U.S.-assembled vehicle originated after 2024. It phases out above $100,000 of MAGI ($200,000 joint).
Casualty Loss
A deductible loss from sudden, unexpected, or unusual events such as fire or storm. For individuals it is currently deductible only if attributable to a federally declared disaster.
Catch-Up Contribution

An additional retirement plan or IRA contribution allowed for individuals age 50 and older above the standard limit. Certain employer plans permit even larger catch-up amounts in the years approaching age 64.
Charitable Contribution Deduction
A deduction for donations of cash or property to qualified organizations, subject to AGI percentage limits. Noncash gifts may require additional substantiation such as a qualified appraisal.
Child and Dependent Care Credit

A credit for a portion of work-related expenses paid to care for a child under 13 or a disabled dependent so the taxpayer can work or look for work. The credit percentage decreases as income rises and requires earned income.
Child Tax Credit (CTC)

A credit for each qualifying child under age 17 who meets dependency and residency tests. A portion may be refundable as the Additional Child Tax Credit, and the credit phases out at higher income levels.
Claim of Right Doctrine

A doctrine requiring income received under an apparent unrestricted right to be reported in the year received, even if it might later have to be repaid. If repayment occurs later, the taxpayer may take a deduction or credit under section 1341.
Clean Vehicle Credit

A credit for purchasing a qualifying new plug-in electric or fuel cell vehicle, subject to manufacturing, sourcing, price, and income limits. Buyers may transfer the credit to the dealer at the point of sale.
Closer Connection Exception

A rule that can override the substantial presence test, allowing a person who was in the U.S. fewer than 183 days in the current year to remain a nonresident if they maintain a tax home and closer ties to a foreign country. It is claimed on Form 8840.
Cohan Rule

A court-developed rule allowing a reasonable estimate of a deductible expense when the taxpayer clearly incurred it but lacks complete records. It does not apply to expenses subject to strict substantiation requirements, such as travel and meals.
Collectibles Gain Rate
The maximum 28% long-term capital gains rate that applies to gains from selling collectibles such as art, coins, and precious metals. It is higher than the general long-term capital gains rates.
Combat Pay Election (Earned Income Credit)

An election allowing service members to include otherwise tax-free combat pay in earned income when it increases the earned income tax credit. The election applies to all of the member's combat pay for the year.
Combat Zone Exclusion
The exclusion of military pay earned in a combat zone: all of it for enlisted personnel and up to a monthly cap for officers. It also postpones filing and payment deadlines.
Considered Unmarried
A married taxpayer who lived apart from the spouse for the last six months of the year and paid more than half the cost of keeping up a home for a qualifying child, allowing head of household filing.
Constructive Receipt

A doctrine treating income as received when it is made available to a taxpayer without substantial restriction, even if not physically in hand. It prevents cash-method taxpayers from deferring income they could have drawn.
Constructive Sale Rule (Section 1259)

A rule triggering gain recognition when a taxpayer enters into transactions that essentially lock in profit on an appreciated financial position, such as a short sale against the box. It prevents indefinite deferral of built-in gains.
Cost Basis
The original value of an asset for tax purposes, generally the purchase price plus acquisition costs. It is the starting point for computing gain, loss, and depreciation.
Coverdell Education Savings Account

A tax-advantaged account for paying qualified education expenses, with tax-free growth and limited annual contributions. Distributions used for qualifying K-12 and higher education costs are excluded from income.
Credit for Other Dependents (ODC)

A nonrefundable credit for dependents who do not qualify for the child tax credit, such as older children and qualifying relatives. It supplements the child tax credit and shares the same income phaseout thresholds.
De Minimis Foreign Tax Election

An election allowing taxpayers with foreign taxes of $300 or less ($600 if married filing jointly) to claim the foreign tax credit directly without filing Form 1116. It simplifies reporting for small amounts of passive foreign income.
Dependent
A qualifying child or qualifying relative for whom a taxpayer may claim certain tax benefits. The dependent must meet specific relationship, support, income, and residency tests.
Dependent Care FSA
An employer plan that allows pre-tax contributions to pay dependent care expenses. The annual limit is $5,000 per household for 2025 and rises to $7,500 beginning in 2026.
Designated Roth Account

A Roth-style account within an employer plan such as a 401(k) or 403(b), funded with after-tax salary deferrals. Qualified withdrawals are tax-free, but it follows employer-plan rules rather than IRA rules.
Disqualifying Disposition (ISO)

A sale of incentive stock option shares before satisfying the required holding periods, converting part of the gain into ordinary compensation income. It eliminates the favorable capital gain treatment for that portion.
Distributable Net Income (DNI)
A measure that limits the distribution deduction of an estate or trust and sets the maximum income taxable to beneficiaries.
Dual-Basis Rule
The rule for gifted property whose fair market value is below the donor's basis at the time of gift: the donee uses the donor's basis for gain and the lower fair market value for loss.
Dual-Status Alien

A person who is both a nonresident alien and a resident alien during the same tax year, typically in the year of arrival or departure from the United States. Such taxpayers follow special rules and generally cannot claim the standard deduction.
Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)

A refundable credit for low-to-moderate income working taxpayers, with the amount based on earned income, filing status, and number of qualifying children. Investment income above a limit disqualifies a taxpayer.
Earned Income Tax Credit Disallowance (Form 8862)

After the EITC is denied for reckless or fraudulent reasons, the taxpayer must file Form 8862 to claim it again in a later year. A two- or ten-year ban may apply depending on the reason for the prior denial.
Educator Expense Deduction
An above-the-line deduction allowing eligible K-12 teachers to deduct a limited amount of unreimbursed classroom supply costs. The dollar limit is indexed periodically for inflation.
Effectively Connected Income (ECI)

Income a nonresident alien earns from a U.S. trade or business, which is taxed at the same graduated rates that apply to U.S. citizens. It is distinguished from fixed or determinable income, which is generally taxed at a flat 30% rate.
Eligible Designated Beneficiary

A beneficiary who may stretch inherited retirement account payments over life expectancy: a surviving spouse, minor child of the owner, disabled or chronically ill person, or someone not more than 10 years younger than the owner.
Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit

An annual credit for qualifying energy-saving improvements to a home such as insulation, windows, doors, and certain heating equipment. It is subject to yearly dollar caps and applies per item category.
Estate Tax
A federal tax on the transfer of a deceased person's taxable estate that exceeds the applicable exclusion amount. It is reported on Form 706 and is unified with the gift tax system.
Estimated Tax
Quarterly payments made on income not subject to withholding, such as self-employment or investment income. Underpaying can trigger an estimated tax penalty unless a safe-harbor amount is paid.
Estimated Tax Penalty

A charge for not paying enough tax during the year through withholding and estimated payments. It is computed like interest on the shortfall and can be avoided by meeting safe-harbor payment thresholds.
Estimated Tax Safe Harbor

A rule that avoids the underpayment penalty if a taxpayer pays at least a specified percentage of the current year's tax or of the prior year's tax through withholding and estimated payments. The prior-year percentage is higher for taxpayers above an income threshold.
Estimated Tax Voucher (Form 1040-ES)

The voucher individuals use to make quarterly estimated tax payments on income not subject to withholding. It helps self-employed and investment-income taxpayers pay tax throughout the year and avoid underpayment penalties.
Excess Business Loss Carryover

The portion of a noncorporate taxpayer's business loss disallowed under the excess business loss limitation, which is converted into a net operating loss carryforward. It then becomes subject to the net operating loss rules in later years.
Excess Business Loss Limitation (Section 461(l))
A rule that limits the amount of net business losses a noncorporate taxpayer can use to offset nonbusiness income in a year. Disallowed losses are carried forward as part of a net operating loss.
Excess Contribution (IRA)
An amount contributed to an IRA above the legal limit or contributed when not eligible. It is subject to an excise tax each year until it is withdrawn or otherwise corrected.
Excess Deferral (Elective Contributions)

Salary deferrals to retirement plans that exceed the annual elective deferral limit, often because an employee participates in plans with two employers. Uncorrected excess deferrals can be taxed twice.
Excess Social Security Tax Credit

A credit for employees who had Social Security tax over-withheld because they worked for two or more employers and exceeded the annual wage base. The excess is claimed as a credit on the individual income tax return.
Exempt Individual
For immigration-based tax rules, a teacher, trainee, student, or foreign government employee whose days in the U.S. do not count toward the substantial presence test for a limited time.
FDAP Income
Fixed, determinable, annual, or periodical U.S.-source income of foreign persons, such as dividends and royalties, generally taxed at a flat 30% by withholding unless a treaty reduces the rate.
Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) Tax
Payroll taxes funding Social Security and Medicare, split between employer and employee. The Social Security portion applies up to an annual wage base, while the Medicare portion has no wage cap.
Filing Status

A category that determines a taxpayer's tax rates, standard deduction, and eligibility for benefits. The five statuses are single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household, and qualifying surviving spouse.
FinCEN Form 114 (Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts)

The report, commonly called the FBAR, that U.S. persons must file electronically when the total value of their foreign financial accounts exceeds $10,000 at any time during the year. It is filed with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, not on a tax return.
FIRPTA
The Foreign Investment in Real Property Tax Act, which taxes foreign persons on gains from U.S. real property interests and requires buyers to withhold, generally 15% of the amount realized.
First-Year Choice
An election that allows a nonresident alien who meets the substantial presence test in the following year to be treated as a resident for part of the first year.
Fixed, Determinable, Annual, or Periodical (FDAP) Income
U.S.-source passive income paid to a nonresident alien, such as interest, dividends, rents, and royalties. It is generally subject to a flat 30% withholding tax unless reduced by a treaty.
Flexible Spending Arrangement (FSA)

An employer-sponsored account funded with pretax salary reductions to pay for qualified medical or dependent care expenses. Health FSAs are generally subject to a use-it-or-lose-it rule with limited carryover or grace period options.
Foreign Earned Income Exclusion

An election allowing a qualifying U.S. taxpayer living abroad to exclude a limited amount of foreign wages and self-employment income from U.S. tax. Eligibility requires meeting either the bona fide residence test or the physical presence test.
Foreign Housing Exclusion

An additional exclusion for taxpayers claiming the foreign earned income exclusion, covering reasonable housing costs abroad that exceed a base amount. Self-employed individuals claim a foreign housing deduction instead of an exclusion.
Foreign Tax Credit Carryover

The ability to carry unused foreign tax credits back one year and forward ten years when foreign taxes exceed the annual limitation. This preserves the benefit of taxes that could not be used currently.
Foreign Tax Credit Limitation

A cap that prevents the foreign tax credit from offsetting U.S. tax on U.S.-source income. The limit equals U.S. tax multiplied by the ratio of foreign-source taxable income to total taxable income, computed separately by income category.
Foreign Tax Credit vs. Deduction Choice

Taxpayers who pay foreign income taxes may elect to claim them as a credit or deduct them as an itemized deduction, but generally must apply one method to all foreign taxes for the year. The credit usually provides greater benefit because it reduces tax dollar-for-dollar.
Form 1040
The standard U.S. individual income tax return used to report income, deductions, and credits. Supporting schedules attach to it to detail specific items.
Form 1040-NR
The U.S. income tax return for nonresident alien individuals.
Form 1040-NR (U.S. Nonresident Alien Income Tax Return)
The income tax return filed by nonresident aliens with U.S.-source income or a U.S. trade or business. It applies different rules than the return for U.S. citizens and residents.
Form 1040-SR (U.S. Tax Return for Seniors)

A version of the individual income tax return designed for taxpayers age 65 and older, with larger type and a chart for the standard deduction. It allows the same income and deductions as the standard Form 1040.
Form 1040-V (Payment Voucher)
The voucher a taxpayer includes when mailing a payment for a balance due on Form 1040. It helps the IRS correctly credit the payment to the taxpayer's account.
Form 1040-X (Amended U.S. Individual Income Tax Return)

The form used to correct a previously filed Form 1040 after the original return was submitted. It shows the original figures, the changes, and the corrected amounts, and is generally due within three years of filing or two years of paying the tax, whichever is later.
Form 1041 (U.S. Income Tax Return for Estates and Trusts)

The income tax return filed by a fiduciary for an estate or trust to report income earned by the entity. It allows a deduction for income distributed to beneficiaries, who then report that income on their own returns via Schedule K-1.
Form 1045 (Application for Tentative Refund)

The form individuals, estates, and trusts can use to apply for a quick refund from carrying back a net operating loss, certain credits, or a claim of right adjustment. The IRS processes it on an expedited, tentative basis.
Form 1095-A (Health Insurance Marketplace Statement)
The statement issued by a Marketplace reporting coverage and advance premium tax credit amounts. It supplies the figures needed to complete Form 8962.
Form 1098 (Mortgage Interest Statement)
The information return a lender issues to report mortgage interest of $600 or more received from a borrower during the year. Borrowers use it to support a home mortgage interest deduction.
Form 1098-E (Student Loan Interest Statement)
The information return a lender issues to report student loan interest of $600 or more received during the year. Borrowers use it to claim the student loan interest deduction.
Form 1098-T (Tuition Statement)
The information return an eligible educational institution issues to report qualified tuition and related expenses. Students and families use it to claim education credits or the tuition deduction.
Form 1099
A series of information returns reporting various types of income other than wages, such as interest, dividends, and nonemployee compensation. Payers send copies to the recipient and the IRS.
Form 1099-A (Acquisition or Abandonment of Secured Property)
An information return a lender files when it acquires secured property or learns it has been abandoned. The borrower uses it to determine gain or loss and any related cancellation of debt income.
Form 1099-B (Proceeds From Broker and Barter Exchange Transactions)

The information return brokers issue to report sales of securities and certain other transactions, including proceeds and, when known, cost basis. Taxpayers use it to complete Form 8949 and Schedule D.
Form 1099-C (Cancellation of Debt)
The information return a creditor issues when it cancels $600 or more of a borrower's debt. Canceled debt is generally taxable income unless an exclusion, such as insolvency or bankruptcy, applies.
Form 1099-DA
The information return on which digital asset brokers report gross proceeds (and later basis) from sales of digital assets, beginning with 2025 transactions.
Form 1099-DIV (Dividends and Distributions)

The information return that reports dividends, capital gain distributions, and certain other distributions paid to a taxpayer during the year. Recipients use it to report dividend income on their returns.
Form 1099-G (Certain Government Payments)
The information return that reports government payments such as unemployment compensation and state or local income tax refunds. Recipients use it to determine how much of those payments is taxable.
Form 1099-INT (Interest Income)
The information return that reports interest income of $10 or more paid to a taxpayer during the year. It also reports any federal income tax withheld and early withdrawal penalties.
Form 1099-K (Payment Card and Third Party Network Transactions)

The information return filed by payment settlement entities, such as credit card processors and payment apps, to report the gross amount of reportable transactions. It helps the IRS match business receipts processed through third-party networks.
Form 1099-MISC (Miscellaneous Information)

The information return used to report various payments such as rents, royalties, prizes, awards, and other income not reported on a more specific form. Nonemployee compensation moved to Form 1099-NEC starting in 2020.
Form 1099-R (Distributions From Pensions, Annuities, Retirement or Profit-Sharing Plans, IRAs, Insurance Contracts, etc.)

The information return that reports distributions from retirement accounts, annuities, and similar plans. It shows the gross and taxable amounts and any tax withheld, and includes a code describing the type of distribution.
Form 1116 (Foreign Tax Credit)

The form individuals use to claim a credit for income taxes paid or accrued to a foreign country. The credit is limited to the U.S. tax attributable to foreign-source income within each separate category.
Form 2120 (Multiple Support Declaration)

The form used when no single person provides more than half of a dependent's support but a group together provides over half. It lets the group designate which member may claim the dependent for the year.
Form 2210 (Underpayment of Estimated Tax by Individuals, Estates, and Trusts)

The form used to determine whether a taxpayer owes a penalty for underpaying estimated tax and to compute the amount. It also allows requests for penalty waivers or use of the annualized income method.
Form 2441 (Child and Dependent Care Expenses)
The form used to calculate and claim the child and dependent care credit and to report any employer-provided dependent care benefits. It requires identifying the care provider.
Form 2555 (Foreign Earned Income)

The form used to claim the foreign earned income exclusion and the foreign housing exclusion or deduction. Qualifying taxpayers must meet either the bona fide residence test or the physical presence test.
Form 3520 (Annual Return To Report Transactions With Foreign Trusts and Receipt of Certain Foreign Gifts)
The information return used to report transactions with foreign trusts and the receipt of large gifts or bequests from foreign persons. Failure to file can result in significant penalties.
Form 4684 (Casualties and Thefts)

The form used to report gains and losses from casualties and thefts of personal-use and business property. For personal-use property, deductible losses are generally limited to federally declared disaster areas.
Form 4835 (Farm Rental Income and Expenses)
The form a landowner uses to report income from a crop-share or livestock-share arrangement when not materially participating. It keeps such income off Schedule F and outside self-employment tax.
Form 4868 (Application for Automatic Extension of Time To File U.S. Individual Income Tax Return)

The form individuals file to get an automatic six-month extension to file Form 1040. The extension covers filing only; estimated tax owed must still be paid by the original deadline to avoid penalties and interest.
Form 5329 (Additional Taxes on Qualified Plans and Other Tax-Favored Accounts)

The form used to report additional taxes on early distributions, excess contributions, and missed required minimum distributions from retirement and similar accounts. It is also used to request a waiver of the penalty for a missed RMD when reasonable cause exists.
Form 6252 (Installment Sale Income)

The form used to report income from an installment sale, where at least one payment is received after the year of sale. It calculates the gross profit percentage and the portion of gain recognized each year.
Form 706 (United States Estate (and Generation-Skipping Transfer) Tax Return)

The return filed by the executor of a decedent's estate to report the gross estate, deductions, and estate tax due. It is also used to elect portability of a deceased spouse's unused exclusion amount.
Form 709 (United States Gift (and Generation-Skipping Transfer) Tax Return)

The return used to report taxable gifts that exceed the annual exclusion and to allocate generation-skipping transfer tax exemption. It tracks use of the donor's lifetime gift and estate tax exclusion.
Form 8332
A form by which the custodial parent releases the claim to a child as a dependent to the noncustodial parent, transferring the child tax credit but not head of household status or the EITC.
Form 8332 (Release/Revocation of Release of Claim to Exemption for Child by Custodial Parent)

The form a custodial parent signs to release the right to claim a child as a dependent to the noncustodial parent. The noncustodial parent attaches it to their return to claim the child for certain tax benefits.
Form 8606 (Nondeductible IRAs)

The form used to report nondeductible contributions to a traditional IRA, distributions from IRAs with basis, and conversions to a Roth IRA. It tracks the taxpayer's basis so the same amounts are not taxed twice.
Form 8615 (Tax for Certain Children Who Have Unearned Income)
The form used to figure the kiddie tax on a child's unearned income above an annual threshold. It taxes that excess income at the parents' rate to discourage shifting investment income to children.
Form 8814
A form on which parents may elect to report a child's interest and dividend income on their own return instead of the child filing a return.
Form 8814 (Parents' Election To Report Child's Interest and Dividends)

The form parents use to elect to report a child's interest and dividend income on their own return instead of filing a separate return for the child. It is available only when the child's income meets certain limits and consists solely of interest and dividends.
Form 8814 Kiddie Tax Election Threshold

The limited amount of a child's interest and dividend income that a parent may elect to report on the parent's return instead of filing a separate child return. Exceeding the cap or having other income types makes the election unavailable.
Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home)

The form sole proprietors use to compute the deductible expenses for the business use of their home. It allocates home costs based on the percentage of the home used regularly and exclusively for business.
Form 8833 (Treaty-Based Return Position Disclosure)
The form used to disclose a position that a tax treaty overrides or modifies a provision of the Internal Revenue Code. Failure to file when required can trigger a separate penalty.
Form 8857 (Request for Innocent Spouse Relief)

The form a spouse files to ask the IRS to be relieved of responsibility for tax, interest, and penalties on a joint return attributable to the other spouse. The IRS evaluates innocent spouse, separation of liability, and equitable relief options.
Form 8863 (Education Credits)
The form used to compute the American Opportunity and Lifetime Learning education credits. It reconciles qualified expenses with amounts reported on Form 1098-T.
Form 8880 (Credit for Qualified Retirement Savings Contributions)
The form used to figure the Saver's Credit for low- and moderate-income taxpayers who contribute to retirement accounts. The credit rate depends on income and filing status.
Form 8938 (Statement of Specified Foreign Financial Assets)

The form filed with a tax return to report specified foreign financial assets when their value exceeds reporting thresholds. It is required under the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act and is separate from the FBAR.
Form 8949 (Sales and Other Dispositions of Capital Assets)

The form on which taxpayers list each sale or disposition of a capital asset, showing proceeds, basis, and gain or loss. Totals carry to Schedule D, and the form is also used to make adjustments such as wash sale or basis corrections.
Form 8959 (Additional Medicare Tax)
The form used to calculate the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax on wages and self-employment income above the filing-status threshold. It also reconciles any extra Medicare tax withheld by employers.
Form 8960 (Net Investment Income Tax)
The form individuals, estates, and trusts use to compute the 3.8% net investment income tax. It applies when modified adjusted gross income exceeds the applicable threshold.
Form 8962 (Premium Tax Credit Reconciliation)

The form that reconciles advance premium tax credit payments received through the Marketplace with the actual credit allowed. A taxpayer may owe repayment or receive an additional credit based on year-end income.
Form 8995 (Qualified Business Income Deduction Simplified Computation)
The simplified form used to figure the qualified business income deduction for taxpayers under the taxable income threshold. Higher-income taxpayers use the longer Form 8995-A instead.
Form 8995-A (Qualified Business Income Deduction)

The detailed form for figuring the qualified business income deduction when taxable income exceeds the simplified-computation thresholds. It applies wage and property limits and the specified service business phaseout.
Form 982 (Reduction of Tax Attributes Due to Discharge of Indebtedness)

The form used to exclude canceled debt from income under exceptions such as bankruptcy, insolvency, or qualified principal residence indebtedness. The excluded amount generally requires reducing tax attributes such as basis or carryovers.
Form W-2
A wage and tax statement employers provide to employees and the Social Security Administration. It reports annual wages and the taxes withheld during the year.
Form W-2G
An information return reporting gambling winnings and any federal tax withheld.
Form W-4 (Employee's Withholding Certificate)

The form an employee completes so the employer can determine how much federal income tax to withhold from wages. Employees can adjust withholding for dependents, multiple jobs, and other income or deductions.
Form W-7 (Application for IRS Individual Taxpayer Identification Number)

The application used to request an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number for those not eligible for a Social Security number. It is generally submitted with a tax return and proof of identity and foreign status.
Form W-8BEN
A certificate by which a foreign individual establishes foreign status and claims treaty benefits for payments from U.S. sources.
Form W-9 (Request for Taxpayer Identification Number and Certification)

The form used to request a taxpayer identification number from a payee and to certify that the number is correct and the payee is not subject to backup withholding. Businesses collect it before issuing information returns like Form 1099.
Gambling Loss Deduction

An itemized deduction for gambling losses, limited to the amount of gambling winnings reported as income for the year. Documentation such as a contemporaneous log is needed to substantiate the losses.
Gift Splitting
An election by married couples to treat gifts made by one spouse as made half by each, effectively doubling the annual exclusion.
Gift Tax
A federal tax on transfers of property by gift during a person's lifetime, paid by the donor. An annual exclusion per donee and a lifetime exemption reduce or eliminate tax for most gifts.
Gross Income
All income from whatever source derived unless specifically excluded by law. It includes wages, interest, dividends, business income, rents, and many other items before any deductions.
Grouping Election (Passive Activities)

An election that lets a taxpayer treat multiple business or rental activities as a single activity for applying the passive activity and material participation rules. Proper grouping can make it easier to meet the material participation tests.
Hardship Distribution
A distribution from a 401(k) plan to meet an immediate and heavy financial need. It is taxable and subject to the 10% additional tax unless an exception applies, and cannot be rolled over.
Head of Household

A filing status for unmarried (or considered unmarried) taxpayers who pay more than half the cost of keeping up a home for a qualifying person for more than half the year. It offers a larger standard deduction and more favorable tax brackets than single filing.
Health Flexible Spending Arrangement
An employer plan that reimburses medical expenses with pre-tax dollars. Unused amounts are generally forfeited, subject to a limited carryover or grace period if the plan allows.
Health Savings Account (HSA)

A tax-advantaged account available to individuals covered by a qualifying high-deductible health plan. Contributions are deductible or pretax, earnings grow tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are not taxed.
High-Deductible Health Plan (HDHP)
A health plan with a minimum deductible and a maximum out-of-pocket limit that makes the covered individual eligible to contribute to a Health Savings Account.
Hobby Loss Nine-Factor Test

The set of factors the IRS weighs to decide whether an activity is engaged in for profit, including expertise, time devoted, history of income or losses, and the manner of operation. No single factor controls the determination.
Hobby Loss Presumption

A presumption that an activity is engaged in for profit if it shows a profit in a specified number of years out of a consecutive period. Meeting the presumption shifts the burden to the IRS to show the activity is a hobby.
Hobby Loss Rule
Section 183, which limits deductions for activities not engaged in for profit. Income is fully taxable, and under current law the related expenses are not deductible.
Holding Period
The length of time a taxpayer owns a capital asset, which determines whether a gain or loss is short-term or long-term. It generally begins the day after acquisition and ends on the disposition date.
Housing Allowance (Clergy)
A designated amount of a minister's pay excluded from income tax up to the least of the amount designated, spent, or the fair rental value, but still subject to self-employment tax.
Identity Protection Personal Identification Number
A six-digit number the IRS issues to eligible taxpayers to prevent the misuse of their Social Security number on fraudulent returns. A return filed without the correct number is rejected or delayed.
Identity Protection PIN
A six-digit number issued by the IRS to protect a taxpayer's SSN from being used to file a fraudulent return. It changes each year and must be entered on the return.
Imputed Interest

Interest the tax law treats as charged on certain below-market or interest-free loans, even if little or no interest is actually charged. It can create taxable interest income for the lender and other tax consequences for the parties.
Incentive Stock Option (ISO)

An employer stock option that, if holding requirements are met, produces capital gain rather than ordinary income on sale. The spread at exercise is, however, an adjustment for alternative minimum tax purposes.
Income Averaging (Schedule J)
An election for farmers and fishermen to spread elected farm income over the three prior years to lower tax.
Income in Respect of a Decedent (IRD)
Income earned by a decedent but not received before death, taxed to the recipient with no step-up in basis, with a deduction for estate tax paid on it.
Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN)

A tax processing number the IRS issues to individuals who must file or be reported on a U.S. return but are not eligible for a Social Security number. It is used for tax purposes only and does not confer work authorization or immigration status.
Injured Spouse Allocation (Form 8379)
A request a spouse files when a joint refund is, or will be, applied to the other spouse's separate past-due debt. It lets the injured spouse recover their share of the joint refund.
Insolvency Exclusion
The exclusion of canceled debt income to the extent that liabilities exceed the fair market value of assets immediately before the cancellation. It is claimed on Form 982.
Installment Sale Pledge Rule

A rule treating proceeds from pledging certain installment obligations as deemed payments that accelerate recognition of installment gain. It limits using the installment method to defer tax while still accessing cash.
Involuntary Conversion
The destruction, theft, or condemnation of property. Gain can be deferred under section 1033 if proceeds are reinvested in similar property within the replacement period, generally two years.
Involuntary Conversion (Section 1033)

The replacement of property lost through casualty, theft, or condemnation, where gain can be deferred if proceeds are reinvested in similar property within a set period. The deferral preserves basis in the replacement property.
Itemized Deduction

Specific allowable expenses reported on Schedule A, such as mortgage interest, state and local taxes (capped), charitable gifts, and medical costs above a threshold. A taxpayer itemizes only when the total exceeds the standard deduction.
Kiddie Tax
Rules taxing a child's unearned income above a threshold at the parents' marginal rate. It prevents shifting investment income to children in lower brackets.
Lifetime Learning Credit (LLC)
A nonrefundable credit of up to $2,000 per return for qualified tuition and related expenses. It has no enrollment-level requirement and can be claimed for an unlimited number of years.
Like-Kind Exchange 180-Day Exchange Period

The deadline by which replacement property must be received in a deferred like-kind exchange, measured from the transfer of the relinquished property. It can be shortened if the tax return due date arrives first.
Like-Kind Exchange 45-Day Identification Period
The window in a deferred exchange within which the taxpayer must identify potential replacement property in writing. Missing the deadline disqualifies the exchange from deferral.
Long-Term Capital Gain
Gain from the sale of a capital asset held more than one year. Long-term gains generally qualify for preferential tax rates of 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income.
Marginal Tax Rate
The tax rate applied to the last dollar of taxable income. The U.S. uses a progressive bracket system where higher portions of income are taxed at higher rates.
Market Discount

The excess of a bond's stated redemption price over a holder's purchase price when bought in the secondary market below face value. Gain attributable to accrued market discount is generally taxed as ordinary income.
Material Participation
Regular, continuous, and substantial involvement in a business activity, measured by a set of tests such as the 500-hour test. Meeting it allows losses to be treated as nonpassive.
Material Participation Tests

The set of tests used to determine whether a taxpayer participates in an activity on a regular, continuous, and substantial basis. Meeting any one test makes the activity non-passive, so losses are not limited by the passive activity rules.
Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System

The standard U.S. depreciation system assigning property to recovery periods and applying accelerated methods. It determines how the cost of business assets is deducted over their assigned class lives.
Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI)

AGI with certain deductions and excluded income added back, with the specific items varying by tax benefit. MAGI is used to determine eligibility and phaseouts for items like IRA deductions, the premium tax credit, and education credits.
Nanny Tax

The common name for the employment taxes a household employer owes on wages paid to domestic workers above the annual threshold. These taxes are reported on Schedule H of the employer's individual return.
Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT)
A 3.8% tax on the lesser of net investment income or the excess of MAGI over a threshold. It applies to higher-income individuals, estates, and trusts.
Net Operating Loss 80% Limitation
A rule limiting post-2017 net operating loss deductions to 80% of taxable income computed before the deduction. It prevents fully wiping out taxable income with carryforwards in a single year.
Net Operating Loss Carryforward

A business loss from a year when deductions exceed income that may be applied against taxable income in future years. Post-2017 losses generally offset only up to 80 percent of taxable income in the carryforward year.
Net Unrealized Appreciation (NUA)

The increase in value of employer securities held in a retirement plan over their cost basis. When such stock is distributed in a lump sum, the appreciation can be taxed at capital gains rates rather than as ordinary income.
Net Unrealized Appreciation Election

An election to roll over employer stock from a qualified plan into a taxable account, paying ordinary tax only on the stock's cost basis at distribution. The built-in appreciation is later taxed at capital gain rates when sold.
Nonaccountable Plan
An employer reimbursement or allowance arrangement that does not meet the accountable plan rules. Payments under it are treated as taxable wages subject to withholding and employment taxes.
Nonbusiness Bad Debt

A bad debt unrelated to a trade or business, deductible only as a short-term capital loss in the year it becomes totally worthless. Unlike business bad debts, no partial worthlessness deduction is permitted.
Nonqualified Stock Option (NQSO)

An employer stock option that generates ordinary compensation income equal to the spread between fair market value and the exercise price at exercise. The employee's basis in the shares includes that recognized income.
Nonrecourse Debt
Debt for which the lender can look only to the collateral, not the borrower personally. On foreclosure the amount realized is the full debt, so there is no cancellation of debt income.
Nonrefundable Credit
A credit that can reduce tax liability only to zero, with no refund of any excess. Examples include the Child and Dependent Care Credit and the Lifetime Learning Credit.
One-Rollover-Per-Year Rule

A limit allowing only one tax-free 60-day IRA-to-IRA rollover during any rolling 12-month period across all of a taxpayer's IRAs. Trustee-to-trustee transfers and Roth conversions are not counted against this limit.
Optional Method (Self-Employment Tax)

An election allowing certain low-income or farm taxpayers to compute self-employment earnings using a set formula rather than actual net profit. It can preserve Social Security credits or qualify the taxpayer for earned-income-based benefits.
Ordinary Income Recapture
The treatment of gain on the sale of depreciable property as ordinary income to the extent of prior depreciation, as under section 1245 for personal property.
Original Issue Discount (OID)

The difference between a debt instrument's stated redemption price at maturity and its lower issue price. The discount is treated as interest that the holder generally includes in income over the life of the instrument rather than at maturity.
Original Issue Discount Accrual
The annual inclusion in income of the discount on a bond issued below face value, even though no cash is received until maturity. Holders increase their basis by the accrued amount each year.
Passive Activity

A trade or business in which the taxpayer does not materially participate, including most rental activities. Losses from passive activities are generally deductible only against passive income, with disallowed amounts carried forward.
Passive Activity $25,000 Rental Allowance

A special allowance letting actively participating rental real estate owners deduct up to $25,000 of passive losses against other income. The allowance phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of modified adjusted gross income.
Passive Activity Loss

A loss from a trade or business in which the taxpayer does not materially participate, or generally from any rental activity. Such losses are deductible only against passive income, with the excess suspended and carried forward.
Passive Activity Loss (PAL) Carryover
Disallowed passive losses carried to future years until offset by passive income or the activity is fully disposed of. A fully taxable disposition generally frees up suspended losses.
Penalty-Free Early Distribution Exception

A circumstance such as disability, certain medical costs, first-home purchase, or higher education that exempts an early retirement distribution from the 10% additional tax. The distribution may still be subject to ordinary income tax.
Phantom Income

Taxable income reported to a taxpayer without an accompanying cash distribution, common with partnership allocations, original issue discount, and forgiven debt. It can create tax due even when no money is received.
Physical Presence Test

A qualifying test for the foreign earned income exclusion met when a taxpayer is physically present in a foreign country for at least 330 full days during any 12 consecutive months. Unlike the bona fide residence test, it is purely a day-count rule.
Portability
The election allowing a surviving spouse to use the deceased spouse's unused estate tax exclusion (DSUE), made on a timely filed Form 706.
Premium Tax Credit
A refundable credit that helps pay for health insurance purchased through the Marketplace, reconciled on Form 8962 against advance payments.
Premium Tax Credit (PTC)
A refundable credit that helps eligible individuals afford health coverage purchased through the Marketplace. It is reconciled on Form 8962 against any advance payments made during the year.
Pro-Rata Rule
The rule that treats all of a taxpayer's traditional, SEP, and SIMPLE IRAs as one account when figuring the taxable part of a distribution or conversion that includes after-tax basis.
Pro-Rata Rule (IRA Distributions)

A rule requiring that each distribution or conversion from traditional IRAs be treated as a proportional mix of pretax and after-tax amounts. It prevents taxpayers from cherry-picking only nondeductible basis when converting to a Roth.
Provisional Income
Adjusted gross income (without Social Security), plus tax-exempt interest, plus half of Social Security benefits. It is compared to base amounts to determine how much of the benefits is taxable.
Qualified Business Income

The net ordinary income from a qualified U.S. trade or business operated as a sole proprietorship, partnership, or S corporation. It is the base for the Section 199A deduction and excludes investment-type income and reasonable compensation.
Qualified Business Income Threshold

The taxable income level at which the qualified business income deduction begins to apply wage and property limits and the specified service business restriction. Below the threshold, the deduction is generally a straightforward 20% of qualified income.
Qualified Charitable Distribution (QCD)

A direct transfer from an IRA to a qualified charity by a taxpayer age 70 and a half or older, up to an annual limit. It is excluded from income and can count toward the required minimum distribution.
Qualified Charitable Distribution Limit

The annual cap on amounts an IRA owner age 70 1/2 or older can transfer directly to charity tax-free, which is indexed for inflation. The distribution counts toward the required minimum distribution but is excluded from gross income.
Qualified Dividend
A dividend from a U.S. or qualified foreign corporation that meets the holding period (more than 60 days in the 121-day period around the ex-dividend date), taxed at capital gain rates.
Qualified Dividends
Dividends from domestic and certain foreign corporations that meet holding period requirements. They are taxed at the lower long-term capital gains rates rather than ordinary income rates.
Qualified Joint Venture

An election allowing a married couple operating an unincorporated business together to file as two sole proprietors instead of a partnership. Each spouse reports a share of income and self-employment tax on a separate Schedule C.
Qualified Opportunity Fund

An investment vehicle that invests in designated low-income communities and offers tax benefits for reinvested capital gains. Investors can defer and potentially reduce gain and exclude future appreciation if holding requirements are met.
Qualified Overtime Deduction
A deduction (2025–2028) for the premium portion of overtime pay required by the Fair Labor Standards Act, up to $12,500 ($25,000 joint), phasing out above $150,000 of MAGI ($300,000 joint).
Qualified Principal Residence Indebtedness Exclusion
An exclusion for canceled mortgage debt on a taxpayer's main home, available when the law extends it. Excluded amounts reduce the home's basis rather than producing taxable income.
Qualified Tips Deduction

A deduction of up to $25,000 (tax years 2025–2028) for voluntary tips received in occupations that customarily receive tips. It is allowed to itemizers and non-itemizers and phases out above $150,000 of MAGI ($300,000 joint).
Qualified Tuition Program (529 Plan)

A state-sponsored savings or prepaid plan that grows tax-free and pays qualified education expenses without tax. Earnings on nonqualified distributions are taxable and subject to an additional penalty.
Qualifying Child

A dependent who meets the relationship, age, residency, support, and joint return tests under the dependency rules. A qualifying child must generally be under 19 (or 24 if a full-time student) and not provide more than half of their own support.
Qualifying Relative

A dependent who is not a qualifying child but meets the relationship or member-of-household, gross income, support, and not-a-qualifying-child tests. The dependent's gross income must be below the annual exemption threshold and the taxpayer must provide more than half of their support.
Qualifying Surviving Spouse
A filing status available for two years after a spouse's death for a taxpayer with a dependent child who has not remarried. It allows use of joint return rates and the higher standard deduction.
Real Estate Professional
