A taxpayer who spends more than 750 hours and more than half of personal service time in real property trades or businesses in which the taxpayer materially participates, allowing rental losses to be nonpassive.
Real Estate Professional Status

A tax status allowing a taxpayer who spends enough qualifying hours in real property businesses to treat rental real estate as non-passive. It permits otherwise passive rental losses to offset other income when material participation is met.
Recharacterization (IRA Contribution)

Treating a contribution made to one type of IRA as if it had been made to the other type, within the allowed time. It can no longer be used to undo a Roth conversion but still applies to certain contributions.
Recognized Gain
The portion of realized gain that is actually included in taxable income. Some gains are deferred or excluded by law, so recognized gain may be less than realized gain.
Recourse Debt
Debt for which the borrower is personally liable. On foreclosure, the amount realized is the property's fair market value, and any forgiven excess can be cancellation of debt income.
Recovery Rebate Credit

A refundable credit claimed on a return to reconcile economic impact (stimulus) payments authorized during the COVID-19 period. Taxpayers who received less than they were entitled to could claim the difference on their return.
Refundable Credit
A credit that can reduce tax below zero and result in a refund of the excess. Examples include the EITC and the refundable portion of the Child Tax Credit.
Related-Party Installment Sale Rule

A rule that can accelerate installment gain to the original seller if a related buyer resells the property within two years. It prevents families from deferring tax indefinitely through intra-family resales.
Required Beginning Date

The date by which a retirement account owner must begin required minimum distributions, generally April 1 of the year after the owner reaches the applicable age (73, or 75 for those born in 1960 or later).
Required Beginning Date (Retirement Distributions)

The deadline by which a retirement account owner must begin taking required minimum distributions, generally tied to reaching a specified age. Missing it can trigger an additional tax on the amount not distributed.
Required Minimum Distribution (RMD)

The minimum amount that must be withdrawn annually from most tax-deferred retirement accounts once the account owner reaches the required beginning age. Failure to take the RMD triggers an excise tax on the shortfall.
Residential Clean Energy Credit

A credit for a percentage of the cost of qualifying solar, wind, geothermal, and battery storage property installed at a home. It is nonrefundable but any unused amount carries forward to future years.
Rollover

A transfer of retirement funds from one qualified plan or IRA to another that is tax-free if completed within 60 days or done directly between trustees. IRA-to-IRA rollovers are limited to one per 12 months.
Roth Conversion

The transfer of funds from a traditional IRA or other pretax retirement account into a Roth IRA. The converted pretax amount is included in taxable income in the year of conversion in exchange for future tax-free qualified withdrawals.
Roth IRA

An individual retirement account funded with after-tax dollars where qualified distributions, including earnings, are tax-free. Contributions are not deductible and the account is not subject to lifetime RMDs for the owner.
SALT Cap
The limit on the itemized deduction for state and local taxes. It is $40,000 for 2025 ($20,000 if married filing separately), phasing down for high earners, and reverts to $10,000 in 2030.
Saver's Credit
A nonrefundable credit for lower-income taxpayers who contribute to retirement accounts such as IRAs or 401(k) plans. The credit rate depends on AGI and filing status.
Saver's Match (Retirement Savings Contributions)

A federal contribution beginning in 2027 that deposits a percentage of an eligible person's retirement savings directly into their account, replacing the older nonrefundable Saver's Credit. It is paid by the Treasury rather than reducing tax liability on a return.
Savings Incentive Match Plan for Employees (SIMPLE) IRA

A retirement plan for small employers that combines employee salary deferrals with mandatory employer matching or nonelective contributions. It carries lower limits than a 401(k) and a higher early-withdrawal penalty during the first two years.
Schedule 1-A
The 2025 schedule used to claim the new deductions for tips, overtime, car loan interest, and the senior deduction.
Schedule 8812 (Credits for Qualifying Children and Other Dependents)
The schedule used to figure the Child Tax Credit, the credit for other dependents, and the refundable additional child tax credit. It reconciles any advance payments and applies income phaseouts.
Schedule A (Itemized Deductions)

The schedule on which individuals list itemized deductions such as medical expenses, state and local taxes, mortgage interest, and charitable contributions. Taxpayers itemize when the total exceeds the standard deduction.
Schedule B (Interest and Ordinary Dividends)
The schedule used to report taxable interest and ordinary dividends when the amounts exceed a threshold. It also asks about foreign accounts and certain foreign trusts.
Schedule D (Capital Gains and Losses)

The schedule that summarizes a taxpayer's short-term and long-term capital gains and losses from Form 8949 and other sources. It computes the net capital gain or the deductible capital loss for the year.
Schedule E (Supplemental Income and Loss)

The schedule used to report income and loss from rental real estate, royalties, partnerships, S corporations, estates, and trusts. Pass-through items from Schedule K-1 generally flow to this schedule.
Schedule F
The form used by farmers to report farm income and expenses on a cash or accrual basis.
Schedule F (Profit or Loss From Farming)
The schedule a farmer uses to report income and expenses from a farming business. Net farm profit or loss flows to Form 1040 and is generally subject to self-employment tax.
Schedule H (Household Employment Taxes)
The schedule individuals use to report Social Security, Medicare, and unemployment taxes for household employees such as nannies. It is filed with the employer's personal income tax return.
Schedule J (Income Averaging for Farmers and Fishermen)
A schedule that lets farmers and fishermen spread elected farm income over the three prior years' brackets. It can reduce tax in a high-income year following lower-income years.
Schedule SE (Self-Employment Tax)

The schedule used to calculate self-employment tax owed on net earnings from self-employment. It also computes the deduction for one-half of the self-employment tax that the taxpayer may take above the line.
Section 1031 Like-Kind Exchange

A deferral of gain when real property held for business or investment is exchanged for other real property of like kind. After 2017 it applies only to real estate, and boot received can trigger partial gain recognition.
Section 1033 Replacement Period

The time, generally two years (longer for condemned business or investment real estate), within which proceeds from an involuntary conversion must be reinvested to defer gain. The period starts at the end of the year the gain is first realized.
Section 1041 Transfer
A transfer of property between spouses, or between former spouses incident to divorce, on which no gain or loss is recognized and the recipient takes the transferor's basis.
Section 1202 Qualified Small Business Stock

Stock in certain C corporations that, if held more than five years, may allow a shareholder to exclude a large percentage of gain from gross income. The corporation must meet active business and gross asset requirements at issuance.
Section 121 Exclusion

An exclusion of up to $250,000 ($500,000 for married filing jointly) of gain on the sale of a principal residence. The taxpayer must generally have owned and used the home as a main residence for at least two of the prior five years.
Section 121 Home Sale Exclusion

An exclusion of up to 250000 dollars of gain, or 500000 for joint filers, on the sale of a main home. The taxpayer generally must have owned and used the home as a principal residence for two of the prior five years.
Section 1231 Gain

Net gain from the sale of depreciable property and real property used in a trade or business held more than one year. It generally receives favorable long-term capital gain treatment, while a net Section 1231 loss is treated as ordinary.
Section 1245 Recapture

A rule requiring gain on the sale of depreciable personal property to be taxed as ordinary income to the extent of prior depreciation deductions. Only gain beyond the recapture amount may qualify as Section 1231 capital gain.
Section 1250 Unrecaptured Gain Rate

The maximum 25% capital gains rate applied to the portion of gain on depreciable real estate attributable to prior straight-line depreciation. It bridges the gap between ordinary recapture and the lower long-term capital gain rates.
Section 1252 Recapture (Farm Land)

A recapture provision treating part of the gain on certain farmland as ordinary income to the extent of previously deducted soil and water conservation expenditures. It applies when the land is disposed of within a set holding period.
Section 1341 Claim of Right

A rule providing relief when a taxpayer must repay income reported in an earlier year under a claim of right. The taxpayer may deduct the repayment or take a credit equal to the prior year's tax on that income, whichever is more favorable.
Section 1341 Repayment Credit

A provision allowing a taxpayer who must repay income previously reported under a claim of right to choose either a deduction or a credit for the tax effect of the prior inclusion. The taxpayer uses whichever method produces the greater benefit.
Section 1411 Net Investment Income

The category of investment income such as interest, dividends, capital gains, and passive activity income that is subject to the 3.8% net investment income tax. It is reduced by allocable investment expenses.
Section 1411 Net Investment Income Tax

An additional 3.8 percent tax on net investment income for individuals, estates, and trusts above set income thresholds. It applies to items such as interest, dividends, capital gains, and passive activity income.
Section 162 Ordinary and Necessary Business Expense

The general rule allowing a deduction for ordinary and necessary expenses paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business. The expense must be helpful and appropriate for the business and not a capital expenditure or personal cost.
Section 179 Expensing

An election to deduct the full cost of qualifying business property in the year placed in service rather than depreciating it. The deduction is subject to an annual dollar cap, a phase-out, and a business income limitation.
Section 199A Deduction

A deduction of up to 20 percent of qualified business income for owners of pass-through businesses. It is subject to taxable income thresholds, wage and property limits, and restrictions for specified service businesses.
Section 212 Expenses (Production of Income)

Expenses paid for the production or collection of income or for managing income-producing property. Many such miscellaneous deductions for individuals are currently suspended, though some still apply to specific situations.
Section 263A Uniform Capitalization

Rules requiring certain direct and indirect costs of producing or acquiring inventory to be capitalized into the cost of goods rather than deducted currently. They defer deductions until the related goods are sold.
Section 267 Related Party Rules

Provisions that disallow loss deductions on sales between related parties and defer certain deductions until the related payee includes the income. They prevent taxpayers from creating artificial losses among family members or controlled entities.
Section 274 Substantiation Rules

Rules requiring detailed records to support deductions for travel, meals, gifts, and listed property. They also limit or disallow deductions for entertainment and impose a general limit on business meals.
Section 280A (Vacation Home and Home Office Rules)

The Internal Revenue Code section limiting deductions for the business or rental use of a dwelling also used personally. It governs home office deductions and the treatment of mixed personal and rental use of vacation homes.
Section 453 Installment Sale

A method allowing a seller to report gain as payments are received rather than all in the year of sale. It applies when at least one payment is received after the year of sale and spreads the tax over the collection period.
Section 461 Economic Performance

A requirement that an accrual-basis taxpayer may deduct an expense only when the underlying services, property, or use actually occurs. It is the final prong of the all-events test for deducting accrued liabilities.
Section 83(b) Election

An election to include the value of restricted property, such as unvested stock, in income at grant rather than at vesting. It starts the capital gain holding period early but risks paying tax on property that may later be forfeited.
Self-Employed Health Insurance Deduction

An above-the-line deduction allowing self-employed individuals to deduct health, dental, and qualifying long-term care premiums for themselves and their families. It is limited to net self-employment earnings and is unavailable for months the taxpayer could join an employer plan.
Self-Employment Tax

The Social Security and Medicare tax paid by self-employed individuals on net earnings from self-employment. It covers both the employer and employee portions, and one-half is deductible above the line.
Self-Employment Tax Deduction

An above-the-line deduction equal to the employer-equivalent portion of self-employment tax, roughly half of the total. It places self-employed taxpayers closer to parity with employees whose employer share is not taxed.
Self-Rental Rule

A rule recharacterizing net rental income from property leased to an activity in which the taxpayer materially participates as nonpassive. This prevents using such income to absorb unrelated passive losses.
Senior Deduction

An additional $6,000 deduction (2025–2028) per taxpayer age 65 or older by year end, phasing out at 6% of MAGI above $75,000 ($150,000 joint). It is in addition to the extra standard deduction for age.
SEPP (72(t))

Substantially equal periodic payments from a retirement account that avoid the 10% early distribution tax, calculated by one of three IRS-approved methods and continued for at least five years or until age 59½.
Series EE and I Bond Education Exclusion

An exclusion allowing interest on certain U.S. savings bonds to be tax-free when proceeds pay qualified higher education expenses. The exclusion phases out at higher modified adjusted gross income levels.
Short-Term Capital Gain
Gain from the sale of a capital asset held for one year or less. Short-term gains are taxed at ordinary income tax rates.
Simplified Employee Pension (SEP)

An employer-funded retirement arrangement that contributes to traditional IRAs for employees, with high contribution limits tied to compensation. It is popular with self-employed individuals because of its simplicity.
Solo 401(k)

A 401(k) plan covering a business owner with no employees other than a spouse, allowing both employee deferrals and employer contributions. The dual capacity lets self-employed savers reach high total contributions.
Sourcing Rules

The set of rules that determine whether income is treated as U.S. source or foreign source, which controls foreign tax credit limits and taxation of nonresident aliens. Different rules apply to wages, interest, dividends, rents, and sales of property.
Specified Service Trade or Business

A field such as health, law, accounting, consulting, or financial services where the principal asset is the reputation or skill of its employees. Owners above the income thresholds lose part or all of the Section 199A deduction.
Spousal IRA

An arrangement allowing a working spouse to fund an IRA for a nonworking or low-earning spouse based on the couple's joint compensation. It lets a married couple double their household IRA contributions when only one spouse has earnings.
Standard Deduction

A fixed dollar amount that reduces taxable income, available to taxpayers who do not itemize. The amount depends on filing status, age (65 or older), and blindness, and is adjusted annually for inflation.
Step-Up in Basis
The adjustment of an inherited asset's basis to its fair market value at the decedent's death. It can eliminate the income tax on appreciation that occurred during the decedent's lifetime.
Stepped-Up Basis

The adjustment of an inherited asset's basis to its fair market value on the decedent's date of death. This step-up can eliminate appreciation that occurred during the decedent's lifetime for income tax purposes.
Straddle Loss Deferral

A rule deferring losses on one position of an offsetting investment straddle to the extent of unrecognized gain on the other position. It limits the ability to harvest losses while retaining economic exposure.
Student Loan Interest Deduction
An above-the-line deduction for interest paid on a qualified education loan, capped at an annual maximum and phased out at higher incomes. It is available even to taxpayers who do not itemize.
Substantial Presence Test

The day-counting formula used to determine whether a noncitizen is a U.S. resident alien for tax purposes. It is met with 31 days in the current year and a weighted 183-day total across the current and two prior years.
Substantially Equal Periodic Payments (Rule 72(t))

A schedule of withdrawals computed under approved methods that lets a taxpayer take IRA or plan distributions before age 59 1/2 without the early-distribution penalty. Modifying the payments before the required period ends triggers retroactive penalties.
Tax Attribute Reduction

The required reduction of items such as net operating losses, credits, and asset basis when canceled debt is excluded from income. It defers, rather than forgives, the tax benefit of the discharged debt.
Tax Benefit Rule

A rule requiring a taxpayer to include a recovered amount in income if deducting it in a prior year produced a tax benefit. A common example is a state tax refund that is taxable only to the extent the earlier deduction reduced tax.
Tax Credit
A dollar-for-dollar reduction of tax liability, more valuable than a deduction of the same amount. Credits may be nonrefundable, refundable, or partially refundable.
Tax Home
The general area of a taxpayer's main place of business or work, regardless of where the family home is located. It is used to determine deductible travel expenses while away from home.
Tax Treaty Benefit
A provision in a bilateral income tax treaty that reduces or eliminates U.S. tax on certain income for residents of the treaty country. Taxpayers often disclose treaty-based positions on Form 8833.
Taxable Income

The amount of income subject to tax after subtracting deductions from gross income. For individuals it equals AGI minus the standard or itemized deductions and the qualified business income deduction.
Ten-Year Rule
The requirement that most non-spouse beneficiaries of inherited retirement accounts withdraw the entire balance by the end of the tenth year after the owner's death.
Three-Property Identification Rule
A safe harbor allowing a like-kind exchange taxpayer to identify up to three replacement properties regardless of their value. Alternative rules permit more properties subject to value limits.
Tip Income Allocation (Form 8027)

Large food and beverage establishments must report and, when reported tips fall below 8% of gross receipts, allocate the shortfall among tipped employees. The allocated amount appears on each employee's Form W-2 even though no extra cash was distributed.
Traditional IRA
An individual retirement account where contributions may be deductible and earnings grow tax-deferred. Distributions are generally taxable as ordinary income and are subject to RMD rules.
Trump Account
A children's IRA-type account created by the 2025 tax act. Contributions of up to $5,000 per year begin July 4, 2026, and eligible children born in 2025–2028 receive a $1,000 federal seed.
Trustee-to-Trustee Transfer
A direct movement of retirement funds between custodians without the owner receiving the money. It is not subject to the once-per-year IRA rollover limit or to withholding.
Tuition and Education Credit Coordination

The rule that the same education expenses cannot be used for more than one tax benefit, such as claiming both the American Opportunity Credit and the Lifetime Learning Credit for one student. Taxpayers must allocate qualified expenses among available benefits.
Unadjusted Basis Immediately After Acquisition

The original cost basis of qualified depreciable property without reduction for depreciation, used in one prong of the Section 199A wage-and-property limit. It rewards businesses that own significant capital assets.
Underpayment Penalty (Form 2210)

A penalty for not paying enough tax through withholding or estimated payments during the year, avoided by safe harbors of 90% of the current-year tax or 100% (110% for high earners) of the prior-year tax.
Unrecaptured Section 1250 Gain

The portion of gain on the sale of depreciable real property attributable to prior straight-line depreciation. It is taxed at a maximum capital gains rate of 25 percent rather than the lower long-term capital gain rates.
Vacation Home 14-Day Rule

A rule under which a dwelling rented for fewer than 15 days during the year produces no taxable rental income and allows no rental deductions. The personal-use threshold also affects how mixed-use property expenses are split.
W-2 Wage Limitation

A limit on the Section 199A deduction for higher-income taxpayers based on the W-2 wages paid by the business. The deduction cannot exceed the greater of 50 percent of wages or 25 percent of wages plus a property factor.
Wash Sale

A sale of stock or securities at a loss where substantially identical securities are bought within 30 days before or after the sale. The loss is disallowed and added to the basis of the replacement securities.
Wash Sale Adjustment

The basis and holding period adjustment required when a loss is disallowed because substantially identical securities are bought within 30 days before or after the sale. The disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement shares.
Wash Sale Replacement Property

Substantially identical stock or securities purchased within 30 days before or after a loss sale, which triggers the wash sale rule. The disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement property.
Wash Sale Rule

A rule disallowing a loss on the sale of a security when substantially identical securities are bought within thirty days before or after the sale. The disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement security.
Withholding
Amounts an employer or payer deducts from wages and certain payments and remits to the IRS toward the recipient's tax liability. The amount is based on the employee's Form W-4 elections.
Worthless Security Deduction

A capital loss allowed when a security becomes completely worthless during the year, treated as if sold on the last day of the tax year. Partial declines in value do not qualify until the security is sold or fully worthless.
Accrual Method
An accounting method that recognizes income when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands. It generally applies the all-events test to determine timing.
Accumulated Adjustments Account

An S corporation account that tracks post-1982 income and losses that have already been taxed to shareholders. Distributions from this account are generally tax-free returns of previously taxed income.
Accumulated Adjustments Account (AAA)
An S corporation account that tracks undistributed income already taxed to shareholders, used to determine the tax treatment of distributions.
Accumulated Earnings Tax
A penalty tax on C corporations that retain earnings beyond reasonable business needs to avoid shareholder-level tax on dividends. It is imposed in addition to regular corporate income tax.
Adjusted Current Earnings
A measure used in the corporate AMT calculation historically to adjust alternative minimum taxable income. It captures economic income items not otherwise reflected in regular taxable income.
Affiliated Group
A group of corporations connected through 80% vote-and-value ownership to a common parent, eligible to file a consolidated return.
Alternate Valuation Date

An estate election to value assets six months after death rather than on the date of death, available only if it lowers both the gross estate and the estate tax. It cannot be used selectively for individual assets.
Annual Gift Tax Exclusion

The amount a donor may give to each recipient each year without using the lifetime exemption or filing requirements, indexed for inflation. Gifts of a present interest below the limit are not reported.
Bankruptcy Estate
A separate taxable entity created when an individual files chapter 7 or 11 bankruptcy, which files Form 1041.
Basis (Partner's Outside Basis)

A partner's tax basis in their partnership interest, which limits the losses they can deduct and affects gain on disposition. It increases with contributions and income and decreases with distributions and losses.
Basis Adjustment (S Corporation Stock)
The yearly recomputation of a shareholder's stock basis for income, losses, and distributions. Stock basis limits deductible losses and determines the taxability of distributions.
Bipartisan Budget Act Partnership Audit Regime

The centralized partnership audit rules under which adjustments and any resulting tax are generally assessed and collected at the partnership level. It replaced the older TEFRA procedures for most partnerships.
Bonus Depreciation
An additional first-year depreciation allowance for qualifying new or used property placed in service. The applicable percentage is set by statute and has been phasing down in recent years.
Boot
Cash or non-like-kind property received in an otherwise tax-deferred exchange. Receiving boot causes gain to be recognized up to the amount of the boot received.
Boot Received (Like-Kind Exchange)
Non-like-kind property or cash received in an otherwise tax-deferred exchange, such as cash or relief from debt. Gain is recognized to the extent of the boot received.
Built-In Gains Recognition Period

The period after a corporation converts from C to S status during which gains on appreciated assets held at conversion may be subject to the built-in gains tax. Selling such assets within the period can trigger a corporate-level tax.
Built-In Gains Tax

A corporate-level tax imposed on an S corporation that was formerly a C corporation when it disposes of appreciated assets within the recognition period. It prevents avoidance of double taxation on gains that accrued while a C corporation.
Built-In Gains Tax Recognition Period

The window, generally five years after an S election, during which a former C corporation's built-in gains can trigger entity-level tax. Selling appreciated assets during this period accelerates the tax.
C Corporation
A corporation taxed as a separate entity at the corporate level under Subchapter C. Its earnings can be taxed twice when distributed as dividends, once to the corporation and again to shareholders.
Carryforward
The application of a current-year tax attribute, such as a loss or credit, to a future tax year. Carryforwards arise when an item cannot be fully used in the year it is generated.
Cash Method
An accounting method that recognizes income when actually or constructively received and expenses when paid. Many small businesses and individuals use this simpler method.
Charitable Lead Trust
A trust that pays income to charity for a term, after which the remaining assets pass to noncharitable beneficiaries. It is often used to transfer wealth at reduced transfer-tax cost.
Charitable Remainder Trust

An irrevocable trust that pays income to noncharitable beneficiaries for a term and then transfers the remainder to charity. It provides a current charitable deduction and can defer gain on contributed appreciated assets.
Complex Trust

A trust that may accumulate income, distribute principal, or make charitable contributions in a given year. It is taxed on income it retains and may claim a distribution deduction for amounts paid to beneficiaries.
Constructive Dividend

An economic benefit a corporation provides to a shareholder that the IRS recharacterizes as a taxable dividend. Examples include excessive compensation, below-market loans, or personal use of corporate property.
Constructive Dividend (Disguised Distribution)

A benefit a corporation provides to a shareholder that is treated as a dividend even though it is not formally declared, such as excessive compensation or personal use of corporate property. It is taxable to the shareholder to the extent of earnings and profits.
Controlled Foreign Corporation (CFC)
A foreign corporation more than 50% owned by U.S. shareholders who each own at least 10%.
Controlled Group (Corporations)

A group of corporations connected through common ownership that must share certain tax benefits such as bracket amounts and credit limits. The rules prevent splitting a business to multiply tax advantages.
Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax (CAMT)
A minimum tax on the adjusted financial statement income of corporations with very high average annual earnings. It ensures highly profitable corporations pay a baseline level of tax.
Corporate Capital Loss Rules

Rules under which a C corporation may deduct capital losses only against capital gains, carrying excess losses back three years and forward five years. Unlike individuals, corporations cannot deduct net capital losses against ordinary income.
Corporate Charitable Contribution Limit
The cap, generally 10% of taxable income computed with modifications, on a C corporation's deductible charitable contributions. Excess contributions carry forward for five years.
Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)
The direct cost of producing or acquiring the goods a business sells during the year. It is subtracted from gross receipts to determine gross profit and is not itself an itemized expense.
De Minimis Safe Harbor
An annual election to expense items costing $2,500 or less per invoice or item ($5,000 with an applicable financial statement) instead of capitalizing them.
De Minimis Safe Harbor Election

An election under the tangible property regulations allowing a business to immediately expense low-cost items rather than capitalize them, up to a per-item or per-invoice dollar threshold. The threshold is higher for taxpayers with an applicable financial statement.
Deposit Penalty (Employment Taxes)
A penalty imposed when an employer fails to make required federal tax deposits on time, in the right amount, or by the proper method. The penalty rate increases with the length of the delay.
Depreciation
The systematic deduction of the cost of tangible business or income-producing property over its useful life. It reflects the wear, tear, and obsolescence of an asset used to produce income.
Depreciation Recapture

The treatment of gain on the sale of depreciable property as ordinary income to the extent of prior depreciation deductions. It prevents converting ordinary deductions into preferentially taxed capital gain.
Disguised Sale

A transaction in which a partner's contribution of property and a related distribution from the partnership are recharacterized as a taxable sale. The rules generally apply when transfers occur within a two-year window unless an exception is met.
Distributable Net Income

A trust or estate concept limiting the amount of income that can be taxed to beneficiaries and defining its character. It caps the income distribution deduction and ensures income is taxed only once between the entity and its beneficiaries.
Distributive Share
A partner's allocated portion of partnership income, gain, loss, deduction, or credit, reported on Schedule K-1. It is taxed to the partner whether or not actually distributed.
Dividends Received Deduction

A deduction allowed to a C corporation for a portion of dividends received from another domestic corporation. The percentage depends on the recipient's ownership stake and reduces double or triple taxation of corporate earnings.
Dividends-Received Deduction (DRD)
A deduction that allows a C corporation to reduce taxable income on dividends received from other domestic corporations. The percentage depends on the ownership stake in the paying corporation.
Earnings and Profits

A corporate tax measure of economic ability to pay dividends, similar to but distinct from taxable income and retained earnings. Distributions are treated as taxable dividends to the extent of current and accumulated earnings and profits.
Earnings and Profits (E&P)
A measure of a corporation's economic capacity to pay dividends, which determines whether distributions are dividends, return of capital, or capital gain.
Earnings and Profits Adjustment

The set of modifications to taxable income used to compute a corporation's earnings and profits, which determines how much of a distribution is a taxable dividend. Adjustments include differences in depreciation and certain disallowed items.
Electing Small Business Trust (ESBT)
A trust that may hold S corporation stock if all beneficiaries are eligible shareholders; the S portion is taxed at the highest trust rate.
Estate Fiscal Year Election

An estate's ability to choose a fiscal year ending on the last day of any month, unlike trusts which generally must use a calendar year. It provides flexibility in timing income recognition for beneficiaries.
Estate Income in Respect of a Decedent (IRD)
Income a decedent had a right to receive but had not yet recognized at death, such as unpaid wages or IRA distributions. It is taxed to the recipient and does not receive a stepped-up basis.
Excess Net Passive Income Tax

A corporate-level tax imposed on an S corporation with accumulated earnings and profits when passive investment income exceeds 25% of gross receipts. Sustained excess passive income for three years can terminate the S election.
Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA)

The federal law imposing a payroll tax on employers to fund the administration of state unemployment programs. Employers generally receive a credit against the FUTA rate for state unemployment taxes paid.
First-In, First-Out (FIFO) Inventory Method
An inventory method that assumes the oldest goods are sold first. In times of rising prices it generally results in lower cost of goods sold and higher taxable income than LIFO.
Form 1023 (Application for Recognition of Exemption Under Section 501(c)(3))
The application an organization files to be recognized as a tax-exempt charity under section 501(c)(3). Smaller eligible organizations may use the streamlined Form 1023-EZ.
Form 1023-EZ
A streamlined application for exemption for organizations expecting gross receipts of $50,000 or less and assets of $250,000 or less.
Form 1024 (Application for Recognition of Exemption Under Section 501(a) or Section 521)

The application certain non-charitable organizations file to seek recognition of tax-exempt status, such as social welfare or business league organizations. It is used for exemptions outside the 501(c)(3) charitable category.
Form 1065 (U.S. Return of Partnership Income)

The annual information return that a partnership files to report its income, deductions, gains, and losses. The partnership itself pays no income tax; instead each partner receives a Schedule K-1 reporting their share of items.
Form 1096 (Annual Summary and Transmittal of U.S. Information Returns)
The summary form used to transmit paper information returns such as Forms 1099 to the IRS. It reports the totals of the accompanying forms and is not needed when filing electronically.
Form 1099-NEC (Nonemployee Compensation)

The information return used to report payments of $600 or more made to independent contractors and other nonemployees for services. Payers furnish a copy to the recipient and file a copy with the IRS.
Form 1120 (U.S. Corporation Income Tax Return)

The income tax return filed by a C corporation to report its income, deductions, credits, and tax liability. The corporation is a separate taxpayer that pays tax at the corporate rate on its taxable income.
Form 1120-F
The income tax return of a foreign corporation with U.S. income.
Form 1120-S (U.S. Income Tax Return for an S Corporation)

The annual return filed by an S corporation to report income, deductions, and credits that pass through to shareholders. Each shareholder receives a Schedule K-1 reporting their pro rata share of the corporation's items.
Form 1120-W (Estimated Tax for Corporations)
The worksheet corporations use to figure required quarterly estimated tax payments. Large corporations face stricter rules limiting reliance on the prior-year safe harbor.
Form 1128
The application to adopt, change, or retain a tax year.
Form 1139 (Corporation Application for Tentative Refund)

The corporate counterpart to Form 1045, used by C corporations to claim a quick refund from a carryback of a net operating loss or certain credits. The IRS reviews and processes it on an expedited basis.
Form 2553 (Election by a Small Business Corporation)

The form a qualifying corporation files to elect S corporation status so that income passes through to shareholders. It generally must be filed within roughly two and a half months of the start of the tax year the election is to take effect.
Form 3115
The application for a change in accounting method.
Form 3115 (Application for Change in Accounting Method)

The form a taxpayer files to request IRS consent to change an accounting method, such as switching depreciation methods or moving between cash and accrual. It includes a section 481(a) adjustment to prevent income from being omitted or duplicated.
Form 3520
A return reporting transactions with foreign trusts and receipt of large foreign gifts.
Form 4562 (Depreciation and Amortization)

The form used to claim depreciation, the section 179 deduction, and amortization, and to report information on listed property. It summarizes a taxpayer's depreciation deductions across assets and businesses.
Form 4626 (Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax)

The form applicable corporations use to compute the corporate alternative minimum tax based on adjusted financial statement income. It applies to very large corporations meeting average-income thresholds.
Form 4797 (Sales of Business Property)

The form used to report sales and exchanges of business property, including section 1231 gains and losses and depreciation recapture under sections 1245 and 1250. Net results flow to other parts of the return depending on character.
Form 5471
An information return for U.S. persons with ownership or control in certain foreign corporations.
Form 5471 (Information Return of U.S. Persons With Respect to Certain Foreign Corporations)
The information return certain U.S. persons must file regarding their ownership in or officer or director status with foreign corporations. Failure to file can result in substantial penalties.
Form 5472
A report of certain transactions between a 25% foreign-owned U.S. corporation or disregarded entity and related foreign parties.
Form 5472 (Information Return of a 25% Foreign-Owned U.S. Corporation or a Foreign Corporation Engaged in a U.S. Trade or Business)

The information return used to report reportable transactions between a U.S. corporation that is 25% foreign-owned, or a foreign corporation doing business in the U.S., and related parties. It helps the IRS monitor cross-border related-party dealings.
Form 5500
The annual return/report for employee benefit plans, due the last day of the seventh month after the plan year ends.
Form 5500 (Annual Return/Report of Employee Benefit Plan)

The annual report filed for many employer-sponsored retirement and welfare benefit plans to satisfy reporting requirements under the tax code and ERISA. Smaller plans may file the simplified Form 5500-SF or 5500-EZ.
Form 7004 (Application for Automatic Extension of Time To File Certain Business Income Tax Returns)
The form businesses use to request an automatic extension of time to file returns such as Forms 1065, 1120, and 1041. It extends the filing deadline but not the time to pay any tax due.
Form 8300
A report of cash payments over $10,000 received in a trade or business, due within 15 days.
Form 8594
The report of how the purchase price in an asset acquisition is allocated among seven asset classes.
Form 8621
An information return for shareholders of a passive foreign investment company.
Form 8832 (Entity Classification Election)

The form an eligible business entity files to choose how it is taxed, such as electing to be treated as a corporation or, for an eligible entity, as a disregarded entity or partnership. This is often called the check-the-box election.
Form 8865
An information return for U.S. persons with interests in certain foreign partnerships.
Form 8919 (Uncollected Social Security and Medicare Tax on Wages)

The form a worker uses to report and pay their share of Social Security and Medicare taxes when they were misclassified as an independent contractor instead of an employee. It ensures the employee share is paid without the higher self-employment rate.
Form 940 (Employer's Annual Federal Unemployment Tax Return)

The form employers use to report and pay Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA) tax, which funds unemployment compensation. FUTA tax is paid entirely by the employer and is not withheld from employee wages.
Form 941 (Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return)

The quarterly return employers file to report wages paid, federal income tax withheld, and both the employer and employee shares of Social Security and Medicare taxes. Most employers file this each calendar quarter.
Form 943 (Employer's Annual Federal Tax Return for Agricultural Employees)

The annual return used by employers of farmworkers to report federal income tax withheld and Social Security and Medicare taxes on agricultural wages. It replaces Form 941 for qualifying farm employers.
Form 944
The annual employment tax return for very small employers, filed in place of quarterly Form 941.
Form 944 (Employer's Annual Federal Tax Return)

A simplified annual employment tax return for the smallest employers whose total annual liability for income tax and Social Security and Medicare taxes is $1,000 or less. Eligible employers must be notified by the IRS that they may file it instead of Form 941.
Form 945
The annual return for withholding on non-payroll payments such as pensions, gambling, and backup withholding.
Form 945 (Annual Return of Withheld Federal Income Tax)

The form used to report federal income tax withheld from nonpayroll payments, such as pensions, gambling winnings, and backup withholding. It is separate from the employment tax returns used for payroll.
Form 970
The election to use the LIFO inventory method.
Form 990 (Return of Organization Exempt From Income Tax)

The annual information return that most tax-exempt organizations file to report their finances, governance, and activities to the IRS and the public. Smaller organizations may file Form 990-EZ or the electronic Form 990-N (e-Postcard).
Form 990-EZ
A shorter annual return for exempt organizations with gross receipts under $200,000 and assets under $500,000.
Form 990-N (e-Postcard)
An electronic notice for small exempt organizations with normal annual gross receipts of $50,000 or less.
Form 990-T
The return for reporting unrelated business income, required when gross unrelated income is $1,000 or more.
Form SS-4 (Application for Employer Identification Number)

The form a business or other entity uses to apply for an Employer Identification Number, the federal tax ID used for filing returns and reporting employment taxes. It can be filed online, by fax, or by mail.
Form SS-8 (Determination of Worker Status for Purposes of Federal Employment Taxes and Income Tax Withholding)
The form a worker or business files to ask the IRS to officially determine whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor. The IRS reviews the facts and issues a determination.
Form W-2c (Corrected Wage and Tax Statement)

The form an employer files to correct errors on a previously issued Form W-2, such as wrong wages, withholding, or a Social Security number. The employer also files Form W-3c to transmit the correction.
Form W-3 (Transmittal of Wage and Tax Statements)
The summary form an employer files with the Social Security Administration to transmit all paper Forms W-2 for the year. It totals the wages and taxes reported on the accompanying W-2s.
Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax

A separate transfer tax on gifts or bequests that skip a generation, such as transfers from a grandparent to a grandchild. It supplements estate and gift taxes to prevent avoidance across generations.
Gift-Splitting Election
An election by a married couple to treat gifts made by one spouse as made one-half by each, doubling the available annual exclusions. Both spouses must consent on a gift tax return.
Grantor Trust

A trust whose income is taxed directly to the person who created or controls it because that person retains certain powers or benefits. The trust itself is generally disregarded for income tax purposes.
Guaranteed Payment

A payment to a partner for services or use of capital determined without regard to partnership income. It is deductible by the partnership and is ordinary income to the receiving partner, also subject to self-employment tax.
Heavy Highway Vehicle Use Tax
An annual excise tax on vehicles of 55,000 pounds or more, reported on Form 2290.
Hobby Loss Rules
Rules denying loss deductions for an activity not engaged in for profit. The IRS uses factors and a presumption of profit in certain years to distinguish a business from a hobby.
Hot Assets

Partnership unrealized receivables and inventory items that produce ordinary income rather than capital gain when a partnership interest is sold or certain distributions occur. They prevent partners from converting ordinary income into capital gain.
Inside Basis
A partnership's adjusted basis in the individual assets it holds. It generally equals the sum of partners' outside bases when no special basis adjustments apply.
Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) Inventory Method
An inventory method that assumes the most recently acquired goods are sold first. In times of rising prices it generally increases cost of goods sold and lowers taxable income.
Like-Kind Exchange

A deferral of gain or loss when business or investment real property is exchanged for other real property of like kind under Section 1031. Recognition is deferred to the extent no boot is received, and the rules now apply only to real property.
Listed Property
Certain assets such as passenger automobiles that are subject to special depreciation and recordkeeping rules. Business use must exceed 50% to use accelerated depreciation methods.
Lower of Cost or Market (Inventory Valuation)
An inventory valuation method that values goods at the lower of their cost or current market value. It allows recognition of declines in inventory value but is not available to taxpayers using LIFO.
Mark-to-Market Trader Status

The status of a securities trader who qualifies as conducting a trade or business of trading and elects mark-to-market accounting. Qualifying traders report gains and losses as ordinary and may deduct trading expenses as business expenses.
Mid-Quarter Convention
A depreciation convention required when more than 40% of the year's depreciable personal property basis is placed in service in the last quarter.
Mixing Bowl Transaction (Sections 704(c)(1)(B) and 737)

Partnership rules that trigger gain when contributed appreciated property, or other property, is distributed within seven years to or from the contributing partner. They prevent using a partnership to disguise a taxable exchange of property.
Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System (MACRS)
The standard depreciation method for most tangible property placed in service after 1986. MACRS assigns assets to recovery period classes and applies prescribed conventions and accelerated methods.
Net Operating Loss (NOL)

The excess of allowable business deductions over gross income for a tax year. Under current rules an NOL is carried forward indefinitely and may offset up to 80% of taxable income in a carryforward year.
Nonrecourse Liability

A partnership debt for which no partner bears personal economic risk of loss because the lender's only remedy is the secured property. It is generally allocated among all partners according to specified tiers of profit-sharing.
Other Adjustments Account

An S corporation account that records tax-exempt income and related expenses that do not flow through the accumulated adjustments account. It affects the ordering and taxability of distributions when the corporation has earnings and profits.
Outside Basis
A partner's or shareholder's adjusted basis in their interest in a pass-through entity. It limits deductible losses and determines gain on a sale or distribution.
Partnership

An unincorporated business of two or more persons who carry on a trade or business and share profits and losses. It files an information return (Form 1065) and passes income through to partners via Schedule K-1.
Partnership Capital Account Maintenance
The bookkeeping rules that track each partner's equity, adjusted for contributions, distributions, and allocated income and loss. Proper maintenance supports the validity of special allocations.
Partnership Minimum Gain

The gain a partnership would recognize if it disposed of property subject to nonrecourse debt for no more than the debt balance. It supports special allocations of nonrecourse deductions under the substantial economic effect rules.
Partnership Representative

The single person designated to act for a partnership under the centralized audit regime, with sole authority to bind the partnership and its partners. The role replaced the former tax matters partner.
Partnership Technical Termination (Historical)

A former rule that deemed a partnership terminated when 50% or more of capital and profits interests changed hands within 12 months. The rule was repealed for tax years after 2017 but appears in older fact patterns.
Pass-Through Entity
A business such as a partnership, S corporation, or sole proprietorship whose income passes through to owners and is taxed at the owner level. The entity itself generally pays no federal income tax.
Passive Foreign Investment Company (PFIC)
A foreign corporation that meets a 75% passive income test or a 50% passive asset test, subject to special tax rules.
Passive Investment Income Tax (S Corporation)

A corporate-level tax that can apply when an S corporation with accumulated earnings and profits has excessive passive investment income. Prolonged excess passive income can also terminate the S election.
Patronage Dividend
A distribution by a cooperative to its patrons based on the business they did with it, deductible by the cooperative.
Penalty for Failure to Furnish Information Returns

A penalty imposed on businesses that fail to file correct information returns, such as Forms 1099, or to furnish correct payee statements by the deadline. The amount per return increases the longer the failure continues.
Per Diem
A daily allowance for lodging, meals, and incidental expenses while traveling for business. Using federal per diem rates can simplify substantiation of these expenses.
Personal Holding Company

A closely held corporation with mostly passive income that may owe an extra tax on undistributed personal holding company income. The tax encourages such corporations to distribute earnings rather than retain them to shield shareholders.
Personal Holding Company (PHC)
A closely held corporation with mostly passive income, subject to a 20% tax on undistributed PHC income.
Personal Holding Company Tax
An additional tax on closely held corporations with a high proportion of passive income that is not distributed. It discourages using a corporation to shelter investment income.
Personal Service Corporation

A corporation whose principal activity is performing services in fields such as law, health, or accounting and that is substantially owned by employee-owners. It is taxed at a flat corporate rate and faces restrictions on fiscal years.
Portability Election (DSUE)
An estate tax election allowing a surviving spouse to use the deceased spouse's unused estate and gift tax exclusion amount. It is made by timely filing an estate tax return even when no tax is due.
Post-Termination Transition Period

A grace period after an S election ends during which the former corporation can make tax-free distributions from its remaining accumulated adjustments account. It allows shareholders to extract previously taxed income.
Private Foundation
A section 501(c)(3) organization that does not meet the public charity tests, subject to excise taxes on self-dealing, undistributed income, and net investment income.
Prohibited Transaction (Plan)
A transaction between a plan or IRA and a disqualified person, such as a loan, subject to a 15% initial excise tax.
Public Support Test
A test showing that a charity receives at least one-third of its support from the general public (or 10% with facts and circumstances).
Push-Out Election
An election under section 6226 allowing a partnership to push audit adjustments through to the reviewed-year partners instead of paying the imputed underpayment itself.
Push-Out Election (Partnership Audit)

An election under the centralized audit regime allowing a partnership to pass audit adjustments through to the partners who were partners in the reviewed year. The partners then pay any resulting tax on their own returns.
Qualified Business Income (QBI) Deduction

A deduction of up to 20% of qualified business income from pass-through entities and sole proprietorships under Section 199A. It is subject to taxable income thresholds and limitations based on wages and qualified property.
Qualified Improvement Property
Interior improvements to nonresidential buildings placed in service after the building, with a 15-year recovery period and eligibility for bonus depreciation.
Qualified Intermediary (Like-Kind Exchange)

An independent party that holds the proceeds from the sale of relinquished property and uses them to acquire the replacement property in a deferred like-kind exchange. Using one keeps the taxpayer from having actual or constructive receipt of the funds.
Qualified Nonrecourse Financing

Real estate debt borrowed from a qualified commercial lender or government with no personal liability that is nonetheless treated as at-risk. It allows a taxpayer to deduct losses tied to real property financed without recourse.
Qualified Subchapter S Subsidiary (QSub)

A wholly owned subsidiary that an S corporation elects to treat as part of the parent rather than as a separate corporation. Its assets, income, and deductions are treated as the parent's for tax purposes.
Qualified Subchapter S Trust (QSST)
A trust that may hold S corporation stock if it has one income beneficiary who elects to be treated as the owner of the S stock.
Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT)
An entity that invests in real estate and distributes at least 90% of its taxable income, avoiding entity-level tax on distributed income.
Reasonable Compensation

The wages an S corporation must pay shareholder-employees for services before making distributions. The IRS can recharacterize distributions as wages if compensation is unreasonably low to avoid payroll taxes.
Reasonable Compensation Audit Adjustment (S Corporation)

An IRS recharacterization of S corporation distributions as wages when shareholder-employees are underpaid to avoid payroll taxes. The adjustment imposes the employer and employee shares of employment tax plus penalties.
Recapture (General)
The reversal of a prior tax benefit when a triggering event occurs, such as recapturing depreciation or credits. The recaptured amount is added back to income or tax in the year of the event.
Recapture of Section 179

The addition of previously expensed Section 179 amounts back to income when business use of the property drops to 50% or less. The amount recaptured is the excess of the deduction over allowable depreciation.
Recourse Liability

A partnership debt for which at least one partner or related person bears the economic risk of loss. It is allocated to the partners who would have to pay it if the partnership could not, increasing their outside basis.
Residual Method
The method of allocating purchase price in an asset acquisition by assigning value to asset classes in order, with the remainder going to goodwill (Class VII).
Routine Maintenance Safe Harbor
A safe harbor allowing deduction of recurring work expected to be performed more than once during the property's class life to keep it operating.
S Corporation

A corporation that elects to pass income, deductions, and credits through to shareholders for federal tax purposes. It avoids corporate-level tax, is limited to one class of stock and a capped number of eligible shareholders, and files Form 1120-S.
S Corporation Accumulated Adjustments Account Ordering

The sequence used to determine the taxability of S corporation distributions, drawing first from the accumulated adjustments account, then from earnings and profits, and then from remaining basis. The ordering affects whether distributions are tax-free or dividends.
S Corporation Inadvertent Termination Relief

Relief allowing the IRS to overlook an accidental termination of S status if the corporation acts promptly to correct the disqualifying event. The corporation is treated as having remained an S corporation throughout.
Schedule C
The form a sole proprietor uses to report income and expenses from a business. Net profit flows to Form 1040 and is generally subject to self-employment tax.
Schedule K-1
A statement reporting each owner's share of income, deductions, and credits from a partnership, S corporation, estate, or trust. Owners use it to report their share on their individual returns.
Schedule K-2 and K-3 (International Items)

Supplemental schedules to partnership and S corporation returns that report items relevant to partners' or shareholders' foreign tax calculations. They provide standardized international information formerly described in footnotes.
Schedule L (Balance Sheets per Books)
The schedule on business returns that presents the entity's beginning and ending balance sheet based on its books and records. It reports assets, liabilities, and equity for the tax year.
Schedule M-1 (Reconciliation of Income (Loss) per Books With Income per Return)
The schedule on corporate and partnership returns that reconciles financial statement net income with taxable income. It identifies differences such as nondeductible expenses and timing items.
Schedule M-2 (Analysis of Unappropriated Retained Earnings or Partners' Capital Accounts)

The schedule that analyzes changes in retained earnings or partners' capital during the year, including income, distributions, and other adjustments. It helps reconcile equity from the beginning to the end of the year.
Schedule M-3 (Net Income (Loss) Reconciliation)
A more detailed book-to-tax reconciliation required of larger corporations and partnerships. It provides greater transparency than Schedule M-1 about differences between financial and taxable income.
Schedule UTP (Uncertain Tax Position Statement)

A schedule on which certain large corporations disclose federal income tax positions for which they have recorded a financial-statement reserve. It improves IRS visibility into aggressive tax positions.
Section 1031 Deferred Exchange Election

The arrangement in which a taxpayer exchanges business or investment real property and uses a qualified intermediary to defer gain, identifying replacement property within 45 days and closing within 180 days. Gain is deferred only to the extent the exchange meets the like-kind requirements.
Section 1059 Extraordinary Dividend

A rule reducing a corporate shareholder's stock basis by the nontaxed portion of a large dividend received shortly after acquiring the stock. It curbs combining the dividends-received deduction with a later loss on sale.
Section 1202 Exclusion
An exclusion of gain on the sale of qualified small business stock held more than five years. The excludable percentage depends on the stock's acquisition date.
Section 1231 Property

Depreciable property and real property used in a trade or business and held more than one year. Net Section 1231 gains are treated as long-term capital gains while net losses are treated as ordinary losses.
Section 1244 Stock

Stock of a qualifying small business corporation that allows shareholders to deduct losses as ordinary rather than capital. The ordinary loss is limited to $50,000 per year ($100,000 on a joint return).
Section 1245 Property
Depreciable personal property such as machinery and equipment. On sale, gain is recaptured as ordinary income to the extent of prior depreciation deductions.
Section 1250 Property
Depreciable real property such as buildings. Unrecaptured Section 1250 gain attributable to depreciation is taxed at a maximum rate of 25% to the extent it exceeds straight-line amounts.
Section 1361 S Corporation Eligibility

The set of requirements a corporation must meet to elect S status, including a 100-shareholder limit, only allowed shareholders, and a single class of stock. Failing any requirement can terminate the election.
Section 1362 S Corporation Election

The Internal Revenue Code provision under which an eligible corporation elects to be taxed as an S corporation, made on Form 2553. The election remains in effect until it is revoked or terminated by losing eligibility.
Section 1366 Pass-Through (S Corporation)

The rule that an S corporation's income, deductions, losses, and credits flow through to shareholders in proportion to their stock ownership. Shareholders report these items on their own returns whether or not amounts are actually distributed.
Section 1368 Distribution (S Corporation)

The rules governing the taxation of distributions from an S corporation, which depend on the accumulated adjustments account, earnings and profits, and the shareholder's stock basis. Distributions are generally tax-free up to basis but may be taxable when earnings and profits exist.
Section 1374 Built-In Gains Tax
A corporate-level tax on gains recognized during the five-year recognition period after a C corporation converts to S status, to the extent the gain was built in at conversion.
Section 1377 Election

An election allowing an S corporation to close its books when a shareholder fully terminates an interest, so income is allocated based on actual results before and after the change. Without it, items are prorated by days held over the year.
Section 1377(a)(2) Election (S Corporation)

An election available when a shareholder fully terminates their interest in an S corporation, allowing the year to be split into two periods. It assigns income and loss based on actual results in each period rather than a daily proration.
Section 163(j)
The limit on business interest deductions to business interest income plus 30% of adjusted taxable income, with an exemption for small businesses.
Section 163(j) Limitation

A cap on the deduction of business interest expense, generally limited to business interest income plus 30 percent of adjusted taxable income. Disallowed interest is carried forward to future years, with exceptions for small businesses.
Section 168(k) Bonus Depreciation Election

The provision allowing an additional first-year depreciation deduction for qualifying new and used property placed in service during the year. Taxpayers may elect out of bonus depreciation by class of property if it is not beneficial.
Section 174A
The 2025 provision allowing current deduction of domestic research and experimental expenditures for tax years beginning after 2024.
Section 179 Deduction

An election to expense the full cost of qualifying business property in the year it is placed in service, rather than depreciating it over time. The deduction is subject to annual dollar limits and a taxable income limitation, and phases out above an investment threshold.
Section 179 Expensing Election

An election to deduct the cost of qualifying business property in the year it is placed in service, up to an annual dollar limit. The deduction phases out when total purchases exceed a threshold and cannot create or increase a loss.
Section 197 Intangible
An acquired intangible such as goodwill, a customer list, or a covenant not to compete, amortized over 15 years.
Section 199A Specified Service Trade or Business Limitation

A rule that phases out the qualified business income deduction for certain service fields, such as health, law, and consulting, once taxable income exceeds a threshold. Above the upper limit, no deduction is allowed for income from these businesses.
Section 263A (Uniform Capitalization Rules)

Rules requiring certain direct and indirect costs of producing or acquiring inventory to be capitalized rather than currently deducted. Small businesses meeting a gross receipts threshold may be exempt.
Section 280E (Trafficking in Controlled Substances)

A provision that disallows business deductions and credits for businesses trafficking in controlled substances under federal law. It significantly affects state-legal cannabis businesses, which may still deduct cost of goods sold.
Section 280F
The provision that caps annual depreciation on passenger automobiles.
Section 291 Recapture (Corporate)

A rule requiring a C corporation to treat 20% of the additional gain that would have been ordinary under Section 1245 as ordinary income on the sale of Section 1250 property. It increases the ordinary portion of a corporation's real estate gain.
Section 331 Liquidation
A complete liquidation in which a shareholder treats amounts received as full payment for stock, producing capital gain or loss.
Section 332 Liquidation (Subsidiary)
The tax-free liquidation of a subsidiary into a parent corporation that owns at least 80% of the subsidiary. The parent generally takes a carryover basis in the assets received.
Section 336 and 337 Liquidation Rules

Provisions governing gain or loss recognition when a corporation distributes assets in liquidation, with Section 337 providing nonrecognition on distributions to an 80% corporate parent. They coordinate corporate-level results with the shareholder rules.
Section 351 Control

The requirement that transferors of property to a corporation own at least 80 percent of voting power and other stock immediately after the exchange. Meeting it allows the transfer to be tax-free, with gain deferred through carryover basis.
Section 351 Exchange
A transfer of property to a corporation in exchange for stock by persons who control at least 80% of the corporation afterward, deferring gain except for boot.
Section 351 Tax-Free Incorporation

The rule allowing no gain or loss to be recognized when property is transferred to a corporation solely for stock, provided the transferors control the corporation immediately afterward. It lets owners incorporate a business without an immediate tax cost.
Section 357(c)
The rule that treats liabilities assumed in a section 351 exchange as gain to the extent they exceed the basis of the property transferred.
Section 368 Reorganization

A statutorily defined corporate restructuring, such as a merger, stock-for-stock exchange, or asset acquisition, that can be completed without immediate taxation. Each qualifying type lets shareholders defer gain when continuity and business-purpose requirements are met.
Section 444 Fiscal Year Election

An election that lets certain partnerships, S corporations, and personal service corporations use a tax year other than the required year. It generally requires a deposit or payment to offset any deferral of tax.
Section 444 Required Payment
The payment a pass-through entity must make to maintain a fiscal year elected under section 444. It approximates the tax deferral benefit the entity gains from not using a calendar year.
Section 475 Mark-to-Market Election

An election available to qualifying securities or commodities traders to treat their holdings as sold at year-end fair market value. It converts gains and losses to ordinary and exempts qualifying trades from the wash sale rule.
Section 481(a) Adjustment

A one-time cumulative adjustment that prevents income from being duplicated or omitted when a taxpayer changes an accounting method. A positive adjustment increasing income is often spread over several years, while a decrease is generally taken in one year.
Section 501(h) Election
An election by a charity to be subject to specific expenditure limits on lobbying rather than the substantial part test.
Section 530 Relief
Relief from federal employment taxes for a business that had a reasonable basis for treating workers as independent contractors and filed required returns consistently.
Section 645 Election (Trust as Part of Estate)
An election to treat a qualified revocable trust as part of the decedent's estate for income tax purposes. It allows the trust to use the estate's favorable fiscal-year and other tax rules.
Section 691(c) Deduction

An income tax deduction available to recipients of income in respect of a decedent for the portion of estate tax attributable to that income. It mitigates the double taxation of being subject to both estate and income tax.
Section 704(b) Book Capital Account

A partner's economic stake in a partnership tracked under the substantial economic effect rules, reflecting contributions, distributions, and allocated income or loss. It can differ from the tax capital account because book values may use fair market value while tax capital uses adjusted basis.
Section 704(c)
The rule that built-in gain or loss on property contributed to a partnership is allocated to the contributing partner.
Section 704(c) Allocation
A rule requiring that built-in gain or loss on property contributed to a partnership be allocated to the contributing partner. It prevents shifting pre-contribution tax results to other partners.
Section 707 Partner-Partnership Transactions

Rules governing payments between a partner and the partnership, distinguishing services or property provided as an outsider from those provided as a partner. The character affects timing, deductibility, and self-employment treatment.
Section 721
The rule that no gain or loss is recognized when property is contributed to a partnership in exchange for an interest.
Section 721 Contribution (Partnership)

The rule that generally no gain or loss is recognized when a partner contributes property to a partnership in exchange for a partnership interest. The contributing partner's basis carries over into both the interest and the contributed property.
Section 731 Distribution (Partnership)
The rules governing recognition of gain or loss on distributions from a partnership to a partner. Gain is generally recognized only when cash distributed exceeds the partner's outside basis.
Section 734(b) Adjustment

A basis adjustment to remaining partnership assets triggered by certain distributions when a Section 754 election is in effect or a substantial basis reduction occurs. It prevents distortion between a distributee partner's outside basis and the partnership's inside basis.
Section 736 Payments (Retiring Partner)

The rules classifying payments made to a retiring partner or a deceased partner's successor as either for the partner's interest in partnership property or as other income. The classification affects whether amounts are capital or ordinary.
Section 743(b) Adjustment

A basis adjustment to partnership assets, made only for the buying partner, when a partnership interest is transferred by sale or death and a Section 754 election is in effect. It aligns the new partner's share of inside basis with the price paid for the interest.
Section 751 (Hot Assets)

Rules that treat gain on unrealized receivables and substantially appreciated inventory as ordinary income when a partnership interest is sold or distributions change partners' shares of those assets.
Section 752 Liability Allocation

The rules governing how partnership debts are shared among partners and treated as deemed contributions or distributions of cash. An increase in a partner's share of liabilities raises outside basis, while a decrease lowers it.
Section 754 Basis Adjustment Election

A partnership election that allows it to adjust the basis of partnership property when a partnership interest is transferred or certain distributions occur. It aligns a buying or distributee partner's inside basis with their outside basis.
Section 754 Election

A partnership election that allows the inside basis of partnership assets to be adjusted when a partner sells an interest or when a partner receives certain distributions. Once made, it applies to all later transfers and distributions until revoked with IRS consent.
Self-Dealing
Certain transactions between a private foundation and a disqualified person, subject to a 10% initial excise tax on the self-dealer.
Separate Share Rule (Estates and Trusts)

A rule treating substantially separate and independent interests of different beneficiaries as distinct shares when computing distributable net income. It prevents one beneficiary from being taxed on income economically belonging to another.
Separately Stated Items

Income, deduction, and credit items that a pass-through entity reports individually to owners because they may affect each owner's return differently. Examples include capital gains, charitable contributions, and Section 179 expense.
SIMPLE IRA
A retirement plan for employers with 100 or fewer employees requiring either a 3% match or a 2% nonelective contribution.
Simple Trust

A trust required to distribute all of its income currently, that makes no charitable contributions and distributes no principal during the year. Its beneficiaries are taxed on the income whether or not it is actually paid out.
Small Business Health Care Tax Credit
A credit of up to 50% of premiums for qualifying small employers that buy coverage through the SHOP Marketplace, claimed on Form 8941.
Specified Cooperative (Section 199A(g))

An agricultural or horticultural cooperative eligible for a separate domestic production-style deduction under the qualified business income rules. Its patrons face special coordination rules for their own deductions.
State Unemployment Tax Act (SUTA)
State-level payroll taxes that employers pay to fund unemployment benefits in their state. Timely SUTA payments generally produce a credit that reduces the employer's federal FUTA liability.
Statutory Employee
A worker classified as an employee for some employment tax purposes but who reports income on Schedule C. Specific categories include certain drivers, insurance agents, and home workers.
Substantial Economic Effect

The standard a partnership allocation must meet to be respected for tax purposes, requiring that allocations reflect the partners' real economic arrangement. Allocations failing the test are reallocated according to partners' interests.
Supplemental Wages
Wages such as bonuses and commissions paid in addition to regular wages, for which employers may withhold at a flat 22% rate.
Throwback Rule (Trusts)

A historical rule, still applicable to certain foreign trusts, that taxes beneficiaries on accumulated distributions as if received in the years earned. It can add an interest charge for the deferral period.
Tier System (Trust Distributions)

The ordering rules that determine how distributable net income is allocated between beneficiaries entitled to required distributions and those receiving discretionary amounts. First-tier beneficiaries are taxed before second-tier beneficiaries.
Top-Heavy Plan
A retirement plan in which key employees hold more than 60% of total account balances, triggering minimum contributions for non-key employees.
Trust Distribution Deduction

A deduction that passes taxable income from an estate or trust to beneficiaries to the extent of distributable net income. It prevents the same income from being taxed at both the entity and beneficiary levels.
Trust Fund Taxes

The portion of employment taxes that an employer withholds from employees' wages, including income tax withholding and the employee share of Social Security and Medicare. The employer holds these amounts in trust for the government and must remit them.
Unified Credit (Estate and Gift Tax)
The credit that shelters the lifetime exemption amount from combined gift and estate taxes. Using exemption against lifetime gifts reduces the amount available at death.
Uniform Capitalization (UNICAP) Rules

Rules requiring certain direct and indirect costs to be capitalized into the cost of inventory or property a taxpayer produces or acquires for resale. The capitalized costs are recovered through cost of goods sold or depreciation rather than deducted currently.
Unrelated Business Income Tax

A tax on income that a tax-exempt organization earns from a regularly carried-on trade or business unrelated to its exempt purpose. It places exempt entities on equal footing with taxable businesses competing in the same market.
Unrelated Business Taxable Income (UBTI)
Income of an exempt organization from a regularly carried-on trade or business not substantially related to its exempt purpose, taxed on Form 990-T.
Voluntary Classification Settlement Program (VCSP)
An IRS program that lets employers reclassify workers as employees prospectively with reduced employment tax liability and no penalties or interest.
Work Opportunity Tax Credit
A credit for hiring members of certain targeted groups, requiring certification on Form 8850 within 28 days of the hire date.
Worker Classification

The determination of whether a worker is an employee or independent contractor based on behavioral and financial control and the relationship. Misclassification can lead to back employment taxes and penalties.
30-Day Letter
A letter proposing adjustments from an examination that gives the taxpayer 30 days to request an Appeals conference. Failing to respond typically leads to a statutory notice of deficiency.
Accuracy-Related Penalty

A penalty of generally 20% of the underpayment attributable to negligence, disregard of rules, or a substantial understatement of tax. It can be avoided with reasonable cause and good faith or adequate disclosure of a position.
Adequate Disclosure

The act of clearly revealing the facts of a tax position on the return, often via Form 8275, which can reduce or eliminate accuracy-related and preparer penalties. The disclosure must give the IRS enough information to identify the issue.
Administrative Costs Recovery (Section 7430)

The ability of a prevailing taxpayer to recover reasonable administrative and litigation costs when the government's position was not substantially justified. The taxpayer must have exhausted administrative remedies.
