Allowable Living Expenses (Collection Financial Standards)

The standardized expense amounts the IRS uses to determine how much income a taxpayer needs for basic necessities when evaluating ability to pay. These standards cover categories such as food, housing, transportation, and out-of-pocket health care.
Alter Ego Liability

A theory allowing the IRS to collect a taxpayer's debt from an entity or person that is essentially indistinguishable from the taxpayer. It applies when the separate identity is a sham used to shield assets from collection.
Annual Filing Season Program
A voluntary IRS program giving unenrolled preparers who complete CE a Record of Completion and limited representation rights.
Annual Filing Season Program (AFSP)

A voluntary IRS program that gives a record of completion to non-credentialed return preparers who complete continuing education and agree to certain standards. Participants gain limited representation rights before the IRS for returns they prepared.
Appeals (IRS Independent Office of Appeals)
An independent IRS function that resolves tax disputes without litigation. It offers an impartial review of examination and collection determinations based on the hazards of litigation.
Assessment Statute Expiration Date

The last day, generally three years after a return is filed, on which the IRS may assess additional tax. The period extends to six years for substantial omissions of income and is unlimited for fraud or unfiled returns.
Assessment Statute Expiration Date (ASED)
The date after which the IRS may no longer assess additional tax, generally three years from filing, six years for substantial omissions, and unlimited for fraud or nonfiling.
Audit Reconsideration

A process by which the IRS reevaluates the results of a prior audit or a substitute for return when the taxpayer provides new information or disputes the assessment. It can be requested when the taxpayer did not appear for the audit or has additional documentation.
Automated Underreporter (AUR)
The IRS program that matches information returns with filed returns and issues notices such as CP2000.
Automated Underreporter (AUR) Unit

The IRS function that compares amounts reported on tax returns with information returns filed by third parties and identifies discrepancies. It issues notices such as the CP2000 to propose corrections when amounts do not match.
Automated Underreporter Program
An IRS matching system that compares amounts reported on a return with information returns from third parties. Mismatches generate a notice proposing additional tax, commonly known as a CP2000.
Bankruptcy Automatic Stay (Tax Collection)

The injunction that arises when a taxpayer files bankruptcy, halting most IRS collection activity such as levies and lawsuits. Certain tax debts may still be nondischargeable and survive the bankruptcy.
Best Practices (Circular 230)

The aspirational standards in Circular 230 encouraging practitioners to communicate clearly, establish relevant facts, and advise clients on the import of conclusions. They guide professional conduct without imposing direct penalties.
Burden of Proof (Section 7491)

The general rule that the taxpayer bears the burden of proving the IRS is wrong, with the burden shifting to the IRS in limited circumstances when the taxpayer meets recordkeeping and cooperation requirements. It determines who must persuade the court on a factual issue.
Censure (Circular 230)
A public reprimand of a practitioner under Circular 230 that allows continued practice but creates a formal record of misconduct. It is the least severe of the principal disciplinary sanctions.
Centralized Authorization File (CAF)

The IRS database that records powers of attorney and tax information authorizations so the agency knows who is authorized to act for or receive information about a taxpayer. Representatives are assigned a CAF number used on these forms.
Centralized Authorization File Number
A unique number the IRS assigns to a representative to track powers of attorney and tax information authorizations. It links a practitioner to the taxpayers they are authorized to represent.
Certificate of Discharge (Federal Tax Lien)

A document that removes the federal tax lien from a specific piece of property, often to allow a sale, while the lien remains on the taxpayer's other property. It is requested using a dedicated IRS application.
Circular 230

Treasury Department regulations governing practice before the IRS by attorneys, CPAs, enrolled agents, and other practitioners. It sets standards of conduct, due diligence duties, and disciplinary procedures.
Civil Fraud Penalty
A penalty equal to 75 percent of the portion of an underpayment attributable to fraud. The IRS bears the burden of proving fraud by clear and convincing evidence.
Closing Agreement (Form 906)

A binding written agreement between the IRS and a taxpayer that conclusively settles a tax matter, signed on Form 866 or Form 906. Once executed, it generally cannot be reopened except for fraud or misrepresentation.
Collection Appeals Program

A faster but more limited appeals process for disputing certain IRS collection actions such as liens, levies, and rejected installment agreements. Unlike a due process hearing, its decision cannot be taken to Tax Court.
Collection Appeals Program (CAP)

An IRS appeals process that lets taxpayers challenge certain collection actions, such as a proposed or actual lien, levy, or seizure, before or after the action occurs. Unlike a Collection Due Process hearing, a CAP decision cannot be taken to the Tax Court.
Collection Due Process (CDP) Hearing

A hearing before the IRS Independent Office of Appeals that a taxpayer may request after a lien filing or final levy notice. It allows the taxpayer to dispute the collection action and propose alternatives, with the right to judicial review.
Collection Due Process Hearing

A taxpayer's right to an independent appeals hearing after the IRS files a tax lien or issues a levy notice. It allows challenges to the collection action and consideration of alternatives before enforcement proceeds.
Collection Statute Expiration Date

The date, generally ten years after assessment, on which the IRS's legal right to collect a tax debt expires. Certain events such as bankruptcy or installment requests can suspend and extend this period.
Collection Statute Expiration Date (CSED)
The date after which the IRS may no longer collect an assessed tax, generally ten years after assessment, subject to suspension events.
Community Property Relief (Section 66)

Relief from the operation of community property laws for a spouse who did not know of and did not benefit from the other spouse's omitted community income. It is distinct from innocent spouse relief on joint returns.
Competence (Circular 230)

A Circular 230 requirement that a practitioner possess the necessary knowledge, skill, and preparation for the matter handled. Competence may be gained through study or association with knowledgeable colleagues.
Conflict of Interest (Circular 230)

A situation where representing one client is adverse to another or limited by the practitioner's own interests, permissible only with informed written consent. Circular 230 sets the conditions for proceeding despite the conflict.
Contingent Fee (Circular 230)

A fee based on whether a position is sustained, which Circular 230 generally prohibits for preparing original returns. Limited exceptions exist, such as for certain refund claims and IRS examinations.
Continuing Education Requirement (Enrolled Agent)

The mandate that an enrolled agent complete a set number of continuing education hours each year and over each renewal cycle, including ethics hours. Failure to meet the requirement can result in inactive or terminated status.
Continuous Wage Levy

A levy on a taxpayer's wages or salary that remains in effect each pay period until the debt is paid, the levy is released, or the collection statute expires. It differs from a one-time levy on a bank account.
CP2000 Notice

An IRS notice generated when income reported on third-party documents, such as Forms W-2 and 1099, does not match the amounts on the taxpayer's return. It proposes changes to tax, payments, or credits and invites the taxpayer to agree or dispute the adjustments.
Currently Not Collectible (CNC)

A status the IRS assigns when a taxpayer cannot pay any of their tax debt without causing financial hardship. Collection activity is suspended, though interest and penalties continue to accrue and the liability remains.
Currently Not Collectible Status

A designation the IRS assigns when collecting a tax debt would create financial hardship, temporarily pausing active collection. Interest and penalties continue to accrue and the account is periodically reviewed.
De Novo Review (Refund Litigation)

The standard under which a federal district court or the Court of Federal Claims hears a tax refund suit fresh, without deference to the IRS determination. The taxpayer must first pay the tax and file a refund claim.
Designated Payment (Employment Taxes)

A voluntary payment a taxpayer directs to be applied to the trust fund portion of employment taxes to limit personal liability. The IRS generally honors valid designation instructions on voluntary payments.
Diligence as to Accuracy (Circular 230)

A Circular 230 standard requiring practitioners to exercise due diligence in preparing documents and in determining the correctness of representations made to the IRS and clients. Reliance on others' work must itself be reasonable.
Direct Pay (IRS)
A free electronic service allowing individuals to pay tax directly from a bank account without registering an account. Payments can be scheduled and confirmation is provided immediately.
Disbarment (Circular 230)
The most severe Circular 230 sanction, barring a practitioner from representing taxpayers before the IRS. A disbarred practitioner must generally wait years before petitioning for reinstatement.
Dischargeability of Taxes in Bankruptcy

The set of rules determining whether income tax debts can be eliminated in bankruptcy, generally requiring that the returns were filed and the taxes are old enough. Trust fund and fraud-related taxes are typically nondischargeable.
Dishonored Check Penalty
A penalty imposed when a payment to the IRS, such as a check or electronic payment, is not honored by the financial institution. The amount depends on the size of the payment.
Disreputable Conduct
Conduct defined in Circular 230 §10.51 that can lead to sanctions, including willful failure to file returns and giving false information.
Docketed Case (Appeals)
A case that has been petitioned to the Tax Court but is referred to Appeals for possible settlement before trial. Many docketed cases resolve in Appeals without a hearing.
Doubt as to Collectibility Offer in Compromise

A type of offer in compromise based on the IRS conclusion that the full tax debt cannot be collected because the taxpayer's assets and income are insufficient. The offer amount is generally tied to the taxpayer's reasonable collection potential.
Doubt as to Liability Offer in Compromise

A type of offer in compromise based on a genuine dispute about whether the assessed tax is actually owed. It is appropriate when the taxpayer believes the liability itself is incorrect rather than merely unaffordable.
Due Diligence

The requirement that paid preparers take reasonable steps to verify eligibility for certain credits and head of household status. For credits like the EITC, CTC, and education credits, preparers must complete Form 8867 and keep records.
Effective Tax Administration Offer
An offer in compromise based on economic hardship or public policy reasons even where the taxpayer could pay in full.
Effective Tax Administration Offer in Compromise

A type of offer in compromise available when the tax is correct and could technically be paid, but collecting it in full would cause economic hardship or be unfair and inequitable. It is reserved for unusual circumstances.
Electronic Federal Tax Payment System (EFTPS)
The Treasury system businesses and individuals use to schedule and make federal tax deposits and payments electronically. Most employers are required to deposit employment taxes through it.
Electronic Filing Identification Number
A number the IRS assigns to an authorized e-file provider that identifies the firm transmitting electronic returns. It is required to participate in the IRS electronic filing program.
Electronic Filing Identification Number (EFIN)
A number issued to firms that are authorized IRS e-file providers.
Electronic Return Originator
An authorized IRS e-file provider that originates the electronic submission of returns it prepares or collects from taxpayers. It must follow specific identity-verification and signature procedures.
Enrolled Agent (EA)

A federally licensed tax practitioner authorized to represent taxpayers before the IRS in all matters. Enrollment is earned by passing the Special Enrollment Examination or through qualifying IRS experience.
Enrolled Agent Renewal Cycle

The three-year period over which an enrolled agent must complete required continuing education and renew enrollment based on the last digit of their Social Security number. Renewal also requires a valid preparer tax identification number.
Equivalent Hearing

A hearing with the IRS Independent Office of Appeals that a taxpayer may request when the deadline for a Collection Due Process hearing has passed. It offers similar review but does not preserve the right to petition the Tax Court.
Erroneous Refund Claim Penalty (Section 6676)
A penalty equal to 20% of an excessive refund or credit claim that lacks a reasonable basis. It targets aggressive overclaims for refunds even when no tax is otherwise understated.
Estate Tax Lien (Section 6324)
A special lien that attaches to a decedent's gross estate for ten years to secure payment of estate tax, arising automatically without filing. It is separate from the general federal tax lien.
Examination (Audit)
An IRS review of a taxpayer's return and supporting records to verify that income, deductions, and credits are correct. Audits may be conducted by correspondence, in an IRS office, or in the field.
Examination Closing Conference
The meeting in which an examiner explains proposed audit changes and the taxpayer can agree, provide additional information, or pursue appeal. Agreement is usually documented on a consent form.
Failure-to-File Penalty
A penalty for not filing a return by the due date, generally 5% of unpaid tax per month up to 25%. It is larger than the failure-to-pay penalty and is reduced by the latter when both apply.
Failure-to-Pay Penalty
A penalty for not paying tax owed by the due date, generally 0.5% of unpaid tax per month up to 25%. It continues to accrue until the balance is paid.
Fast Track Settlement

An expedited dispute resolution program in which an Appeals official helps the taxpayer and the examining function reach a settlement while the case is still in examination. It can resolve issues much faster than the traditional appeals route.
FBAR
The FinCEN Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts, required for aggregate foreign accounts over $10,000.
Federal Payment Levy Program

An automated program that continuously levies certain federal payments, such as some Social Security benefits and vendor payments, to collect unpaid tax. It generally applies a fixed percentage to each payment.
Federal Tax Lien
A legal claim that attaches to all of a taxpayer's property when a tax debt is assessed and remains unpaid after demand. It secures the government's interest against other creditors.
Final Notice of Intent to Levy (LT11/Letter 1058)

The notice the IRS sends before levying that informs the taxpayer of the right to a Collection Due Process hearing. Requesting a hearing within 30 days generally suspends levy action while the case is considered.
First-Time Abatement

An administrative waiver that removes certain penalties for a taxpayer with a clean compliance history over the prior three years. It applies to failure-to-file, failure-to-pay, and failure-to-deposit penalties.
First-Time Penalty Abatement (FTA)
An administrative waiver of certain penalties for a taxpayer with a clean compliance history for the prior three years. It commonly applies to failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties.
Flora Rule
The requirement that a taxpayer generally must pay the full tax assessed before suing for a refund in district court or the Court of Federal Claims.
Flora Rule (Full Payment)

The judicial doctrine requiring a taxpayer to fully pay an assessed deficiency before suing for a refund in district court or the Court of Federal Claims. It distinguishes refund forums from the prepayment Tax Court.
Form 1040-X
The amended U.S. individual income tax return.
Form 1139
The corporate application for a quick refund from a carryback of a net operating loss or credit.
Form 12153 (Request for a Collection Due Process or Equivalent Hearing)

The form a taxpayer files to request a hearing with the IRS Independent Office of Appeals after receiving a lien or levy notice. Filing it within the deadline preserves the right to challenge the collection action and to petition the Tax Court.
Form 12203
A request for an Appeals review of a case where the total amount for any period is $25,000 or less, without a formal written protest.
Form 23 (Application for Enrollment to Practice Before the IRS)
The application a candidate files after passing all parts of the Special Enrollment Examination to become an enrolled agent. It triggers a suitability and tax compliance check.
Form 2848 (Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative)

The form a taxpayer uses to authorize a representative to act on their behalf before the IRS. It grants authority to receive confidential information and perform specified acts such as signing agreements.
Form 433-A
The collection information statement for individuals, listing assets, income, and expenses.
Form 433-A (Collection Information Statement for Wage Earners and Self-Employed Individuals)

The detailed financial disclosure form individuals submit so the IRS can evaluate their ability to pay a tax debt. It reports income, living expenses, assets, and liabilities for collection decisions like installment agreements or offers in compromise.
Form 433-B (Collection Information Statement for Businesses)

The financial disclosure form a business submits to show its income, expenses, assets, and liabilities when negotiating collection of a business tax debt. The IRS uses it to determine reasonable collection potential.
Form 433-F (Collection Information Statement)

A shorter financial statement individuals use to provide income, expense, asset, and liability information for certain collection determinations, such as streamlined installment agreements. It is less detailed than Form 433-A.
Form 4549
The report of income tax examination changes.
Form 656
The application for an offer in compromise.
Form 656 (Offer in Compromise)

The form a taxpayer submits to propose settling a tax debt for less than the full amount owed. It must usually be accompanied by a financial statement and an application fee and initial payment unless a low-income waiver applies.
Form 8275 (Disclosure Statement)

A form taxpayers and preparers use to disclose positions not otherwise adequately disclosed, helping avoid certain accuracy and preparer penalties. Adequate disclosure can satisfy the reasonable basis standard.
Form 8275-R (Regulation Disclosure Statement)

A variant of the disclosure statement used specifically to disclose a position contrary to a Treasury regulation. Such positions require a higher standard than ordinary contrary-to-substantial-authority positions.
Form 870
A waiver of restrictions on assessment, allowing the IRS to assess an agreed amount without a notice of deficiency.
Form 870 (Waiver of Restrictions on Assessment)

A form by which a taxpayer agrees to proposed audit adjustments and waives the right to receive a notice of deficiency before assessment. Signing it speeds assessment but does not bar a later refund claim.
Form 872
A consent to extend the time to assess tax beyond the normal assessment statute.
Form 872 (Consent to Extend the Time to Assess Tax)
An agreement extending the statute of limitations on assessment beyond the normal period. Taxpayers are not required to sign, but refusal may prompt the IRS to issue a notice of deficiency.
Form 8821
A tax information authorization allowing a designee to inspect or receive confidential tax information, but not to represent the taxpayer.
Form 8821 (Tax Information Authorization)

A form that authorizes a designated person to receive and inspect a taxpayer's confidential tax information. Unlike Form 2848, it does not allow the designee to represent the taxpayer or advocate on their behalf.
Form 8821 Tax Information Authorization (Limited Scope)

An authorization that lets a designated person receive and inspect a taxpayer's confidential tax information for specified matters and years. Unlike a power of attorney, it does not allow the designee to represent or advocate for the taxpayer.
Form 8867
The paid preparer's due diligence checklist for the EITC, child tax credit, American opportunity credit, and head of household status.
Form 8867 (Paid Preparer's Due Diligence Checklist)

The checklist a paid preparer must complete and submit when a return claims certain credits, such as the Earned Income Tax Credit or Child Tax Credit, or head of household status. It documents the preparer's compliance with due diligence requirements.
Form 8879
The IRS e-file signature authorization used when a taxpayer signs a return with a PIN.
Form 8879 (IRS e-file Signature Authorization)

The form a taxpayer signs to authorize an electronic return originator to enter or generate the taxpayer's personal identification number and electronically file the return. It serves as the signature authorization for e-filed returns.
Form 8948
A preparer's explanation for not filing a return electronically.
Form 8948 (Preparer Explanation for Not Filing Electronically)

The form a paid preparer attaches to a paper-filed return to explain why it was not e-filed when the e-file mandate would otherwise apply. Common reasons include taxpayer choice to paper file or an approved hardship waiver.
Form 911 (Request for Taxpayer Advocate Service Assistance)

The form used to request help from the Taxpayer Advocate Service when a taxpayer faces economic harm or cannot resolve a problem through normal IRS channels. The Advocate works independently within the IRS to assist eligible taxpayers.
Form 9465 (Installment Agreement Request)

The form taxpayers use to request a monthly payment plan when they cannot pay their full tax liability at once. It lets the taxpayer propose a payment amount and due date subject to IRS approval and applicable fees.
Fraud Penalty (Civil Fraud)
A civil penalty of 75% of the underpayment attributable to fraud. The IRS bears the burden of proving fraud by clear and convincing evidence.
Fraudulent Failure-to-File Penalty
An enhanced failure-to-file penalty, generally 15% per month up to 75%, imposed when the failure to file is due to fraud. It replaces the ordinary failure-to-file rate in fraud cases.
Frivolous Position
A tax position with no basis in law that is patently improper or advanced merely to delay or impede tax administration. Asserting one can trigger substantial penalties and disciplinary action.
Frivolous Return

A return that lacks information to judge its accuracy or takes a clearly unfounded position to delay or impede tax administration. Filing one can trigger a specific penalty in addition to other consequences.
Frozen Refund
A refund the IRS holds while it reviews a return for potential issues such as identity theft, questionable credits, or unfiled prior-year returns. The refund is released once the matter is resolved.
Golsen Rule
The rule that the Tax Court follows the precedent of the court of appeals to which a case would be appealed.
Guaranteed Installment Agreement

A payment plan the IRS must accept for individuals who owe $10,000 or less, have filed and paid on time for the past five years, and agree to full payment within three years. It cannot be refused if the statutory conditions are met.
Hazards of Litigation
The uncertainty of prevailing in court that the IRS Independent Office of Appeals weighs when settling a case. This standard allows Appeals to compromise based on litigation risk, unlike examiners.
Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN)

A six-digit number issued by the IRS that helps prevent fraudulent returns from being filed under a taxpayer's Social Security number. The correct IP PIN must be entered for the return to be accepted.
Information Document Request (IDR)
A formal written request an examiner issues during an audit asking the taxpayer to provide specific records or explanations. Timely, complete responses help keep an examination on track.
Information Return Penalty Tiers

The graduated penalty structure for late or incorrect information returns such as Forms 1099 and W-2, with amounts increasing the longer the delay continues. Intentional disregard carries a much higher, uncapped penalty.
Injunction Against Tax Preparer
A court order, sought by the government, barring a preparer from preparing returns or engaging in specified conduct due to repeated misconduct. It is a remedy separate from monetary penalties.
Innocent Spouse Equitable Relief (Section 6015(f))

A catch-all form of innocent spouse relief available when it would be unfair to hold a spouse liable but the other relief provisions do not apply. The IRS weighs factors such as hardship, knowledge, and abuse.
Innocent Spouse Relief

Relief that frees a spouse from joint liability for tax, interest, and penalties resulting from an understatement caused by the other spouse. The requesting spouse must show they did not know and had no reason to know of the error.
Installment Agreement

An arrangement allowing a taxpayer to pay an outstanding tax liability over time in monthly payments. Various types exist, including streamlined and guaranteed agreements, depending on the balance owed.
Intentional Disregard (Information Returns)
A knowing or reckless failure to comply with information reporting requirements, which removes the dollar caps on the related penalties. It results in significantly higher per-return penalties.
Internal Revenue Code (IRC)

The body of federal statutory tax law enacted by Congress and codified in Title 26 of the United States Code. It is the primary source of authority for federal income, estate, gift, and employment taxes.
Internal Revenue Manual (IRM)

The IRS's internal guidebook of policies and procedures that employees follow in administering the tax law. It is not legally binding on taxpayers but is useful for understanding how the IRS operates.
Jeopardy Assessment
An immediate assessment and collection of tax the IRS makes when it believes delay would endanger collection. It bypasses normal deficiency procedures but allows the taxpayer to seek prompt review.
Knowledge of Client Omission (Circular 230)

A Circular 230 duty requiring a practitioner who learns of a client's noncompliance or error to promptly advise the client of it and its consequences. The practitioner is not required to correct it without the client's consent.
Letter 1153
The letter proposing assessment of the trust fund recovery penalty, with 60 days to appeal.
Levy

A legal seizure of a taxpayer's property or rights to property to satisfy a tax debt. The IRS can levy wages, bank accounts, and other assets after notice and demand and a final notice of intent to levy.
Levy Exemption

The portion of wages, certain benefits, or specific property that the law protects from IRS levy. Examples include a minimum amount of weekly wages and certain public assistance and disability payments.
Levy Release

The IRS action ending a levy when the tax is paid, the collection period expires, the levy creates economic hardship, or releasing it will facilitate collection. A release does not by itself eliminate the underlying liability.
Lien (Federal Tax Lien)

A legal claim against a taxpayer's property arising when a tax liability is assessed and remains unpaid after notice and demand. A Notice of Federal Tax Lien may be filed publicly to establish priority against other creditors.
Lien Self-Releasing Provision
Language on the notice of federal tax lien causing the lien to release automatically once the collection statute expires. It avoids the need for a separate release document in most cases.
Limited Representation Rights

The authority of certain non-credentialed preparers, such as Annual Filing Season Program participants, to represent clients only before specific IRS functions and only for returns they prepared and signed. It is narrower than the unlimited rights of enrolled agents, attorneys, and CPAs.
Listed Transaction

A transaction the IRS has formally identified as a tax avoidance scheme or one substantially similar to it. Participants and advisers face heightened disclosure requirements and steep penalties for noncompliance.
Loper Bright
A 2024 Supreme Court decision ending Chevron deference, so courts use independent judgment in interpreting statutes.
Material Advisor

A person who provides material aid or advice on a reportable transaction and earns fees above a threshold, triggering separate reporting and list-maintenance duties. The role carries its own penalties for noncompliance.
Math Error Authority

The IRS power to correct certain obvious errors, such as arithmetic mistakes or clearly invalid entries, and adjust the tax without issuing a notice of deficiency. The taxpayer has a limited time to request that the change be reversed and handled through normal deficiency procedures.
Math Error Notice

A notice the IRS issues to correct arithmetic or certain other clear errors on a return without a full audit, adjusting the tax accordingly. Taxpayers have a limited window to request that the adjustment be reversed.
More-Likely-Than-Not Standard

The highest commonly used confidence level, meaning a position has a greater than 50 percent chance of being upheld on its merits. It is required to avoid penalties on certain reportable transactions and tax shelters.
National Taxpayer Advocate

The head of the Taxpayer Advocate Service, an independent organization within the IRS that helps taxpayers resolve problems and reports systemic issues to Congress. The office issues annual reports identifying the most serious problems facing taxpayers.
Negligence Penalty
An accuracy-related penalty for failing to make a reasonable attempt to comply with the tax laws or to keep adequate records. It applies when a taxpayer disregards rules without a good-faith basis.
Negotiation of Client Refund Check (Circular 230)
A Circular 230 prohibition barring a practitioner from endorsing or negotiating a client's tax refund check. It prevents preparers from intercepting refunds owed to clients.
Nominee Liability

A theory the IRS uses to reach property that a taxpayer has placed in another person's or entity's name while retaining control or benefit. It allows the IRS to attach a lien or levy to assets the nominee holds for the taxpayer.
Notice of Deficiency

A formal IRS letter, often called a ninety-day letter, stating a proposed tax increase and the taxpayer's right to petition the Tax Court. The IRS generally cannot assess the tax until the petition period ends.
Notice of Deficiency (90-Day Letter)
A formal IRS notice stating a proposed additional tax and the taxpayer's right to petition the Tax Court. The taxpayer generally has 90 days (150 if abroad) to respond before assessment.
Notice of Federal Tax Lien
A public document the IRS files to alert creditors that a federal tax lien exists against a taxpayer's property. Filing establishes the government's priority relative to many other creditors.
Offer in Compromise

An agreement allowing a taxpayer to settle a tax debt for less than the full amount owed when full payment is unlikely or would cause hardship. The IRS evaluates the taxpayer's reasonable collection potential before accepting.
Offer in Compromise (OIC)

An agreement that settles a tax liability for less than the full amount owed. The IRS may accept it based on doubt as to collectibility, doubt as to liability, or to promote effective tax administration.
Office of Professional Responsibility
The IRS office responsible for enforcing the ethical standards of Circular 230 against practitioners who represent taxpayers. It can censure, suspend, or disbar practitioners for misconduct.
Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR)

The IRS office responsible for interpreting and enforcing Circular 230 standards of practice. It investigates practitioner misconduct and can impose censure, suspension, or disbarment from practice before the IRS.
Offset (Refund Offset)

The application of a taxpayer's refund to certain past-due debts, such as federal or state taxes, child support, or other federal obligations. The Treasury intercepts the refund through the offset program before paying any balance to the taxpayer.
Partial Payment Installment Agreement

A payment plan in which monthly payments will not fully satisfy the tax debt before the collection statute expires. The IRS periodically reviews the taxpayer's finances, and the remaining balance may go uncollected when the statute runs.
Penalty Abatement
The reduction or removal of an assessed penalty, granted for reasonable cause, statutory exceptions, or administrative waivers. The taxpayer generally must show the failure was beyond their control.
Petition (United States Tax Court)
The document a taxpayer files to begin a case in the Tax Court, generally within 90 days of a notice of deficiency. Filing it lets the taxpayer dispute the deficiency before paying the tax.
Power of Attorney
A written authorization allowing a representative to act for a taxpayer in tax matters before the IRS. It defines the tax types, periods, and acts the representative is permitted to perform.
Practice Before the IRS

Activities such as corresponding with the IRS, representing taxpayers at examinations and appeals, and preparing documents that constitute formal representation. The scope of permitted practice depends on the representative's credentials.
Preparer Tax Identification Number
A number every paid tax return preparer must obtain and include on returns they prepare for compensation. It identifies the preparer to the IRS without disclosing a personal Social Security number.
Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN)

An identification number that paid tax return preparers must obtain and renew annually with the IRS. It must be used in place of the preparer's Social Security number on returns they prepare for compensation.
Private Letter Ruling (PLR)

A written determination the IRS issues to a specific taxpayer about how the tax law applies to a proposed transaction or set of facts. It binds the IRS only for the requesting taxpayer and may not be cited as precedent by others.
Protective Claim
A refund claim filed to preserve a taxpayer's rights when entitlement depends on a future event.
Protest Letter (Appeals)

A written statement requesting an appeals conference and setting out the taxpayer's disagreements with proposed adjustments. A formal protest is required when the disputed amount exceeds the threshold for a small-case request.
Qualified Offer (Section 7430)

A written settlement offer a taxpayer makes that, if the government later obtains a less favorable judgment, can entitle the taxpayer to recover litigation costs. It encourages reasonable settlement of tax disputes.
Reasonable Basis

A relatively low but meaningful standard requiring that a tax position is reasonably based on at least one significant tax authority. It is generally enough to avoid the negligence penalty if the position is also disclosed.
Reasonable Cause

A basis for penalty relief when a taxpayer shows they exercised ordinary business care and prudence but were still unable to comply. Examples include serious illness, natural disasters, or reliance on incorrect professional advice.
Reasonable Collection Potential (RCP)
The IRS measure of how much a taxpayer can realistically pay toward a tax debt, based on the net value of assets plus future income. It is the key figure in evaluating an offer in compromise.
Record of Account Transcript
A combined IRS transcript that merges the tax return transcript and the tax account transcript for a period. It provides both the originally reported figures and subsequent account changes.
Refund Claim (Form 843)

A claim for refund or abatement filed on Form 843 for certain taxes, penalties, interest, and fees, other than the income tax shown on a return. It is commonly used to request penalty abatement or to recover erroneously assessed amounts.
Refund Statute Expiration Date
The deadline for a taxpayer to claim a refund, generally the later of three years from filing or two years from payment. After this date the taxpayer loses the right to recover overpaid tax.
Reportable Agreement Penalty (Section 6707A)

A penalty distinct from the underpayment penalty that applies for failing to include reportable transaction information with a return. The amount is a percentage of the tax benefit derived from the transaction.
Reportable Transaction Disclosure (Form 8886)

The requirement that taxpayers disclose participation in transactions with potential for tax avoidance, including listed and confidential transactions. Failure to disclose triggers a separate penalty under Section 6707A.
Responsible Person (Trust Fund Recovery)

An individual who has the duty and authority to collect, account for, and pay over withheld employment taxes. A responsible person who willfully fails to remit trust fund taxes can be held personally liable through the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty.
Return of Client Records (Circular 230)

A Circular 230 rule requiring practitioners to promptly return a client's records needed to comply with tax obligations, even in a fee dispute. The rule protects clients from having records held hostage.
Return Preparer Office

The IRS office that administers the preparer tax identification number program and oversees preparer registration and competency standards. It works alongside the Office of Professional Responsibility on preparer matters.
Revenue Agent Report (RAR)
The document a revenue agent issues at the close of an examination explaining proposed adjustments and the resulting tax change. It typically accompanies a 30-day letter offering appeal rights.
Revenue Procedure

An official IRS statement of procedures and practices that taxpayers and the IRS follow, such as how to make an election or obtain consent. It provides administrative guidance rather than substantive legal interpretation.
Revenue Ruling
An official IRS interpretation of how the tax law applies to a particular set of facts, published for general guidance. Taxpayers in similar circumstances may rely on it.
Sanctions Under Circular 230

The disciplinary actions the Office of Professional Responsibility may impose on practitioners, including censure, suspension, disbarment, and monetary penalties. They are pursued through administrative proceedings.
Section 6015 Innocent Spouse Relief

Relief that frees a spouse from joint liability for tax understatements caused by the other spouse when it would be unfair to hold both responsible. It includes traditional, separation of liability, and equitable relief forms.
Section 6020(b) Return

The statutory authority allowing the IRS to prepare and execute a return for a nonfiler from available data. The resulting assessment lets the IRS begin collection even though the taxpayer never filed.
Section 6501 Assessment Limitation Period

The statute that generally limits the IRS to three years after a return is filed to assess additional tax. The period extends to six years for substantial omissions of income and remains open indefinitely for fraud or unfiled returns.
Section 6502 Collection Limitation Period

The statute that generally gives the IRS ten years from the date of assessment to collect a tax. Certain events, such as bankruptcy or a pending offer in compromise, can suspend and extend this period.
Section 6511 Refund Limitation Period

The statute that limits when a taxpayer may claim a refund, generally to three years from filing the return or two years from paying the tax, whichever is later. Claims filed after the period expires are barred.
Section 6662A Penalty
An accuracy-related penalty applying specifically to understatements arising from reportable transactions. The penalty rate increases when the transaction was not adequately disclosed.
Section 6672 Penalty

The statutory authority for the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty, imposing personal liability on any responsible person who willfully fails to collect or pay over employment taxes. The penalty equals 100 percent of the unpaid trust fund amount.
Section 6694
The preparer penalty for understatements due to unreasonable positions (a) or willful or reckless conduct (b).
Section 6694 Preparer Penalty

A penalty on a tax return preparer for understatements caused by unreasonable positions or willful or reckless conduct. The penalty increases substantially when the conduct is intentional or reckless rather than merely unreasonable.
Section 6695 Preparer Penalty

A set of penalties on preparers for procedural failures such as not signing returns, not furnishing copies, or failing due diligence on certain credits. Each violation carries its own fixed dollar penalty per occurrence.
Section 6695(g)
The preparer penalty for failure to meet due diligence requirements, assessed per failure and indexed for inflation.
Section 6700 Penalty

A penalty imposed on organizers or sellers of abusive tax shelters who make false or fraudulent statements about tax benefits. It targets the promotion of arrangements designed to improperly reduce tax.
Section 6701 Penalty
A penalty on any person who aids or assists in preparing a document knowing it will be used to understate another person's tax liability. It applies to advisors beyond the formal return preparer.
Section 6707 Penalty (Material Advisor)
A penalty on a material advisor who fails to timely file the required disclosure of a reportable transaction. The penalty is substantially larger for listed transactions.
Section 6707A Penalty
A penalty for failing to disclose participation in a reportable or listed transaction, calculated as a percentage of the tax benefit claimed. It applies in addition to any underpayment penalty.
Section 6713 Penalty
A civil penalty for the unauthorized disclosure or use of taxpayer return information by a preparer. It applies per disclosure and complements the criminal penalties for the same misconduct.
Section 7216
A criminal provision penalizing preparers who knowingly or recklessly disclose or use return information.
Section 7216 Disclosure Rules

A criminal provision prohibiting tax return preparers from knowingly disclosing or using a client's return information without proper consent. Violations can result in fines and imprisonment in addition to civil penalties.
Section 7345 Passport Certification

A rule allowing the IRS to certify a seriously delinquent tax debt to the State Department, which can deny, revoke, or limit a passport. The certification is reversed once the debt is resolved or falls below the threshold.
Section 7525 Privilege
A confidentiality privilege for tax advice communications with federally authorized tax practitioners in noncriminal tax matters.
Seizure
The physical taking of a taxpayer's property, such as a vehicle or real estate, to satisfy a tax liability through later sale. It is a form of levy used when other collection efforts fail.
Separation of Liability Relief (Section 6015(c))

A form of innocent spouse relief that divides an understatement between spouses who are divorced, separated, or no longer living together. Each former spouse becomes responsible only for their allocated portion.
Six-Year Assessment Period (Substantial Omission)
An extended assessment period that applies when a taxpayer omits more than 25 percent of gross income from a return. It gives the IRS six years instead of three to assess additional tax.
Small Tax Case (S Case)
Informal Tax Court procedure for disputes of $50,000 or less per tax year, with decisions that cannot be appealed.
Special Enrollment Examination (SEE)

The three-part examination administered to candidates seeking to become enrolled agents, covering individuals, businesses, and representation and procedures. Passing all parts within the allowed window is required for enrollment.
Statute of Limitations

The legal time limit during which the IRS may assess additional tax or a taxpayer may claim a refund. Assessment is generally three years from the filing date, extending to six years for substantial omissions and indefinitely for fraud or no return.
Statutory Notice of Balance Due (CP14)
The first IRS notice telling a taxpayer that they owe a balance on an assessed tax. It begins the formal billing process and starts the sequence of collection notices.
Statutory Notice of Deficiency

A formal IRS letter informing a taxpayer of a proposed deficiency and the taxpayer's right to petition the Tax Court, generally within 90 days. Until that period expires or the petition is resolved, the IRS may not assess or collect the proposed tax.
Streamlined Filing Compliance Procedures
IRS procedures with reduced penalties for U.S. taxpayers whose failure to report foreign assets was non-willful.
Streamlined Installment Agreement

A simplified payment plan available for balances within a specified threshold that does not require a detailed financial statement. The taxpayer agrees to pay the balance within a set number of months, often through direct debit.
Subordination (Federal Tax Lien)

An IRS agreement that allows another creditor's interest to move ahead of the federal tax lien on specific property. It is often used so a taxpayer can refinance or obtain a loan that ultimately helps pay the tax debt.
Substantial Authority

A standard, stronger than reasonable basis but less than more likely than not, requiring that the weight of authorities supporting a position is substantial relative to those opposing it. Meeting it can protect against the substantial understatement penalty.
Substantial Understatement
An understatement of income tax exceeding the greater of 10% of the correct tax or $5,000. It is one basis for the accuracy-related penalty.
Substantial Understatement Penalty

A type of accuracy-related penalty applying when the understated tax exceeds the greater of ten percent of the correct tax or a set dollar amount. Disclosure with a reasonable basis or substantial authority can prevent it.
Substitute for Return

A return the IRS prepares on a taxpayer's behalf when that person fails to file, using available income information. It generally allows only the standard deduction and one exemption, often overstating the tax owed.
Substitute for Return (SFR)
A return the IRS prepares on a taxpayer's behalf when the taxpayer fails to file. It is generally based on reported income without favorable deductions or credits, often producing a higher liability.
Substitute for Return Assessment

A return the IRS prepares and assesses on a taxpayer's behalf when the taxpayer fails to file, generally using third-party income data and minimal deductions. The taxpayer can replace it by filing an accurate original return.
Substitute for Return Reconsideration

The process by which a taxpayer who failed to file and was assessed under a substitute for return submits an original return to reduce the assessment. Filing the correct return often lowers the tax computed by the IRS.
Summons (IRS)
A legal demand the IRS uses to compel production of records or testimony from a taxpayer or third party. Failure to comply can be enforced through the federal courts.
Suspension of the Collection Statute (Tolling)

The pausing of the ten-year collection period during events such as a pending installment agreement request, an offer in compromise, a Collection Due Process hearing, or bankruptcy. The suspended time is added back, extending the deadline.
Systemic Advocacy

The Taxpayer Advocate Service function that identifies and addresses widespread problems affecting many taxpayers rather than individual cases. It pursues changes to IRS procedures and recommends legislative fixes.
Tax Account Transcript
An IRS record summarizing a taxpayer's account activity for a period, including assessments, payments, penalties, and key dates. Practitioners use it to verify balances and statute expiration dates.
Tax Compliance Check (Enrollment)
The review the IRS conducts to confirm an enrollment applicant has filed required returns and paid or arranged to pay any tax owed. Noncompliance can delay or deny enrollment.
Tax Court
A federal court where taxpayers can dispute a proposed deficiency before paying the tax. A petition must generally be filed within 90 days of a statutory notice of deficiency.
Tax Court Small Tax Case Procedure
A simplified, less formal Tax Court procedure available for disputes that do not exceed a dollar threshold per tax year. Decisions in these cases are final and cannot be appealed to a higher court.
Tax Preparer Penalty
Penalties imposed on paid preparers for conduct such as understating liability, failing to sign returns, or failing due diligence. They are separate from penalties imposed on the taxpayer.
Tax Shelter Promoter Investigation
An IRS examination focused on persons organizing or selling abusive tax avoidance arrangements rather than on individual return positions. It can lead to injunctions and promoter penalties.
Taxpayer Assistance Order

An order the Taxpayer Advocate Service can issue to direct the IRS to take or refrain from an action to relieve a significant hardship a taxpayer faces. It is a tool for stopping or reversing harmful IRS actions.
Taxpayer Bill of Rights

A set of ten fundamental rights, such as the right to be informed and the right to appeal, that the IRS has adopted to summarize taxpayer protections. It frames how the IRS is expected to interact with taxpayers.
Termination Assessment

An immediate assessment the IRS may make during the current tax year when it believes a taxpayer is acting to defeat collection, such as planning to leave the country or conceal assets. It ends the taxpayer's tax year early to permit prompt collection.
Third-Party Contact Notice

The advance notice the IRS must generally provide before contacting people other than the taxpayer, such as banks or customers, during an investigation. It informs taxpayers that outside inquiries may occur.
Thirty-Day Letter

A preliminary IRS letter proposing changes from an examination and inviting the taxpayer to request an Appeals conference within thirty days. Failing to respond typically leads to a statutory notice of deficiency.
Timely Mailing Rule
The rule under section 7502 that treats a return as filed on the postmark date if mailed on or before the due date through the USPS or a designated delivery service.
Tolling
The suspension of a statute of limitations period due to specified events such as bankruptcy, time abroad, or pending offers. The clock stops running and resumes when the triggering condition ends.
Transaction Code (TC)

A three-digit numeric code the IRS records on a taxpayer's account transcript to mark actions such as filing, assessment, payment, or refund. Practitioners read these codes to track the status and history of an account.
Transferee Liability
The responsibility of a person who receives assets from a taxpayer for that taxpayer's unpaid tax, up to the value of the assets received. It prevents avoiding tax by transferring property to others.
Treasury Regulation
The official rules the Treasury Department issues to interpret and implement the Internal Revenue Code. Regulations carry significant authority and may be final, temporary, or proposed.
Trust Fund Recovery Penalty

A penalty equal to the unpaid withheld income and employee Social Security and Medicare taxes assessed personally against responsible persons who willfully fail to pay them over. It allows the IRS to collect payroll trust fund taxes from individuals.
Trust Fund Recovery Penalty (TFRP)

A penalty equal to the unpaid trust fund portion of employment taxes (withheld income and the employee FICA share) assessed against responsible persons who willfully fail to collect or pay them over. It can be assessed personally against owners, officers, or others with control.
Trust Fund Recovery Penalty Interview (Form 4180)
The IRS interview used to determine who is a responsible person and acted willfully for purposes of the trust fund recovery penalty. Responses help the IRS decide whom to assess.
Trust Fund Recovery Penalty Statute Coordination

The interaction of the assessment statute for the trust fund recovery penalty with the underlying employment tax liability. The penalty has its own assessment period tied to the related employment tax returns.
Underreporter Notice Response

The taxpayer's reply to an automated underreporter notice, agreeing, partially agreeing, or disputing proposed changes based on unmatched information returns. A timely, documented response can prevent assessment of the proposed tax.
United States Tax Court
A federal court where taxpayers can dispute a proposed deficiency before paying the tax. Filing a petition within the deadline halts assessment and collection while the case is pending.
Unlimited Representation Rights
The authority to represent any taxpayer on any tax matter before any IRS office, held by enrolled agents, CPAs, and attorneys. It is broader than the limited rights of certain other preparers.
Wage and Income Transcript
An IRS record listing information returns reported under a taxpayer's identification number, such as Forms W-2 and 1099. It helps reconstruct income when records are missing.
Wage Garnishment

A continuous levy on a taxpayer's wages that requires an employer to send part of each paycheck to the IRS until the debt is paid or released. A portion of pay is exempt based on filing status and dependents.
Whipsaw (Tax Controversy)

A situation in which the IRS takes inconsistent positions against two related taxpayers to protect revenue, since the correct outcome for one favors the other. It commonly arises in disputes such as innocent spouse cases or alimony disputes between former spouses.
Willfulness (Trust Fund Recovery Penalty)

The element requiring that a responsible person knowingly and intentionally failed to pay over trust fund taxes, or recklessly disregarded a known risk. It does not require evil intent, only a voluntary, conscious, and intentional choice to use the funds elsewhere.
Withdrawal of Notice of Federal Tax Lien

An IRS action that removes the public Notice of Federal Tax Lien as if it had never been filed, which can help the taxpayer's credit and finances. It may be available when filing was premature, the debt is being paid by direct debit, or withdrawal serves both parties.
Written Information Security Plan (WISP)
A written plan describing the administrative, technical, and physical safeguards that tax professionals use to protect client data.
